Dedication TO THE MEMBERS OF THE MISSOURI JUDICIARY AND THE MISSOURI BAR WHOSE LIVES AND EFFORTS ARE DEVOTED TO THE CONTINUING TASK OF USING AND IMPROVING THE MATERIALS AND THE PROCESSES DISCUSSED IN THESE VOLUMES IN THE INTEREST OF ULTIMATE JUSTICE AMONG THE PEOPLE OF A GREAT STATE

PREFACE 

In the preparation of these volumes it has been my purpose to render some assistance to the members of the legal profession of Missouri in the everyday tasks that confront them in their offices and in the courts, in helping them determine some of the principles of substantive law on various subjects and suggesting methods of applying the law in the various tribunals of this State and in the agencies and departments of the Government of the State where the interests of their clients are considered and determined. To the practicing attorney of long experience, much that is herein contained is elementary and may not be of frequent helpfulness. This must needs be true of any general practice book. Certainly, authors of such works cannot, by virtue of their productions of this character, make any claim to erudition. 

But this does not dispense with the absolute necessity for such a book in a lawyer's library. Regardless of how elemental the text or how commonplace the form, every lawyer must sometimes reassure himself of the position he takes in any legal controversy, and any practice book ought to furnish him an avenue of approach to the authority upon which he can make his position secure. It should help him find his foundations.

Nor can any lawyer pride himself in resourcefulness sufficient to enable him to have at all times the things he needs for every given situation in his practice. The practice and form book should help him over those places he may have not been before, or perchance serve as a reminder of the things he has observed on those highways of the profession he may have previously traveled but with which he has not remained familiar.

It is not hoped for this work that it will help every lawyer to meet every situation he confronts, but it is believed that it will be a helpful guide on the ordinary tasks that confront him in his general practice. 

It is not claimed that all of the law in Missouri is stated on the various subjects treated, but it is believed that those principles relative to procedure are sufficiently set out and the basic authority for them cited so as to make it possible for this work to render occasional assistance even to the most skilled attorney.

vi 

PREFACE 

An effort has been made to cover the principal procedural points in all the courts in our judicial system, including those tribunals exercising judicial and quasi-judicial powers, and those departments of the Government that exercise some measure of judicial and administrative control over various interests affecting the population of the State.

References to the Constitution of Missouri of 1875 and to the last revision of the Statutes and to the Session Acts of Missouri are made in parentheses in the text, instead of in the annotations. In all instances where a section number is enclosed in parentheses in the text, unless it is accompanied by other explanatory matter, the section number refers to the 1929 Revision of the Official Missouri Statutes or Missouri Statutes Annotated. 

In the annotations I have followed the plan of citing the last decision by the Supreme Court of this State first and the other decisions by the Supreme Court of Missouri in the reverse chronological order in which they have been rendered, citing the last decisions first and ending with the oldest decision last. Following this, I have cited the last decision of any Court of Appeals of Missouri on the same proposition and all other decisions of the Courts of Appeals in reverse chronological order, citing the oldest of such decisions last. 

To the large number of members of the bench and bar of this State who have so generously counseled and cooperated with me in planning and executing this work, and to the loyal help of those who have assisted me in the preparation of the manuscript and reading the proof, and particularly to my publisher, the Thomas Law Book Company, which has rendered constant assistance and encouragement, I express here my grateful appreciation. 

Cape Girardeau, Missouri, 25 November, 1935.

R. H. L.

I. CHARACTER, FUNCTIONS AND PROCEDURE OF MUNICIPAL COURTS Section 1. 

Character and Power. 

Judicial power is vested in municipal courts by the Constitution of Missouri (Art. 6, Sec. 1). The method and extent of the exer cise of such power by municipal courts is controlled by the Legislature, as there is no other constitutional limit upon our control of such courts except the superintending control vested by the 

Constitution in circuit courts. Such courts are not courts of 

1 Sec. 23, Art. 6, Mo. Const. 1875 provides: "The circuit court shall exercise a superintending control over criminal courts, probate courts, county courts,

MUNICIPAL COURTS 

record (Sec. 1826), although municipal corporation courts almost universally keep records of the business conducted within them. 

They belong in that classification of courts usually designated inferior courts.2

Sec. 2. Functions, Jurisdiction and Procedure. 

The principal function of municipal courts is to hear complaints for the violation of city ordinances, the violation of which is made punishable by provision of the law and ordinances of the cities in which the courts operate. Their jurisdiction is fixed by the charters of the cities in which such courts operate and by the state law governing cities not having special charters. Pleadings and procedure in such courts are similar to pleadings and procedure in criminal actions generally. Defendants in such proceedings are not required to file any formal written pleadings. 

II. IN CITIES OF THE FIRST CLASS Sec. 3. Jurisdiction, Qualification and Selection of Police Judges. 

The police judge has exclusive jurisdiction over all cases arising under any ordinance of the city (Sec. 6163). The office of police judge is created by statute (Sec. 6127). The police judge is elected at the same time as the other elective officials of the city. He holds his office for a term of two years, or until his successor is elected and qualified. His duties are prescribed by ordinance (Sec. 6127). In case of the sickness or absence from the city of the police judge, some justice of the peace resident within the city may be designated by said police judge to act in his stead, and if no one is so designated the mayor acts as police judge. Judgments rendered by such justices acting as police judge have the same force and effect as judgments rendered by the police judge (Sec. 6163). 

Sec. 4. Informations, Warrants and Arrests. 

All persons arrested by the police for a violation of any city ordinance are brought before the judge of the police court (Sec. 6370). municipal corporation courts, justices of the peace, and all inferior tribunals in each county in their respective circuits.'' 'Bailey vs. Winn, 113 Mo. 155, 20 S. W. 21. 4

CITIES OF THE FIRST CLASS 

The mayor, councilmen, chief of police and all police officers and all officers of the city who are conservators of the peace have power to arrest or cause to be arrested, with or without process, all persons who shall break the peace or be found violating any ordinance of the city or laws of the state, commit for examination and, if necessary, to detain such person overnight or on the Sabbath in the city prison or any other safe place, until they can be brought before the judge of the police court (Sec. 6458). A warrant shall issue from the police court in all cases in favor of the city for a violation of any ordinance, by-law, or other regulation, when any person shall make oath or assertion that such violation has been committed, or upon information by the city counselor or assistants (Sec. 6457). 

St. Joseph is the only city in Missouri operating as a city of the first class. The following forms may be used in proceedings in the police court in that city or any other city that may hereafter become a city of the first class.

Sec. 5. Procedure. 

Judge.

In ordinary practice, when a complaint is made that some person has violated the provisions of some ordinance, or when a person is arrested, the city counselor or his assistant files with the police judge an information describing the character of the complaint or the nature of the infraction of the ordinance. When such complaint is filed, if the person charged is not in the custody of the

MUNICIPAL COURTS 

court, the judge of the police court issues a warrant for the arrest of such person. When such person is brought into the court, he may immediately plead guilty and let the judge of the police court enter judgment, or he may give bond to be approved by the police judge for his appearance at some day fixed by the judge, or he may be confined in jail until such time as the court fixes for a hearing of the charges against him.

Hearings of the charges may be held before the police judge, or, if the defendant desires, he may have a jury pass upon the charges made in the information. Jury trials in such cases are infrequent. 

The large majority of prisoners are accused persons being willing to submit the charges against them to the police judge. 

Sec. 6. Appeals. 

Appeals in all cases tried before a police judge may be taken to the court having criminal jurisdiction located in the county in which such city is located. Such appeals may be taken by either the city or by the defendant or defendants. Such appeals shall be taken in the time and manner provided by law in relation to appeals from judgments of justices of the peace in cases of misdemeanor, except that the city is not required to execute any bond. All cases appealed from the police court are tried de novo by the criminal court. Any judgment rendered by such criminal court shall be enforced in the same way as a judgment of the police court, in the absence of an appeal (Sec. 6163).

Sec. 7. Commitment.

Any person sentenced by the police court for any offense cognizable by the court, who shall fail or neglect to pay any fine or penalty or cost imposed for any misdemeanor or breach of any ordinance of the city, may be kept in the workhouse, house of correction or detention, or other place of confinement provided for the purpose, subject to labor on the streets (Sec. 6163).

III. IN CITIES OF THE SECOND CLASS Sec. 8. Jurisdiction, Powers, Qualifications, Term and Vacancy of Police Judge.

The municipal judge has exclusive original jurisdiction to hear and determine all offenses against the ordinances of the city. The municipal judge of a city of the second class is an elective officer (Sec. 6512). Like other elective city officials, in cities of the second class, a municipal judge must be a citizen of the United States and a qualified elector of the State of Missouri and of such city (Sec. 6513). He must qualify within thirty days after his election or forfeit his right to his office (Sec. 6521). He is elected for a term of four years, or until his successor is elected and qualified (Sec. 6512), subject, however, to being removed by recall (Sec. 

6526). Vacancies in the office of municipal judge are filled by special election, except in those cases where a vacancy occurs within six months of the next regular election, and then such vacancies are filled at the general election (Secs. 6504; 6518-6520).

The municipal judge has power to administer oaths and enforce due obedience to all orders, rules, and judgments made by him, and to fine or imprison for contempt in the same manner and to the same extent as the circuit court (Sec. 6685). He is ex officio a 10

CITIES OF THE SECOND CLASS 

3 justice of the peace within the limits of the city, with jurisdiction as to crimes and misdemeanors, but has no jurisdiction to hear or determine civil matters (Sec. 6676). In case of the sickness, disqualification or absence from the city of the municipal judge, some justice of the peace resident within the city may be designated by such municipal judge to serve in his place, but if no one is so designated, then the mayor performs the duties of judge of the municipal court until such absence or disqualification shall have ceased. 

Judgments rendered by such justices so acting have the same force and effect as the judgments of the judge of the municipal court. (Sec. 6687.)

Sec. 9. Place and Sessions of Court. 

The city council must provide, at the expense of the city, a suitable court room for the municipal judge, who is required to hold sessions of court in such court room every day except Sunday (Sec. 

6667). Such daily sessions continue until some disposition is made of each case pending. The judge may adjourn any session to such definite hour as he may see fit, and announcement of such adjournment must be made publicly in the court room at the time (Sec. 6672). 

Sec. 10. Cause Instituted by Filing of Complaint, Procedure 

Thereon.

Prosecution for the violation of any city ordinance is instituted by a complaint in which the offense charged is set forth in plain, ordinary language giving the ordinance and section violated. 

Such complaint may contain one or more complaints for the same or different offenses and must be sworn to upon the information and belief of the person who signs the complaint. The filing of such complaint and the procedure thereon are governed by the rules of civil procedure (Sec. 6668).

Municipal Judge. 

When the complaint is filed the municipal judge must issue a warrant directed to the chief of police or policemen or some other person designated for that purpose at any place within the county in which the city is located (Sec. 6671). Such warrant is a direction to the officer to whom it is given to arrest the person charged and bring him before the municipal judge.

Sec. 12. Appearance Bonds and Liability Thereon. 

Persons arrested when the municipal court is not in session may be permitted to give bond for their appearance before the municipal judge at the hour of the next regular session of court, at which time the municipal judge may require a new bond if such cause is continued to a later day, or may approve by endorsement thereon the bond previously given (Sec. 6673). If the prisoner does not give the required bond, he is confined in the city jail until tried for the offense he is alleged to have committed, which trial shall be set in the next regular session of the municipal court, unless for good cause shown the case shall be by the court continued to some later date. For a breach of such appearance judgment may be entered by the police judge against the principal and sureties for the amount thereof, and such judgment, when properly entered, has the same force and effect as ordinary civil judgments by a justice of the peace. An appeal may be taken from such judgment to the court having general civil jurisdiction in that county and in the time and in like manner as appeals from civil judgments in justice courts.

Sec. 13. Trials. 

Municipal Judge. 

A defendant arrested for the violation of a city ordinance is entitled to trial by jury as in prosecutions before a justice of the peace (Sec. 6666). Neither the defendant nor the City has the right to a change of venue from the municipal judge (Sec. 6666). Trial on the complaint shall be had either before the municipal judge or before a jury presided over by the municipal judge. Witnesses may be subpoenaed by the municipal judge. At the instance of either side an attachment to compel the attendance of witnesses may be issued (Sec. 6669). The complaint may include any number of persons charged with the same offense and growing out of the same general state of facts or occurrences. No proceedings shall be dismissed or the defendant discharged by reason of any informality or irregularity in the complaint. The complaint may be amended 15

MUNICIPAL COURTS 

by leave of court without prejudice to the proceedings at any time before the final submission of the cause. (Sec. 6675.) Should the trial be continued, the municipal judge may announce to the witnesses the hour and day on which the cause is reset for hearing. He shall enter the names of such witnesses on his docket. This verbal notice shall be as valid and binding on the witnesses as a subpoena, and it is not necessary that such witnesses be subpoenaed. If either party require it, witnesses shall furnish a personal bond in such amount as may be fixed by the municipal judge as he may deem just and reasonable to secure the attendance of such witnesses at the trial. If the defendant plead or be found guilty by the municipal judge or by verdict of the jury, the municipal judge shall declare and assess the punishment prescribed by ordinance and render judgment accordingly, together with costs of suit, and that defendant be committed until judgment is complied with. (Sec. 6678.) 

If a defendant is committed, he may be discharged upon the payment of the fine and costs or upon perfecting an appeal (Sec. 6680).

Sec. 14. Appeals. 

In all cases before the municipal judge, an appeal may be taken from his judgment to the court having criminal jurisdiction, except from judgments on a plea of guilty. Such appeals must be taken in the time and manner for appeals from justices of the peace in civil cases. Such appeals may be taken by either the city or defendant, but the city shall not be required to give bond on appeals. (Sec. 6681.)

Sec. 15. 

Procedure Under Commission Form of Government. 

Cities of the second class may adopt a commission and managerial form of government (Secs. 6718a-6718p, Laws 1933, p. 284), but 17

MUNICIPAL COURTS 

where such form of government is adopted the procedure followed and forms used in municipal courts remain the same, unless modified by ordinance (Sec. 67180, Laws 1933, p. 284, Sec. 15).

IV. IN CITIES OF THE THIRD CLASS Sec. 16. Jurisdiction, Powers, Qualifications, Term and Vacancy of Police Judge.

The police judge in cities of the third class has exclusive original jurisdiction to hear and determine all offenses against the ordinances of the city (Sec. 6759). He must be a resident of the city and at the time of his election he must not be in arrears for any unpaid city taxes or forfeiture or defalcation in office (Sec. 6743). The office is elective and the police judge is elected with the other elective officers of the city every two years (Sec. 6723). He may be removed for cause shown after a hearing before the council sitting as a court of impeachment or before the council independent of the mayor (Sec. 

6729). He is, ex officio, a justice of the peace within the limits of the city, with jurisdiction to hear or determine civil matters (Sec. 

6766). He has jurisdiction for petit larceny committed within the city. Courts take judicial notice of the statutory powers of a police judge. If he be absent, sick, or disqualified from acting, it becomes the duty of the mayor to designate a justice of the peace of the same city to act as police judge until such absence or disqualification shall cease. If a vacancy occurs in the office at a greater time than six months before a general municipal election, then a special election shall be held to fill such vacancy. In case of a vacancy in such office within less than six months of the general election, same shall be filled by some justice of the peace or other competent, eligible person of the city, to be appointed by the mayor. (Sec. 6759.) The mayor has no right to appoint a layman as police 4 5 Should a contestant for the office owe delinquent taxes he may remove his disqualification by paying his taxes on election day or prior thereto. The police judge has power to administer oaths and enforce obedience to all orders, rules and judgments made by him and may fine and imprison for contempt in the same manner and to the same extent as the circuit court (Sec. 6775).

Sec. 17. Place and Sessions of Court. 

It is the duty of the council to provide, at the expense of the city, a suitable court room for the police judge, and he shall hold his court in such court room and his court shall be open every day but 

Sunday (Sec. 6760).

Sec. 18. Docket. 

While municipal courts are not among those courts that are designated by statute as courts of record (Sec. 1826), a police judge is required to keep a docket (Sec. 6761). In such docket, he is required to enter the name of the complainant, the nature and character of the offense, the date of the trial, the names of all witnesses sworn or examined, the finding of the court or jury, the judgment of fine and costs, the date of payment, the date of issuing the commitment, if any, and every other fact necessary to show the full proceedings in the case.

Sec. 19. Cause Instituted by Filing of Complaint, Procedure 

Thereon.

Cases arising before a police judge are instituted by the filing of a complaint in writing, which complaint must set forth the charges or offenses in plain and concise terms. Such complaint may contain one or more counts for the same or different offenses. It should give the ordinances and sections thereof violated, and, following the formal parts thereof, should conclude with a charge that same was against the peace and dignity of the city. It must be sworn to either by the city attorney or some other person, who 'City of Cape Girardeau vs. Goehring (Mo. A.), 12 S. W. (2d) 761. 19

MUNICIPAL COURTS 

must state that the facts stated in the complaint are true, or upon the information and belief of the person so verifying or making the complaint he believes them to be true. The proceedings on the complaint are governed by the rules of civil procedure (Sec. 6761).

Sec. 21. Appearance Bonds, Forfeiture and Actions on. 

When a person is brought before a police judge under a warrant issued and served in the manner heretofore indicated, such person has the right to give a bond conditioned upon his appearance at such time and place as may be fixed by the police judge to appear and answer the charges filed against him (Sec. 6763). In case of the breach of any such bond, the same may be declared forfeited and action against the principal and surety, or either, may be prosecuted by the mayor. Such action shall be in the name of the City as plain- 21

MUNICIPAL COURTS 

tiff and may be prosecuted in the circuit court on transcript of the proceedings before the police judge (Sec. 6764). The same form for bond in such cases may be used as that prescribed for cities of the second class.

Sec. 22. Trials. 

A defendant in a police court action is entitled to trial by jury as in prosecutions before the justice of the peace (Sec. 6763), but no change of venue is allowed in any case before a police judge for the violation of a city ordinance (Sec. 6759). Trial may be had before either the police judge or a jury. A defendant is not required to file any pleading. The complaint may be amended by leave of court at any time before or during the trial and prior to retirement of jury or finding by police judge (Sec. 6765). Such complaints may include any number of persons charged with the same offense, and no proceedings shall be dismissed or defendant discharged by reason of any informality or irregularity in any complaint. The rules in civil procedure govern trials for violation of city ordinances. Proceedings for the conduct of the trial follow those in civil cases before justices of the peace, so that an instruction may be given calling attention to the fact that a defendant did not testify. Either side has the right to call witnesses in its behalf, and it is the duty of the police judge to summon all persons named as witnesses at any trial before him. Attachments may be issued to compel the attendance of witnesses (Sec. 6769). Continuances may be had upon the application of the parties, and when such continuances are granted it is the duty of the police judge to notify verbally the witnesses present to attend before him on the day set for the trial to testify in the case, and such verbal notice is as valid as a summons (Sec. 6768). If a defendant pleads guilty, or is found guilty either by the police judge or a jury, it is the duty of the police judge to declare and assess punishment prescribed by ordinance and render judgment accordingly for costs of suit and that defendant stand committed until judgment is complied with (Sec. 6770). If defendant is convicted and sentenced and does not pay his fine, he may be committed.

Sec. 23. Appeals. 

Except in cases of judgments on a plea of guilty, appeals may be taken. Such appeals may be by either the City or the defendants. 

They must be taken in the time and manner provided for in appeals from justices of the peace in cases of misdemeanors. The City shall not be required to execute any bond. Upon appeal, the appellate court shall proceed with the cause as in cases of appeals from judgments of justices of the peace in cases of misdemeanors. (Sec. 

6773.) 10 An appeal lies by the City as well as by the defendant.11

An appeal must be taken on the same day that judgment is rendered.12 10 Appeals from Justices and judgments in cases of misdemeanors are governed by Sec. 3448. 11 

City of Mexico vs. Harris, 115 Mo. A. 707, 92 S. W. 505; City of Poplar

MUNICIPAL COURTS Sec. 24. Under Alternative or Commission Form of Government. 

Cities of the third class in Missouri may operate under the alternative or what is more generally known as the commission form of government (Secs. 6906-6929). Some Missouri cities of the third class have adopted this form of government. As a result of their adoption of such form of government such cities do not alter their preexisting classification as cities of the third class.18 Under such form of government, a mayor and councilmen are elected by the vote of the people every two years (Secs. 6907-6910). Police judges under the commission form of government, like other non-elective officials, are selected by the mayor and council (Sec. 6915). In other respects, municipal courts in cities operating under the alternative form of government as cities of the third class have the same functions and jurisdiction, and the practice before them is in all respects similar to or identical with that in municipal courts of such cities not operating under the commission form of government. 

Sec. 25. The City Manager Plan. 

Since 1921, cities of the third class in Missouri have had the right to adopt what is known as the city manager form of government (Secs. 6930-6945). Under this form of government, the city council is elected by the vote of the people (Sec. 6931), and the council appoints a city manager, a city clerk, city assessor and city treasurer (Sec. 6938). All other officers and employes of the city are appointed and may be removed by the city manager under rules and regulations governing the same, made by the council (Sec. 6938). 

Subject to the differences noted, the operation of municipal courts under the city manager plan is no different from that of municipal courts in cities not operating under such form of government. 

V. IN CITIES OF THE FOURTH CLASS Sec. 26. Jurisdiction, Powers, Qualifications and Term of Police 

Judge.

In cities of the fourth class the mayor and board of aldermen may by ordinance provide for the election of a police judge, who shall be 

18 Barnes vs. City of Kirksville, 266 Mo. 270, 180 S. W. 545. 24

CITIES OF THE FOURTH CLASS 

elected at the regular city elections. In case of the absence, sickness or disability of such police judge, or vacancy in such office, the mayor is required to perform the duties of the police judge until the disability is removed or the vacancy filled (Sec. 6972). When a police judge is elected, he and the mayor have exclusive, original jurisdiction to hear and determine all offenses against the ordinances of the city (Sec. 6977). The mayor or police judge shall have power to administer oaths and enforce due obedience to all orders, rules and judgments made by him within the scope of his authority, and may fine and imprison for contempt of court in the same manner and to the same extent as the circuit court (Sec. 6992). They shall have the power to put to work any person convicted and sentenced for violation of a city ordinance (Sec. 6987). The police judge or the mayor has the power to summon all persons whose testimony may be deemed necessary and to enforce attendance by attachment if necessary (Sec. 6985). The mayor or police judge shall hold court in a room provided for the purpose by the board of aldermen and such court must be open every day except Sunday (Sec. 6978).14 The police judge is required to keep a docket in which he shall enter every case coming before him and the proceedings therein (Sec. 6977).

Sec. 27. Proceedings in Cases Before the Police Judge Initiated Upon Complaint. 

All prosecutions for violation of a city ordinance are instituted before the police judge, or the mayor serving as such, upon a formal complaint. Such complaint may be made by the marshal or any policeman who makes the arrest and takes the person charged into custody (Sec. 6979), or by some person other than a city official.15

The complaint must be sworn to by such officer or person making same (Sec. 6979). It must be sufficiently definite to inform the defendant of the offense of which he is charged.16 A complaint was held sufficiently verified where sworn to before the mayor, who signed his name and affixed the seal of the city but did not show his official capacity." Complaints may include any number of persons "City of Richland vs. Null, 194 Mo. A. 176, 185 S. W. 250. 

15 Ibid. "City of Marshall vs. Standard, 24 Mo. A. 192. 11 

City of Clarence vs. Patrick, 54 Mo. A. 462. 25

MUNICIPAL COURTS 

charged with the same offense, and no proceedings shall be dismissed or the defendant discharged by reason of any informality or irregularity in the complaint. Such complaint may be amended at any time before or during the trial prior to the retirement of the jury or the finding of the police judge (Sec. 6983).

Sec. 28. Warrants. 

Warrants issued by the mayor or police judge shall be directed to the city marshal, the sheriff, or any constable of the county in which the city is located. Such warrant shall be executed by the marshal or any policeman of the city or by the sheriff or any constable of the county at any place within the limits of the county and not elsewhere, unless such warrants are endorsed in the manner provided for warrants in criminal cases, and when so endorsed shall be served in other counties as provided for warrants in criminal cases. (Sec. 6980.)

The form of warrants and returns used in cities of the fourth class may follow generally the forms of such warrants used in other cities. 

Sec. 29. Pleas and Bonds. 

A defendant arrested on a complaint signed before a police judge in a city of the fourth class is not required to file any formal pleading. The practice is for the defendant to be brought before the police 26

CITIES OF THE FOURTH CLASS 

judge and asked what plea he desires to enter. If he announces that he desires to enter a plea of guilty, a judgment of conviction may be entered against him (Sec. 6979) and a judgment fixing the punishment rendered accordingly (Sec. 6986). If the defendant enters a plea of not guilty and asks to be tried, it becomes the duty of the mayor or police judge to try him immediately, unless, for good cause shown, the hearing should be continued to another day. If the trial is postponed to another day, the police judge or mayor must cause the defendant to enter into a bond with sufficient security, conditioned that he will appear at the time and place appointed to answer the complaint alleged against him. If he fails to enter into such bond, the defendant shall be committed to prison (Sec. 6981). Should there be a breach of such bond, the same shall be deemed forfeited and prosecution against the principal and surety, or either of them, may be made (Sec. 6982).

Sec. 30. Trials. 

The police judge or mayor has no right to grant a change of venue in a case instituted before him (Sec. 6977). A trial may be had before the police judge or before a jury. If the trial is before a jury, the proceeding is the same as in prosecutions before a justice of the peace (Sec. 6981). A unanimous verdict of the jury is necessary for a conviction of violation of a city ordinance.18 If the trial results in a conviction, the defendant may be released only upon the payment of fine and costs, or upon perfecting an appeal (Sec. 6988). 

He cannot procure a discharge by tendering property on which to levy execution.19 If a defendant is acquitted, he is entitled to be discharged and released upon his bond.

Sec. 31. Appeals. 

Appeals may be taken by either the city or the defendant from judgments before a police judge or mayor. Such appeals go to the court having criminal jurisdiction. No appeal can be taken from a judgment on a plea of guilty. Appeals must be taken in the time and manner provided by statute in relation to appeals from judgments 18 

King City vs. Duncan, 238 Mo. 513, 142 S. W. 246. "In re Miller, 44 Mo. A. 125. 27

MUNICIPAL COURTS 

of justices of the peace in misdemeanor cases. Upon such appeal the appellate court proceeds in the same manner as is provided in cases of appeals from judgments of justices of the peace in cases of misdemeanor. (Sec. 6990.) 20

VI. IN CITIES UNDER SPECIAL CHARTERS Sec. 32. Municipal Courts. 

All cities and towns having a population of less than ten thousand and more than three thousand, and acting under special charters, may by ordinance provide for the election of police judges in such cities. Such judge shall be elected at the regular city election and when elected shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all offenses against the ordinances of such cities. When a police judge is thus elected, the jurisdiction of the mayor to hear and determine cases for violation of city ordinance by the charter of such cities shall be held to refer to the police judge elected (Sec. 7284.) 

Such officer is elected for a term of four years (Sec. 7318). The jurisdiction and powers of and the proceedings before such police judge are prescribed by ordinance.

VII. IN TOWNS AND VILLAGES Sec. 33. Powers and Duties of Municipal Court in Towns and Villages. 

The chairman of the board of trustees is the chief judicial representative of towns and villages. He has exclusive original jurisdiction to hear and determine all offenses against the ordinances of the town or village (Sec. 7112). He has the power to enforce due obedience to all orders, rules and judgments made by him and the power to fine or imprison for contempt in the same manner and to the same extent as the circuit court (Sec. 7126). It is his duty to provide, at the expense of the town, a suitable room in which to hold court, and his office shall be open every day except Sunday for the transaction of business. He is required to keep a suitable docket at the expense of the town (Sec. 7112). 

* Noll vs. Alexander (App.), 282 S. W. 739. 

28

TOWNS AND VILLAGES Sec. 34. Complaints. 

Prosecutions of cases before the chairman of the board of trustees are instituted by the filing of a written complaint, unless the complaint is made by the marshal, assistant marshal, or regular policeman. In either of the latter cases, the complaint need not be in writing if the defendant is present in court and in custody. In all other cases the complaint must be in writing and verified. The complaint is invalid unless it refers to a particular ordinance violated.21 Where the complaint is not in writing, the record of the trial must recite the presence of the defendant in court.22 A complaint is sufficient if it properly notifies the defendant of the offense with which he is charged.28 A complaint may be sworn to by the town attorney, the town marshal, or by any other person competent to testify in the cause (Sec. 7114).

Sec. 35. Warrants and Returns. 

Upon the filing of a complaint, the chairman of the board shall forthwith issue his warrant for the arrest of the accused, which shall be directed to the town marshal, the sheriff, or any constable of the county. Such warrant may be served by any such officer anywhere within the limits of the county and not elsewhere, unless such warrant is endorsed in the manner provided for warrants in criminal cases, and when so endorsed shall be served in other counties as provided for warrants in criminal cases (Sec. 7114). Such warrants shall be returnable forthwith (Sec. 7115). Form of warrants and returns follows generally those prescribed for use in cities. 

Sec. 36. Appearance and Bond.

When a defendant is thus brought before a chairman of a board, the regular practice is to ask him what plea he desires to enter. If he enters a plea of guilty, the chairman of the board may assess his fine and fix his punishment as prescribed by ordinance (Sec. 7121). 

If the defendant pleads not guilty, he is entitled to an immediate trial. If there is good cause for continuing the case to another day, he may be discharged upon giving bond for his appearance (Sec. 

7116). If he cannot give bond, and the case is continued, he shall be committed to prison. In case he gives bond for his appearance and does not appear, the bond is forfeited and forfeiture may be enforced against the principal and the surety in an action before the chairman of the board of trustees (Sec. 7117).

Sec. 37. Trials. 

Trials may be had before the chairman of the board, who is authorized to summon witnesses and enforce their attendance by attach- 30

ment, if necessary (Sec. 7119). If, during the course of the trial, it appears that the charge is one that should be prosecuted under the state law, the proceedings may be stopped and a complaint made before a justice of the peace (Sec. 7118). The guilt of the defendant must be established beyond a reasonable doubt.24 Other proceedings in the trial follow generally proceedings in the trial of cases before a justice of the peace. If the defendant is acquitted, he shall be immediately discharged; if he is found guilty he shall be committed unless he pays the fine and costs or perfects an appeal (Sec. 7122). 

Sec. 38. Appeals. 

An appeal may be taken by the defendant to the circuit court or other appellate court. Such appeal shall not be allowed unless the defendant within two days enters into a bond with good and sufficient security, to be approved by the board of trustees, conditioned for the personal appearance of the defendant before the appellate court on the first day of the next term thereof (Sec. 7124). Such appeals are governed by rules applicable in civil cases.25 

VIII. IN THE CITY OF ST. LOUIS Sec. 39. Municipal Courts: Their Creation, Jurisdiction and Powers. 

The City of St. Louis operates under special charter government authorized by the Constitution of Missouri for all cities having more than one hundred thousand inhabitants (Art. 9, Sec. 16). The charter of the City of St. Louis is specially authorized by the Constitution (Art. 9, Sec. 20). By ordinance, the city is divided into two judicial districts.26 And for each district there is a city court presided over by a judge.27 The city courts are located in the Municipal 

Courts Building. These courts have jurisdiction over all cases arising under the St. Louis Charter or any ordinance of the city. They have the power to punish for contempt, enforce orders and judg- 

City of Stanberry vs. O'Neal, 166 Mo. A. 709, 150 S. W. 1104; Town of Glenwood vs. Roberts, 59 Mo. A. 167. 25 

Village of Marble Hill vs. Caldwell, 189 Mo. A. 286, 176 S. W. 294. 

"Gen. Ord. of St. Louis 1926, Ch. 6, Art. 1, Sec. 62.

MUNICIPAL COURTS 

ments, and render final judgment on any forfeited bond in such court.28 These courts have jurisdiction of all suits for the recovery of any fine, forfeiture or penalty for the breach of any ordinance, and such suits are in the nature of civil actions.29 

Sec. 40. Judges, Their Qualifications, Selection and Terms of Office. 

City court judges are appointed by the mayor for four-year terms.30 To be eligible for such office, a person must be at least thirty years of age, a licensed and practicing attorney for at least five years prior to appointment, a citizen of the United States, and a resident of the City of St. Louis for three years next preceding his appointment.31 

Sec. 41. Procedure.

The city counselor of the City of St. Louis is charged with the duty of preparing all charges and prosecuting in the city courts all actions on behalf of the city.32 Prosecutions are initiated by charges usually prepared by an assistant city counselor and the defendant is brought into court by a summons.3 

33 The defendant is authorized to demand a jury, and if the jury is called it may consist of six persons, unless the parties agree to a less number.34 The witnesses may be subpoenaed by either party and trials conducted before the court as is customary in other courts of like kind.

Sec. 42. Appeals. 

All appeals from the judgment of the city court go to the St. Louis

IX. IN THE  Sec. 43. Municipal Courts: Their Creation, Jurisdiction and Powers. 

As in the case of St. Louis, Kansas City operates under a special charter authorized by the Constitution of Missouri for cities having more than one hundred thousand inhabitants (Art. 9, Sec. 16). This special charter was adopted February 24, 1925, and by it a municipal court, with two or more judges and with such divisions as the council may determine, was created.86 

This court has jurisdiction of all cases arising under the charter and any ordinances of the city and such other jurisdiction as may be conferred by law. It has concurrent jurisdiction with the circuit court in suits for the collection of taxes for the enforcement of special tax bills and assessments, the abatement of nuisances or growing out of the abatement of nuisances, and of the proceedings for taking and damaging property for public use, for the establishment of restrictions on the use of property and of easements thereon and therein, and for ascertaining damages caused by change of grade or other exercise of the power of eminent domain and making assessments to 

36 Kansas City Charter, Art. 13, Sec. 395. 

40

pay compensation therefor. This court also has jurisdiction to try any person arrested for an offense against the city which is also an offense against the state."7

The charter grants to this court the powers of a circuit court for enforcing its process and orders, to summon and compel the attendance of witnesses, and, when a jury is allowed, to summon and compel the attendance of jurors, to pass upon the competency of evidence, and instruct the jury.38

Sec. 44. Judges: Their Qualifications, Selection and Terms of Office. 

The judges of the municipal court are elected from the city at large for terms of four years and until their successors are elected and have qualified. Such judges shall have been for five years prior to their election members in good standing of the bar of Jackson County. The compensation of the judges is fixed by the council at not less than $4,800 per year. 

Sec. 45. Procedure. 39 Cases for the violation of city ordinances usually arise upon information made and signed by a complaining witness before an assistant city counselor or upon an information filed in the first instance by an assistant city counselor. A warrant is then issued by the clerk of the municipal court and the defendant is brought before the court. The defendant is not required to file a pleading. He may give a bond for his appearance. Further proceedings follow generally those which prevail in other municipal courts.40 The rules of practice are prescribed and regulated by ordinance.¹¹ 

Sec. 46. Appeals. 

Appeals may be taken from the municipal court to the circuit court of Jackson County, Missouri, in a manner and upon the conditions prescribed by ordinance.42

I.  Sec. 47. Origin and Growth in England. 

The genesis of justice courts as known in the judicial system of Missouri is found in the exigencies employed by Edward III, King of England, from 1327-1377, to maintain a usurped throne, and the response made by parliament to the demands of the emergency thus placed on the sheriffs of the king's dominions in keeping the peace, by providing that the king could assign additional officers to act as conservators of the peace. Not long thereafter, these peace officers of the king were granted power by the parliament (34 Edward III, ch. 1) to try felony cases, following which they became known as justices.¹ 1 In 1 Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England, 350-351, the following interesting account is given: "When Queen Isabel, the wife of Edward 

II, had contrived to depose her husband by a forced resignation of the crown, 66

In the course of time these officers became known to the common law and in the English judicial system as justices of the peace. In the beginning they exercised no judicial functions, and after they were given power by statute to try criminal cases their duties were not confined alone to that function, but they were empowered to discharge a great variety of ministerial functions and became important agencies in the operation of local government. Because and had set up his son Edward III in his place; this, being a thing then without example in England, it was feared would much alarm the people: especially as the old king was living, though hurried about from castle to castle, till at last he met with an untimely death. To prevent therefore any risings, or other disturbance of the peace, the new king sent writs to all the sheriffs in England, the form of which is preserved by Thomas Walsingham, giving a plausible account of the manner of his obtaining the crown; to-wit, that it was done ipsius patris beneplacito: and withal commanding each sheriff that the peace be kept throughout his bailiwick, on pain and peril of disinheritance, and loss of life and limb. And in a few weeks after the date of these writs, it was ordained in parliament that, for the better maintaining and keeping of the peace in every county, good men and lawful, which were no maintainers of evil, or barretors in the country, should be assigned to keep the peace. And in this manner, and upon this occasion, was the election of the conservators of the peace taken from the people, and given to the king; this assignment being construed to be by the king's permission. But still they were only called conservators, wardens, or keepers of the peace, till the statute 34 Edw. III. c. 1, gave them the power of trying felonies; and then they acquired the more honorable appellation of justices."' 'In People ex rel. Lawrence vs. Mann, 97 N. Y. 530, 1. c. 533-534, the court said: ". . . . Justices of the peace had been known to the common law of 

England for a century and a half before America was discovered. They were in their original institution men conservators of the peace, exercising no judicial function. It is said in Burn's Justice (Vol. 3, 19th ed., page 4), that by the statute 1 Edw. III, which is the first statute that ordains the assignment of justices of the peace by the king's commission, they had no other power but only to keep the peace. But from time to time their powers were enlarged, and they came to constitute a very important agency in the administration of local government in England. They discharged a great variety of duties connected with the support of the poor, the reparation of highways, the imposition and levying of parochial rates and other local affairs. (See enumeration in Stat. 16, Geo. II, Chap. 18.) They were invested with judicial powers for the first time (it seems) by the statute 34, Edw. III, Chap. 1, which gave them power to try felonies, but then only when two or more acted together, and not singly, and it is said by Blackstone (Vol. 1, page 349), 'they then acquired the more honorable appellation of justices.' I do not find that they ever exercised in England jurisdiction in civil courses.

3 of the dignity attached to the office of justice of the peace in England, and the high character of qualifications therefor required by statute, men of prominence and influence were attracted to the office. And, owing to the great diversity of duties of an important public nature imposed upon these officers, the services they performed were largely of a beneficent nature, the privileges accorded them were rare and highly coveted, and the exactions from them often severe. By virtue of the fact that they were required by * In 1 Blackstone, pp. 352-353, it is said: "Touching the number and qualifications of these justices, it was ordained by statute 18 Edw. III, c. 2, that two or three, of the best reputation in each county, shall be assigned to be keepers of the peace. But these being found rather too few for that purpose, it was provided by statute 34 Edw. III, c. 1, that one lord and three or four of the most worthy men in the county, with some learned in the law, shall be made justices in every county. But afterwards the number of justices, through the ambition of private persons, became so large, that it was thought necessary, by statute 12 Ric. II, c. 10, and 14 Ric. But this rule is now disregarded, and the cause seems to be (as Lambard observed long ago) that the growing number of statute laws, committed from time to time to the charge of justices of the peace, have occasioned also (and very reasonably) their increase to a larger number. 

And, as to their qualifications, the statutes just cited direct them to be of the best reputation, and most worthy men in the county; and the statute 13 Ric. II, c. 7, orders them to be of the most sufficient knights, esquires, and gentlemen of the law. Also by statute 2 Hen. V. st. 1, c. 4, and st. 2, c. 1, they must be resident in their several counties. And because, contrary to these statutes, men of small substance had crept into the commission, whose poverty made them both covetous and contemptible, it was enacted by statute 18 Hen. VI, c. 11, that no justice should be put in commission if he had not lands to the value of 20£ per annum. And, the rate of money being greatly altered since that time, it is now enacted by statute 5 Geo. II, c. 18, that every justice, except as is therein excepted, shall have 100£ per annum clear of all deductions; and, if he acts without such qualification, he shall forfeit 100£. This qualification is almost an equivalent to the 20£ per annum required in Henry the Sixth's time; and of this the justice must now make oath. Also it is provided by the act 5 Geo. II, that no practicing attorney, solicitor, or proctor, shall be capable of acting as a justice of the peace.' 4

Sec. 48. Transplanted to America. 

These justice courts that had functioned in England for nearly three centuries before the landing of the Pilgrims were transplanted to America by the English Colonists. During the American Colonial period, these courts occupied an important position in local administration in the various communities. They occupied positions in public affairs and exercised powers much like the justice courts of the mother country of which they were a striking counterpart, and these powers were gradually enlarged to meet the demands of expanding communities down to the time of the Revolution." Folservice. And therefore if a well-meaning justice makes any undesigned slip in his practice, great lenity and indulgence are shewn to him in the courts of law; and there are many statutes made to protect him in the upright discharge of his office; which, among other privileges, prohibit such justices from being sued for any oversights without notice beforehand; and stop all suits begun, on tender made of sufficient amends. But, on the other hand, any malicious or tyrannical abuse of their office is usually severely punished; and all persons who recover a verdict against a justice, for any wilful or malicious injury, are entitled to double costs."' 

51 Blackstone 352. 

Scott, "The Courts of the State of New York," 305. 'In People ex rel. Lawrence vs. Mann, 97 N. Y. 530, 1. c. 534-535, it was said: "The office of justice of the peace was brought here by the English colonists. From the earliest colonial period it has existed in this country. . . . 

But from the earliest colonial period until this time (1737), justices of the peace here, as in England, have been invested with various and important functions connected with local administration, quite independent of their judicial authority and a glance (page 535) at the statutes will show how important a part these officers have had in the administration of the poor laws, the highway acts, the adjustment of town changes, and indeed in nearly every department of local administration. It is important to notice that the judicial function exercised by justices of the peace was a graft upon their original authority, and that the enlargement of their powers has not been in this direction alone, but that by gradual accretion they have come to constitute a most important factor in the corporate administrative life of towns and counties. The gradual growth of their powers and functions furnishes a good illustration of the manner in 69

lowing the Revolution, as the different colonies adopted constitutional government, the existence of these courts was generally recognized, and thereafter the position of these courts and the extension of their functions became a subject of legislative enactment in the various states. Their jurisdiction was extended beyond that of trying criminal cases, and was made to include the right to try civil cases involving small sums and controversies connected with limited property rights. 

Sec. 49. In Missouri.

Out of this background of nearly five centuries of experience, the justice courts in Missouri grew. Shortly after the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, the vast territory acquired was divided into two districts for the temporary purposes of government, and the Governor and judges of the Indiana territory were authorized to serve as a legislative body for that part of Louisiana embracing Missouri, and were given power to establish in that district inferior courts and prescribe their jurisdictions and duties. This legislative body, in the exercise of the power thus granted to it, passed an act which became effective October 1, 1804, by which it divided which institutions grow up and adopt themselves to the changing conditions and demands of society, until they are brought to subserve, in the most effective way, the public interests.''

Characteristic of this development of justice courts during the colonial period and following the Revolution throughout the American colonies is the following account thereof in the state of New York found in Scott's "The 

Courts of the State of New York," pp. 305-306: "From the first settlement of the English in the province of New York, justices of the peace held town courts, and were members of all the other tribunals held in the colony. After the 

Revolutionary War, these courts were continued by different legislative enactments. "" Chapter 44 of the laws of 1780, passed February 26 of that year, empowered justices of the peace, mayors, recorders, and aldermen to try all cases involving one hundred pounds or less; all actions on cases of debt, slander, trespass, replevin, or for damages, where the amount demanded was less than one hundred pounds, were heard before one of the justices of the peace of any of the counties, or mayor, recorder, or alderman for the cities of New York and Albany and the Borough of Westchester.'' • Territorial Laws of Missouri, pp. 5-6. 70

the territory into districts, created an organization of courts for each district, and provided that a competent number of justices of the peace in every district be nominated and appointed by the Governor.10 Jurisdiction of such courts and practice therein were prescribed by another act.11 Later, after government in the territory became better organized, this territorial governing body, by an act which became effective July 4, 1807, provided for the appointment in every township of one or more persons as justices of the peace, whose jurisdiction in criminal cases extended over the whole district and in civil cases over the township for which they were commissioned.12 At the same time the jurisdiction of these courts in civil cases was made to extend to controversies involving sums not exceeding $60, their judgments in cases where the sum demanded did not exceed $10 were made final, and the procedure for such courts was prescribed in detail. 18 Jurisdiction of such courts and procedure before them were modified at various times during the period of Missouri's territorial government.14 In 1814, jurisdiction in civil causes was extended to cover controversies involving not exceeding the sum of $90.15 By an act approved February 1, 1817, it was made unlawful for a plaintiff to file a suit in the circuit court for any sum within the jurisdiction of a justice of the peace.16 

The first Constitution of Missouri, adopted in 1820, provided that in each county there should be appointed as many justices of the peace as the public good may be thought to require, whose powers and duties and duration in office shall be regulated by law." Pursuant thereto, the first General Assembly of Missouri provided that that legislative body proceed to appoint a sufficient number of persons in each county, and not more than eight for each township, as justices of the peace.18 It further provided that justices of the

Sec. 50. Character and Classification. 

Justice courts constitute a class in our judicial system, and the office of justice of the peace is a constitutional office.22 Each constitution of Missouri has authorized the appointment or election in each county of as many justices of the peace as the public good may require,23 and whose powers, duties, and duration in office are regulated by law.24 They do not come within that classification of courts designated as courts of record (Sec. 1826). But they do come within that classification of tribunals known as subordinate or inferior courts and are subject to the superintending control of courts of superior rank (Const., Art. VI, Sec. 23). Justices of the peace are officers of the township in which they have their offices (Sec. 2136).25

Sec. 51. Number and Term of Justices. 

Each municipal township is entitled to two justices of the peace, but in case there is in any such township an incorporated town or city having a population of over two thousand inhabitants and less than one hundred thousand inhabitants, such town or city is entitled to an additional justice of the peace, who must be a resident of such town or city (Sec. 2136). In all townships containing seventy-five thousand inhabitants and not over one hundred and fifty thousand inhabitants, according to the last decennial census, there shall be four justices of the peace (Sec. 2366). In all cities which have three hundred thousand inhabitants or more, there shall be one justice of the peace for each district, and there shall be five districts for the first one hundred thousand population in such cities and an additional district for every additional one hundred thousand and for every fractional part of one hundred thousand exceeding fifty thousand of population (Secs. 2394, 2395). In counties under township organization there shall be two justices of the peace for each township (Sec. 12268), but in all townships having a population of over two thousand there may be an additional justice of the peace for every two thousand inhabitants until the population reaches six thousand, after which the number of justices shall not be increased (Sec. 12269). In counties not under township organization, and outside Kansas City and the City of St. Louis, an additional justice of the peace may be appointed by the county court for any township, upon a petition presented to such court, signed by twelve or more qualified voters of any township of the county, setting forth that such petitioners live more than five miles from the nearest justice of the peace in their township (Sec. 2137). If the county court acts upon such petition, it must appoint an additional justice living in the immediate neighborhood of the petitioners and at least five miles from any other justice of such township (Sec. 2137).

Justices are elected for a term of four years, or until their successors are elected, commissioned, and qualified (Secs. 2138, 2144), except in counties under township organization, where they are elected for a term of two years (Sec. 12267). 73

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 52. Qualifications and Eligibility. 

A justice of the peace must be a citizen of the United States and an inhabitant of Missouri for twelve months and of the township for which he is chosen six months next before his election (Sec. 

2141).26 In St. Louis and in Kansas City, a person must have been an inhabitant of the city for twelve months prior to his election or appointment, in order to be eligible for justice of the peace (Sec. 2400). 

No clerk of the circuit court or county clerk or the deputy of either shall hold or exercise the office of justice of the peace (Sec. 2139). 

But in counties having township organization, the same persons may be elected members of the township board and justices of the peace and hold both offices (Sec. 12268).

Sec. 53. Election of and Election Contests. 

Elections of justices of the peace are conducted at the same time and in the same manner as elections of other officers (Secs. 2136, 2138, 2142, 2394, 12267, 12268). In case of a tie vote or an election contest for the office of justice in any township, the county court is given statutory authority to determine who is elected (Sec. 

2143). And in an early case it was held that under this statutory authority county courts had exclusive original jurisdiction to determine such election contests.27 But that part of the statute (Sec. 

2143) authorizing a county court to determine who is elected justice as between those receiving an equal vote has been held unconstitutional.28 Since justices of the peace are township officers, 29 and since the statute gives county courts jurisdiction of election contests of township offices (Sec. 10339), and specifically of election contests for justices of the peace of any township (Sec. 2143), it would appear that such courts have exclusive original jurisdiction to determine election contests between justices of the peace,30 except in

Sec. 54. Certificate of Election. 

When the county courts have ascertained who are elected as justices of the peace, certificates of election are issued by such courts to the justices elected. These certificates are signed by the president, witnessed by the clerk, and delivered to the persons entitled thereto (Sec. 2145). Should the court seal be omitted inadvertently from the commission, the validity thereof is not affected. On the back of each certificate the clerk of the county court is required to endorse a statement that the person for whom it is intended shall qualify according to law within twenty days after the receipt of same, and in default thereof such certificate is void (Sec. 2146). 31

Sec. 56. Oath and Certificate Must Be Recorded. 

Within thirty days after the receipt of the certificate of election, and before entering upon the discharge of his duties, such justice must cause the certificate of election and his oath of office to be recorded in the office of the clerk of the county court (Sec. 2148). 

These constitute his commission and the evidence of his official right to act. He cannot perform any official acts as justice of the peace until his commission has been recorded (Sec. 2151). Failure to record the certificate and oath by such justice is deemed a refusal of the certificate (Sec. 2148), and one who fails to qualify after election may be ousted by his predecessor.32 When the clerk of the county court records the certificate of election, he must certify to the Governor the acceptance of the commission (Sec. 2149).

Sec. 57. Vacancies. 

James Prosser, Clerk.

Vacancies in the office of justice of the peace may occur by death, resignation, forfeiture, removal from the district or township, and removal from office. A justice of the peace who is convicted of bribery, perjury, or other infamous crime, or of any misdemeanor in office, shall be removed from office (Sec. 2162). A vacancy occurs in the office when a justice of the peace removes from the township or district for which he was elected (Secs. 2164, 2395; 2381, as amended Laws 1933, p. 209), and when he forfeits his office (Sec. 

2370). A vacancy may also occur by the voluntary resignation of a justice of the peace (Sec. 2163). Resignations must be in writing "State ex rel. Harris vs. McCann, 88 Mo. 386. 77

When a vacancy occurs by the resignation, removal, or disqualification of a justice of the peace, such justice shall immediately thereafter deliver to the clerk of the county court, or to the City Register if in the City of St. Louis, all dockets, records, books, papers, and documents appertaining to his office or relating to any suit, matter, or controversy committed to him in his official capacity (Sec. 2164). When a justice of the peace dies, it is the duty of the clerk of the county court, or of the City Register if in the City of St. Louis, upon the affidavit of any person having any interest in the dockets, records, books, papers, and documents of such justice of the peace, stating the nature of such interest and that such justice is dead, to issue an order in writing to the sheriff directing him to take into custody all such dockets, papers, books, records, and documents and deliver the same immediately to the clerk of the county court, or to the City Register if in the City of St. Louis (Sec. 

2164). Such clerk or register shall cause same to be delivered to some justice of the peace of the township or district in which the vacancy occurred, and such justice shall proceed to dispose of all causes remaining undisposed of as if they had been originally brought before him (Sec. 2165). When a vacancy occurs in the office of justice of the peace, it becomes the duty of the county court in which such vacancy occurs to appoint some person who is competent and qualified, who shall hold his office until the next general election of county officers and until his successor is elected, commissioned, and qualified (Sec. 2140). 78

cannot be held civilly liable for their erroneous judicial acts, even where such acts are performed unlawfully, fraudulently, corruptly, and with malice. 54 Thus, a justice cannot be held personally liable for corruptly and wilfully refusing to enter a judgment for a plaintiff, for in doing this he exercises purely judicial functions.55 For the same reason, a civil action will not lie against a justice on a charge that he issued a warrant against the plaintiff and caused him to be arrested as a vagrant.56 It has also been held that a justice is not liable in damages where, at the instance of the plaintiff, he issued an execution but made it returnable in sixty instead of ninety days, as the law required, whereby plaintiff lost and could not collect from defendant." In that instance, the court held that the issuance of an execution is a judicial act, and for the errors in the performance of any act from the beginning to the end of a suit, including the issuing of an execution, the justice was not liable in damages. This decision that the issuance of an execution is a judicial act has been both upheld 58 and criticized.59 But if, in the performance of his ministerial duties, a justice acts with malice or wilful oppression, he is liable in damages as any other ministerial officer. terial functions as a justice of the peace, it is sometimes difficult to determine when he is civilly liable for official acts and when he is not, but it is evident that the courts are inclined to resolve any doubt on the point in favor of the justice.61 A justice of the peace and the sureties on his official bond are liable for his default in turning over to the county money due it from such justice (Sec. 2371), and he is liable for costs unnecessarily incurred by him in certain criminal prosecutions (Sec. 3838). He is also subject to criminal prosecution for wilful neglect of duty 62 and for accepting a bribe (Sec. 

3930). And if convicted of bribery, perjury, or other infamous crime, or of any misdemeanor in office, he shall be removed from office (Sec. 2162). motives. . . . But there is a limit to this judicial immunity. The civil remedy depends exclusively upon the nature of the duty which has been violated. When duties which are purely ministerial are cast upon officers whose chief functions are judicial, and the ministerial duty is violated, the officer, although for most purposes a judge, is still civilly responsible for such misconduct."' 61 

Thus in Wertheimer vs. Howard, 30 Mo. 420, 1. c. 422, the court said: "The difficulties in drawing a line of distinction between judicial and ministerial acts, in reference to the duties which our statutes have confided to justices of the peace, are not readily removed; and, upon principles of public policy as well as equity, we are not disposed, in determining their responsibilities, to adopt the rules which have been applied to clerks and sheriffs and other mere ministerial officers. The clerical and judicial acts of justices are mingled together from the beginning to the end of a suit, and it is not easy to separate the one from the other. Great inconvenience, we also apprehend, would arise from holding a justice responsible for a blunder in issuing an execution where his intentions have been altogether pure. The office, at least in the great majority of instances, is not one attended with large gains; nor can it generally be relied on for a mere subsistence, but must necessarily be filled by persons whose principal pursuit will not allow an appropriation of much time or labor to the attainment of accurate legal information, even upon those subjects with which they have officially to deal. That the justice is required or allowed to be his own clerk, is not a sufficient reason to divest him of his judicial character whenever he performs an act, which a clerk, under other circumstances, would do. 

We have not been able to see, therefore, that in issuing an execution he is to be held responsible as a mere ministerial officer, but our inclination is to hold all his acts, which from the beginning to the end of a suit the law requires him to perform, as judicial and involving only that responsibility which attends all judicial officers.'' 

State vs. Latshaw, 63 Mo. A. 496. 83

JUSTICE COURTS II.  Sec. 62. General Nature. 

Unlike circuit courts, which exercise general jurisdiction and proceed according to the common law, justice courts are local courts of an inferior nature which exercise a limited statutory jurisdiction only, and within which they are strictly confined. They have no common law jurisdiction 64 and do not proceed according to the course of the common law,65 but derive their authority solely from the statute and can exercise no jurisdiction by implication. They arose to meet local needs and were designed for the convenience of parties litigant who may appear before them and conduct their cases without attorneys.67 They have exclusive original jurisdiction only of cases involving small sums and minor controversies. 68 

The statute excludes them altogether from jurisdiction over many subjects of litigation (Sec. 2168), and in those fields where the statute gives them jurisdiction superior courts see that they are strictly confined.69

Sec. 63. Suits Where Justice Courts Have No Jurisdiction. 

The statute (Sec. 2168) prohibits justice courts from exercising jurisdiction in cases: 

a. Against administrators and executors. b. Of libel, slander, false imprisonment, and malicious prosecution. c. Involving title to real estate. Sec. 64. Appeal Does Not Confer Jurisdiction Where Justice Was Originally Without Jurisdiction. 

A circuit court acquires only that jurisdiction of the subject matter of a case appealed from justice court which was originally conferred by statute on the justice, and in all those cases where the statute expressly denies jurisdiction to justice courts, the circuit court acquires no jurisdiction on appeal. In appeals from justice courts the jurisdiction of the circuit court is wholly derivative, and where the justice has no jurisdiction the circuit court acquires none, and the question of jurisdiction can be raised at any time. Sec. 65. Exclusive Original Jurisdiction. 

Justices of the peace have exclusive original jurisdiction in actions for forcible entry and detainer and for unlawful detainer (Sec. 2449). The law applicable to such cases has been held to constitute a special and preclusive code, so that if its mandatory requirements are not rigidly complied with, the justice court does not acquire jurisdiction in the first instance nor does the circuit court or court of appeals by appeal. Except as otherwise provided by law, justice courts also have exclusive original jurisdiction of civil actions and proceedings for the recovery of money, whether such actions be founded upon contract or tort, or upon a bond or undertaking given in pursuance of law in any civil action or proceeding, or for a penalty or forfeiture given by any statute of this State, when the sum demanded, exclusive of interest and costs, does not exceed fifty dollars and all the defendants reside in the same county (Secs. 2166, 1938), such cases not being originally cognizable by circuit courts

Sec. 66. Concurrent Original Jurisdiction. 

Justice courts have original jurisdiction concurrent with the circuit courts in all counties and cities in all civil actions for the recovery of money, whether such actions be founded upon contract or tort, or upon a bond or undertaking given in pursuance of law, in any civil action or proceeding, or for any penalty or forfeiture given by any statute of this State, when the sum demanded, exclusive of interest and costs, exceeds fifty dollars and does not exceed the maximum jurisdiction of justices of the peace in like cases in any such county or city; and also in all such cases where the sum demanded is less than fifty dollars, and wherein there are two or more defendants, not all of whom reside in the same county (Sec. 

1938).11 Justice courts and circuit courts have concurrent original jurisdiction also in all actions against railroad companies to recover damages for the killing or injuring of horses, mules, cattle, or other animals, without regard to the value thereof or the amount claimed therefor, such justices, of course, having jurisdiction of such cases arising within their respective townships (Secs. 1938, 2166, 2167). 

These courts also have concurrent original jurisdiction in attachment actions when the property attached does not exceed in value the statutory jurisdiction of the justice (Secs. 1274, 2426, 2444) and under certain conditions is not less in value than five dollars (Sec. (1277); in garnishment proceedings (Secs. 1396-1425; 2522-2538); and in actions to enforce mechanics' liens (Secs. 2539-2547; 31563189); and for replevin (Secs. 1624-1647; 2548-2572),12 within the pecuniary jurisdiction of both courts. Sec. 67. Pecuniary Limitations on Jurisdiction. 

In all civil actions and proceedings, whether founded on contract or tort, bond, or undertaking given in pursuance of law in any civil action or proceeding, or for a penalty or forfeiture given by any statute of this State, justice courts have jurisdiction when the sum demanded, exclusive of interest and costs, does not exceed two hundred and fifty dollars (Sec. 2166).18 In counties or cities having over fifty thousand and less than three hundred thousand inhabitants, the pecuniary limitation on the jurisdiction of justices of the peace is three hundred dollars (Sec. 2167). In counties having three hundred thousand inhabitants and less than six hundred thousand inhabitants, the pecuniary limit, exclusive of interest and costs, is five hundred dollars (Sec. 2167). In cities having three hundred thousand inhabitants or over, jurisdiction of justice courts extends to all such civil cases heretofore enumerated, and cases upon special tax bills when the sum demanded, exclusive of interest and costs, does not exceed seven hundred fifty dollars (Sec. 2043). Le Sec. 70. Claims Exceeding Limit Cannot Be Split. 

Where each of two notes is within the jurisdiction of justice courts, jurisdiction lies in an action on one of them, even though the notes were given as part of the same transaction and in the aggregate exceeded the pecuniary limit.32 But in an action on an account, the entire amount of which exceeded the pecuniary limit, plaintiff, by dividing the amount into three separate items, each of which was within the limit, could not have action on each of these items.83 

Splitting of claim or employment of other caprice in order to acquire jurisdiction cannot be tolerated, because it is a fraud upon the law.94 

Sec. 71. Jurisdiction Conferred by Remission of Part of Claim. 

Where plaintiff's claim exceeds the pecuniary limit on the jurisdiction of the justice, jurisdiction may be conferred by a voluntary renunciation by plaintiff of a part of his demand.85 The renunciation may be made by endorsing on the instrument which is the basis for the demand a credit sufficient to reduce the amount within the jurisdiction of the justice, or by filing a statement showing the actual amount of the demand, though that amount exceeds the jurisdiction, but praying for judgment only for an amount within the 77. 32

Sec. 72. Jurisdiction Retained by Remission of Part of Excessive 

Judgment.

Jurisdiction of a cause is not lost if a jury or the justice finds in favor of a party litigant in a sum in excess of that for which a justice is authorized to give judgment, provided that such party remit or release the excess and take judgment for the residue (Sec. 2294). 

This statutory method of conserving jurisdiction where lawfully exercised will not operate as a curative in a case where the original demand exceeded the jurisdiction of the justice and no voluntary renunciation of a part of same was made before the excessive verdict or judgment was entered.48

Sec. 73. Jurisdiction Where Set-offs and Counterclaims Are Filed. 

In an action against a defendant within the pecuniary limit of the jurisdiction of a justice, the defendant may ask a set-off or counterclaim, provided same does not exceed the pecuniary jurisdiction of the justice (Sec. 2218). But the justice cannot entertain a set-off or counterclaim in excess of his jurisdiction. Nor can a defendant prove a set-off in an amount exceeding the jurisdiction where, by giving credit for plaintiff's demand, such counterclaim is reduced within the pecuniary limit.
