Sec. 74. Actions Where There Is No Pecuniary Limit. 

a. Against railroad companies for killing livestock. 

Justice courts have jurisdiction of all actions against any railroad company in this State to recover damages for killing or injuring horses, mules, cattle, or other animals within their respective townships, without regard to the value of such animals or the amount claimed for killing or injuring same (Sec. 2166). But in order for such actions to lie, it must appear on the whole record that the injury occurred either in the township of the justice or in an adjoining township.49 Jurisdiction lies in actions for double damages for killing or injuring livestock, regardless of the amount.50 But it has been held that an action cannot be brought against a railway company for killing a horse and also for injuring harness under two different provisions of the act defining the jurisdiction of a justice, for the purpose of obtaining a judgment beyond the jurisdictional limit. However, if the plaintiff brings two causes of action against a railroad company, one of which is for the conversion of personalty within the pecuniary limit and the other for the killing of an animal, and the two actions together aggregate more than the pecuniary limit, the justice has jurisdiction.52 "Emery vs. St. Louis, etc., Ry. Sec. 75. Territorial Limitations Upon Jurisdiction. 

The statute makes the territorial jurisdiction of a justice of the peace coextensive with the county for which he is elected or appointed (Sec. 2169), except in landlord and tenant cases and in cases of forcible entry and detainer and unlawful detainer, in which cases suit must be brought before a justice in the township where the property to be affected is situated (Sec. 2374).52a A justice cannot hold court or perform official functions outside of the district for which he was appointed; and if he attempts to do so, his acts are void.53 

His authority to act officially is confined to the limits of his county,54 within which he has jurisdiction of unlawful detainer and forcible entry and detainer cases (Sec. 2449),55 and of all landlord and tenant actions (Sec. 2374), and suits in replevin,56 when brought within the proper venue (Secs. 2170, 2173, 2374).

Sec. 78. Jurisdiction of Ex Parte Proceedings. 

A justice court is always open for the conduct of ex parte proceedings.78 For the purpose of conducting such proceedings, such as entering a judgment by confession, it is not necessary that the court be opened by formal announcement, but for this and the transaction of any other ex parte business, the justice court is always open.70 An example of the service a justice is often called upon to render ex parte is that relating to taking up of stray animals (Secs. 12824-12860).

Sec. 79. Venue. 

a. Generally.

Action cognizable by a justice of the peace shall be brought before some justice of the township either:

First, wherein the defendants, or one of them, reside, or in any adjoining township;

Second, wherein the plaintiff resides, and the defendants, or one of them, may be found; 

76 State ex rel. Harris vs. Galloway (App.), 24 S. W. (2d) 710. 

76 Dorroh vs. Jones (App.), 247 S. W. 460. "State ex rel. Shaw State Bank vs. Pfeffle (App.), 293 S. W. 512. 

78 Hoppenbrock vs. Dial, 137 Mo. A. 75, 119 S. W. 496. 

70 Sullivan vs. Bambrick-Bates Construction Co., 86 Mo. A. 151. 100

Third, if the defendant is a nonresident of the county in which the plaintiff resides, the action may be brought before some justice of any township in such county where the defendant may be found; 

Fourth, if the defendant is a nonresident of the State, or has absconded from his usual place of abode, the action may be brought before any justice in any county in this State wherein defendant may be found; and

Fifth, any action against a railroad company for killing or injuring horses, mules, cattle, or other animals, shall be brought before a justice of the peace of the township in which the injury happened, or in any adjoining township (Sec. 2170). b. In counties of from 300,000 to 600,000 inhabitants. 

Actions cognizable before a justice of the peace in counties having a population of more than three hundred thousand and less than six hundred thousand inhabitants shall be brought before some justice of the township exactly as heretofore related for such suits before justices generally, except that as to the first subdivision or classification thereof the suit must be brought in the township wherein the defendants, or one of them, reside, and not in any adjoining township. 

In such counties it is also provided that actions instituted before any justice of the peace shall be tried at the place where such justice has his office or court and in the district over which he presides as such. 

Such justice is required to issue process, assume jurisdiction, and render judgment at the place where his court is located and within the district where he presides. Furthermore, when such justice removes his office or place of holding court out of the district for which he was elected or appointed, he shall be deemed to have vacated his office (Sec. 2171). The constitutionality of this provision of the statute has been upheld.80 c. In municipal townships containing 100,000 to 300,000 inhabitants.

The foregoing rules applicable to the place of bringing actions before justices of the peace generally apply in cities having a population of from one hundred thousand to three hundred thousand inhabitants, except that where justices of the peace are paid a salary every action cognizable by a justice against a defendant residing in "State ex rel. Hollaway vs. Knight (Sup.), 21 S. W. (2d) 767. 101

JUSTICE COURTS 

such township must be brought before some justice of the peace of such township and none other, and any judgment rendered contrary to such exception shall be null and void, except in actions by attachment (Sec. 2175). d. Where there is no justice, or justice is disqualified. 

When there is no justice in the township where a suit before a justice should be brought, or when all of the justices of such township are interested in the suit or are otherwise disqualified, such suit may be brought before any justice in the county where the plaintiff resides (Sec. 2173). e. Where several persons jointly liable.

Where several persons jointly liable to a suit reside in different townships in the same county, suits may be brought in any township against all such persons wherein any of such defendants reside, or in any adjoining township (Sec. 2172). f. When one justice may act for another. 

In townships having two or more justices any one may act for the other whenever such other is unable to act for any cause or reason. 

But in such case the incapacitated justice must enter in his docket a request for the other justice to act before such other justice shall have jurisdiction (Sec. 2176). g. Livestock injury and crop damage cases against a railroad company. 

Actions against a railroad company for killing or injuring livestock and for crop damages, when brought before a justice of the peace, must be brought in the township where the injury occurred, or in an adjoining township (Secs. 2170, 4761). This is essential to jurisdiction; the point cannot be waived by the appearance of the defendant; and if a judgment is rendered in such a case where such jurisdictional facts do not affirmatively appear on the face of the proceedings, the judgment will not stand.81 It has long been the 81

Foreign insurance companies.

If the defendant, garnishee, or proposed garnishee in an action before a justice is a foreign insurance company, the justice has authority to issue process and have same served by a constable or sheriff in the city or county where the Superintendent of Insurance resides or has his office (Sec. 2169). And it has been held that since the statute (Sec. 2170) provides that where the defendant is a nonresident of the State the action may be brought before any justice in any county where the defendant may be found, a foreign insurance company is a resident of every county and township in the State and suit may be instituted in any county regardless of the residence of plaintiff. 84

III. PROCEDURE IN CIVIL CASES A. IN ORDINARY ACTIONS 1. Proceedings Preliminary to Filing Suit: 

Sec. 80. Where Plaintiff Sues as Poor Person. 

If a person desiring to file a suit in a justice court is unable to pay the costs and expenses of the suit or give security therefor, he will avoid delay by applying to the justice for leave to sue as a poor person. The statute authorizes justice courts, in their discretion, before a suit is filed or after it has been commenced, to permit such persons to sue without giving security for costs (Sec. 2205). The application should state the facts showing plaintiff's inability to pay the costs or give security and should be accompanied by an oath that the facts stated are true. 83 'Haggard vs. A. & P. Ry. Sec. 81. Where Plaintiff Voluntarily Gives Security for Costs. 

The statute provides that if the plaintiff is a nonresident of the county or shall become a nonresident after the commencement of a suit, or if from any cause the justice shall be satisfied that he is unable to pay the costs, the justice shall rule the plaintiff, on or before the day in the rule named, to give security for the payment of costs in such suit, and if the plaintiff fail on or before the day of such rule named to file the obligation of a responsible person of the county whereby he shall bind himself to pay all costs that have accrued or may accrue in such action, or to deposit a sum of money equal to the costs that have accrued and will probably accrue in the same, the justice of the peace, on motion; shall dismiss the suit, unless security is given before the motion is determined (Sec. 2203). If the plaintiff is in such condition before suit is filed that he is liable to be required to file security for costs, he should file such security before the time of the filing of the suit. He may file a bond for the costs and make such deposit for costs as may be required by the justice. (Sec. 2203.)

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 82. Where Plaintiff Is an Infant. 

Any plaintiff except an infant may appear and conduct his suit either in person or by agent or attorney in a justice court (Sec. 

2207). No suit can be instituted by an infant plaintiff until a next friend for such infant shall have been appointed. While a written application of a minor for appointment of a next friend to institute a suit is not required,85 it is good practice in all cases to have written application for the appointment of a next friend filed before the justice, and, where the infant is more than fourteen years of age and entitled to select a guardian, the person applying for the appointment of a next friend should have such infant join in the application.

2. Pleadings: 

Sec. 83. Generally. 

Formal pleadings such as are used in circuit courts have never been required in justice courts in Missouri. 88 From the beginning, proceedings in civil actions before justices of the peace have been of "This form may be used when the application is filed by the minor alone or may also be used as an additional evidence of the obligation the proposed next friend is willing to assume.

In the practice before justice courts during the Territorial Period in Missouri, the statute required that the plaintiff file a formal petition with the justice stating the nature of his claim and requesting the issuance of process against the defendant. The justice thereupon endorsed on such petition a summons against the defendant who was served "by producing the original petition and summons, and informing him of the contents thereof, or by leaving a copy of it at his dwelling house, in the presence of one or more of his family or neighbors, at least four days before the time of hearing." Territorial Laws, Ch. 46, pp. 171-172. 

In 1825, the Legislature of Missouri passed an act requiring that in all suits brought in justice courts "a brief statement of the cause of action, and the amount claimed, shall be made in writing and filed with the justice; and the same, or a copy, annexed to the summons as aforesaid: but form in such state- 107

JUSTICE COURTS 

a summary nature without the usual formal pleading," other than the instrument sued on or a brief statement of the nature of the claim; and as to such statements as the statute requires to be filed, strict rules of pleadings are not, and never have been, applied.⁰⁰ So careful has the Legislature been to conserve the practice of informality in proceedings before justices of the peace that in 1843 it passed an act to construe a former law relative to proceedings before justices of the peace, in which it stated that the meaning of the act was, that to entitle the defendant to a continuance a written pleading was not necessary.91 The courts have uniformly held that in civil actions before justices of the peace formal pleadings are not required and strict technical rules of pleading are not applicable.⁹2 

The statute now provides that no formal pleadings on the part of either plaintiff or defendant shall be required in a suit before a justice of the peace, but further requires that before any process shall be issued in any suit the plaintiff shall file with the justice the instruments sued on or a statement of the account or of the facts constituting the cause of action upon which the suit is founded, and the dement shall not be regarded, so as the same be sufficient to apprise the defendant of the nature of the claim again him." Mo. R. S. 1825, Vol. I, pp. 473-474. 

In Brown vs. Fricke (1824), 1 Mo. 440, the first case reported in which the point was considered, the court said: "There are no formal pleadings required in proceedings before justices of the peace.' 

The reason for this informality in pleadings in justice courts, which is directly contrary to the strict rules governing pleadings in circuit courts, was stated in 

Casey vs. Clark, 2 Mo. 12, as follows: "It was doubtless a great object with the Legislature to simplify proceedings before justices of the peace so that every man might be his own lawyer; to that end, they have dispensed with all matters of mere form; but still a substantial statement or declaration of the cause of action, in cases like the present, are required.' 

The filing of a statement upon which a cause of action was based was declared necessary to give a justice jurisdiction of a cause in Odle vs. Clark, 2 Mo. 13.

The tendency away from formality in pleadings in justice courts has been so pronounced that it is uniformly held that much liberality should be indulged respecting the right of recovery under the pleadings. The pleadings in a justice court should always be liberally construed,95 and should not be judged by the rules applicable to formal pleadings in the circuit court. Thus, if a plaintiff relies upon recovering under a law of another state, it is not necessary for him to plead such law in an action before a justice of the peace in order to prove it.97 And a defendant need not plead the statute of limitations either verbally or in writing to rely upon same in defense of an action in justice court.98 The same rules apply in particular actions such as for forcible entry and detainer.99 In any action before a justice every inference and intendment should be resolved in "These provisions of the statute, in exactly the same form in which they now appear, have been in each revision of the statutes since 1879. Sec. 85. In Actions on Notes. 

In a suit on a note before a justice of the peace, the filing of the note with the justice, without any formal petition, is sufficient (Secs. 

2185, 2186). And the filing of a copy of a note has been held sufficient where no objection was made. The statute authorizes the filing of the note itself, or a statement of the cause of action. Delivery of the note to the justice is sufficient filing, though the justice does not mark it filed or make entry in his docket showing the note has been filed. The filing of both the note and a petition or statement of the cause of action thereon is not necessary,¹º but if both are filed the note itself is considered the foundation of the suit and the petition or statement should be ignored.11 Where the suit is against the endorser of a note, the filing of the note alone is sufficient. 12 And where more than one person is liable on the note, a pencil memorandum made on the note and filed with the justice, showing the person plaintiff desires to hold, has been held sufficient.18 The filing of a note by "Among these cases are those cited in the last preceding footnote, to which may be added the following additional cases, where the rule may be said to be stated with clarity and precision: Gnadt vs. Moore (App.), 297 S. Sec. 87. In Actions on Lost Instruments. 

Where the note or instrument in writing is alleged to be lost or destroyed, it is sufficient for the plaintiff to file with the justice the affidavit of himself or some other credible person, stating such loss or destruction and setting forth the substance of the instrument (Sec. 2187). But before a plaintiff can recover upon such lost instrument, he, with two sufficient securities to be approved by the court in which the trial is had, must execute a bond in a penalty at least double the amount of the note or bill, to the adverse party, conditioned to indemnify him against all claims by any other person on account of such note or instrument and against all costs and expenses by reason of such claim (Sec. 2188). Such affidavit is not required where the note or instrument is lost after the filing of the suit.21 But where the note or instrument is lost and no affidavit is filed before the judgment is rendered, the justice acquires no jurisdiction.22 An affidavit of the loss of a life insurance policy which is the subject of an action has been held insufficient and not within the

Sec. 88. In Actions on Accounts. 

In actions on accounts plaintiff must file the account or a statement of the facts constituting the cause of action upon which the suit is founded (Sec. 2185). In ordinary actions on account the filing of the account itself with the justice is sufficient if the account is so prepared that it advises the defendant of the claim and adequately identifies the subject matter and cause of action so as to preclude another action.27 The account when filed as a pleading must state the names of the debtor and creditor, the items, amount, and dates, "Cameron vs. Electric Household Stoves (App.), 78 S. W. (2d) 548; Derossett 

VS. Marsh, 224 Mo. A. 1095, 35 S. W. (2d) 62. 115

Sec. 90. In Actions for Torts. 

Tort actions are usually not founded upon and do not involve an instrument in writing and ordinarily are not susceptible to being stated in the form of an account. Since the statute requires the filing of either the instrument which is the foundation of the action or a statement describing the nature of the action, it is usually necessary in tort cases for plaintiff to file a statement describing his complaint, although such statement is sometimes made in the form of an account. In making such statement, the rules applicable to pleadings in justice courts generally apply, that is, the statement must be specific enough to advise the defendant of the nature of the claim and to bar another action on the same claim. But if in an action for negligence a plaintiff elects to charge specific grounds of negligence, and (App.), 26 S. W. (2d) 832; Lauman vs. Walker (App.), 249 S. Sec. 92. Where Defendant Should File Pleading. 

a. Where execution of written instrument is denied.

If a suit, set-off or counterclaim is founded upon an instrument of writing purporting to have been executed by the opposite party, and same is filed with the justice, it shall be received in evidence at the trial unless the party charged to have executed the same, before the jury is sworn or the trial submitted to the justice, denies the execution thereof on oath taken before some justice, or by an affidavit filed with the justice, and taken before any court or officer authorized to administer oaths (Sec. 2231). While it has been held that an affidavit denying execution may be filed for the first time in circuit court on appeal,57 it is always good practice to file such affidavit or oath denying execution.

c. Where statute of limitations is relied upon. 

It has been held that where a statute of limitations is relied upon as a defense to an action in justice court, it is not necessary to plead it either in the justice court or in the circuit court when the case arrives there on appeal. But the rule in justice court seems to follow the general rule to the extent that if the defendant relies on a statute of limitations as a bar to the cause of action, he should raise the point in some manner in the justice court."⁰ Some confusion exists as to how the courts intend that the point be raised in jus- 59 60 

Wickersham vs. Jarvis, 2 Mo. A. 279. 

Hornsby vs. Stephens, 65 Mo. A. 185. 

Cooksey vs. Kansas City, St. Joseph & Council Bluffs R. R., 17 Mo. A. 132. 

In Revelle vs. The St. Louis, Iron Mountain & Southern Ry. Co., 74 Mo. 438, 1. c. 442-443, Sherwood, J., said: "Besides, even if we admit that the statement shows upon its face that the statutory bar existed to plaintiff's action, the proper course for the defendant to have pursued was either to have pleaded the statute, or to have filed a motion to dismiss, or, if the cause had been tried de novo in the circuit court, to have asked an instruction covering the point. . . . 

The general rule is, that a party relying on the statute as a bar, must plead it the formality with which he makes his plea or the manner in which he urges his point, depending to a great extent upon the forum in which he makes this defense.'' 

Krause vs. Spurgeon (App.), 297 S. W. 434; Gregg vs. Carroll, 201 Mo. A. 473, 211 S. W. 914. 126

tice court, 61 or whether the same rule prevails where the account filed shows on its face that it is barred by a special statute as prevails in a case where a claim is barred by a general statute.62 The occasion for the confusion perhaps lies in the fact that there has not yet been clearly stated a rule harmonizing for justice practice, the rule prevailing in justice courts permitting a defendant to show any defense without a pleading, with the rule prevailing in courts of record requiring a special pleading of a defense of the statute of limitations. Unquestionably, where such defense is available in a case pending in justice court it would be following the course of caution to take certain advantage of the defense by filing an answer in justice court pleading it.

A defendant may set off any demand he has against the plaintiff, provided he owed it at the commencement of the action, and the amount of the demand does not exceed the jurisdiction of the justice (Sec. 2218). To entitle the defendant to set off such demand, he must give notice thereof in court, either verbal or written, before the jury is sworn or the case submitted to the justice; and when the setoff or counterclaim is founded upon an instrument of writing executed by plaintiff, or by his testator or intestate, or upon an account, he must at the time of giving such notice file with the justice such instrument or a bill of items of such account (Sec. 2219). Sec. 94. Amendment of Pleadings and Proceedings in Justice Courts. 

The statutes direct that any justice may, in open court, in furtherance of justice, and on such terms as may be proper, amend, on motion of either party, any statement, account, set-off, counterclaim, summons, return, or other proceeding, and add new parties as coplaintiffs or co-defendants, and correct a mistake in the name of the party (Sec. 2239). Under this statutory authority to permit amendments, it is the policy of the courts to exercise liberality in favor of the party seeking to amend.78 An amended statement may be filed by plaintiff without giving new notice to the defendant, where no new defendants are joined.79 A statement may be amended to bring a case within the pecuniary jurisdiction of a justice 80 and to show other jurisdictional facts,81 and an appellate court will reverse a cause to permit an amendment to be made showing such facts, 82 but an appellate court will not reverse a cause to permit an amendment to show an omitted jurisdictional fact where it affirmatively appears that jurisdiction over the subject matter of the cause had not attached and could not be made to attach in the justice court.83 In an action in replevin, a justice properly permitted the filing of an amended affidavit so as to show jurisdictional facts, 84 as a circuit court should do when a like case reaches that court on appeal where such amendment has not been made but leave is there asked to make the amendment.85 Likewise, a justice and a circuit court should per- "Lesan Adv. Sec. 95. Amendments in Circuit Courts in Cases Appealed From Justice Courts. 

a. Statutory authority for.

The statute authorizes circuit courts to allow amendments of pleadings in cases appealed from justice courts in all cases when substantial justice will be promoted by the amendments and no new item or cause of action is included in an amendment (Sec. 2360), and the addition of new parties, plaintiff or defendant, necessary to a complete determination of the cause of action, so long as the same cause is tried on appeal as was tried before the justice (Sec. 2358) and no set-off or counterclaim is pleaded in the circuit court that was not pleaded before the justice, in all those cases where the summons was personally served on the defendant (Sec. 2359). b. Courts generally construe authority liberally. 

Conforming to the plain intent of the statutes authorizing such amendments, circuit courts construe these statutes as remedial, and follow a liberal policy in allowing amendments within the restrictions

Sec. 96. Demurrers and Motions in Justice Courts. 

If a statement, complaint, or counterclaim is defective and cannot be corrected so as to state a cause of action, plaintiff should attack same in the justice court. This cannot be done by demurrer, as demurrers are unknown in justice practice. 3. Parties. 

Sec. 97. Generally. 

In justice courts the rule applicable as to parties in actions generally applies, and the subject being more completely covered elsewhere,34 it will not be treated here except as to some particular points that should be kept in mind in justice practice. The tendency toward extreme informality and the practice of extending leniency towards justice court proceedings, together with the statutes favoring amendments, both in justice courts (Sec. 2239) and in circuit courts before (Sec. 819) and after (Sec. 822) judgment, should not lure one having cases in justice court into neglect of some things that when once done cannot be corrected, even with all the intendments employed to assist. Thus, the naming of the exact party defendant is jurisdictional, and if an entirely different defendant is named from the person sought to be held, judgment will not stand against the intended defendant not named in the original statement.35 Moreover, the real party in interest must sue in his name, for his cause of action cannot be maintained in the name of another as agent.36 31

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 98. Plaintiff. 

Any plaintiff, except an infant, may appear and conduct his suit either in person or by agent or attorney (Sec. 2207), but this does not mean that the suit can be prosecuted in the name of the agent or attorney; and if a suit is instituted in an agent's name, it is error to permit an amendment substituting the principal's name as plaintiff, and the case may be dismissed. Substitution of an entirely different party plaintiff for the one who brought the action is not permissible under the statutes authorizing amendments, either in the justice court 38 or in the circuit court on appeal," for the reason that to allow such a substitution would be in effect to permit the institution of an entirely new suit by way of an amendment.4º An infant can sue only by next friend, and in such suits the proceedings should be conducted in the manner elsewhere discussed.4¹ 

Sec. 99. Defendant. 

Defendants, except infants, may appear in person or by agent or attorney and defend suits brought against them. Where a defendant appealed from a judgment in a justice court in which there was defective service, and in which it had otherwise appeared, the appeal constituted a general appearance and had the effect of waiving the defects in the service.42 An infant defendant can defend by guardian only, and if a judgment is entered against an infant defendant for whom no guardian was appointed, it is voidable and may be set aside in a direct proceeding.48 After an infant defendant has been served, no further proceedings can be taken in the case until a guardian is appointed, and a guardian may be appointed

4. Commencement of Actions. 

Sec. 101. The Docket of the Justice. 

Justice courts are not courts of record, but their business and the manner of conducting it are regulated by statute; and among the regulations prescribed is that each of them must keep a docket, in which he shall enter:

First, the title of all causes commenced before him; 

Second, the time when the first process was issued against the defendant, and the particular nature thereof; 

Third, the time when the parties appeared before him, either with or without process, or upon the return of process; 

Fourth, a brief statement of the nature of the plaintiff's demand "A court of record is defined by Ballentine as a court whose judgments may be revised by writs of error and whose proceedings and judgments import absolute verity and, until revised, protect all who obey them. 141

JUSTICE COURTS 

and the amount or description and value of the property claimed, and, if a set-off or counterclaim is pleaded, a similar statement of the nature of the set-off or counterclaim and the amount claimed; 

Fifth, every adjournment, stating at whose request and at what time;

Sixth, the time when the trial was had, stating whether the same was by jury or by the justice; 

Seventh, the verdict of a jury, and when rendered; 

Eighth, the judgment rendered by the justice, and the time of rendering the same;

Ninth, the time of issuing execution, and the name of the officer to whom delivered, and an account of the debt, damages and costs, as the same was endorsed on the execution; 

Tenth, the fact of an appeal having been made and allowed, and when made and allowed (Sec. 2177).

County courts are required to furnish justices of the peace with dockets, records and blanks used by them and by constables (Sec. 

2178). In cities of 300,000 inhabitants and over, the municipal assembly of such cities is required to furnish dockets and records and provide rooms and offices for justices and clerks and constables and for the proper care of same, and whatsoever else may be necessary for the proper conduct of their business (Sec. 2420). a. Subject to supervisory control of circuit courts. 

The courts recognize the statutory duty of justices of the peace to keep a careful record of the court proceedings before them.50 

And, through their right to exercise a superintending control of justice courts, circuit courts have a right to direct justices of the peace to correct erroneous entries of judgments in their dockets without resort to extraordinary remedies.51 In making entries required by law to be kept in his docket, a justice of the peace acts in a ministerial capacity,52 and, as a ministerial as well as an inferior 

50 In State vs. Ancell, 62 S. W. (2d) 443, l. c. 447, the Supreme Court recently observed: "It thus appears that in matters both civil and criminal in which a justice of the peace exercises the functions of a court, with authority to adjudicate controversies and render judgments, he is required by the statute to keep a docket of his proceedings and enter certain facts therein.' "Carter vs. Louisiana Purchase Exposition Co., 124 Mo. A. 530, 102 S. W. 6. 

52 Ibid. 142

judicial officer, is subject to the constant supervisory control of superior courts. 53 b. Justice alone responsible for, although entries may be made by clerk.

The mechanics of record-keeping may be delegated by a justice to a clerk, 54 but neither the responsibility therefor nor the consequence of errors committed in the course of making the entries shifts from the shoulders of the justice, because the statute makes the justice alone responsible, the clerk having no legal status.55 The authority of a justice to make entries in his docket ceases with the expiration of his term of office, and entries made by him thereafter are null.56 c. Nunc pro tunc entries, amendments and corrections. 

A justice has no power to make nunc pro tunc entries in his docket.57 The statute contemplates that the justice make entries of proceedings promptly as they occur, and when he renders judgment he is required to enter same forthwith on his docket (Sec. 2293). 

After a justice enters the record of a judgment in his docket, he is without power or authority to correct mistakes or supply omissions without the consent of all parties, and perhaps after obtaining such consent he should not make corrections and amendments except un-

W. 6, the court said: " 'Superior courts, on motion, and by rules or orders, command the performance of ministerial duties by officials, and this usage has prevailed time out of mind. It is an everyday occurrence for courts to grant rules on justices of the peace and clerks of inferior courts, to perfect their transcripts, send up complete records, or do other ministerial acts. State vs. Howell, 117 Mo. 307, 23 S. W. 263. . . . These orders are made in causes, the parties to which are before the court, but frequently are ex parte in the sense that the officials to whom they are directed have not been served previously with process. In fact they are treated as process to him, and he may show cause, if he can, against obeying the order.. "In our opinion, the superintending power of superior tribunals in ministerial matters ought to be given free play by the use of all available agencies and procedures which can be resorted to without prejudice to the rights of litigants."' After such transcript is filed, the judgment has the same dignity and effect as a judgment of the circuit court and is under the control of the court where the transcript is filed (Sec. 2301). e. Irregularities in docket entries not to affect judgment. 

No judgment rendered by a justice of the peace shall be deemed invalid, stayed, or in any way affected by neglect or failure of the justice to enter the same within the time prescribed or by reason of any informality in entering or giving such judgment or other entry required to be made in the docket, or for any other default or negligence of the justice or constable by which neither party shall be prejudiced (Sec. 2313). Thus it has been held that the omission of the dollar mark in stating the amount of the judgment does not render the judgment void.65 Nor does the failure of a justice to keep proper record of a search warrant render the warrant invalid.66 Failure of the justice to date or sign judgment does not invalidate same,67 nor does the entry of a judgment three days after it was rendered affect it.68 f. Entry in docket imports verity. 

When an entry required by law to be made in a docket of the justice is regularly entered, it imports verity and is the best and only evidence as to the fact covered by such entry. Such judgment generally cannot be collaterally attacked except for fraud, accident, or mistake. But where the record of the justice is regular on its face, it is not subject to collateral attack.70 As to records which the law does not require the justice to keep, the rule is otherwise, it being generally held that such records do not import verity, but may be impeached."¹ 65

Not subject to change by parol evidence. 73 When the docket of a justice is silent as to facts required by law to be entered therein, the justice may be called upon to testify as to the omitted facts.72 And the justice and his clerk may testify as to correctness of dates on transcript when the records have been changed. But a justice cannot be required to contradict, vary, or explain away the facts stated in his docket." Nor is parol evidence admissible to controvert recitals in a transcript of a justice or to contradict, vary, or impeach entries in a justice docket of matters required by law to be entered therein.75 h. Open to inspection.

The statute requires that the dockets of justice of the peace be kept open at all times for inspection on the part of persons interested, and upon request and tender of fees therefor, justices of the peace shall make out and deliver to the demandant a full and complete copy, all duly certified as the law directs, of such proceedings in their custody and recorded in their dockets as may be requested. (Sec. 2180). Failure to abide by such requirement subjects the justice to a fine of not less than $10, and liability to the party injured in double the amount of damages caused thereby (Sec. 2181).

Sec. 102. Terms and Time of Holding Court. 

There are no terms of justice courts. The statute requires that every justice hold court as often as may be necessary and on any day except Sunday, and that when the justice requires it, the constable of the township be in attendance in person or by deputy (Sec. 2182). 

Such courts, therefore, are always open for the transaction of business, and trials before them can be held, process made returnable, and cause adjourned on any day of the year, except Sunday (Sec. 

2182), including even a holiday." 77 

Sec. 103. When and How Suits May Be Commenced. 

The statute authorizes the institution of suits before justices of the peace, either by the voluntary appearance and agreement of the parties, or by process (Sec. 2183). Several causes of action by the same plaintiff may be joined in one suit and one writ may be directed to several defendants, unless by such joinder the jurisdiction of the justice is exceeded (Secs. 2190, 2191). 

a. By agreement. 

Where the parties to a controversy mutually agree to submit their cause to a justice, they may do so by voluntarily appearing and 

76 Sullivan vs. Bambrick-Bates Construction Co., 86 Mo. A. 151, 1. c. 155. "Bear vs. Youngman, 19 Mo. A. 41. 149

JUSTICE COURTS 

agreeing before the justice that suit may be filed and the cause submitted without the issuance and service of process. Where this is done, the action is deemed commenced at the time the case is docketed (Sec. 2183).

b. By process. 

Where suit is commenced by process, either a summons may be issued and served on defendant or his property attached. In either event, the suit is commenced at the time the writ is delivered to the constable to be served, and that time is determined by a notation the constable is required to make on the writ at the time he receives it (Sec. 2183). The time the suit is commenced cannot be determined 150

from an entry on the docket of the justice, for such entry is no evidence of the time the writ was delivered, as the law does not require the justice to enter such fact on his docket, and his docket is evidence only of such matters as he is required to record.78 If the constable fails to note on the writ the time of receiving it, evidence may be admitted to show such time.79 The fact may be of consequence, for if the period of limitation runs prior to the delivery of the writ to the constable, the action is barred.80

Sec. 104. Process, Its Issuance, Content and Form. 

In all cases not specially provided for, the process is a summons (Sec. 2193) issued and signed by the justice granting same, dated on the date issued (Sec. 2192), and running in the name of the State of Missouri (Art. 6, sec. 38; Secs. 754, 2192).81 Every summons must be directed to the constable of the township in which the justice who granted the same resides, or in which the defendant, or one of the defendants, resides, except where it is otherwise specially provided. 

This summons is a command to the defendant or defendants to appear before the justice who issued the same, at a time and place named in the summons, not less than ten, nor more than thirty, days from the date thereof, to answer the complaint of the plaintiff and stating also the nature of the suit and sum demanded (Sec. 2193). The statute also provides that the justice shall endorse on the summons the amount of plaintiff's demand, with the costs that have accrued; and if the defendant shall pay to the officer serving the summons the amount claimed and costs, the summons shall be returned satisfied and the suit thereupon be dismissed. But the failure of the justice to so endorse such summons shall in nowise affect the same or any service or proceeding in the case (Sec. 2194). The form of summons is prescribed by statute (Sec. 2195). "Fabien vs. Grabow, 134 Mo. A. 193, 114 S. W. 80; Heman vs. Larkin, 99

Sec. 105. Service of Process. 

a. By whom.

When process is issued, it is delivered by the justice to the constable to whom it is directed. If the justice is satisfied that such process will not be executed for want of an officer to be had in time to execute the same, or if the constable is a party to the pending suit or is otherwise interested in the result thereof, the justice may empower any suitable person not a party to the suit to execute the same, by endorsing upon such process authorization for service thereof.

Sec. 107. Defects in Process and Service Waived by General Appearance. 

96 or If the process issued is defective or if it has been defectively served, the defendant should take advantage of it by a limited appearance for the purpose of quashing the summons or return, dismissing the cause. For it is generally held that if a defendant has been served with a defective process or in an irregular manner and thereafter generally appears, he thereby waives any defects in the process and service. Such waiver may result from an appearance only for the purpose of consenting to a continuance," or for any other acts relative to resisting the cause.100 If a defendant first appears for the purpose only of presenting a motion to quash the service or dismiss the case, and after these motions are overruled files an answer, participates in the trial, and then appeals to circuit court, where he again takes part in the trial, his appearance becomes general and he waives defective process and service.¹ But if the defendant does not appear in justice court and a judgment by default is there rendered on a defective service, the defendant may perfect an appeal from justice court, and when the case reaches the circuit court limit his appearance there only for the purpose of presenting a motion to quash or dismiss, and not thereby waive defective process or service.2

5. Proceedings Following Service of Process. 

Sec. 108. Defendant May Pay Constable. 

Defendant has the statutory right to pay the constable the amount of plaintiff's demand, either before or after a suit is commenced against him (Sec. 2202), and thus save himself further costs and the perfecting an appeal from a judgment of a justice does not operate to waive defective process or service and confer jurisdiction over the person. * This and the last preceding form may be filed in justice court where process or service thereof may be attacked. If the motion should be there overruled, defendant should refuse to take any further action or appear further in any other capacity. Should judgment be rendered against the defendant in justice court, the defendant may thereafter appeal and refile such motions in circuit court. 

Or, if defendant does not file such motions in justice court or appear therein for any purpose, and judgment is rendered against him, he may appeal from such judgment. After the case reaches circuit court on appeal, and defendant has not theretofore filed his motion to quash or dismiss, he may file similar motions in the circuit court or refile those first filed in the justice court. If the motions are overruled in circuit court, defendant should then take no other part in the case whatever nor appear in circuit court further for any purpose. If he does appear for any other purpose and take any action anywhere in the stage of the proceedings in justice court or circuit court relative to the subject matter of the action, his appearance will be considered general and his right to object to defects in the process, service or return thereof, waived. 158

trouble of appearing in justice court. And if defendant offers to pay the constable the amount of plaintiff's demand and the constable directs defendant to pay the amount to the justice, which defendant does, the defendant complies with his statutory privilege and cannot thereafter be held for further costs.¹ 

Sec. 109. Defendant May Tender Amount Due. 

5 If the defendant does not pay the constable what he owes plaintiff until after the suit is commenced, and still desires to avail himself of the statutory right to avoid further costs, he must pay the entire amount he owes plaintiff, with all the costs that have accrued up to that time; and if he does so and plaintiff does not accept the amount but continues the prosecution of the suit, and does not recover judgment for a larger amount, exclusive of interest and costs thereafter accrued, than the sum paid to the constable, the plaintiff must pay all costs accruing after such payment (Sec. 2226). But a payment of the amount of the demand to the justice instead of to the constable after the suit was commenced has been held insufficient, as was a deposit in a bank of the amount sued for, not including costs, to the credit of the justice instead of to the constable. If there is a tender only, and no deposit is made, it has the effect only of preventing the running of interest or accumulation of damages after the time of the tender (Sec. 2225). Defendant also has the statutory right to relieve himself of the obligation to pay costs by making a tender of what he owes plaintiff, either before or after the commencement of the suit; and if, after such tender, the suit is filed and defendant deposits the amount due, or the thing involved, with the constable of the township, the defendant shall recover costs (Sec. 2224). It has been held that this right to make a tender is but a recognition of the common law rule that a tender could be made and pleaded when the demand was in the nature of a debt and the sum was certain or capable of being made certain; but it could not be made when the action was for unliquidated damages, the amount of which was to be determined by a jury, and that the statute did not extend the rule to apply to cases where unliquidated damages are demanded.' And 'Berrel vs. Davis, 44 Mo. 407. 'J. H. North Furn. & Carpet Co. vs. Davis, 86 Mo. A. 296. 

Road District No. 41 vs. Jackson, 208 Mo. A. 194, 231 S. W. 1043. 'Joyner vs. Bentley, 21 Mo. A. 26. 159

JUSTICE COURTS 

9 8 this interpretation of the statute has been uniformly followed. Obviously, the statute does not apply to actions originally brought in circuit courts. But the statute does not follow the common law rule in allowing a tender but a retention of the thing tendered by the defendant until accepted by plaintiff, for in order for defendant to take advantage of the statutory right to relieve himself of costs after suit is brought, he must make the tender and deliver the thing tendered to the constable of the township in which suit is brought, and when he does so he is relieved of the obligation for costs, regardless of what the constable does with it.10

If the tender is first made to the constable of the township to which the case goes on change of venue, who keeps it until after judgment is rendered and an appeal taken to the circuit court, and then returns it to the defendant, who again tenders it to plaintiff and deposits it with the clerk before the trial begins in the circuit court, the statute is complied with.11 When money is demanded, tender made by check is sufficient and will stop the running of interest on the debt, but to avail defendant it must not be withdrawn.12 A tender to the constable followed by a payment of the amount tendered operates as a payment of the demand, so that thereafter plaintiff is not only denied the right to recover costs but defendant is also estopped from denying that the amount tendered is due.18 If plaintiff accepts the amount tendered when paid to him by the officer with whom it was deposited by defendant, the operation of the statutory privilege accorded defendant is complete, and plaintiff cannot thereafter both retain the amount and continue the prosecution of the suit.¹4

Sec. 111. Defendant May Appear and Resist the Action. 

If the defendant is less than twenty-one years of age, he should appear by his guardian, if he has one, and if not, he should have a guardian appointed for him in the manner heretofore discussed.16 

If he is more than twenty-one years of age, he may appear in person or by agent or attorney (Sec. 2210). He may attack the proceedings and take such steps and make such defenses as are available. a. By demanding security for costs.

If plaintiff has not already filed security for costs or obtained permission to prosecute the action as a poor person, either of which he may do in the manner hereinbefore discussed, and if the plaintiff is a nonresident of the county, or shall have become a nonresident since the filing of the suit, the defendant should demand that plaintiff be required to give security for the payment of the costs of the suit, and if security is not given as may be required, the defendant should move for a dismissal thereof (Sec. 2203). The statutory requirement that security be given for costs in those cases where plaintiff is a nonresident or the justice is satisfied that he is unable to pay the costs, is mandatory; and if the defendant desires to take advantage thereof, he must see that security for costs is required in justice court, for it has been frequently held that where plaintiff wins in justice court he cannot be required to give security for costs after the case reaches the appellate court on appeal.18

The defendant may raise the question of the sufficiency of the pleading, statement or complaint filed by asking that same be made more definite and certain or by motion to strike out or by motion to dismiss.19 If defendant desires to attack the process or return, he may do so by motion to quash or by motion to dismiss; but, for getting such motions presented, he should appear specially and for no other purpose and refuse to take any action whatever to resist the case on its merits. Or, he may make no appearance whatever in justice court until after a judgment is rendered against him on defective process or service, and then he may either appear specially and ask that judgment be set aside (Secs. 2251, 2252), or appeal and file motion to quash or dismiss in the circuit court.20 c. By filing set-off or counterclaim.

If defendant has any demand against plaintiff which he owned at the time the action was commenced, and which he could plead in a court of record, and which does not exceed the jurisdiction of the justice, he may file same as a set-off or counterclaim against plaintiff's cause of action (Sec. 2218). This counterclaim should conform to all the requirements of a statement of an original cause of action by a plaintiff,21 and notice thereof, either verbally or in writing, must be given before the jury is sworn or the trial submitted to the justice (Sec. 2219).22 If the counterclaim is founded upon an instrument of writing executed by plaintiff or by his testator or intestate, he must at the time of giving such notice file with the justice such instrument or a bill of items of such account (Sec. 2219). 

Where a set-off or counterclaim has been filed, judgment shall be entered for defendant for costs, if the counterclaim is equal in amount to plaintiff's debt. If it is for less than plaintiff's debt, plaintiff is entitled to judgment for the residue only, with costs. If it is "Skillman vs. Ballew (App.), 27 S. W. By moving the consolidation of causes against him. 

Whenever several suits shall be pending before a justice of the peace by the same plaintiff against the same defendant for causes of action which may be joined, or whenever several suits shall be pending before the same justice of the peace against several defendants for the same cause of action, the justice before whom the same may be prosecuted shall, upon motion of the defendant, order such suits to be consolidated, if it appear that the causes of action are such as may be joined in the same suit, that the questions which will arise in both actions are substantially the same, or that no defense is intended, or that the defense will be substantially alike in both cases (Sec. 2235). An order consolidating suits cannot be made when the effect will be to increase the amount involved beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the justice, but the number of actions may be reduced by consolidation and so as to permit plaintiff to still recover his entire demands (Sec. 2236).24 But suits instituted at different times and before different justices cannot be consolidated. 25 When consolidations are ordered, costs are equitably divided between the parties by the justice (Sec. 2237), and the plaintiff is not permitted to recover costs in several causes that may have been brought in a single action in the first place (Sec. 2238). e. By resisting case on its merits. 

Defendant may appear and file an answer, or in the trial of the case, without an answer, set up such defenses as he may have.20

After suit is filed and process served, plaintiff, in the interest of perfecting the proceedings, may do either of the following things: "State ex rel. a. If a minor, have next friend appointed. 

Sometimes, by inadvertence or mistake, a suit for a minor may be instituted without the previous appointment of a next friend. 

Should this be done and plaintiff make discovery of the error, he may ask that a next friend be appointed. In fact, the suit cannot be dismissed for failure to have such appointment previously made if some suitable person will file with the justice his written consent to become next friend and be responsible for the costs when the exception is taken. (Sec. 2209.) b. Where defendants are not all served.

Where defendants are not all served or some are not served in time, the plaintiff may direct the justice either to discontinue as to all not served and those not served in due time, and proceed against those that are bound to appear, or he may continue the suit until another day and take new process against those that are not served or not served in time (Sec. 2215). But a plaintiff cannot take a judgment against a defendant properly served and at the same time continue the case as to another defendant not served, for there can only be one judgment and that must dispose of all the parties to the cause.27 This is the general rule prevailing in other courts, 28 but a second continuance to bring in other defendants will not be allowed except by consent of all those who appear (Sec. 2216). If plaintiff is not present to direct the course to be pursued when all defendants have not been served, the justice may continue the cause and issue new process for those not served when necessary (Sec. 2217). c. Amend, add new parties or correct names of parties. 

If the proceedings are irregular, plaintiff may take advantage of the opportunity the statute gives him, in common with the defendant, to move the amendment of his statement or account, or the summons, writ or other proceeding; or he may ask that new parties plaintiff or defendant be added or the mistake in the name of a party corrected (Sec. 2239). If new parties defendant are added and they do not voluntarily appear in open court and enter their appearance, the cause must be continued and summons issued and served on them as other parties (Sec. 2240).

Sec. 113. Proceedings Where Either Plaintiff or Defendant Does 

Not Appear. a. Justice must wait three hours.

If a summons is returned showing that it has been duly served, the justice shall wait three hours after the return time stated in the summons before he takes any action, unless the parties sooner appear (Sec. 2215). b. Where defendant fails to appear.

But if a defendant who has been duly served or who has once appeared and the case has been adjourned, neglects to appear within three hours after the return of the process or the adjourned time, the statute requires the justice to proceed in the manner following: "First, if the suit be founded upon an instrument of writing, filed with the justice at the commencement of the action, and purporting to have been executed by the other party, and the demand of the plaintiff is liquidated by such instrument, the justice shall, whether the plaintiff appear or not, render judgment with costs against the defendant by default, for the amount which shall appear by such instrument to be due to the plaintiff, after allowing the proper discounts for all payments endorsed thereon; second, if the suit be not founded on an instrument of writing, and the plaintiff appear in person or by his agent, the justice shall proceed to hear his allegations and proofs, and shall determine the cause as the very right thereof shall appear from the testimony, and if it appear from such testimony that the plaintiff is entitled to recover, judgment shall be rendered by default against the defendant for so much as the testimony shows the plaintiff is entitled to, together with costs; and if it do not appear that the plaintiff ought to recover, judgment shall be given for the defendant as upon a verdict against the plaintiff. (Sec. 2249.) 

A judgment of a justice against a defendant who was present by attorney when the judgment was rendered but took no part in the hearing was not a judgment by default.29 Nor is a judgment by confession a default judgment. Likewise, a judgment rendered after a defendant pleads to the merits and then withdraws and a jury renders a verdict against him, is not one in default.³ "Borgwald vs. Fleming, 69 Mo. 212. 31 "Wade vs. Swope, 107 Mo. A. 375, 81 S. W. 471. "State ex rel. Shenault vs. Hopper, 72 Mo. A. 171. 165

c. When plaintiff fails to appear.

If plaintiff fails to appear, except where the suit is on an instrument of writing, the justice shall render judgment of nonsuit against him, with costs, and this even though defendant has been duly served and makes default (Sec. 2249). And in all other cases not otherwise specially provided for, if plaintiff fails to appear in person or by agent or attorney within three hours after the time appointed for the trial, the justice shall render judgment of nonsuit against him, with costs (Sec. 2250). A judgment of nonsuit can be entered only when plaintiff fails to appear in person or by agent or attorney,82 and such judgment is the only judgment that can be rendered when he fails to appear, except when the suit is on a written instrument. 88 

Plaintiff may appeal from such judgment.³ 84 Moreover, the judgment does not bar a new suit on the same cause of action.85

Sec. 114. Judgment of Nonsuit and by Default May Be Set Aside. 

Every justice of the peace shall have power, on the application of the party aggrieved, or his agent, and for good cause shown, to set aside the judgment of nonsuit and by default, upon the payment of all costs then accrued. Every such application shall be made within ten days, or twenty days if the party be a nonresident of the state, after the rendering of the judgment; and if in the meantime any execution has been issued, the justice may revoke the same in the manner provided for revoking an execution after an appeal has been allowed, and with the like effect. The justice shall, in all cases, make an entry in his docket of every such application, and of the day on which it was made, together with his orders thereon (Sec. 2251). Thus, at the request of defendant and for good cause shown, a justice may set aside a judgment by default, but he cannot set aside such judgment at the request of plaintiff," nor until all costs that have accrued are paid.88 The application must be made within the time the statute allows, and in computing the time the general rule obtains that the first day after judgment is excluded and the last day included."⁰ 39

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 115. Effect on Proceedings. 

a. Where there is a transfer of interest in suit.

In case of a transfer of any interest in the action, other than that occasioned by death, marriage, or other disability of a party to a suit, the action shall be continued in the name of the original party, if the party to whom the transfer is made will indemnify the party in whose name the suit is to be continued, against all costs and damages that may be occasioned thereby, or the court may allow the person to whom the transfer is made to be substituted in the action; and in all such cases the party to whom the transfer is made may be required by the court, upon the application of the party who made the transfer, either to give such indemnity, or to cause himself to be substituted in the action; and upon his omission to do so the court shall order the suit to be dismissed (Sec. 2241). b. Where justice fails to hold court on appointed day. 

No suit shall be deemed discontinued or abated by reason of the failure of the justice to hold court at the appointed day, nor by reason of any adjournment before the business pending in such court is disposed of; but the same shall be continued and proceeded upon as if no such failure or adjournment had happened. (Sec. 2242.) c. Where vacancy in office of justice occurs.

A suit pending before a justice whose office becomes vacant does not abate. In cases of such vacancy, plaintiff may either let the action remain until a successor to the justice is appointed or elected, or he may commence suit before some other justice. If he elects to pursue the latter course, he is entitled to withdraw the instrument on which the first suit is brought from the person having custody of the records of the late justice, who shall make a memorandum in the docket of the withdrawal. (Sec. 2243.)

On this 2d day of February, 19...., Arch Roe, plaintiff herein, appeared before me and asked leave to withdraw the promissory note he holds against Lucius May, and which note was the subject of this suit and is hereinbefore more particularly described; and the said 

Arch Roe having satisfactorily shown me that since the death of 168

H. Howe, another justice of the peace of Township, and the said note was thereupon delivered by me to the said Arch Roe. 

Ralph Day,

Having custody and charge of the official records of Howard Smith, deceased, until his successor is chosen. d. Where plaintiff dies.

Suit does not abate upon the death of a plaintiff in those cases where, by law, the action survives to the executor or administrator of the deceased, but in all such cases such executor or administrator is authorized to become a party to the suit (Sec. 2244). After receiving notice of the death of a plaintiff, a justice should make an entry of the fact upon his docket and issue a citation or notice directed to his executor or administrator requiring him to appear before the justice on a day named in the citation, not less than fifteen nor more than thirty days after such citation or notice is issued, and be made a party to the suit (Sec. 2245). If, after such notice is served and such executor or administrator neglects or refuses to appear to become a party to the suit, the justice shall thereupon render judgment of nonsuit against such executor or administrator for all costs of the suit (Sec. 2246).

Where joint plaintiff or defendant dies.

If a suit is by two or more plaintiffs or defendants and one or more of them shall die before judgment, the suit does not thereby abate, but the cause of action survives to the surviving plaintiff or plaintiffs and against the surviving defendant or defendants. When suggestion of such death is made, the justice should enter same on his docket, after which the suit may proceed as though death had not occurred (Sec. 2247). It has been held that where one of two plain- 170

tiffs in joint possession of real estate before entry dies, the survivor is entitled to all damages from forcible entry and detainer.** f. Where defendant dies.

When a sole defendant dies after being properly served with process and before judgment in any case in which the cause of action by law survives, the death of the defendant shall be suggested and the justice shall immediately make an entry thereof on his docket and shall cease all further proceedings in the cause and certify and return to the court of his county having probate jurisdiction a transcript of all entries made in his docket in the cause, together with all papers relating to the suit and filed therein, in the same manner and within the same time as upon an appeal; and upon the filing of the proceedings and papers in the office of the clerk, the court shall become possessed of the cause and shall proceed as in cases of other demands against an estate, ten days' previous notice thereof having been given to the executor or administrator, or such notice having been waived by him (Sec. 2248). But this does not apply to suits by attachment and other suits which probate courts cannot dispose of.45

Sec. 116. Change of Venue. 

Either party shall be entitled to a change of venue if, before the jury is sworn or a trial before the justice commenced, he shall file an affidavit charging either that: (1) The justice is a material witness for him, without whose testimony he cannot safely proceed to trial; (2) the justice is near of kin to either party, stating in what degree; (3) he cannot have a fair and impartial trial before such justice on account of his bias or prejudice; (4) he cannot have a fair trial in the township on account of bias or prejudice of the inhabitants of such township. The affidavit may be made by the party or his agent or attorney. (Sec. 2254.) If a justice transfers a cause to another justice without application of either party, a reviewing court will assume the parties consented and waived the irregularity, in the absence of a showing to the contrary. A change of venue may be “Keyser vs. Rawlings, 22 Mo. 126.

Sec. 120. Continuances. 

a. By consent of parties or by order of justice. 

Upon the return day, if a jury be required, or if the justice be actually engaged in other official business, the justice may adjourn the trial to another day without the consent of either party in any case, where it appears necessary (Sec. 2259). This applies to attachment actions as well as other suits.65 Or the trial may be adjourned upon the application of either party for good reason shown, to some day certain, not exceeding twenty days from the return day of the writ (Sec. 2260). And a justice may be compelled by mandamus to grant a continuance when good cause is shown." b. Because of absent material evidence.

A continuance may be had upon application of either party supported by his own oath or affidavit or the oath or affidavit of some other person that a material witness or evidence in the case cannot be produced (Sec. 2261). But in order for a party to procure a continuance on this account, the affidavit must comply with all the statutory requirements therefor. 67 c. Sec. 121. Procuring Witnesses For by Subpoena. 

a. At whose instance.

For the purpose of establishing his case, a party to a cause usually finds it necessary to rely upon the testimony of other persons besides himself. Sometimes such persons may voluntarily, or at the request of the party for whom they expect to testify, appear and serve as witnesses when called upon. Nothing in the law prevents a person from thus voluntarily serving as a witness. Again, persons whose testimony may be pertinent to an issue in a trial may not desire to appear voluntarily as witnesses, either because their voluntary appearance may be construed as an indication of bias in favor of the person in whose behalf they appear or prejudice against the other 177

JUSTICE COURTS 

party to the cause, or because it may preclude them from receiving pay for their services as witnesses through the regular channel of costs. And still again the desired witness may not be willing to serve at the instance of either party to the controversy and thus refuse to heed their requests to serve. The statute provides for both parties a remedy against leaving their actions open to the hazards of trials without material witnesses by directing the justice to issue subpoenas to witnesses at the instance of either party, and including all witnesses ordered at the same time by one of the parties in a single subpoena. (Sec. 2263.) b. Who subject to.

Any witness in the county where the cause is tried or in an adjoining county and within twenty miles of the place of trial may be compelled to attend as a witness in justice court upon a subpoena issued by a justice (Sec. 2264). Even a person confined in jail or prison may be compelled to attend a trial before a justice in either a civil or criminal proceeding upon a special writ or process issued for that purpose (Secs. 1745-1746). c. By whom and how served.

A subpoena may be served either by a constable or by any other person, and it shall be served by reading the same to the witness or delivering to him a copy thereof. In all those cases where the witness shall refuse to hear such subpoena read or to receive a copy thereof, the offer of the constable or such other person to read the same or to deliver a copy thereof, and such refusal, shall be a sufficient service of such subpoena. (Sec. 2265.) A party to a cause may serve subpoenas upon his own witnesses, but if he does so he is not entitled to have his fees therefor charged as costs in the case.68

Sec. 122. Procuring Witnesses by Attachment. 

a. When.

Eldon James. 

Whenever it shall appear to the satisfaction of the justice that any person duly subpoenaed to appear before him in a suit shall have failed without just cause to attend as a witness in conformity to such subpoena, and the party in whose behalf the subpoena was issued, or his agent, shall make oath that the testimony of such witness is material, the justice shall have power to issue an attachment to compel the attendance of such witness (Sec. 2266). b. To whom directed and how served.

Every such attachment may be directed to any constable of the county in which the witness resides, and shall be executed in the same 179

JUSTICE COURTS 

manner as a warrant in a criminal case, and the fees of the officer for issuing and serving the same shall be paid by the person against whom the same shall have been issued, unless he show reasonable cause, to the satisfaction of the justice, for his omission to attend, in which case the party requiring such attendance shall pay all costs of such attachment (Sec. 2267). c. Attached witness, how discharged.

If any witness so attached shall show a reasonable excuse for not appearing, as required by the subpoena, he shall be discharged, either with or without payment of the costs of the attachment, in the discretion of the justice; but if he fail to show any good and sufficient reason for not attending, he shall be fined in such sum as the justice shall think reasonable to impose, not exceeding ten dollars, and may be committed until such fine and costs are paid, in like manner as persons may be committed for the nonpayment of fines and costs in criminal cases (Sec. 2268).

Sec. 123. Adverse Party May Be Called as Witness. 

In trials before justices of the peace, either party may call on his adversary to testify as a witness in the cause, and may cause him to be subpoenaed in the same manner and with like effect as any other witness. If the party, after being duly subpoenaed, fail to attend the trial personally, or, being present, shall refuse to be sworn and testify, if plaintiff, his suit may be dismissed, or if defendant his answer, set-off or counterclaim may be stricken out and not allowed, at the option of the adverse party. (Sec. 2273.)

Sec. 124. Reattendance May Be Required Without New Subpoena. 

When any cause shall be continued by the justice, it shall be his duty forthwith to call before him all witnesses summoned in the cause and verbally notify such as may attend to appear before him to testify in the cause on the day set for trial, which verbal notice shall be in all respects as valid as a summons; and the justice shall enter in his docket the fact of notice and the names of the witnesses notified. No summons shall thereafter issue to any witness notified as directed. (Sec. 2270.)

Sec. 125. Witnesses Liable in Damages for Non-Attendance. 

Every person subpoenaed as aforesaid and neglecting to appear shall, if his fees have been tendered to him, also be liable to the party in whose behalf he may have been subpoenaed for all damages which such party may have sustained by his nonattendance (Sec. 2269).

Sec. 126. Litigant Liable for Costs of Unnecessary Witnesses. 

If either party subpoena more than three witnesses to prove any one fact, or shall subpoena any person or persons and not examine them as witnesses on the trial, he shall pay the costs occasioned by 181

JUSTICE COURTS 

such surplus or unnecessary witness or witnesses, unless the testimony of such unexamined witnesses shall be rendered unnecessary by admissions of the opposite party on the trial (Sec. 2271).

Sec. 127. Competency and Oath of Witnesses. 

Every witness is required to have administered to him an oath or affirmation before he gives any testimony. If he is objected to as an incompetent witness, such objection must be tried and determined by the justice (Sec. 2272). 

118. FORM OF OATH OF WITNESS 

Do you solemnly swear (or affirm) that the evidence you are about to give relating to the matter now in issue shall be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help you God?

Sec. 128. Trials, When Held. 

Every suit shall be tried on the day named in the process, when the same has been duly served, or on the day to which it shall have been adjourned, unless it be continued or otherwise disposed of by the justice (Sec. 2274).

Sec. 129. Trials Before Justice. 

In all cases where the parties appear in person or by agent or attorney and in which the parties to the cause, or one of them, do not demand a jury before the trial begins, the trial proceeds before the justice (Secs. 2275, 2276). The proceedings upon the trial with respect to the examination of witnesses, the submission of evidence and argument, and the order and conduct of the trial, shall, when no other provision is made by law, be governed by the usage and practice in the circuit court, so far as the same may be applicable (Sec. 2286).

Sec. 130. Special Provisions of Law Governing Trials in Justice 

Courts. a. Consideration of bond or note may be impeached.

In any action pending in a justice's court, or in any court on an appeal therefrom, the foundation of which is a bond or note, the 182

obligor or maker of such bond or note may impeach its consideration and show a partial or total failure thereof and reduce or prevent the plaintiff's recovery accordingly; nor shall such defense be precluded by reason of the existence of any contract, verbal or otherwise, made with the obligee or payee, which would give a right of action in the obligor or maker, in the event of a partial or total failure of the consideration of the bond or note (Sec. 2229). Even though the execution of a note sued on before a justice was not procured by fraud, a defendant has the right to impeach its consideration by showing only a partial or total failure thereof. Want of consideration may be established by proof of false representation made to defendant on which he relied, to his damage." And if a complete failure of consideration is shown, the original payee in the note cannot recover." The rule extends to and applies against assignees (Sec. 2230). b. But not in hands of innocent holder. 69 This special statutory provision authorizing the impeachment of the consideration of bonds or notes in suits in justice courts does not apply to innocent holders of bills of exchange or negotiable promissory notes (Sec. 2230). c. Execution of instrument sued on need not be proved unless denied under oath.

If any suit, set-off or counterclaim be founded upon any instrument of writing purporting to have been executed by the opposite party, and the same shall have been filed with the justice, such instrument shall be received in evidence on the trial, unless the party charged to have executed the same, before the jury is sworn or the trial submitted to the justice, shall deny the execution thereof, on oath, taken before some justice, or by an affidavit filed with the justice and taken before any court or officer authorized to administer oaths (Sec. 2231). This special statutory provision relating to trials in justice courts follows the rule relating to the same subject in effect in superior courts, and in fact the rule was enforced in justice courts

Sec. 131. The Right to Trial by Jury. 

Either party to a cause may demand that the case be tried before a jury, provided that the demand for a jury trial is made before the trial begins (Sec. 2276). The right to trial by jury is an ancient common law right solemnly recognized by the Seventh Amendment to the Constitution of the United States as one that should be preserved.75 Although this provision of the Federal Constitution is not applicable to actions in State courts,76 and under more recent decisions is not held of such vital consequence in the Federal Judiciary," the right, even in modern practice, is preserved exactly as

A jury in a justice court is made up of six men, unless by agreement of the parties a smaller number may be used (Sec. 2276). The

Jurors are obtained for service in justice courts upon summons issued by the justice and directed to the constable of the township wherein the cause is to be tried. Twelve men are summoned unless the parties agree upon a jury of less than six, in which case six more than the parties have agreed upon are summoned. (Sec. 2277.)

If it shall appear to the justice that a jury, from any cause, cannot be had in his township to try the case, he shall order the constable to summon a jury from the body of the county (Sec. 2278).
