122. FORM OF OATH TO JURY TO TRY CAUSE 

You, and each of you, do solemnly swear that you will well and truly try the matter in difference between James Smith, plaintiff, and Ed Jones, defendant, and a true verdict give according to the law and evidence, so help you God? (Sec. 2281.) b. Submission of evidence.

All proceedings after the jury is sworn to try the case with respect to the examination of witnesses, the submission of evidence and argument, and the order and conduct of the trial, are governed by the usage and practice in the circuit court, so far as same are applicable and when no other provisions are made by law (Sec. 2286). c. Justice cannot take case from jury.

The members of a jury in a justice court are the sole judges of the law and the facts, and a justice has no right to instruct the jury to find a verdict for one of the parties.85 d. Instructions and argument of counsel.

Instructions are not ordinarily given in justice courts, for the obvious reason that they are not as effective as another weapon used by counsel in their argument to juries. The argument of counsel proceeds in justice courts in the same manner, perhaps with less formality, particularly as to points of law, as in circuit court. In fact, the arguments before a justice may cover a much wider range than arguments in circuit courts. The statutes may be read to show the jury what the Legislature has enacted as the law, and decisions may be read to show the jury how courts have construed the law. 

Books on any subject may be read in the argument to juries. e. Juries kept together.

After a jury is sworn, the members of it shall sit together and hear the evidence, which must be delivered publicly in their presence, 85 State ex rel. Schonhorst vs. Cline, 85 Mo. A. 628. 188

and argument, and after the case is submitted the jury shall be kept together in some convenient place or room in charge of the constable, until the members have agreed upon a verdict or have been discharged by the justice (Sec. 2282). 

f. Verdicts. 

Two-thirds or more of the jurors concurring may return a verdict (Sec. 2276). The verdict must be in writing, and if concurred in by all of the members of the jury it may be signed by the foreman. If rendered by less than the entire number, it shall be signed by all who agree with it. (Sec. 2276.) When the jury has reached a verdict, it is delivered publicly to the justice, who is required to enter it upon his docket (Sec. 2283), where it has the effect of a formal judgment immediately, even though no other judgment is entered on the docket.86 A justice has no power to set aside a verdict.s 87 A verdict has the force of a formal judgment when it is entered on the docket.88

We, the jury, find for the defendant in the sum of ....... dollars.

Whenever the justice shall be satisfied that the jury cannot agree upon a verdict, after having consulted upon it a reasonable time, he may discharge them and continue the case to another day, to be tried before another jury, to be summoned and impaneled in the same manner, unless the parties agree that the justice may decide the case upon the evidence already before him, or upon a new hearing of the same (Sec. 2284).

7. Judgments.

Sec. 134. Judgments Generally. 

The statute (Sec. 1070) defines a judgment as the final determination of the right of the parties in the action. It is the last word in a judicial controversy.89 Judgments regularly entered by a justice of the peace in cases in which the justice has jurisdiction and in which he is authorized to enter final judgments, and from which no appeal is taken, are as binding and effective as judgments of any other courts. The statute authorizes justices of the peace to enter judgments of the following kinds: (1) Judgments by confession (Sec. 2287); (2) nonsuit (Secs. 2249, 2250, 2289); (3) consent or offer (Sec. 2227); (4) default (Sec. 2249); (5) judgments upon his own findings (Secs. 2275, 2290-2294); (6) or according to the verdict of a jury (Secs. 2275, 2290-2294), after trial and submission of the cause.

Sec. 135. Judgments by Confession.⁰⁰ 

The statute authorizes a justice of the peace to enter a judgment by confession of the defendant in any case where the amount confessed does not exceed the amount for which a justice is authorized to render judgment (Sec. 2288). But the statute does not authorize a justice to render a judgment of confession unless the following requisites are complied with: First, the defendant must personally appear before the justice in open court; second, the confession must be in writing, signed by the defendant, or by some person by him thereto lawfully authorized, and filed with the justice (Sec. 2288).

In all those cases where process has been regularly issued and served, and the defendant appears, the requirement of the statute that judgment by confession must be in writing, does not apply.⁹1 

In such cases, if the defendant orally confesses that he has no de-

Sec. 140. Judgments for Infant Plaintiffs. 

In cases instituted by an infant plaintiff, or through his next friend, judgments may be entered that are as binding as in other cases, but such judgments cannot be based merely on the consent of the minor, for he is without discretion, nor on the consent of the next friend, because he is not vested with either the power or the duty to consent to such judgment.16 In all such cases, the court is charged with the duty of protecting the minor's interest, and it is only when the judgment of the court is based upon facts judicially ascertained upon a real, and not a perfunctory, hearing that its judgment is binding upon him.17 Thus, where a defendant consented to a judgment against him in favor of a minor plaintiff and caused all papers to be prepared for the appointment of a next friend and for the entry of the judgment, and all parties appeared before the justice, who entered a judgment without hearing any "McCormick Harvesting Machine Co. vs. Hill, 104 Mo. Robison vs. Floesch Const. Co., 291 Mo. 34, 236 S. W. 332. "Gilliland vs. Bondurant (Sup.), 59 S. W. (2d) 679; Robison vs. Floesch 

Const. Co., 291 Mo. 34, 236 S. W. 332. 197

Sec. 141. Judgment According to Verdict of Jury. 

If the cause is tried by jury, the justice is required to enter judgment according to the verdict of the jury (Sec. 2275). The duty to enter judgment on a verdict has been held to be purely ministerial, so that failure to enter the right judgment does not deprive the verdict of its force.20 If, according to the verdict of the jury, no sum is found in favor of the plaintiff, the justice shall enter judgment for the defendant (Sec. 2290). But if any sum shall be found by the verdict of the jury in favor of the plaintiff, the justice is required to enter a judgment in favor of the plaintiff for that sum (Sec. 2292). If a verdict is for the plaintiff without specifying any amount, judgment should be entered for the defendant, as such verdict is equivalent to judgment for the defendant,21 and man-

Sec. 142. When Judgment Should Be Entered. 

In cases where a plaintiff shall be nonsuited, or withdraw his action, and where judgment shall be confessed or where a verdict shall be rendered, the justice shall forthwith render a judgment and enter the same in his docket; in all other cases, he shall render judgment and enter the same in his docket within three days after the cause shall have been submitted to him for his final decision (Sec. 2293). But it has been held that a failure to enter judgment within three days after the submission does not invalidate the judgment,25 and the entry of a judgment in the docket of the justice more than three days after the date of rendition has been held sufficient, regardless of the statutory provision.26 In fact, a judgment has been upheld when entered any time during the incumbency of the justice who rendered the judgment, even where the judg- "State ex rel. Sec. 144. Nature and Effect of Judgments. 

The general rule that justice courts are inferior tribunals with limited statutory jurisdiction only, do not proceed according to the course of the common law,³¹ and no intendments can be allowed in their favor,32 applies to judgments of justices of the peace.s " Drake vs. Bagley, 69 Mo. A. 39.

30 Leith vs. Shingleton, 42 Mo. A. 449. "Ballentine, p. 1024, makes the following interesting observation about this phrase so frequently repeated in decisions concerning the nature of the procedure of justice courts: "The expression (proceeding according to the course of the common law) has a certain rotundity of sound which is quite pleasing to the ear but leaves no definite impression upon the understanding. It is simply equivalent to a knowing look or a solemn shake of the head, and doubtless it was first used in that sense. When first employed its use was harmless, for there was then no mode of procedure except such as the common law prescribed; but its continued use where the modes of the common law have been superseded is mischievous. The most accurate writers do not use the expression when speaking of the present or cognate rules. The only distinction which they make is represented by the words 'superior' and 'inferior,' 'limited' and 'general,' and such, in our judgment, is the only distinction which exists.'

And this rule is applicable to judgments of justices of the peace because the statute (Sec. 2177) requires the justice to enter judgments on his docket, and as to any proceedings the law requires the justice to make a record of in his docket, the record, when regular on its face, imports verity. And in all cases where the court has had competent jurisdiction of the parties and subject matter, the judgments of justice courts are as conclusive as judgments of courts of record, both as a merger or bar and as an estoppel as to any particular matter of fact adjudicated.35

Sec. 146. Direct Attack on Judgments. 

A judgment of a justice of the peace may be corrected by a direct proceeding in equity where it appears that same was entered as a result of fraud, accident or mistake.42 But a circuit court cannot, on a motion, correct a judgment of a justice, the transcript of which has been filed in circuit court, when the justice records are in the hands of another who has succeeded him, and if it attempts to do so it will be stopped by prohibition.43 A judgment of a justice cannot be contradicted nor changed by parol evidence," and this for the reason that a judgment regularly entered imports verity, and where such judgment is clear, unambiguous, and was entered without fraud, accident or mistake, it is the best and only competent evidence as to what judgment the justice in fact rendered, so that such judgment cannot be contradicted by parol, even though parol evidence indicates that the justice announced at the conclusion of the trial he would enter judgment for one party but judgment was actually entered for the other party.45 But if a judgment of a justice is regularly entered and it appears on the face of the proceedings that the justice had jurisdiction, the judgment is final and binding, even though it was entered as a result of fraud, accident or mistake, and the proper way to attack such judgment is by a direct proceeding in equity to have same set aside.46 40 * 1 Freeman, Judgments (5th ed.), p. 735, Sec. 354. Sec. 147. Execution on Judgment, How Stayed. 

The execution upon a judgment rendered by a justice of the peace may be stayed for any length of time agreed upon by the parties to the judgment, and for the purpose of protecting plaintiff in agreeing to such stay of judgment he may require that some responsible person, to be approved by him enter into a recognizance in a sum sufficient to secure the judgment and costs (Secs. 2295-2296).

Sec. 148. Judgments May Be Set Off, How. 

The statute provides that if there be mutual justices' judgments between the same parties, upon which the time for appealing has elapsed, one justice, on the application of either party and reasonable notice thereof to the other, may be set off by the justice before whom the judgment against which the set-off is proposed may be (Sec. 2297). But a debt exempt from attachment and execution is not subject to set-off. If the judgment proposed as a set-off was rendered before another justice, the party proposing such set-off must produce before the justice a transcript of such judgment, upon which there shall be a certificate of the justice rendering the judgment that there was no appeal or existing execution thereon, and that such transcript was obtained for the purpose of being set off against the judgment to which it is offered as a set-off. The justice granting such transcript shall make an entry thereof in his docket, and all further proceedings on such judgment shall be stayed unless such transcript be rendered without the proper justice's certificate thereon that it has not been allowed in set-off (Sec. 2298). 

47 Wagner vs. J. H. North Furn. & Carpet Co., 63 Mo. A. 206. 203

JUSTICE COURTS 

If any justice shall set off one judgment against another, he shall make an entry thereof in his docket, and execution shall issue only for the balance which may be due after such set-off. If a justice shall allow a transcript of judgment rendered by another justice to be set off, he shall file such transcript among the papers relating to the judgment in which it is allowed in set-off. If he shall refuse such set-off, he shall so certify on the transcript and return same to the party who offered it (Sec. 2299).

Sec. 149. Transcripts of Judgments. 

Jonathan Cromwell, 

Every justice before whom any judgment shall be recovered, or his successor in office, or the officer who shall be in possession of the 204

docket containing the same, shall, on demand of any person in whose favor the same shall have been rendered, or of any person interested therein, whether by assignment or otherwise, give to such person a certified transcript of such judgment; and the clerk of the circuit court of the county in which the judgment was rendered shall, upon the production of any such transcript, file the same in his office and record the same in a book to be kept for that purpose, and forthwith enter the same in his docket of circuit court judgments and note therein the date and hour of its filing (Sec. 2300). Such a transcript may be filed before an execution is issued by the justice,48 but if an appeal is taken from such judgment a transcript cannot be filed, or, if filed, is ineffective.49 A transcript cannot be filed of a judgment more than three years old, unless such judgment has been revived.50 Several judgments may be included in one transcript.51 but a judgment of a justice of the peace does not prove itself, even though properly and duly authenticated.52 The provision of the statutes relating to the filing of transcripts of judgments must be substantially complied with in order to give judgments force and effect, so that if the transcript is not certified as a correct transcript of the judgment by the justice or officer regularly in charge of the docket of the justice who renders the judgment, there is no authority for such transcript to be filed, and, if filed, it creates no lien and is of no effect whatever.58

Sec. 150. Lien of Judgments. 

Every such judgment, from the time of filing the transcript, shall have the same lien on the real estate of the defendant in the county as is given to judgments of circuit courts, and shall be under the control of the court where the transcript is filed; may be revived and carried into effect in the same manner and with like effect as judgments of circuit courts, and executions issued thereon may be directed to and executed in any county in this State; and the party obtaining said judgments, or his attorney, shall have the option of suing out an execution out of the court where the transcript is filed, without being first required to sue out an execution from the justice court where said judgment was obtained, and without being required to file a supplemental transcript or certificate of the justice showing the suing out and the return of an execution from the justice court (Sec. 2301). After a transcript of such judgment is filed in the office of the circuit clerk of the county where such judgment was rendered, a transcript of the record thereof, certified by the clerk and showing the time of filing, and attested by his seal, may be filed, docketed and recorded in the office of the clerk of the circuit court of any other county in the same manner as judgments of courts of record, and when so filed in such other county such judgment shall be a lien upon the real estate of the person against whom the judgment was rendered, and situate in the county where such certified transcript is filed (Sec. 1144).54 Such lien exists for the same time and to the same extent as the lien of the judgment or decree in the county where the same was rendered, and a transcript of a judgment or decree reviving a judgment or decree or the lien thereof may be filed, docketed and recorded in the same manner and with like effect as an original judgment or decree (Sec. 1145).55

The lien of such judgment attaches at the time it is filed in the office of the circuit clerk, and from that time such lien has the same force and effect as that of a judgment of a circuit court.56 From the time such judgment transcript is filed in the office of the clerk of the circuit court, such judgment is under the control of the judge of the "Mahen vs. Tavern Rock, Inc., 37 S. Sec. 151. Expiration of Unrevived Judgment. 

The statute forbids the suing out of an execution on a judgment of a justice at any time after the expiration of three years from the date of the judgment, unless such judgment be revived (Sec. 2304). 

This statutory provision has been strictly construed. After a lapse of three years from the rendition of a judgment of a justice, no execution can be issued upon such judgment nor a transcript of it filed in the office of the circuit clerk.62 And if a transcript of such unrevived judgment is filed after the lapse of three years, it does not have the effect of creating a lien upon the real estate of the defendant.88 But it has been held that if a transcript of a judgment of a justice is filed in the office of the circuit clerk within three years after the rendition of the judgment, execution on such transcript judgment may be issued out of the office of the circuit clerk after the lapse of three years, even though the judgment has not been revived. However, if no transcript is filed in the office of the circuit clerk and the judgment is not revived and three years elapse, a proceeding to revive the judgment in circuit court after three years cannot be maintained. Nor does the fact that an appeal from the judgment is pending have the effect of extending the statutory period of limitation.66 65

Sec. 152. Judgment May Be Revived. 

a. By scire facias proceeding in circuit court. 

When a transcript of a judgment rendered by a justice of the peace is filed in the office of the circuit clerk, it becomes, for the purposes of execution and revival, a judgment of the circuit court,87 and, thereafter, scire facias proceedings for the revival of such judgment may be had in the same manner and under the same statutory provisions as judgments of circuit courts (Secs. 11061112). In such a proceeding an application for a writ of scire facias is usually filed, and upon that application a writ is issued, which writ, and not an ordinary summons, is served on the defendant. The writ should state sufficient facts to authorize the court to enter a judgment of revival, if the facts are found to be true, and this writ, and not the petition or application for it, is the foundation of the proceeding, so that unless such writ is issued and served, instead of an ordinary summons, the proceeding will fail.68 

b. By citation from justice. 

The fact that a transcript of a judgment of a justice has been filed in circuit court does not preclude the revival of such judgment in justice court, nor the issuance of an execution thereon, but such judgment may be revived and execution issued thereon by the justice who rendered the same, or has the control thereof, notwithstanding the filing of the transcript in the circuit court (Sec. 2302). 

After a revival before a justice of a judgment, the transcript of which has been filed in the circuit court, the filing of a new transcript of the judgment is not necessary, but the judgment is effective as a lien if a certificate by the justice, showing the date of the revival and that the judgment has been revived, is filed with the clerk of the circuit court (Sec. 2302).

one.71 Originally a proceeding to revive a judgment could not be prosecuted in the name of the assignee thereof," for the reason that the statutes did not authorize such proceeding in the name of an assignee," but the statute (Sec. 1139) was amended so as to permit an assignee to revive a judgment in his own name.74 Since a revival proceeding is a continuation of the original suit, and since a transcript of a judgment of a justice becomes in effect a judgment of the circuit court, a scire facias proceeding to revive such judgment in the circuit court must be controlled by the statute applicable to such cases "The decision of Milsap vs. Wildman, 5 Mo. 425, announcing a contrary doctrine, was expressly overruled and all the subsequent cases which had followed that case declared expressive of an erroneous rule in the case of Sutton vs. Cole, 155 Mo. 206, 55 S. W. 1052, which latter case was certified to the Supreme Court by one of the courts of appeals because of the conflict in authority referred to. 

In Sutton vs. Cole, the Supreme Court said: "In Kratz vs. Preston, 52 Mo. A. 

256, Ellison, J., said: 'When the object is to revive a judgment, it cannot be said to be a new suit. It is a continuance of the old action, and merely ancillary thereto, notwithstanding it partakes of the nature of a new action, as before stated, in that it may be pleaded to. I think it apparent that when the writ is used to revive a judgment it is merely a further proceeding in the same action, and is based on the original judgment, which in this case, we have seen, was rendered on defendant's personal appearance. Such a writ is sometimes called a writ of execution 

The result is that Milsap vs. Wildman, 5 Mo. 425, has never been followed by this court, but the contrary doctrine often declared, and that case, in effect, overruled. So, to end all doubt and confusion, Milsap vs. 

Wildman, 5 Mo. 425, is hereby expressly overruled. As Wolff vs. Schaeffer, 4 

Mo. A. 367, Simpson vs. Watson, 15 Mo. A. 430, and Walsh vs. Bosse, 16 Mo. A. 

233, were predicated upon Milsap vs. Wildman, supra, it follows that they can no longer be regarded as stating the law in this state. Being only a continuation of the original action, and simply ancillary thereto, it follows that there can be no change of venue allowed in a scire facias to revive a judgment, because there is no statute specially authorizing it, and the general statute in reference to change of venue has no application.'' 

The rule thus announced in Sutton vs. Cole has been followed in Lawrence

Citations issued to revive judgments shall be directed to the party to be served and placed in the hands of the constable of the township in which the suit is pending, and shall be executed by him in any part of his county. The time and manner of service of such citations, and the fees he shall receive, shall be the same as in the case of service of summons. (Sec. 2311.) Sec. 154. Judgments in Revival Proceedings. 

If the defendant fail to appear after service of the writ of the citation, or, appearing, shall fail to show sufficient cause to the justice why the judgment shall not be revived, the justice shall make an entry on his docket reviving the same from the date of such entry and issue execution, unless otherwise directed, for the amount of what may appear to be due on such judgment, with interest thereon and all costs. But if the defendant shall, on appearing, show and establish that the judgment has been paid or satisfied, and that execution ought not be issued on the judgment of the justice, judgment 214

shall be given against the person filing the affidavit in favor of the defendant for all costs; and such judgment shall forever be a bar against the former judgment (Sec. 2308). A revived judgment shall, upon the entry of the revival, have the same force and effect in all respects as the original judgment (Sec. 2309). And a judgment once revived may be again revived in the same manner and with like effect as the first revival, except that no judgment shall be revived after ten years after the rendition thereof, or from the date such judgment may have been revived (Sec. 2310). The filing of a transcript of an original judgment after a revival thereof is not necessary.78 When a judgment is revived, execution may be based on the old judgment." The judgment entry should declare the original judgment still in force for whatever remains unpaid.80 And if the order of revival contains recital of conditions indicating that a new judgment is entered, such recitals may be regarded as surplusage.81 The statute of limitations as to the revival of a judgment (Sec. 2310) has been construed strictly to mean that limitation shall run from the date of the judgment, or, if the judgment has been revived, from the date of the revival.82

Sec. 157. Form, to Whom Directed and When Returnable. 

The statute prescribes the form for an execution issued by a justice of the peace (Sec. 2317). Except where it is otherwise specially provided, such execution is directed to the constable of the township where the justice resides, and is against the goods and chattels of the person against whom it is issued. The execution must be dated on the day it is issued and be returnable in thirty days from its date, but if the constable collects the amount of the judgment or any part thereof before the return day of the execution he must pay the same to the party entitled thereto. (Sec. 2316.) In those cases where the defendant resides out of the township where the judgment was rendered or where he has goods and chattels out of the same, but in another township in the same county, or where there are several defendants residing in different townships in the same county, the justice shall, at the option of the plaintiff, direct the execution to the constable of the township in which the judgment was rendered, who shall execute the same in any part of his county, or he may direct it to the constable of the township in which the defendants, or any of them, reside, or in which their goods and chattels may be found; or, where judgment is rendered by a justice against the constable of his township, the justice shall direct the execution to the constable of any adjoining township in his county (Sec. 2318). But such execution cannot be directed to or served by a private person.8 "Smith vs. Rogers, 191 Mo. 334, 90 S. W. 1150.

Sec. 158. How Endorsed and When a Lien.

Before delivering an execution, the justice is required by statute to state in his docket and also on the back of the execution an account of the debt, damages and costs and fees due each person, and the rate of interest on the judgment separately (Sec. 2319). The officer receiving the execution is required by statute to endorse on it the time he received same. From the time of the delivery of the execution to the constable, the execution is a lien on the goods, chattels and shares of stocks of the defendant found within the limits within which the constable or other officer can execute the process, but not upon any property exempt by law from execution sale, or which was sold or pledged to an innocent purchaser before the levy of the writ (Sec. 

2319). The statute directs that every fee bill and writ of fieri facias issued by a justice shall have written or printed thereon a true statement of each and every item of all the taxable costs in the case and over against each item so stated there shall be set the amount of money taxed thereunder, and when the same is delivered to the officer authorized to enforce the collection thereof, such officer is required to itemize all the costs to be added thereto by him for his own services. 

The justice issuing the execution, or officer to whom it is delivered, who fails to follow the provisions of the statute governing same shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor and, upon conviction, forfeit his office. (Sec. 2319.) The statute pertaining to executions must be strictly complied with, and if a justice issues an execution without entering in his docket the various items required by statute, the exe- 217

Sec. 159. When a Lien. 

Constable.

From the time of the delivery of the execution to the constable, the execution is a lien on the goods, chattels and shares of stocks of the defendant found within the limits within which the constable or other officer can execute the process, but not upon any property exempt by law from execution sale, or which was sold or pledged to an innocent purchaser before the levy of the writ (Sec. 2319). The lien attaches to all the personal property of the defendant at the time of the delivery of the execution to the officer and to all property that the defendant thereafter acquires.91 But such lien may be displaced by and made subordinate to the lien of another execution which had been previously levied. The lien of an execution is inferior and subordinate to that of a chattel mortgage filed for record prior to the date of the judgment on which the execution was issued, but it is not subordinate to that of a chattel mortgage executed after the delivery of the execution to the officer.94 93

Sec. 160. 

Control of Execution. 

After a justice issues an execution, he has no power to quash it.95 

A court of equity does not have the power to enjoin the levy of an execution that has been issued on a void judgment of a justice of the peace.96 Nor will injunction lie in the circuit court to restrain a justice from issuing an execution.97 Neither can a circuit court compel a justice to change a judgment shown on his docket, nor prevent its enforcement by execution, in the absence of fraud, accident or mistake.98 But if a judgment is void on its face, a motion to quash the execution issued thereon is a proper remedy.99 In a motion to quash, the sufficiency of the petition on which the judgment is based may be inquired into.100

Sec. 161. Renewal of Execution. 

If an execution is not satisfied, it may at the request of the plaintiff be renewed from time to time either by the justice issuing the same or the justice to whom his docket is transferred, by an endorsement on the docket to that effect filed by the justice and dated when made. If any part of the execution has been satisfied, the endorsement of the renewal shall express the sum due on the execution. 

Every such endorsement shall renew the execution for ninety days from the date of the renewal, and no longer; and an entry of such renewal shall be made in the docket of the justice (Sec. 2320). Entry of the date of renewal must be made on the execution to make it valid. But if the endorsement of the date on the renewal and in the docket differ, evidence may be introduced to show the correct date.² 

A justice cannot revive an execution after it is once dead, but he may issue a new execution both before and after the expiration of the old execution.³

Sec. 162. Sale of Property Under Execution. 

The statute directs that the constable, after taking goods and chattels into his custody by virtue of an execution, shall, without delay, give public notice of the time and place when and where they will be exposed to sale, by setting up three advertisements, one in the office of the justice issuing the execution, and one at each of two other of the most public places in the township; but in case the execution issued from another township, then the advertisements shall be set up one at each of the three most public places in the township where the property is found. Such notice shall describe the goods and chattels taken and must be put up at least ten days before the day of sale. (Sec. 2321.) It has been held that the requirement as to notice is directory only. But if a constable's sale is not conducted according to law, it is considered a conversion." Sec. 163. Regulations for Execution Sales. 

Sales under execution by a constable shall be conducted at the time and place as advertised in the notice thereof, and if the goods and chattels be present for inspection of bidders the officer shall expose them to sale at public vendue to the highest bidder, if there be more than two persons present competent to bid (Sec. 2322). No constable or other officer shall, directly or indirectly, purchase any goods or chattels at any sale made by him upon execution (Sec. 

2323). Should such an officer attempt to purchase at his own execution sale, the purchase is absolutely void (Sec. 2323). After the sale, the constable shall, after deducting costs, pay the money over to the party entitled thereto and make return of the execution (Sec. 

2322). It has been held that if an execution is returned unexecuted before the time fixed by law, it is void. A return on an execution reciting that the writ was executed on a certain day named in the return and further stating that no property was found on which to levy the execution, has been held to constitute a sufficient return of nulla bona.8

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 164. Levy on Property of Third Person. 

The statute provides that if a constable levy an execution on any goods or chattels, and any person other than the defendant in the execution claim such property and deliver to the constable a written notice of such claim, verified by the affidavit of the claimant or his agent, describing the property claimed and stating his interest therein, whether it be in whole or in part thereof, and that he is, in good faith, the lawful owner of the interest claimed by him in said property, that the defendant in said execution has no right or title whatever in the interest claimed, and that said claim is not made in collusion with the defendant, for the purpose of vexing, hindering or delaying the plaintiff in obtaining his just rights, the constable, before proceeding to sell such property, shall take of the plaintiff a bond, payable to himself, with good security, and conditioned to indemnify him against all damages and costs which he may sustain in consequence of the seizure and sale of the property on which the execution shall have been levied; and, moreover, to pay and satisfy any person or persons claiming title to such property all damages which such person or persons may sustain in consequence of such seizure and sale (Sec. 2324). This statutory provision is never applicable in favor of a defendant, but it applies only when a claim to the property on which the constable has levied is made by a third party. The claim may be made although claimant has only an interest in the property levied on, and if a claimant gives notice that he is owner of the entire interest in the property and it is later sold, he may recover such interest as he had in the property at the time of the sale.10 For the notice to be effective and binding, it must be sworn to and must contain all the averments required by the statute.11 The remedy applies to both general and special executions. 12 Where a claimant elects to give notice to the constable and the constable gives bond in accordance with the statute, claimant must pursue his remedy on the bond and cannot sue the constable for the property.18 If bond is 'Pierce vs. Kingsbury, 63 Mo. 259; Guinta vs. Jack Daniels Distilling Co., 211

Where a third person claims the property seized by the constable and a bond is given, such bond must be returned to the justice, with the execution, and the claimant may, in the name of the officer to whom the bond is payable, prosecute his or her action on the bond and recover such damages as the jury may assess (Sec. 2325). Claimant is entitled to a copy of the bond, and, when necessary, he may require the justice to produce the original in any court of record (Sec. 2326). If the plaintiff decline or fail to give bond within forty-eight hours after having been notified of a claim to the property by a third person and after the constable has requested the bond, it is the duty of the constable to release the property to the plaintiff, and if he does so plaintiff is barred of any right of action against the constable on that account (Sec. 2326).

Sec. 166. Remedy of Purchaser of Property Belonging to Third Person. 

Any purchaser of property regularly sold by a constable under execution, when such property belongs to some person other than the defendant, whereby the purchaser loses the property or is compelled to pay damages as a result thereof to the real owner, may sue the person against whom the execution or order of sale may have been issued, or the person legally representing him, in any court having jurisdiction, and recover what he paid for such property, with interest thereon from the time of payment (Sec. 2327).

Sec. 167. Payments on Judgment Should Be Made to Constable. 

Any person owing a judgment and desiring to pay same should make his payments thereon to the constable of the township where the judgment was obtained, and take a receipt therefor. A person making such payment is protected even though the constable gives no receipt.22 And the person entitled to the money has his remedy against the constable and his sureties in the same way as if such money had been collected by the constable on execution (Sec. 2328).

But payment of money upon a judgment to the justice, either before or after the execution, shall not be valid against such judgment nor credited thereto, unless paid with the consent of the person to whom the same is due (Sec. 2329). And such payment does not bar an appeal from an insufficient judgment.²

Sec. 169. A Statutory Privilege. 

Constable, Signal Township.

The right to appeal does not inhere in a cause of action, but it is and always has been statutory.25 An appeal is not a matter of right, but is a privilege conferred by statute and can be exercised only in conformity with the statute.26

Sec. 170. Persons Authorized to Appeal. 

From the beginning, the statutes have authorized appeals from judgments of justice courts by any person aggrieved thereby.27 The 544.

It is a remedy which the legislature may in its discretion grant or take away, and it may prescribe in what cases, and under what circumstances, and from what courts appeals may be taken; and, unless the statute expressly or by plain implication provides for an appeal from a judgment of a court of inferior jurisdiction, none can be taken."'

Sec. 171. When Appeal Lies. 

Generally when a party feels aggrieved by a judgment, he may appeal from such judgment,28 though such party is not the only party plaintiff or defendant in the case.29 Such appeal may be taken though no formal judgment is entered on the record.30 An appeal will not lie from an interlocutory order made by a justice, but only from a final judgment on the merits of the case.³¹ It has been held that an appeal will lie from a judgment of revival,32 from a judgment enforcing an agister's lien,33 from a judgment on a plea in abatement after judgment on the merits only, and from a judgment on an interpleader in an attachment suit.55 But a confession of judgment defeats the right of appeal for the purpose of having a plea in abatement reviewed, from a judgment erroneously taxing costs where it does not appear that the defendant moved for a retaxing of the costs,37 and from a judgment which is neither for the plaintiff nor against the defendant except for costs.38

Sec. 172. Statutory Requisites for Appeal. 

No appeal is allowed unless the following statutory requisites are complied with: a. Must be made within time prescribed.

First, the appeal must be made within ten days after the judgment was rendered, except where appellant is a nonresident of the county where the suit was instituted, in which case the appeal must be made within twenty days. b. Appellant must file bond.

Second, the applicant, or some person for him, together with one or more solvent sureties, to be approved by the justice, must, within the time prescribed for appeal, enter into a recognizance before the justice to the adverse party in a sum sufficient to secure the payment of such judgment and the costs of appeal, conditioned that the applicant will prosecute his appeal with due diligence to a decision, and that if, on such appeal, the judgment of the justice be affirmed, or upon a trial anew in the appellate court judgment be given against him, he will pay such judgment, and that if his appeal is dismissed he will pay the judgment of the justice, together with the costs of appeal. The affidavit and bond for appeal filed shall be taken and considered by the appellate court as an entrance of appearance (Sec. 

2341). The statute prescribes the form for the recognizance and requires that it be filed by the parties entering into same, and approved by the justice (Sec. 2342). c. Affidavit for appeal must be filed.

The party applying for appeal, or some person for him, must make an affidavit stating that the application for an appeal is not made for vexation or delay but because he believes the appellant is injured by the judgment of the justice, and stating whether such appeal is from the merits or from an order or judgment taxing costs (Sec. 2343). 

The affidavit may be taken by any officer qualified to administer oaths and must be filed with the justice when the application for appeal is made. Upon request, it shall be the duty of the justice to prepare both the affidavit and the bond. (Sec. 2344.) 229

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 173. Time for Appeal. 

a. Generally.

An appeal can be taken only from a final judgment, and an attempt to appeal before a final judgment is entered is fruitless.89 A failure to appeal and make an affidavit and file a bond within the time prescribed by statute results in a denial of the right to appeal, so that if an appeal is taken after the time expires the circuit court acquires no jurisdiction of the cause.40 And when the circuit court acquires no jurisdiction of the cause by failure of the appellant to take his appeal in time, the parties cannot confer jurisdiction by voluntarily appearing and consenting that the appeal be heard." The statute which authorizes appeals when properly taken, even though the justice does not show the allowance of the appeal in his docket (Sec. 2347), does not save an appellant from the loss of jurisdiction of his cause where the affidavit and bond were not filed in time, although the justice later amended his docket so as to show that the appeal was taken in time. But if the proper steps for appeal have been taken within due time but the allowance of the appeal has not been entered because of the absence of the justice, the right of appeal is not defeated. Where the last day for appeal falls on Sunday, an appeal taken on the following Monday is timely, and for the purpose of determining whether an appeal was taken in time the court will take judicial knowledge of the days of the week." b. By resident appellants.

All resident appellants must appeal within ten days after the judgment was rendered (Sec. 2341). For the purpose of determining the time when an appeal must be taken, the date of the verdict is considered the date of the judgment." And it has been held that an appeal taken within ten days after the justice gave judgment will not be good unless also taken within ten days after the return of the * State ex rel. As against an attack for failure to appeal in time, it is sufficient if the record shows that all the papers were lodged by the justice in the circuit clerk's office less than ten days after the case was tried. An appeal from a default judgment taken within ten days after a motion to set aside the default is overruled, but more than thirty days after the rendition of the judgment, is not taken within the time prescribed by the statute. Where a judgment of nonsuit is set aside and a new trial granted, an appeal may be taken within ten days after the granting of the new trial.¹9 c. By nonresident appellants. 

All appellants not residents of the county where the suit was instituted are allowed twenty days within which to take an appeal (Sec. 2341). The test of whether a foreign corporation doing business in Missouri is entitled to the benefit of the twenty-day limit within which to appeal is whether such corporation has an office or place of business, or an agent transacting business for the company, in the county where the suit was instituted. 50 Thus, where a corporation organized under the laws of Delaware was licensed to do business in Missouri and had an agent in the county of Missouri where the case was instituted, such foreign corporation was held to be a resident of such county and was required to appeal from a judgment against it within ten days.51 Likewise, a foreign insurance company authorized to do business in Missouri and maintaining an office in the City of St. Louis, where a suit against it was tried, was held a resident and required to appeal from a judgment against it within ten days after the judgment was rendered. 52 But if such foreign insurance company does not have an office or agent transacting business for it in the county where the suit was instituted, and service was had on same through the Superintendent of Insurance, it was considered a nonresident of the county and entitled to twenty days "Rutherford vs. Wim, 3 Mo. 15. Sec. 174. Necessity for and Sufficiency of the Affidavit.

The statute prescribes what the affidavit shall contain and directs that an appeal shall not be allowed unless the affidavit containing such provisions is made (Sec. 2343). The affidavit may be made before any officer authorized to take an oath and may be made before a notary public in another state.57 A written statement not in the form of an affidavit and not sworn to is an insufficient compliance with the statute,58 as an affidavit, and not a mere statement in writing, is indispensable to the order granting an appeal.59 The affidavit and recognizance do not constitute notice of appeal. Sec. 175. Essentials and Functions of a Recognizance. 

The recognizance must be signed by the parties entering into the same and must be approved by the justice (Sec. 2342). It must be signed, not only by the appellant but also by one or more solvent sureties to be approved by the justice, and it must be filed within the time prescribed by the statute (Sec. 2341). Compliance with these statutory requirements is a prerequisite to the allowance of an appeal.75 If an appeal is allowed by a justice when the required affidavit and bond have not been filed, the circuit court does not acquire jurisdiction of the case on appeal.76 And a compliance with the prerequisite of filing an appeal bond necessary to the allowance of an appeal cannot be presumed in the face of a judgment dismissing an appeal for lack of affidavit and bond." Leave to sue as a poor person does not dispense with the necessity of filing an appeal bond.78 It is as essential that the bond be filed as that an affidavit be filed," and the fact that a corporation is in the hands of a receiver does not dispense with the necessity of an appeal bond by the receiver.80 The bond should be made to the appellee,81 and if the bond is made payable to the State of Missouri instead of the appellee, the surety cannot be held liable.82 Where the space in an

Sec. 176. Duty of Justice Allowing an Appeal. 

If an appeal is properly made, it is the duty of the justice to allow same and immediately make an entry of such allowance in his docket. The allowance of the appeal has the effect of suspending all other proceedings on the judgment. If, in the meantime, execution shall have been issued, the justice shall give to the appellant a certificate that an appeal in the cause has been allowed, and on presentation of such certificate to the constable the property of the defendant that may have been taken on execution shall be forthwith released by the constable. (Sec. 2345.) The effect of the appeal is to vacate the judgment of the justice until the appeal is determined,92 and to confer jurisdiction of the cause upon the circuit court. 93 

Sec. 177. Power of Circuit Court Over Justice as to Appeals. 

If the justice fails to allow an appeal when it should be allowed, or if, on account of absence, sickness, or any other cause on the part of the justice an appeal cannot be taken in time, the statute provides that the circuit court or other court having jurisdicion of such appeal, or the judge thereof in vacation, on such fact satisfactorily appearing, may by rule and attachment compel the justice to allow the appeal and to return his proceedings in the case, together with the papers required to be returned by him (Sec. 2346). Under this statutory authority, a circuit court has the power to compel a justice to allow an appeal where the filing of an appeal bond was prevented by the absence, sickness, or neglect of the justice. But a circuit court will not grant relief under this statutory authority to an appellant who did not file his affidavit and bond within the time required.95 Nor will the circuit court apply the statutory remedy against a justice who refuses to allow an appeal because appellant refused to present evidence as to the solvency of sureties on his "McAnaw vs. Matthis, 129 Mo. 142, 31 S. And if a circuit court refuses to compel a justice to allow an appeal, certiorari does not lie to review the action of the circuit court, since such action is reviewable by appeal or writ of error." 98

Upon an appeal being made and allowed, the court may by rule and attachment compel a return by the justice of his proceedings in the suit and of the papers required to be returned by him (Sec.

But a justice is not authorized to amend his return on his own motion,100 nor to file an amended transcript for appeal without an order of the circuit court.¹ When it is discovered in the circuit court that a justice has not certified to his return, the circuit court has the power to call upon the justice to add his certificate to the return.2 And the circuit court may compel the justice to amend his record showing the date upon which the appeal was taken, and the power of the circuit court to compel a justice to amend defective records rests within its sound discretion, and its action will not be disturbed on appeal in the absence of abuse. Sec. 178. Appeal Considered Allowed, Though No Entry Thereof Made in Docket of Justice. 

The statute provides that if a justice shall allow an appeal and certify in his certificate the cause of his failure to allow the same at the proper time, the appeal shall be sustained when it would have been competent for the court to order the same to be allowed, and in all cases when the bond and affidavit required shall have been filed or deposited with the justice in due time and the justice shall have returned such appeal to the appellate court, the appeal shall be considered as having been allowed by the justice, although no entry thereof shall appear in the record (Sec. 2347). Because of this statutory provision, appeals are considered allowed where the affidavit and bond are filed, even though no entry thereof appears in the record. And if a sufficient affidavit and bond are filed in time, and a transcript is filed in the circuit court, jurisdiction is thus lodged in the circuit court, though no actual allowance of appeal appeared in the record of the justice. And the circuit court does not err in overruling a motion to dismiss an appeal after the transcript is lodged with the circuit court and the circumstances are such that the justice could have been compelled to grant an appeal.s

Sec. 181. Notice of Appeal. 

If the appeal be not allowed on the same day on which the judgment is rendered, the appellant shall serve the appellee, at least ten days before the first day of the term at which the cause is to be determined, with a notice in writing stating the fact that an appeal has been taken from the judgment therein specified (Sec. 2355).

This statutory provision requiring the service of notice of an appeal is mandatory.16 If the appeal is not taken when the judgment is rendered, and the statutory notice of appeal is not given, the circuit court does not acquire jurisdiction.17 The giving of written notice is jurisdictional, so that the circuit court acquires no jurisdiction of the cause even though the appellee had actual knowledge of the appeal but was not served with written notice.18 Jurisdiction, however, may be waived if the appellee voluntarily appears.¹º If an appeal is taken and no statutory notice given, and the affidavit for appeal bears a date after the judgment, the appeal should be dismissed in circuit court, notwithstanding the fact that the docket entry of the justice shows that the case was appealed immediately after judgment.20

But when the appellee enters his appearance and demands trial, and the appellant fails to appear, the judgment, on motion of the appellee, shall be affirmed. (Sec. 2356.) It has been held that a judgment of a justice court was properly affirmed on motion, where the plaintiff gave no statutory notice of appeal, notwithstanding that at the first term after the case reached the appellate court appellant filed an application for a change of venue." Where a plaintiff resisted the defendant's motion to dismiss a motion to affirm the judgment of the justice court, his action in doing so did not have the effect of entering his appearance.38 Where the appellee waived a notice of appeal, or entered his appearance in circuit court, and the appellant failed to appear, it was the duty of the circuit court to hear the appellee's evidence and render judgment thereon.39 But if no notice of appeal is given, and the appellee does not appear on or before the second day of the first term after the appeal reaches the appellate court, it is error to try the case at such term without the consent of the parties.40 And this rule applies to cases appealed less than ten days before the next term of the court. The appellant is not entitled to a continuance as a matter of right when the appellee enters his appearance on the second day.42 At the return term, if no notice has been given, and the appellee remains silent, a continuance must be granted.43 No appeal shall be dismissed at the first term of the court for failure to give notice. Sec. 184. Effect of Failure to Give Notice Before Second Term. 

The statute provides that if the appellant fail to give notice before the second term of court after the appeal is taken, the judgment shall be affirmed or the appeal dismissed, at the option of the appellee (Sec. 2357). The duty of an appellant in justice court to give notice of his appeal is mandatory.46 If the first term of the court to which the case was appealed began less than ten days after the appeal from justice court was taken, the appellant has until ten days before the third term of the court to give notice of his appeal.""

The giving of such notice is jurisdictional, so that knowledge of the appeal acquired in any other manner is insufficient. 48 In computing the time within which the notice must be given, the rule that obtains follows the general rule in such cases, namely, that the first day should be excluded, and the last day included.49 It has been held that if the appellee, at the first term, stood for trial and appellant failed to prosecute, the appellee was entitled to have judgment.50 Where the appellant failed to give notice ten days before the second term, the appellee was entitled to an affirmance of the judgment.51 The appellee may waive notice of appeal and enter his appearance, thereby giving the circuit court jurisdiction to render judgment."2 

If the appellant dismisses his appeal, judgment of affirmance must be rendered against him and his sureties, and if he fails or refuses to prosecute the appeal same may be dismissed. 53 The practice relative to the necessity for notice of appeal and the effect of a failure to give such notice before the second term of the appellate court after the judgment of the justice was rendered, is uniform.54

a. When cause triable.

c. Set-off and counterclaims not allowed in circuit court when not made before justice.

The statute provides that in cases wherein the summons was personally served on the defendant, no set-off nor counterclaim shall be pleaded in the appellate court that was not pleaded before the justice (Sec. 2359). The courts construe this statute strictly, and hold that a defendant cannot first avail himself of a counterclaim or set-off on appeal." Nor can a defendant by an amended answer set up an additional counterclaim in the circuit court.60 The right of recoupment is prohibited in the circuit court, unless pleaded in justice court.61 Where the suit is on a note, and the defense is a failure of consideration on account of fraud in the procurement of the note, such defense is in the nature of a counterclaim or set-off, and cannot be pleaded for the first time in circuit court.62 

d. Amendment of pleadings. 

The statute authorizes a liberal policy with regard to the amendment of pleadings in circuit court, after the case arrives there on appeal from a justice court (Sec. 2360). We have already discussed the policy of the circuit courts in allowing amendments of pleadings in such cases. 68 e. Practice prevailing in circuit court governs.

The statute provides that trial in the appellate courts of cases that have been appealed from justice courts shall be governed by the practice in circuit court, except that, by agreement of the parties, the case may be tried by a jury of six men (Sec. 2361).

Sec. 186. Judgments Against Appellant and Sureties. 

66 The statute provides that in all cases of appeal from a justice court, if the judgment of the justice be affirmed, or if, on trial anew in the appellate court, the judgment be against the appellant, such judgment shall be rendered against him and his sureties in the recognizance for the appeal (Sec. 2362). And where a defendant appeals from a judgment of a justice, he cannot avoid an adverse judgment by dismissal.70 A judgment cannot be rendered on an appeal from a justice court against a surety on an appeal bond insufficient to sustain an independent action thereon."¹

The statute provides that if, upon an execution being issued upon such judgment, the principal shall not pay such execution, and the officer cannot find sufficient property of such principal to satisfy the same, such execution shall be enforced against the sureties; and the officer shall specify in his return by whom the money was paid, and the time thereof (Sec. 2363). 1. Attachments. 

B. IN PARTICULAR ACTIONS Sec. 187. Nature of the Proceeding. 

Attachment is a statutory proceeding by which an alleged debtor's property is seized under a legal process, known as an attachment writ, and held for the purpose of being used to satisfy a debt which the owner of the property owes, or until it can be determined whether such alleged debtor is, in fact, a debtor and can be compelled to pay the debt. The remedy is always ancillary to and dependent on an action to determine the justice of a demand of the attaching creditor. Its purpose is to aid in the collection of the amount due on such demand, and it may be instituted simultaneously with the action on the demand, or at any stage of the action on the demand before final judgment is entered.72 "In 2 R. C. L., pp. 800-801, it is said: "Attachment is a remedy for the collection of an ordinary debt, proceeding by a seizure under legal process, termed a writ or warrant of attachment, of the property of the debtor. Although for some purposes the issuance of the writ and the seizure of the property thereunder constitute a separate legal proceeding, yet it can have no independent existence. 

The attachment is ancillary to and dependent on a principal proceeding, either at law or in equity, which has for its purpose a determination of the justice of the creditor's demand. It is therefore tantamount to an involuntary dispossession of the defendant prior to any adjudication of the rights of the plaintiff -an execution, so to speak, in advance of trial and judgment. The property of the debtor having thus been levied upon, it is conserved for eventual execution 249

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 188. Statutory Control of Remedy in Justice Courts. 

The remedy by attachment in the justice courts and in courts of record is, and always has been, statutory. As it now exists, it was not known to the common law, although it has been said that the origin of the right of a creditor, under certain circumstances, to attach his debtor's property as security for his demand, is of great antiquity in the English law." The statutes in Missouri have given justices of the peace jurisdiction of attachment proceedings since the Territorial Period." Except where the statutes especially applicable to justices of the peace govern the use of the attachment remedy in justice courts, attachments in justice courts are controlled by the statutes which govern attachments in courts of record (Sec. 2444).75 The general subject of attachments, as the remedy is applied in courts of record, being considered in another division of this work,70 only that part of the subject as it relates to and is governed by statutes especially applicable to justices of the peace will be considered here. 

Sec. 189. Property Subject to Attachment. 

Real estate cannot be attached under an attachment writ issued by a justice (Sec. 2444). But where mining machinery was attached, which machinery was made removable from the real property on which it was located by the terms of a written lease, and which had been treated as personal property, and title to same had after the action shall have proceeded to judgment, unless the debtor procures its release by giving other security in the manner provided by law.' 

This language has been adopted by Ballentine, p. 121, as the definition of 'attachment."

This section shall not be construed to authorize real estate to be attached under an attachment issued by a justice; nor shall that officer have power to appoint a receiver of attached property, nor shall the form of action, or the ordinary mode of proceeding before justices, be considered as changed by anything contained in this section."

Sec. 190. Jurisdiction and Venue. 

Justices of the peace have jurisdiction of attachment actions involving property which does not exceed in value the pecuniary limitation of their jurisdiction. The statute provides that every such action must be brought before a justice of the township wherein the property, credits, or effects of the defendants, or either of them, may be found, or in any adjoining township thereto, or in the township wherein the defendants reside, or in any adjoining township. But in townships which have 150,000 inhabitants and in which the justices of the peace are paid salaries, every such action cognizable before a justice of the peace by attachment against the property, credits, or effects of the defendants, or either of them, found in any such township, shall be brought in some justice court in said township, or in the township where defendants, or one of them, reside, and in no other, and any judgment rendered contrary to such statutory provision is null and void. Sec. 191. Commencement of Attachment Actions. 

Attachment actions are commenced by the filing of an affidavit for attachment (Sec. 2427) and an attachment bond (Sec. 2428). 

The proceeding is separate from and in aid of the original cause of action, and, while the statement of the original cause of action should be separate from the affidavit for attachment, it has been held that the joining of the statement on which the cause of action is based and the affidavit of attachment is not fatal.81 The statute provides that before issuing a writ of attachment the sufficiency of the penalty and the security in the bond shall be approved by the justice and his approval endorsed on the bond. The statute further provides that the account, statement, or instrument to be sued on, together with the affidavit and bond, shall be filed with the justice (Sec. 2429). 

Sec. 192. Affidavit for Attachment. a. How and by whom made.

The statute prescribes the form for an attachment affidavit (Sec. 2427). Such affidavit may be made by a plaintiff or by some person for him (Sec. 1279).82 The affidavit may be made by the plaintiff's attorney,88 and when made by plaintiff's attorney it need not disclose the attorney's means of knowledge.84 The affidavit may be made by an agent for a corporation, and such affidavit has been held good though it failed to state by what authority and in what capacity the affiant acted.85

Sec. 193. Bond in Attachment.

The statute prescribes the form for the attachment bond. In all essential respects, such form should be complied with, but it has 256

been held that a bond which omits part of the statutory conditions is, nevertheless, valid as to the conditions contained in it.2 The statute provides that the assignee of the constable may sue in his own name in a justice's court on any bond assigned, if the penalty of the bond does not exceed $150, and, if such penalty exceed that amount, in any court having jurisdiction (Sec. 2432). The giving of a bond in an attachment proceeding is a prerequisite to the issuance of the attachment writ, its purpose being to secure the defendant in case of a wrongful attachment. The bond and the affidavit together are essential to confer jurisdiction upon the justice to issue the writ and are the means for preventing injustice and damages to a defendant at the hands of an impatient or indiscreet plaintiff.3

Sec. 194. Issuance and Personal Service of Writ. 

The statute provides that writs of attachment shall be issued and returned in like time and manner as ordinary writs of summons, but may be served by the officer to whom they are directed in any township or county in which the suit is instituted, except that writs of attachment against insurance companies not incorporated by, or organized under the laws of, this State may be issued and served as authorized in Section 2169 (Sec. 2431). The statute prescribes the form for the writ of attachment (Sec. 2430). The writ may be directed to a constable of the township where the justice resides, or to the constable of an adjoining township, but it must be served by the constable to whom it is directed. After the property is attached, valid service must be had. The writ may be amended to conform to the facts of service. An officer is liable for failure to perform his duty in the service of an attachment writ, but in a suit on such bond it is necessary to aver that the constable failed to perform his duty. If a constable makes a return showing a levy on and seizure of property, he is estopped from pleading in an action on his bond that he was not acting officially."

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 196. Sales of Perishable Property Attached. 

Property likely to perish or materially depreciate in value before the trial, or that can be kept only at much loss or expense, may be sold by the constable upon order therefor of a justice of the peace and on the same notice as goods are required to be sold on fieri facias. 

The proceeds of such sale must remain in the hands of the constable, subject to being disposed of as the property itself would have been. (Sec. 2433.) A purchaser at such sale takes good title.14 If judgment goes for the defendant, he is entitled to recover the proceeds of the sale.15

Sec. 197. Verbal Plea in Abatement Sufficient. 

The statute provides that in all cases where property or effects shall be attached, the defendant may put in issue by a verbal plea in the nature of a plea in abatement on oath, the substance of which shall be noted by the justice on his docket, the existence of facts alleged in the affidavit on which the attachment was sued out (Sec. 

2434). A formal plea in abatement not noted on the docket of the justice is treated on appeal as putting in issue the existence of the facts alleged in the affidavit for attachment.16 If the defendant makes no plea to the affidavit, he thereby confesses the matter stated therein.17 He may amend his plea after the case reaches the circuit court on appeal,18 and he may in the circuit court plead in abatement of the attachment, although he may have defended upon the merits before the justice.19 Where the defendant appears and pleads to the merits, and then withdraws, and a jury renders a verdict against him, the judgment is not by default, and the justice has no power to grant a new trial. If the defendant proceeds to trial on the merits, without denying the allegations of the affidavit, he confesses the matters alleged.20 If no property was seized and the suit was dismissed before the issues were made, plaintiff was not liable on his bond for an attorney's fee of the defendant.21

Sec. 198. Plaintiff Must Prove Facts Alleged in Affidavit. 

After a plea in abatement, the plaintiff must prove the existence of the facts alleged by him as the ground of the attachment. If the issue is found for him, the cause shall proceed, but if the issue be found for the defendant, the attachment shall abate at the cause of the plaintiff, and the plaintiff and his sureties shall be liable on their bond for all damages occasioned by the attachment or other proceedings in the case. But the suit shall proceed to final judgment on the merits of the cause of action sued on. (Sec. 2435.) It has been held that the loss of time is an item of damages for malicious attachment and that a jury can infer value of time lost in the absence of direct proof as to such value.22

Sec. 199. Attachments May Be Dissolved. 

Attachments before justices of the peace, as in courts of record, may be dissolved on motion made in behalf of the defendant, at any time before final judgment, in the following cases:

First, when the affidavit on which the same was founded shall be adjudged by the court insufficient; but no attachment shall be dissolved in such case if the plaintiff shall file a good and sufficient affi- "Helfer vs. Hamburg Quarry Co., 208 Mo. A. 58, 233 S. W. 275. 263

JUSTICE COURTS 

davit, to be approved by the court, in such time and manner as the court shall direct;

Second, when the defendant shall appear and plead to the action, and give bond to the plaintiff, with good and sufficient security to be approved by the court, in double the amount of the property, effects and credits attached, conditioned that such property, effects and credits shall be forthcoming and abide the judgment which shall be rendered in the cause when and where the court shall direct; 

Third, when the defendant shall appear and plead to the action and give like bond and security, in a sum sufficient to satisfy the amount sworn to, in behalf of the plaintiff, with interest and costs of suit, conditioned that the defendant shall pay to plaintiff the amount which may be adjudged in favor of the plaintiff, interest, and all costs of suit. (Secs. 1321, 2444.) When an attachment is dissolved, all proceedings touching the property and effects attached, and the garnishee summoned, shall be vacated, and the suit shall proceed as if it had been commenced by summons only (Sec. 1322).

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 200. Third Persons Claiming Attached Property May Inter plead.

The statutes (Secs. 1325, 2444) authorize any person who claims money, property, effects, or credits that have been attached in the hands of a defendant in an action in a justice court to interplead in the cause in the justice court. Such interplea, whether filed in a justice court or a court of record, must be verified by affidavit, and when such verified interplea is filed issues are made up thereon and tried as like issues by the plaintiff and defendant. (Sec. 1325.)

Statutory authorization of interpleas has long been held applicable to actions in justice courts.28 An interplea is in the nature of a statutory replevin ingrafted on the attachment act.27 The office and purpose of the proceeding is to determine the question of ownership of a specific chattel and the right of the officer to hold it under his writ.28 

26 State ex rel. Hirsch vs. Silverstein, 77 Mo. A. 304. "Green vs. Powell (App.), 46 S. W. (2d) 915; Gate City Natl. Bank vs. Boyer, 161 Mo. A. 143, 142 S. W. 487; Plano Mfg. Co. vs. Cunningham, 73 Mo. A. 376; 

State ex rel. Reeves vs. Barker, 26 Mo. A. 487. 

28 State ex rel. Reeves vs. Barker, 26 Mo. A. 487. In this case the court described the nature of an interplea in an attachment action as follows: "The proceeding of interpleader in the action of attachment is somewhat sui generis. 

It is solely the creature of the statute. It is defined by our supreme court (in 

Burgert vs. Borchert, 59 Mo. 80), to be in the nature of an action of replevin ingrafted on a suit by attachment. Its very office and purpose are to determine the question of ownership of the specific chattel and the right of the sheriff to seize and hold it under his writ. . . . The sheriff represents the plaintiff in the attachment suit in holding the property as the legal custodian. The inter- pleader 'became substituted for the original defendant, and, therefore, a party to the action.'''’ ...

The nature of the proceeding was further discussed in Spooner vs. Ross, 24 

Mo. A. 599, 1. c. 603, as follows: "An interplea is in the nature of a replevin, engrafted by statute on the proceeding in attachment. Certainly, then, it will not lie where the action of replevin will not. The very object of the action in replevin is the recovery of specific personal property, in kind. It partakes in this respect, of the nature of a proceeding in rem. ... "Especially is this true of an interplea. It is a claim for the recovery of the possession of the specific thing. Unlike the action of replevin, no money judg ment in damages can be awarded in lieu of the specific property claimed. It is peculiarily a possessory action, 'the right to present possession of the property being the principal question in controversy.' It involves the exclusive right of the claimant to the immediate possession of the chattel, and the fact of the wrongful detention thereof by the defendant as against the claimant.' 

266

The proceeding on the interplea is separate from the attachment action, and cannot be maintained after the property has been destroyed in the hands of the plaintiff in attachment.29 The proceeding will not lie where an action of replevin cannot be maintained.30 Nor can a claimant interplead after the attachment has ended. But if a justice acquires jurisdiction of an attachment proceeding, he has the right to hear and determine an interplea for the attached property, although such property exceeds in value the pecuniary limitation on the jurisdiction of the justice. 82

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 202. Record, Judgment and Appeal. 

The record of the attachment should be kept separate from that of the interplea.87 Thus when an interplea is filed, the justice should enter the same on his docket as a separate and distinct case and make all entries in his docket relative thereto in the same way that he would do in any other case. As soon as judgment is entered, the docket of the justice should be promptly made to show that fact. 

From a final judgment on an interplea, an appeal lies to the circuit court as in other civil causes. 38

Sec. 203. Judgment. 

The statute provides that when the defendant shall be notified as required by law and shall not appear and answer to the action, judgment by default may be entered, which may be proceeded on to final judgment in like manner as in ordinary actions (Sec. 2438). Such judgment shall bind only the property or effects attached, and no execution shall issue thereon against any other property of the defendant, nor shall any action be brought thereon (Sec. 2439).
