Sec. 204. Transcript Filed and Proceedings on in Circuit Court. 

If, in any case of a suit brought before a justice of the peace by attachment, it shall appear by the return that the defendant has not any goods, effects, or credits liable to be attached by such writ, the justice shall, on the application of the plaintiff, certify a transcript of his docket, together with the process and all the original papers in the cause, to the circuit court or other court having jurisdiction of the cause (Sec. 2440). When same is filed in the circuit court, the clerk of that court shall, if a sufficient bond and affidavit is among the papers, issue an attachment, as in a case originating in the circuit court, and proceedings shall be had thereon in all respects as if the original action had been brought therein (Sec. 2441). But if there is not a sufficient affidavit and bond certified with the docket of the justice and the other papers in the case, the clerk shall not issue a writ of attachment until a sufficient affidavit and bond has been filed (Sec. 2442).

Sec. 205. Duty of Justice on Withdrawal of Note. 

The statute provides that in all cases in which a judgment may have been rendered against a defendant in an attachment without appearance, upon a bond, bill, note, or other instrument in writing, and the plaintiff shall, at any time, desire the withdrawal of the instrument sued on, it shall be the duty of the justice to endorse on said instrument the amount, if any, which has been paid upon the judgment arising from the proceeds of the sale of the attached effects (Sec. 2443). 270

2. Forcible Entry, Unlawful Detainer and Writs of Certiorari. 

Sec. 206. A Special and Preclusive Code. 

The common law affords no civil remedy of forcible entry and detainer, or unlawful detainer, but such remedies are purely statutory." The statutes authorizing and governing actions of forcible entry and detainer, unlawful detainer and certiorari for the removal of such causes to superior courts (Secs. 2445-2521) are complete within themselves, and proceedings under such statutes are not dependent upon and are not governed by the General Code of Civil Procedure or any other statute.12 These statutes constitute a special and preclusive code, and proceedings under them are not measured or determined by the ordinary rules and proceedings in civil cases.48 

The remedies afforded by these statutes have sometimes been referred to as extraordinary remedies,44 but this characterization has doubtless been used to distinguish such remedies from the remedies afforded in ordinary actions at law, and in pursuit of which the procedure prescribed by the Code governs. Justices of the peace have exclusive, original jurisdiction in forcible entry and detainer and unlawful detainer actions.45 In such actions the mandatory requirements of the particular statutes governing the proceedings must be rigidily complied with. The actions being cognizable originally and exclusively by justices of the peace, particular attention will be given to them here.

Sec. 207. Origin and Purpose of the Remedies. 

The remedies of forcible entry and detainer and unlawful detainer were provided by statute to assist in the preservation of the public "11 R. C. L. 1136-1145; Fuhr vs. Dean, 26 Mo. 116; Krevet vs. Meyer, 24 Mo. 107. "Brennan vs. McMenamy, 78 Mo. A. 122, 1. c. 128; Westerhold vs. Boese, 64 

Mo. A. 280, 1. c. 283; Hastings vs. Hennessey, 52 Mo. A. 172, 1 c. 176-177; Carter vs. Tindall, 28 Mo. A. 316, 1. c. 319. 

Gary Realty Co. vs. Kelly, 278 Mo. 450, 214 S. W. 92; State ex rel. Morris 

Bldg. & Inv. Co. vs. Brown (App.), 72 S. W. (2d) 859; Purcell vs. Merrick, 172 

Mo. A. 412, 158 S. W. 478; Holman vs. Hogg, 83 Mo. A. 370; Schwoerer vs. 

Christophel, 64 Mo. A. 81. "Brennan vs. McMenamy, 78 Mo. A. 122. "State ex rel. Morris Bldg. & Inv. Co. vs. Brown (App.), 72 S. W. (2d) 859. "Purcell vs. Merrick, 172 Mo. A. 412, 158 S. W. 478. 271

JUSTICE COURTS 

peace as between persons claiming possession of real estate. Under the common law, such remedies were not available, but a party having title to land and the right of entry had the conceded right to recover possession as against a person offering forcible resistance. At common law, a person having a right of entry to real estate in the possession of another might enter forcibly and subject himself only to an indictment for a breach of the peace. The common law did not compel him to make restitution of the possession thus forcibly taken. 

The statutory remedy of forcible entry and detainer was conceived for the purpose of providing for restoration of possession to one forcibly ejected and to take away inducement to persons to redress themselves at the expense of the peace of the community. The general purpose of such statutes is to preserve for a party in peaceable and quiet possession of real estate the right to continue such peaceable and quiet possession and to afford redress to him if he is ejected by force or violence. Under such statutes, a person who makes a forcible entry or who forcibly detains real estate after a peaceable but unlawful entry, is not only subject to indictment but is also required to restore possession to the party entitled thereto and respond in damages caused by his unlawful acts. In providing for an action of forcible entry and detainer, the object of the statutes was to prevent breaches of the peace and to prevent persons from redressing their grievances in defiance of the law, and to lead them to assert their rights by peaceable and lawful means. Unlawful detainer actions were authorized by the statutes for the purpose of giving to landlords possession against tenants holding over and affording them a right to secure such possession without resorting to forcible ejection. The statutes authorizing these actions have been held statutes 

47 11 R. C. L. 1136-1142, 1165; Krevet vs. Meyer, 24 Mo. 107.

In Krevet vs. Meyer, the court discussed the underlying principles of the actions thus: "By the common law, a person having a right of entry to lands in the possession of another might enter into the possession, and although he was subject to an indictment for any breach of the peace committed in making his entry, yet there was no remedy provided by which he could be compelled to make restitution of the possession thus forcibly taken. In order to correct the evils attending this state of the law, and to take away all inducement to persons to redress themselves at the expense of the peace of the community, several statutes were made which prohibited the forcible entry on the possession of another, and directed that, in the event force was found, restoration of the possession should be made 272

of peace whose object is to prevent opposing claimants for the possession of land from taking the law into their own hands and strug- 

to the party who was forcibly ejected. In the construction of these statutes, all attempts to prevent restoration, by showing that the person guilty of the force had a right of entry, were steadily resisted. Upon the force being found restitution followed as a matter of course, without any regard to the right of the party by whom it had been committed. This was done that men might learn to appeal to the law for injuries done them, and not undertake the redress of their own wrongs.

If the tenant holds over, the landlord cannot enter against his consent, but must resort to his warrant. A possession gained by disseizin will not prevent the disseizor from maintaining his warrant against another having a right of entry, but who enters on his possession without his assent. These cases are not cited as authorities, for we know that they are founded on statutes different from that in force in this state. The object in producing them is to show that the principle on which this proceeding is founded is not novel; that it prevailed in England and in sister states. That principle is, that persons shall not take the law into their own hands, but shall assert their rights by action in a peaceable manner, and not by force." 

In 11 R. C. L., pp. 1136, 1137, it is said: "The privilege allowed by the ancient common law to persons disseized or turned out of possession to use violent methods to reinstate themselves was early found to be prejudicial to the public peace as tending to lawlessness. Several statutes were accordingly passed in England 'to restrain all persons from the use of such violent methods, even of doing themselves justice, and much more if they have no justice in their claim.' . . . The substance and in large degree the quaint phraseology of these early enactments have been retained by the statutes of very many of the states of the Union, where the remedy for a forcible entry and detainer is but one of a civil nature for the restitution of the premises taken by force, and in some cases by acts that would not have been considered forcible under the construction given to the British statutes. . . . The general purpose of the statutes of forcible entry and detainer, both in England and in this country, is that, regardless of the actual condition of the title to the property, the party in peaceable and quiet possession shall not be turned out by a strong hand, violence or terror. One who is guilty of a forcible entry, therefore, or of a forcible detainer after a peaceable but unlawful entry, is not only subject to indictment, but is required to restore possession to the party from whom it was so taken or detained, and in a proper case is often required to pay him treble damages, notwithstanding the fact that the entrant may have had the superior title or the better right to present possession. In affording this remedy of restitution the object of the statutes is to prevent breaches of the peace and criminal disorder which would ensue from the withdrawal of the remedy, and the reasonable hope such withdrawal would create that some advantage must accrue to those persons who, believing themselves entitled to the possession of property, resort to force to gain possession rather than to some appropriate action in the courts to assert their claims. Sec. 208. Statutory Definition of Remedies. 

a. Forcible entry and detainer.

The statutes provide that if any person shall enter upon or into any lands, tenements, or other possessions with force or strong hand, or with weapons, or by breaking open the doors or windows or other parts of a house, whether any person be in it or not, or by threatening to kill, maim or beat the party in possession, or by such words or actions as have a natural tendency to excite fear or apprehension of danger, or by putting out of doors or carrying away the goods of the party in possession, or by entering peaceably and then turning out by force, or frightening, by threats, or other circumstances of terror, the party out of possession, and detain and hold the same-in every such case the person so offending shall be deemed guilty of a forcible entry or detainer (Sec. 2446).⁰⁰ b. Unlawful detainer. 50 The statute provides that when any person shall unlawfully and without force hold over any lands, tenements, or other possessions, after the termination of the time for which they were demised or let to him, or the person under whom he claims, or when any person wrongfully and without force, by disseisin, shall obtain and continue in possession of any lands, tenements or other possessions, and after demand made, in writing, for the delivery of the possession thereof by the person having the legal right to such possession, his agent or tions of forcible entry and detainer which are designed to compel the party out of possession to respect and resort to the law alone to obtain what he claims is his."' 

48 Hewitt vs. Doherty, 25 Mo. A. 326.

This statute provides that: "No person shall enter upon or into any lands, tenements or other possessions, and detain or hold the same, but when entry is given by law, and then only in a peaceable manner. 

Do This definition conforms with that given by Ballentine, p. 515: "An offense committed against the public peace which is committed by violently taking or keeping possession of lands and tenements with menaces, force and arms, and without the authority of law." 274

attorney, shall refuse or neglect to quit such possession, such person shall be deemed guilty of an unlawful detainer (Sec. 2447).51

Sec. 209. Elements of Forcible Entry and Detainer. 

The statute specifies the things which a person may do by which he subjects himself to an action for forcible entry and detainer (Sec. 

2446). It presupposes possession by the party complaining. In order for the action to lie against a defendant, there must be shown a forcible entry on property in the possession of another and a detention of the possession of such property by the entrant. a. Possession of complainant.

It is indispensable, in order to sustain the action of forcible entry and detainer, for complainant to show that he was in the actual possession of the property from which he claims he was ousted.52 The property must have been in the exclusive possession of the complainant at the time of his dispossession, except where one tenant in common has been dispossessed by his co-tenant.58 The fact that he had the legal right to possession will not aid a complainant to make out his case where he cannot show that he has never been in possession.54 

What is such actual possession as will support an action for forcible entry and detainer is a mixed question of law and fact, varying in different circumstances, depending on the character and condition of the property.55 Ordinarily the complainant need not reside on the land, occupy a building thereon, nor have it enclosed. Continuous 56

Thus the fact that a church had not functioned on property with continuous regularity was held not to destroy such continuity of possession as was required to enable it to maintain an action of forcible entry and detainer.58 And building a fence to enclose vacant lots indicates an intention to remain in possession, though no other acts of occupancy occurred.59 If the deeds performed by complainant on the property are open and visible indicia of possession, and if they constitute such overt acts as indicate dominion and a purpose to occupy and not to abandon the premises,61 they will be sufficient evidence of possession upon which to base an action of forcible entry and detainer. 62 But the possession must be exclusive, for such possession as one holds by way of easement is not sufficient." Possession by an agent or a tenant of the complainant will support the action,64 and if tenant leaves, the landlord comes into sole possession, though not personally present.65 If a tenant holds over after his term expires, he alone is in possession sufficient to maintain forcible entry and detainer against a third person.66

In short, the possession necessary and sufficient to furnish the basis for forcible entry and detainer must be such possession represented by either occasional or continuous occupancy of the premises by the complainant, his agents or tenants, or the performance of such overt acts thereon by them, as indicate an intention to hold possession or exercise dominion over same permanently."7 "Bradley vs. West, 60 Mo. 59.

b. Entry against will of party in possession.

In order for a plaintiff to maintain the action, it is not necessary that he prove a forcible entry. It is sufficient if he show an entry by the defendant against the will of the party in actual possession, 68 and with the intent of interfering with such possession or ousting the one in possession. An entry for the purpose of cutting timber where possession is not held does not give rise to an action for forcible entry and detainer." But while the mere entry for cutting timber is not ordinarily a sufficient entry to meet the requirements of the statute, if the entry is accompanied with an intention to occupy permanently, it is such as will support the statutory element of entry."¹ 

An entry, though it be against the will of the party in possession, is not sufficient to support an action for forcible entry and detainer, if defendant does not take possession or oust the one in possession or undertake to exercise any control over the property upon which the entry was made, for such acts amount only to a trespass.72 Likewise, if an owner enters leased premises and cuts hay which lessee was supposed to cut, and the owner's acts are not accompanied with an intention to take possession of the premises, he is guilty only of a trespass, and not of forcible entry and detainer.73 But if a defendant tears down plaintiff's fence and extends his house on plaintiff's enclosure and declares himself in possession, such acts are of a sufficient overt nature to indicate dominion and purpose to enter for occupying the premises, and will support an action for forcible entry and detainer." The intention accompanying the entry is of primary importance." Thus if a party is in possession of land which de-

Sec. 211. The Kinds of Unlawful Detainer Distinguished. 

The statute authorizes, and the courts recognize, the right of action for unlawful detainer in two different classes of cases (Sec. 2447).87

The first class includes those cases where a person wilfully and without force holds over any lands after the termination of the time for which they were leased to him, and the second includes those cases where persons wrongfully and without force, by disseisin, obtain and continue in possession of lands and refuse to quit possession after demand made in writing. In cases under the first class, a showing of a relationship of landlord and tenant is necessary." 

89 In cases under the second class, a showing of the relationship of landlord and tenant is not necessary." 

90 A further distinction lies in the fact that in cases under the first class no demand in writing for the delivery of the possession is required before the institution of the suit, while in the cases under the second class such a demand is indispensable.⁹1 

Except for these distinctions, actions under the two classes are practically, if not exactly, the same.

Nor is it necessary that plaintiff show that he resided on the land, occupied any building thereon, or had it enclosed. Actual and continuous occupancy of the land is not necessary, provided complainant's acts in connection with the property have been such as to indicate an intention on his part to exercise control and dominion over it.97 But if a complainant has never been in possession of premises purchased or leased by him, he cannot maintain unlawful detainer against his grantor or lessor.98 Nor is a claim of ownership or reputation of possession sufficient." Title, right to, and demand for possession in unlawful detainer.

Complaints in unlawful detainer are sufficient when they contain the allegations required by the statute." The general rule that a pleading in a justice court is entitled to leniency applies in actions of this nature, and if a complaint is imperfectly drawn it will be held sufficient if it contains the substance of the elements required by the statute. And an objection thereto made for the first time in the court of appeals comes too late. A complaint in unlawful detainer with force which failed to allege demand in writing for possession has been held fatally defective.47

Sec. 217. Service of Summons. 

a. Personal service. 

The statute provides that the summons be executed at least five days before the return day thereof," by one of the following 

First, by reading the complaint and summons to the defendant; second, by delivering the defendant a copy of the complaint and summons; third, by leaving a copy of the complaint and summons at the usual place of abode of the defendant, with some member of his family over the age of fifteen years (Sec. 2452). 

b. Service by publication. 

If the officer shall return that the defendant is not found, or that he has absconded or absented himself from his usual place of abode in this State, it shall be the duty of the justice before whom the proceeding is commenced to make an order that notices be set up for ten days in four public places in his township, ward, or district; or, if a daily newspaper be published in his township or city, such notices shall be published for six days in such daily paper, informing the defendant of the commencement of proceedings against him. And on proof of the notice by affidavit of some competent witness, or by affidavit of the publisher, if the notice be published in a newspaper, the justice shall proceed to hear the case as if there had been personal service, and judgment shall be rendered and proceeded in as in other cases. (Sec. 2452.) It has been held that where a defendant joins in an application for certiorari or appears and answers in circuit court, he thereby waives service,72 and where defendants appear generally, the court acquires jurisdiction, even though service has not "Westerhold vs. Boese, 64 Mo. The statute provides that the officer shall, on or before the trial day, return the summons and certify thereon, or annex thereto, how he executed it (Sec. 2453). Such summons is returnable in five days.74

Sec. 219. Plaintiff Non-suited for Failure to Prosecute.

The statute provides that if the complainant fail to attend and prosecute his suit in person, or by agent or attorney, at the time appointed for the hearing of the complaint, he shall be non-suited, and defendant shall recover his costs (Sec. 2454).

Sec. 220. Proceeding Where Defendant Defaults. 

If the defendant, after being duly summoned, does not appear at the time appointed for hearing the complaint, the justice shall proceed with the hearing (Sec. 2455) and may render judgment if he finds that he has jurisdiction and the plaintiff is entitled to relief. 

But in a case where the defendant appeared the day following judgment by default and showed that he had a meritorious defense but was detained on the day of the trial by sickness, and that he had made diligent effort to be present at the trial in person or by agent, it was held that the justice properly set aside the default judgment." 

Sec. 221. Trial Procedure. 

76 When both parties appear at the time appointed for the trial, the justice shall proceed to examine the complaint and proofs of the parties and render judgment according to his findings or the verdict of the jury (Sec. 2456), unless for good cause shown the case is continued, but continuances are granted at the discretion of the justice and not for a longer time than ten days (Sec. 2469). If, before commencing an investigation of the merits of the cause by the hearing of any testimony, either party demands that the cause be tried by a jury, a jury shall be ordered to try the case. Such jury shall 

76 State ex rel. McCann vs. Smyth, 1 Mo. A. 571. 294

consist of the same number of men possessing the same qualifications, summoned in the same manner, and shall be governed by the same provisions regarding trials by and proceedings of juries and the rendition of their verdicts as are, or may be, provided by law for the trial of other civil suits before justices of the peace (Sec. 2457). If the case is tried before a jury, the justice shall, after the jury is sworn, cause the complaint to be read to the jury, and then call upon the complainant to support the same by proof; but the complainant shall not be compelled to make further proof of the forcible entry or detainer than that he was lawfully possessed of the premises and that the defendant unlawfully entered into and detained or unlawfully detained the same (Sec. 2458).

Sec. 222. Production of Testimony. 

a. By personal attendance of witnesses. 

The statute authorizes the justice to issue subpoenas for witnesses on the application of either party, and, if witnesses summoned do no attend, the justice may issue an attachment to compel their attendance (Sec. 2469). b. By depositions of witnesses.

Depositions may be taken to be read at the trial of any such cause in the same manner as in any other causes before justices of the peace (Sec. 2471). Such depositions, if taken and returned according to law, and if competent and relevant, may be read as evidence in the cause: First, if it appear to the satisfaction of the justice that the witness resides out of the county in which the trial is to be had; second, if the witness be dead; third, if by reason of age, sickness, or bodily infirmity, he is unable to attend the trial; fourth, if he be gone out of the county without the collusion, privity, or consent of the party offering the testimony (Sec. 2472).

Sec. 223. Proof Required by Complainant. 

a. Prima facie case in forcible entry and detainer.

The statute provides that a complainant shall not be compelled to make further proof of the forcible entry or detainer than that he was lawfully possessed of the premises, and that the defendant unlaw- 295

JUSTICE COURTS 

fully entered into and detained or unlawfully detained the same (Sec. 2458). The courts have uniformly held that all that complainant needs to show in order to maintain his cause of action is that he was in the actual possession of the property and was forcibly dispossessed by the defendant.” b. Prima facie case in unlawful detainer.

In an action for unlawful detainer, it has been held that a complainant makes a prima facie case by showing his deed, taking pos session of the property, and collecting the rent each month, by showing that a written thirty-day notice to vacate was given, and that defendant refused to vacate, and by proof of a reasonable value of the premises. By such proof, complainant shows all that is required by the statute (Sec. 2447).79 c. Proof of demand in unlawful detainer action.

The statute requires that the demand which a complainant in an unlawful detainer action must show in order to maintain the action must be made either by delivering a copy of the demand to the person in possession, or by leaving such copy with some person above the age of fifteen years, residing on or being in charge of the premises. 

If no person is in the actual occupancy of the premises, such demand must be made by posting a copy thereof on the premises. If the demand is made by an officer authorized to serve judicial process, his return is prima facie evidence of the facts therein stated, but if the demand is made by any other person, the return must be sworn to by such person, and, when sworn to, is prima facie evidence of the facts therein stated. (Sec. 2481.) Reading a copy of the demand to the defendant is not in compliance with the statute; 80 nor does mailing a copy constitute personal service.81 The exhibition of the complainant's deed to the defendant is not necessary.82 If service was not had on the defendant, his agent, or the person in possession, but on a member of his family above the age of fifteen years, a showing 77

Where a complainant in forcible entry and detainer relied on possession through another as his tenant, he was held to have the burden of proving that the latter was his tenant.86 In such action, the burden is on complainant to prove that he was in peaceable possession and that defendant forcibly dispossessed him.87 It has been held that the burden is on the complainant to show that at the time of the entry by the defendant, complainant was in the actual possession of the premises as contradistinguished from constructive possession arising from title.88 In an action of unlawful detainer for premises held over by a tenant after the expiration of his lease, if the tenant claims that there was an extension of his tenancy, the burden is upon the tenant to show an agreement for such extension. e. Where a father and son are joined as defendants and conviction of the father was sought on the ground that he aided and abetted his son and acted in concert with him in forcibly entering and maintaining possession, and there was no evidence of the father's being implicated, whereas the father and son both testified that the father had nothing to do with it, a verdict for the father was approved."

Sec. 224. Merits of Title Not in Issue. 

The statute provides that the merits of the title shall in no wise be inquired into on any complaint in forcible entry and detainer and unlawful detainer actions (Sec. 2467). While it has been held error to admit evidence of title," for the reason that it is not material in such actions and is not in issue," the rule prevails that title can be inquired into if it gives any information tending to show the character and nature of the possession of the premises. Thus, it is improper to say that title is not to be considered for any purpose, for the rule that title is not an issue is to be taken in the sense that title is not tried out as a determinative factor upon which the issues "Koger vs. Ward (App.), 243 S. Sec. 225. Defenses. 

The statute provides that forcible entry and detainer and unlawful detainer actions will not lie as against any person who has had the uninterrupted possession or been in quiet possession of any lands or tenements for the space of three whole years together immediately preceding the filing of the complaint, or who has continued three whole years in the peaceable possession after the time for which the premises were demised or let to him, or those under whom he claims, shall have expired (Sec. 2468). Even where the possession has been obtained under circumstances that will ordinarily justify unlawful detainer, if it appears that the defendant has been in uninterrupted possession for three years, the action cannot be maintained against him.10 Nor can a complainant whose possession has not been held in good faith recover as against a defendant who, with his predecessors, has had possession for three years. 11 An attempted possession of a part of a tract by a complainant when the entire tract was in the possession of the defendant for three years does not give the complainant the right to maintain the action.12 The fact that a tenant has been in possession for three years before the commencement of the unlawful detainer is no bar as against the right of the landlord to maintain unlawful detainer, for the tenant's possession is the landlord's, and is sufficient to support the landlord's action.13 Nor will such defense by a tenant who has held possession under the complainant's grantor, or under the prior owner, prevail as against the complainant.¹¹ 'Hafner Mfg. Co. vs. City of St. Louis, 262 Mo. 621, 172 S. W. 28.

12 Kennedy vs. Prueitt, 24 Mo. A. 414. 

13 Kaulleen vs. Tillman, 69 Mo. 510. "Gillett vs. Mathews, 45 Mo. 307. 300

The statute provides that when any forcible entry and detainer, or unlawful detainer, shall be made upon any lands or other possessions, against the provisions of the statutes, the person having the lawful possession shall, against the wrongdoer, be considered as entitled to such quantity, extent and limits of lands as by the patent, grant, concession, deed, survey, donation, settlement or preemption right, such person or those under whom he claims can, by the laws of the United States or of this State, have and lawfully claim in and to such premises (Sec. 2474). And under this provision of the statute it has been held that one forcible entry cannot be offset against another.15 Where no legal survey has been made of such possession, the improvement of the person entitled to the possession shall be in the middle of the tract as near as may be, making the survey as near in a square as may be, not to interfere with any established survey or line, or any conditional line agreed upon by the adjoining proprietors or possessors (Sec. 2475).

It is no defense to an action for forcible entry and detainer that the complainants had once left the possession with an intention not to return.16 In an action for unlawful detainer, equitable rights or interests which defendant thinks himself entitled to cannot be set up as a defense.1

Sec. 226. Amendments. 

The statute authorizes any justice in open court and at any time, in furtherance of justice and on such terms as may be proper, on the motion of either party, to allow any complaint, summons, writ or other proceeding to be amended and to permit new parties as coplaintiffs or codefendants to be added and to correct a mistake in the name of either party (Sec. 2470). The statute provides that no cause removed to the circuit court by certiorari or appeal shall be dismissed for any informality, insufficiency or imperfection in the affidavit or recognizance, if a sufficient affidavit or recognizance be filed within such time as shall not delay the other party (Sec. 

2510). And the statute further authorizes the circuit court to proceed to hear, try and determine such causes removed thereto by

2516). Under these statutory provisions, it is generally held that amendments may be made either in the justice court or in the circuit court to correct defects or informalities that are not of a jurisdictional nature. 18 If the complaint and original proceedings are sufficient to give the justice jurisdiction, any other defect may be cured by amendment.19 While it is the general policy of the courts to favor the allowance of amendments, and to exercise liberality in granting the right to amend in furtherance of justice,20 amendments cannot be made in forcible entry and detainer and unlawful detainer actions so as to constitute a material change in the cause of action.21 Under the liberal policy of allowing amendments, it has been held that defective description of the property in the complaint may be amended if the original complaint contained any description at all,22 and that an affidavit to the complaint may be amended if the affidavit in the original complaint was sufficient to confer jurisdiction.28 And where an amended affidavit was filed in circuit court, and the clerk omitted to attach the seal of the court thereto, advantage could not first be taken of the omission in the appellate court. 24 The statute does not require that the complaint allege the amount of damages sustained, and it has been held that a complaint may be amended striking out the amount of damages claimed, and that a complaint thus amended will support a judg-

Sec. 227. Requisites of Verdict for Complainant. 

The statute provides that whenever the verdict of the jury or the finding of the justice shall be for the complainant, damages shall be assessed as well for waste and injury committed upon the premises found to be forcibly or unlawfully detained, as for all rents and profits due and owing up to the time of the rendering of the verdict or finding of the justice, and a statement of the monthly value of the rents and profits of the premises (Sec. 2459). Sec. 228. Judgment on Verdict for Complainant. 

The statute provides that if the verdict of the jury or the finding of the justice be for the complainant, the justice shall record the same, and the judgment shall be that the complainant have restitution of the premises found by the jury or justice to have been forcibly or unlawfully detained, and recover of the defendant double the sum assessed by the jury or found by the justice, for his damages; and also double the sum found by the jury or justice, per month, for rents and profits, from the day of rendering the verdict, or of the finding, until restitution be made, together with costs (Sec. 2464). It has been held that the provision authorizing double damages is not unconstitutional.38 The judgment need not be drawn according to any particular verbal formula, but it must contain a description of the land corresponding with the description contained in the complaint, and it must be based upon the verdict

Sec. 229. Verdict for Defendant 

The statute prescribes the form of verdict where a finding is for the defendant (Sec. 2460). If the justice or jury find the defendant not guilty, it is the duty of the justice to record the finding or verdict and give judgment accordingly, and for costs, and to issue an execution therefor in the ordinary form, against the goods and chattels of the complainant (Sec. 2463). 

191. FORM OF VERDICT FOR DEFENDANT 

We, the jury, find the defendant not guilty in manner and form as charged in the complaint.58

Sec. 230. Correction of Verdict and Docket Entries. 

The statute provides that no verdict shall be set aside for informality, but the justice shall, in the presence of the jury, correct the verdict in matters of form, changing no matter of substance (Sec. 2462). The statute requires that the justice enter on his docket the names of the jurors, their verdict, and the judgment thereon (Sec. 2466).

The justice may issue an execution against the defendant which shall contain a clause of restitution and generally conform with the judgment (Sec. 2465). An execution may be issued for damages and costs after there has been a restitution of the premises.54

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 233. Removal to Circuit Court by Certiorari. 

Actions for forcible entry and detainer or for unlawful detainer may be removed to the circuit court in the county in which same are pending by certiorari, to be issued by the clerk and served on the justice at any time after service has been had, and before the day of trial (Sec. 2483). This proceeding is not one of review.56 A case of this nature may be removed to the circuit court by certiorari, notwithstanding mistrials by the justice." The transcript of the justice must show jurisdiction, or the circuit court acquires none on certiorari.58 The case may be transferred any time before the trial actually occurs, and after a case may have been continued.59 Notice must be given as of appeals from justices' courts (Sec. 2491).

Sec. 234. When Granted and How Made. 

Application must be made for certiorari before the day of trial by the applicant's filing with the clerk a copy of the complaint, together with an affidavit and recognizance (Sec. 2484).6⁰ a. On application of complainant. 60 Where complainant makes application for the writ, he, or some credible person for him, shall make an affidavit stating that affiant verily believes that the complainant is justly entitled to recover the possession of the premises described in the complaint (Sec. 2485).

The complainant, or some responsible person for him, must also enter into a recognizance, filed by himself, with one or more sureties to be approved by the clerk, which recognizance must be in favor of the defendant and in a sum sufficient to secure the payment of all costs, conditioned that the complainant shall prosecute his suit with effect and without delay, pay all costs that may be adjudged against him, and otherwise abide the judgment of the circuit court (Sec. 2486).

The statute provides that when a certiorari shall be served on the justice before the day of the trial, and not otherwise, he shall stay all further proceedings and certify to the circuit court of the county a complete transcript of his docket and all proceedings had before him, together with the original papers filed in the cause, and file the same in the office of the clerk of the circuit court within ten days after the service of the certiorari (Sec. 2490). The circuit court may compel the justice to make a return (Sec. 2517). Notice of the application for a writ of certiorari shall be given as in cases of 61

Sec. 237. Requisites for Appeal. 

A party desiring to appeal must make an application therefor and file an affidavit and recognizance for appeal within ten days after rendition of the judgment (Sec. 2494). a. Affidavit for appeal.

The affidavit must be made by the appellant, or some credible person for him, and shall state that the affiant verily believes that the appellant is aggrieved by the judgment of the justice, and that he does not take the appeal for vexation or delay, but that justice may be done (Sec. 2496). The affidavit must conform with this provision of the statute, as the general rule relative to appeals has no application to cases of this kind. Where the affidavit is defective, it may be amended (Sec. 2510), and an opportunity should be given to make such amendment." b. Sec. 238. Appeal Returnable When. 

day of 19..... When the judgment of the justice is rendered during the vacation of the circuit court, the appeal shall be returnable to the first day of the next term thereof; but if the judgment be rendered during the term of such court, the appeal shall be returnable within six days after the rendition of the judgment (Sec. 2495). The statute fixing a return time where the judgment is rendered during a term of the circuit court must be strictly complied with, as no variance therefrom will be permitted.80 The responsibility for filing the appeal is on the appellant, so that if he directs the clerk to file the transcript in the circuit court and the clerk fails to do so in time, appellant cannot obtain relief because of such failure.81 Following the statute, it has been held that if a judgment in such case is rendered during a term of the circuit court, the appeal must be filed in six days.82 And in determining what consists of six days,

For the purpose of determining whether a judgment is rendered during the vacation of the circuit court, the courts have held that the word "vacation" means all that period between the end of one term and the beginning of another, and not merely the intervals between the actual sessions of court during the term.87 

Sec. 239.

Execution. 

If a justice renders judgment he may issue an execution at any time after judgment, but such execution shall not be levied until after the expiration of the time allowed for the taking of an appeal (Sec. 2502), except where it appears to the officer having charge of the execution that the defendant therein is about to remove, conceal or dispose of his property, so as to hinder or delay the levy, in which case the rents and profits, damages and costs may be levied before the expiration of the time allowed for taking an appeal (Sec. 2503). 

When the appeal is perfected, the justice shall note that fact on his docket, and thereupon all further proceedings on the judgment shall be stayed, and the execution, if any, shall be returned, upon notice of the appeal being served on the officer having charge thereof (Sec. 2504). It has been held that a constable and his sureties are liable on his bond for execution of a writ of restitution within ten days.88

Sec. 242. New Bond May Be Required. 

The circuit court may, in any case where it shall appear that the amount or security in a recognizance is insufficient, or for any other substantial defect, order a new recognizance to be filed within such time as shall not delay the trial (Sec. 2511). A refusal to continue a cause upon the filing of a new bond is not erroneous.⁹⁹ A motion to dismiss because the penalty in the bond is too small is not the same as a motion for a new bond.100

Sec. 244. Proceedings on Dismissal or Default of Parties. 

If a defendant appellee defaults after the case is removed to circuit court either by certiorari or appeal, judgment may be rendered against him by default, but if such defendant is appellant and he defaults, the judgment of the justice may be affirmed or the appeal dismissed (Sec. 2513). In case of a judgment by default, a jury, or the court if no jury be required, shall assess the monthly value of the premises, and the damages and judgment shall be rendered on the verdict accordingly (Sec. 2515). The circuit court may assess damages in such case."

Sec. 246. Writs of Restitution and Rerestitution. 

The Supreme, appellate and circuit courts, respectively, shall have power to issue writs of restitution, or rerestitution, or executions with clauses to that effect, as occasion may require, to enforce their judgments in all cases for forcible entry and detainer and unlawful detainer (Sec. 2519).

The officer having charge of a writ of restitution or rerestitution, or execution with a clause to that effect, shall have power to expel and remove from the premises mentioned the defendant therein named, his servants and others under his control, and all other persons who shall have entered thereon after the commencement of the suit otherwise than by process of law, and to deliver to the plaintiff possession thereof (Sec. 2520).

Sec. 247. Changes of Venue. 

Either party shall be entitled to change of venue in any suit for forcible entry and detainer and unlawful detainer, if he shall, before the jury is sworn or the trial is commenced before the justice, file an affidavit that the justice is a material witness for him, without whose testimony he cannot safely proceed to trial, or that the justice is near of kin to either party, stating in what degree, or that he cannot have a fair and impartial trial before such justice on account of his bias or prejudice, or that he cannot have a fair trial in the township or district on account of bias or prejudice of the inhabitants of such township or district, which affidavit may be made either by the party to the suit pending or by said party's agent or attorney. Where such change of venue is granted, the justice shall forthwith make out and certify a transcript of the

3. Garnishments. 

Sec. 249. Definition. 

A garnishment is a proceeding by which the money or property of a debtor which is in the hands of a third party may be reached by process and applied to the payment of an obligation the debtor owes his creditor.11 'Scheerer vs. Waltner (App.), 29 S. W. (2d) 193. 

10 Chap. 117, Landlord and Tenant. 

"In 12 R. C. L., p. 775, the proceeding is discussed as follows: "The term of garnishment as used today means a proceeding or process whereby the property, money or credits of one person, generally called the debtor, and in the possession of or owing by another, generally designated the garnishee, are applied to the payment of the debt of the debtor, by means of process issuing against the debtor and the garnishee. The person instituting the proceedings is generally referred to as the creditor or plaintiff, the person indebted to the creditor is called the debtor or defendant, and the person in whose possession is 321

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 250. Nature and Purpose of the Remedy. 

Garnishment is purely a statutory proceeding,12 of a strictly legal nature, and is a means of obtaining satisfaction of a judgment by reaching credits due to a losing defendant in the main suit.18 A garnishment is not a new suit, although, after the proceeding is instituted, for the purpose of reaching the defendant's credits, the issues between the garnishee and the plaintiff are tried as ordinary issues between a plaintiff and a defendant.14 The object of a garnishment proceeding is to impound a specific sum of money belonging to the defendant and owing by the garnishee.15 The proceeding in justice court must conform with the statutes especially applicable to and which govern the practice in such cases in justice courts (Secs. 2522-2538). The general subject is considered elsewhere in this work,16 and only that part of the subject relating to special garnishment proceedings in justice courts will be considered here.

Sec. 251. When Garnishee May Be Summoned in Justice Court. 

The statute provides that if there be not sufficient goods and chattels whereon to levy an execution, the constable shall summon in writing, as garnishees, such debtors or other persons having in their possession or under their control money, property or effects of the defendant in the execution as may be named to him by the plaintiff or his agent, to appear before the justice at a time and place to be specified in the summons, not less than five nor more than fifteen days from the service of the same, to answer such interrogatories as may be exhibited against them touching their indebtedness, or their possession or control of money, property or the property sought to be reached and who is indebted to the debtor is called the garnishee or trustee, the latter being garnished or warned by the creditor not to settle with the debtor but to answer to the suit of the creditor.''

This statutory provision authorizing garnishment proceedings and directing when and how they shall be instituted must be strictly complied with.¹ In garnishment proceedings the pecuniary limitation upon the jurisdiction of the justice controls, and a justice may enter a judgment for an amount within his jurisdiction although the indebtedness of garnishee exceeds the pecuniary limitation of the jurisdiction of the justice.18 But jurisdiction does not lie until there has been issued and served a garnishment summons and until the return thereof shows that service has been had, as the rule in such proceedings is against conferring jurisdiction by consent or by waiver.19 A summons requiring the appearance of the garnishee in less than five days may be quashed, and cannot be amended to require appearance more than fifteen days after the date of the service.20 The constable's return on the garnishment notice is evidence of service.21 In such proceeding a judgment may be rendered by default.22

It is not necessary that interrogatories in a garnishment proceeding before a justice be in writing.27 

Sec. 253. 

Default of Garnishee.

If a garnishee is duly summoned and fails to appear or to make full and direct answer upon oath to the interrogatories, the plaintiff may take judgment against him by default, which may be proceeded on to final judgment in like manner as in cases between plaintiff and defendant. At the option of the plaintiff, the justice may attach the body of the garnishee until he answer the interrogatories. Where the garnishee is a corporation and fails to answer, the justice shall, on motion of the plaintiff, compel the corporation to answer by attaching the body of the president, secretary, treasurer, auditor, paymaster, or deputy paymaster of such corporation, in which case. the corporation shall be liable for all the costs accruing by reason of such attachment. (Sec. 2526.) 

Sec. 254. 

Answer of Garnishee.

The statute provides that any garnishee, being summoned, may, at his option, appear and answer the interrogatories before the return day of the attachment (Sec. 2524). Such garnishee may file his answer in writing under oath with the justice; or the justice may, at his request, write the answer of the garnishee to each interrogatory separately, and file the answer as a paper in the cause (Sec. 2525). If the answer of the garnishee is not denied in proper time, it shall be taken to be true and sufficient (Sec. 2532). And if, by answer not denied, it shall appear that the garnishee is possessed of property or effects of the defendant or is indebted to the defendant, the justice shall assess the value of such property or effects, and ascertain the amount of such indebtedness, and shall render judgment for the proper amount in money, unless the same "Laughlin vs. January, 59 Mo. 383. 325

Sec. 255. Plaintiff May Deny Garnishee's Answer. 

The statute provides that on the same day on which the answer is made, or at such other time as the justice shall direct, the plaintiff may deny the answer of the garnishee, or any part thereof (Sec.

2527). Such denial must be in writing and must show what part of the answer is denied and what is not denied, and same must be filed as a paper in the cause (Sec. 2528). The plaintiff's denial should contain a special averment of the facts as will advise the garnishee what issues he is called upon to meet, and if the denial is limited to a general denial it cannot be amended on appeal.29 Denial must be made before the justice within the time allowed by the statute, and if it is not circuit court should not permit the filing of a denial after the case reaches that court on appeal.30 (Caption.)

Sec. 256. Trial of Issues Between Plaintiff and Garnishee. 

a. Same as between plaintiff and defendant in ordinary case. 

The statute provides that all issues between the plaintiff and a garnishee shall be tried as ordinary issues between plaintiff and defendant, and costs may be adjudged for or against either party, as in ordinary actions (Sec. 2529). If, upon the trial, property, effects or money of the defendant are found in the hands of the garnishee, the justice or jury shall find what property or effects, and the value thereof, or what money, are in his hands. Unless he discharge himself as authorized by law, by paying or delivering over such property or money to the constable forthwith, or as soon as may be, then the justice shall enter up judgment against the garnishee for the value or amount in money as found. (Sec. 2530.) "Rees vs. Peck-King Mortgage Co., 206 Mo. A. 690, 230 S. W. 666.

JUSTICE COURTS 

b. Procedure in garnishments in courts of record prevails. 

The statutes governing procedure in garnishments in courts of record (Secs. 1415, 1417 and 1418) are made applicable to garnishments before justices of the peace. Under those sections, if the answer of the garnishee is not excepted to or denied, and it shall appear that the garnishee is possessed of property or effects of the defendant, or is indebted to the defendant, the court shall make the garnishee a reasonable allowance for his trouble and expenses in answering, to be paid out of the funds or proceeds of the property or effects confessed in his hands (Secs. 1417 and 1418). 

Sec. 257. Garnishee May Discharge Himself by Surrendering

Property. 

A garnishee having in his possession property, money or effects of the defendant, may discharge himself by surrendering and paying the same, or so much thereof as shall be sufficient to satisfy the debt and interest or damages and costs, to the constable and take his receipt therefor at any time before final judgment against him (Sec. 

2531). If he has money in his hands belonging to the defendant he may discharge himself by delivering the money to the constable.³¹ 

Sec. 258. Interpleas. 

The statute authorizes any person claiming property, money, effects or credits attached, to file his interplea, in writing, in the cause, supported by affidavit; and verbal issues may be taken to such interplea and be tried as issues between plaintiff and defendant in ordinary cases and without unnecessary delay (Sec. 2535). When a claimant interpleads, an issue is made up and must be tried as an original cause between plaintiff and defendant, and the issue raised by the interplea must be tried and determined before the trial of the issue between the plaintiff and the garnishee.32 The interplea is in no sense part of the cause of action, but it is an assertion of an independent right.33 Not only must an interplea be tried and de- "Fullerton vs. Kelliher, 48 Mo. 542; Cassidy Co. vs. Estep, 63 Mo. A. 540. "Ladd, Patrick & Co. vs. Couzins, 35 Mo. 513; Kahmke vs. Weber, 187 Mo. A. 

698, 173 S. W. 76. "Giett vs. McGannon, 74 Mo. A. 209; Wolff vs. Vette, 17 Mo. A. 36. 328

termined separately, but the record of the proceedings on the interplea should also be kept distinct from the record of the proceedings on the garnishment. 34 The statute requires the justice to file the interplea and note the filing of same and the substance of the issues upon his docket (Sec. 2536). The issues on the interplea may be tried by a jury,35 and the issues as to whether the defendant fraudulently conveyed his property to his wife, who is the interpleader, can be investigated in the proceedings.36 A change of venue lies in an interpleader proceeding.37 It has been held that where the claimant failed to interplead before the justice he may file his interplea in the circuit court after the case reaches that court on appeal.88 But in a garnishment proceeding where a third person has filed an interplea and the interplea has been disposed of, and subsequently a judgment is entered in the garnishment action, the interpleader has no right of appeal from the judgment in the garnishment action.39

Sec. 259. Judgment on Interplea Must Precede Judgment on Garnishment. 

Before a judgment is rendered against the garnishee in whose hands or possession the property, money, effects or credits may be, a judgment disposing of the interplea must be rendered (Sec. 2537). 

In entering a judgment on the issues raised by the interplea, costs may be adjudged for or against either party as in ordinary actions (Sec. 2538). An appeal may be taken from the judgment of a justice on an interplea before the final determination of the garnishment proceeding.40 And a judgment in favor of the interpleader is a bar to further action by the plaintiff in the garnishment proceeding." 

Sec. 260. Judgment in Garnishment Proceeding. 

The statute provides that there shall be no final judgment rendered against a garnishee until there shall be final judgment against the defendant (Sec. 2534), and it has been held that where a judgment is void for want of jurisdiction a garnishee must, for his own protection, set up its validity,42 as a garnishment proceeding cannot be based on a void judgment.48 

4. Mechanic's Lien. 

Sec. 261. Nature of the Remedy. 

A mechanic's lien is a claim for the price of labor and material furnished in erecting and repairing a building or structure, which, 40 Smith vs. Sterritt, 24 Mo. 260; Weisenecker vs. Kepler, 7 Mo. 52. "Richardson vs. Watson, 23 Mo. 34; Richardson vs. Jones, 16 Mo. 177. 42 

Hopkins vs. Huff, 67 Mo. A. 394; McPike Drug Co. vs. Wilson (App.), 237 

S. W. 1044. 43 

Chicago Herald Co. vs. Bryan, 195 Mo. 590, 92 S. W. 906. 330

by operation of special statutes, is given the right to priority of payment and may be enforced by a sale of such building or structure and the land on which it stands. Such liens are wholly statutory and were unknown to the common law.45 The mechanic's lien statutes have been held to be highly remedial in nature and entitled to be liberally construed to effectuate their beneficent purpose.46 

The statutes in Missouri authorize the enforcement of mechanic's liens in justice courts where the amount claimed does not exceed the pecuniary limits of the jurisdiction of such courts (Secs. 25392547). 47 Since the general subject is treated elsewhere in this work,* only the proceedings relating to the enforcement of mechanic's liens in justice courts prescribed by the statutes governing such proceedings will have our attention here. 

Sec. 262.

Jurisdiction. 

A special statute prescribes the jurisdiction of justices of the peace in mechanic's lien proceedings (Sec. 2539). By that statute, justices of the peace in counties or cities having over 50,000 inhabitants, are vested with jurisdiction in all actions brought to enforce mechanic's liens as provided by law for enforcing such liens in circuit courts, when the amount or balance claimed to be due does not exceed $250.00, while in all counties having less than 

50,000 inhabitants, justices have such jurisdiction where the amount or balance claimed does not exceed $150.00 (Sec. 2539). The provisions of the statutes prescribing jurisdiction must be strictly complied with, and a justice does not acquire jurisdiction unless the action is brought before him in the county where the land sought to be charged is located,48 and unless the debt sued for is within the pecuniary limitation of the justice. Sec. 263. Persons Entitled to Lien. 

Under the provisions of the mechanic's lien statutes relative to liens in justice courts, the statute authorizing liens to persons in courts of record determine who are entitled to such liens in such actions in justice courts. Under that statute, every mechanic or other person who shall do or perform any work or labor upon, or furnish any materials, fixtures, engine, boiler, or machinery for any building, erection or improvements upon land, or for repairing the same, under or by virtue of any contract with the owner or proprietor thereof, or his agent, trustee, contractor or subcontractor, shall have for his work or materials a lien upon such building, erection or improvements, and upon the land on which the same are situated, to the extent of one acre, and if upon a building or structure in a township or village, then upon the lot or land upon which the building or structure is situated, provided such mechanic or other person complies with the law giving him a right to such lien. (Sec. 3156.) It has been held that the surviving partner of

Sec. 264. Lien Must Be Filed in Circuit Clerk's Office. 

The statute provides that any person entitled to such lien, after having complied with the mechanic's lien law by filing with the clerk of the circuit court, within the time prescribed, a statement of his account and a description of the property upon which the lien is intended to apply, with the name of the owner or contractor, or both, if known to the person filing the lien, verified by the oath of himself or some credible person for him, as required by law (Sec. 

2540), may institute his action therefor before a justice of the peace within the time prescribed for filing such actions after the filing of such lien. A lien does not lie for the razing of a building,54 but when such work is done in repairing, a lien does lie.55 The filing of such lien is a condition precedent to the right to maintain an action to enforce a lien.56 Such remedy must be filed within the time and according to the provisions of the general mechanic's lien law (Sec. 3161).

Sec. 266. Notice of Claim of Lien. 

The general statute on mechanic's liens, which is applicable to liens enforced in justice courts, provides that every person except the original contractor, who may wish to avail himself of the benefit of the mechanic's lien law shall give ten days' notice before the filing of the lien to the owner, owners, or agent, or either of them, that he holds a claim against such buildings or improvements, setting forth the amount and from whom the same is due. Such notice 335

JUSTICE COURTS 

may be served by any officer authorized by law to serve process in civil actions, or by any person who would be a competent witness. 

When served by an officer, his official return, endorsed thereon, shall be proof thereof, and when served by any other person, the fact of such service shall be verified by affidavit of the person so serving. (Sec. 3175.) Such notice is not process," but the object of it is to warn the property owner against paying the original contractor while outstanding claims exist in favor of laborers and material men.61 The notice must be in writing and must be properly signed."2

Sec. 267. Notice of Suit. 

The statute provides that before the commencement of any suit to enforce a mechanic's lien, the plaintiff shall file with the clerk of the circuit court a notice showing when and before what justice of the peace such suit will be instituted (Sec. 2541). The notice must be filed prior to the commencement of the suit, and if the suit is filed on the same day that notice is filed, evidence of priority must be produced.63 Filing has been held to be accomplished when the notice is deposited in the office of the clerk, and if such fact can be established by other evidence, the absence of the usual indorsement of the filing by the clerk will not invalidate the notice. The notice may be signed by the claimant, or by his agent or attorney. It must give the name of the justice, but it need not give his local address. 65 

The suit is deemed commenced if the petition is actually filed with the justice within the time prescribed in the notice.66

Sec. 268. Suit Instituted by Filing Statement. 

Before any process shall be issued, the plaintiff must file with the justice a statement of the facts constituting his cause of action, and a description of the property sought to be charged with the lien (Sec. 2541). The filing of such statement is jurisdictional, and if the statement filed misdescribes the property it is proper that the execution be quashed because of lack of jurisdiction."7 Suit to enforce a lien may be instituted later on the same day the lien claim is filed." 

But a failure of the justice to file or docket a statement lodged with him will not prejudice the action, if such statement is actually filed before process is issued." The statement must allege that the materials went into the building on which a lien is claimed." Sec. 269. Time for Filing Suit. 

Under the statutes governing mechanic's lien actions in justice courts (Sec. 2540), suits must be brought to enforce mechanic's liens in justice courts, as well as courts of record, within ninety days 340

after filing the lien. Unless the action to enforce the lien is instituted within that time, the lien expires. (Sec. 3172.) The statute making this provision is one of limitation,74 and unless a suit to enforce a mechanic's lien is filed within ninety days, it is barred.75 

The suit must be brought against all the necessary parties within the required time to save it from the operation of this statute of limitations.70

Sec. 270. Process. 

The statute directs that process and proceedings in a mechanic's lien cause be as nearly as practicable the same as provided by law in other suits before justices of the peace (Sec. 2540). The service of process either personal or by constructive notice has been held to be a prerequisite to the right to maintain the action and to enforce a lien." If the defendant cannot be summoned, the statute provides that the justice shall enter an order on his docket, requiring the plaintiff to give notice to such defendants by four written or printed advertisements, set up at four public places in the county, that a suit has been instituted against him to enforce a mechanic's lien against the property, describing it, stating the amount claimed to be due and on what account, and when and where said cause will be heard before such justice; which advertisements shall be set up at least twenty days before the time set for the hearing of the case (Sec. 2543). It has been held that the finding by a justice that the defendant has absconded from his usual place of abode and cannot be found in this county is not sufficient to authorize an order of publication, as it does not appear that defendant could not have been summoned by leaving a copy of the summons at his usual place of abode with a member of "McPherrin vs. Lumbermen's Supply Co., 211 Mo. Sec. 271. Trial and Judgment. 

Pine Tree Lumber Company,

By Elmer C. Boone, President. 

The statute provides that if any defendant, after having been summoned or notified according to law, shall not appear to the action, judgment by default shall be entered against him (Sec. 2542).

Where service has been had, or the debtor appears, the case may be tried by a justice or a jury, as other cases are tried before justices of the peace. If the finding be for the plaintiff, and sustaining the lien, the judgment shall be that he recover the amount of indebtedness found to be due, with costs of suit, with the addition that if sufficient property of the debtor cannot be found to satisfy such judgment and costs, the same, or the residue thereof, shall be levied out of the property charged with the lien, which said property shall be correctly described in the judgment. But if the finding be for the plaintiff and the lien be not sustained, the judgment shall be in the ordinary form, and may be enforced against the property of the debtor as ordinary judgments of justices of the peace. (Sec. 2542.) 

If the debtor has not been served with a summons, and has not appeared, but has been notified as provided by law, the judgment, if 343

JUSTICE COURTS 

for the plaintiff, shall be that he recover the amount of indebtedness found to be due, and costs of suit, to be levied out of the property charged with the lien therefor, which property shall be correctly described in the judgment (Sec. 2544). A judgment on constructive service is against the property, and in such judgment that property must be accurately described.81

Sec. 272. Transcript of Judgment Must Be Filed. 

The statute provides that if the judgment be for the enforcement of the lien against the property as hereinbefore provided, it shall be the duty of the justice, upon demand of plaintiff and payment of fees therefor, to make out and forthwith file with the clerk of the circuit court of his county a certified transcript of such judgment. Such transcript shall be recorded in the same manner and with like effect as provided for recording transcripts of judgments of justices of the peace, and the said judgments shall be enforced and execution issued thereon in all respects as on judgments of a like nature rendered in 

81 Lecoutour vs. Peters, 57 Mo. A. 449.

the circuit court. The justices cannot issue execution to enforce the lien of any such judgment against the property therein described. (Sec. 2545.) 82

Sec. 273. Appeals. 

The statute authorizes any party aggrieved by any judgment of a justice of the peace in a mechanic's lien action to appeal therefrom to the circuit court, in the manner and with like effect as in other cases (Sec. 2547). The circuit court does not have any power over the case other than the justice had, so that, since a justice has not power to declare whether a lien thus sought to be enforced is prior or subsequent to a mortgage, the circuit court had not such power on appeal.83

Since the statute applicable to appeals in mechanics' lien cases does not provide for a special appeal bond, the ordinary bond may be given.84 

5. Replevin. 

Sec. 274. Nature and Purpose of the Action. 

Replevin has been defined as a proceeding by which the owner recovers possession of his own, and is said to be one of the most ancient and well-defined writs known to the common law.8 The action is founded on a tortious taking and detaining, is somewhat analogous to an action of trespass, is in the nature of a proceeding in rem to regain possession of personal property and of a proceeding in personam to recover damages for its detention.80 The right to maintain the action depends upon plaintiff's right of possession and a wrongful seizure and detention by the defendant. The purpose of the action is to recover possession of the identical property and damages for its detention, the right of property not being in issue.87 The action

takes its name from the writ involved in the proceeding, and, while the action was long known to the common law,88 it is controlled almost entirely by statute, and proceedings relative to the use of the remedy in justice courts are governed solely by special statutes applicable to replevin actions in such courts (Secs. 2548-2572). The subject is treated generally in another part of this work," so that the discussion of the subject here will be confined merely to the use of the proceeding in justice courts. 

Sec. 275.

Jurisdiction. 

In all counties or cities having over fifty thousand inhabitants, justices of the peace shall have jurisdiction of actions for the recovery of specific personal property when the value of the property sought to be recovered and the damages claimed for the taking or detention and for injuries thereto shall not exceed, in the aggregate, Three Hundred and Fifty Dollars; and in all counties having less than fifty thousand inhabitants justices of the peace shall have such jurisdiction when the value of the property sought to be recovered, and the damages claimed for the taking or detention and for all injuries thereto, shall not exceed, in the aggregate, Two Hundred and Fifty Dollars (Sec. 2548). In townships of 200,000 and less than 

400,000 inhabitants, the pecuniary jurisdiction of justices of the peace in replevin actions is limited to Five Hundred Dollars, for the value of the property sought to be recovered and the damages claimed for the taking or detention and for injuries thereto (Sec. 2375).

Justices in such townships have jurisdiction of replevin suits coextensive with the county.⁹0 

Justices in cities with 300,000 inhabitants and over have jurisdiction in replevin actions when the value of the property sought to be recovered and the damages claimed for the taking and detention and for injuries thereto, shall not exceed, in the aggregate, Seven Hundred and Fifty Dollars (Sec. 2405). In such cities, the jurisdiction of the justice is co-extensive with the city in which he shall be elected (Sec. 2404). Such jurisdiction as justices may exercise within the pecuniary limits fixed by statute is not exclusive, but is concurrent

In other words, in ordinary replevin actions, the jurisdiction of justices of the peace and the circuit court is concurrent where the property involved is of the value of more than Fifty Dollars and less than Two Hundred and Fifty Dollars. The jurisdiction of the justice depends on the property being in the county, irrespective of the township, and lack of jurisdiction over the person of the defendant, who lives in another township than that in which the suit is brought, has been held waived by the defendant's appearance and trying the case without objection to jurisdiction or venue, where the court had jurisdiction of the property.92 Jurisdiction is determined by the named value, regardless of the actual value of the property involved, but where the judgment is in behalf of the defendant there is no limit to the amount of the judgment.94 Jurisdiction in circuit court on appeal is limited by the jurisdiction in the justice court, so that if the justice court did not have jurisdiction the circuit court acquired none by appeal.95 

And a plaintiff cannot amend in the circuit court by reducing the amount sued for so as to give jurisdiction. Sec. 276. Requisites of Statement. 

a. Where defendant may retain property.

Actions in replevin or for the recovery of the possession of specific personal property are instituted by the filing of a written statement on the part of the plaintiff. The statute requires that such written statement be verified by the affidavit of the plaintiff, his agent or his attorney, that to the best of his knowledge and belief the facts and allegations in such statement are just and true. This statement by the plaintiff must allege:

First, that he is lawfully entitled to the possession of the property claimed, sufficiently describing it; 

Second, that it is wrongfully detained by the defendant at the county in which the suit is brought, naming it; 

Third, the actual value thereof;

Fourth, that the same has not been seized under any process, execution or attachment against the property of the plaintiff; 

Fifth, in case the property has been injured, it should state how or in what manner, and the amount of damages, if any, plaintiff ought to recover for such injuries or for the taking and detention, or detention, thereof;

Sixth, if the plaintiff claim the possession of the property before judgment, he shall also state that he will be in danger of losing his "Stevens vs. Reberert, 186 Mo. A. 456, 171 S. W. 638; Saunders vs. Scott, 132 Mo. A. 209, 111 S. W. 874; Malone vs. Hopkins, 40 Mo. A. 331; Gottschalk vs. Klinger, 33 Mo. A. 410. 

100 Alexander vs. McFarland, 203 Mo. A. 229, 213 S. W. 488; Knoche vs. Perry, 90 Mo. A. 483. 348

said property, unless it be taken out of the possession of the defend ant. (Sec. 2549.) 

If a suit is filed based on such statement and the plaintiff gives bond and has the property delivered to him under a replevin writ, the defendant may retain the property by giving bond for delivery 

(Sec. 2555). 

b. Where defendant cannot retain property.

The plaintiff may file a replevin suit and take possession of the specific property under a replevin writ in all those cases where defendant cannot give a delivery bond and retain possession of the property. To prevent defendant from retaining the property the plaintiff must add to the allegations heretofore set out the additional allegations that the property described in the statement was wrongfully taken and that the plaintiff's right of action accrued within one year. When such allegations are contained in the statement, defendant does not have the right to give bond and retain the property. 

(Sec. 2549.) c. Jurisdictional facts. 

The statement must allege facts required by the statute, and if a statement of facts sufficient to give the justice jurisdiction appears in the statement, such statement will not be held insufficient because of some immaterial departures from the precise words of the form used by the statute.¹ d. Title and right to possession of plaintiff.

A statement is sufficient if it alleges that the plaintiff is lawfully entitled to the possession of the property, as it is not necessary that the statement allege ownership in the plaintiff.2 The nature and source of title need not be stated. The statement must contain an allegation that the defendant wrongfully detains the property, as this is the gist of a replevin action.* 'Berry vs. Kauffman, 70 Mo. 186; Sieckman vs. Arwein, 10 Mo. It has been held that where a statement contained an allegation that the property was valued at a certain sum, it was sufficient." 

But if the description and value of the property is stated in language so vague as to make identification impossible, as that plaintiff is entitled to corn of the value of about one hundred dollars, it is insufficient." 

f. Verification of statement. 

The affidavit to the statement is essential to the jurisdiction of the justice, and if there is no such statement the justice acquires no jurisdiction. The statement and affidavit need not be separate instruments but may be incorporated together in the form of a verified statement. The statement is sufficient when verified by an agent,¹º and the fact that the agency is not sworn to is not fatal to the action.¹¹
