Sec. 279.

Service of Process and Execution of Writ. 

If no bond is filed and summons is issued, the officer executes the summons in the same manner as in ordinary civil actions (Sec. 2554). 

If a replevin writ is issued, the statute directs that the constable shall execute the writ by taking the property therein mentioned and delivering it to the plaintiff, or to his agent or attorney (Sec. 2555). 

However, a delivery bond may be given by the defendant, who may thereupon retain possession (Sec. 2555). The constable is empowered to break open doors and enclosures to execute the order for the delivery of the property, if, upon public demand, they be not opened (Sec. 2559). 

Sec. 280.

Procedure Where Defendant Retains Possession. 

In order for the defendant to retain possession of the property described in the replevin writ, the defendant must, with one or more sufficient sureties to be approved by the constable, execute a bond to the plaintiff, to the effect that they are bound in double the value of the property as set forth in plaintiff's statement, for the delivery of said property to the plaintiff, if said delivery be adjudged, and in default of such delivery, for the payment of the assessed value of such property and for the payment of all damages for injuries to the same and for the taking and detention, or detention, thereof, and all costs that may be adjudged against him in the action. If the defendant require it, the constable shall hold the property forty-eight hours to enable him to furnish said bond, and if the same be not furnished in that time the constable shall deliver the property to the plaintiff, who shall have the right to retain the same to abide the event of the suit. (Sec. 2555.) It should be borne in mind that the defendant does not have the right to give bond and retain possession 354

of the property unless the plaintiff states in his affidavit that the property was wrongfully taken and that his cause of action accrued within one year.

Sec. 281. Sureties on Bonds and New Bonds. 

E. F.

The sureties in any bond or undertaking required in this action shall be resident householders or freeholders in the county and worth the amount for which the bond is given, exclusive of property exempt from execution, and after paying all just debts (Sec. 2557). If the justice should, at any time before trial, be satisfied that any bond given in the action is not good and sufficient, he shall order a new one with solvent sureties to be given; and if the party ordered to give such new bond shall fail to do so within forty-eight hours after such order shall be made, and the party so failing to give such bond shall have the property, the justice shall make a further order that the constable retake the property and deliver it to the other party, and shall deliver to the constable an order to that effect, which shall be directed and executed in the same manner as an order for the taking and delivery of the property to the plaintiff (Sec. 2558). JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 282. Constable Allowed Reasonable Charge for Keeping Property. 

The statute provides that the justice shall allow the constable reasonable charges for taking, keeping, handling and delivering the property described in a replevin writ, such charges to be taxed as costs in the suit (Sec. 2560).

Sec. 283. Trial. 

Either party may demand a jury and the cause may be tried by the justice or a jury as other civil cases are tried in justice courts 

(Sec. 2563). 

Sec. 284. Verdict and Judgment for Plaintiff. a. Where property is delivered to plaintiff.

In all cases where the property has been delivered to the plaintiff and is in his possession at the time of the trial, and the justice or jury shall find for the plaintiff, they shall assess his damages for the taking and detention, or detention, of the property, and for all injuries thereto, and the justice shall render judgment for recovery of said property and for the damages assessed with costs of suit, against the defendant. But if the plaintiff was entitled to the possession of the property at the issuing of the writ, but shall not be entitled to it at the time of the trial, or shall have special interest only in the same, the justice or jury shall find according to the facts, and assess the value of his right or interest in the same, and the justice shall give judgment accordingly. (Sec. 2564.) b. Where property is not delivered to plaintiff.

When the plaintiff does not ask for the possession of the property pending the suit, or fails to file the bond required of him, or when the property claimed has not been taken from the possession of the defendant, the cause shall proceed as if the same had been taken by the officer; and if it shall appear from the testimony on the trial that the property was in the possession of the defendant at the date of the issue of the writ or summons, and that plaintiff was entitled to the possession of the same and the defendant wrongfully detained the 356

same from plaintiff, the justice or jury shall find for the plaintiff accordingly and assess the value of the property and damages for the taking or detention of the same, and injuries thereto, and the justice shall render judgment that the plaintiff recover said property and the damages assessed, with costs of suit, and that if said property shall not be found, or at the discretion of the plaintiff, he shall recover the assessed value of the said property, with the damages assessed, and costs of suit (Sec. 2565). A constable's failure to seize the property does not affect the court's jurisdiction.27 When appellant has possession of the property he cannot dismiss the appeal or take a nonsuit and thereby avoid an order against himself for the return of the property or a judgment against himself and his sureties. 28

Where a transcript of a judgment in a justice court is filed in the circuit clerk's office, circuit court has jurisdiction to order same modified so as to conform to statute.29 The production of evidence at the trial to the effect that the property was in the possession of the defendant at the time the summons was issued is a necessary part of plaintiff's case, without which he cannot prevail. The measure of damages recoverable by the plaintiff is not the value of the property at the time it was taken from the plaintiff, with damages for the detention, but it is the value of the property at the date of the trial, with damages for the caption and detention, the latter of which are not measured by the standard of six per cent interest, but includes damages for depreciation, if any, since the taking and before the trial. The trial of a case in circuit court on appeal being de novo, the form of verdict in circuit court is controlled by the statutes governing replevin actions in courts of record.82 A judgment for the assessed value of the property, as requested by plaintiff, is not invalid, though it is not in the alternative, and such judgment is not subject to collateral attack by motion to quash execution.88 81 "Gibson vs. Ball, 159 Mo. c. Where defendant retains property.

If the defendant has given a bond for the delivery of the property, and retained the same, and the finding shall be for the plaintiff, the justice or jury shall also assess the value of the property and the damages for all injuries thereto and for the taking and detention, or detention, of the same, and the judgment shall be against the defendant and his sureties, that defendant shall return and deliver the property or pay the assessed value thereof, at the election of the plaintiff, and the plaintiff recover the damages so assessed, and the costs of suit (Sec. 2566). The circuit court on appeal has no power to vacate a judgment of a justice, the only way by which it has any control over such judgment being by trying the cause de novo and thereafter entering such judgment as may appear proper. It has been held that though a delivery bond is obtained, if the property was not in defendant's possession when the suit was brought, an action of replevin cannot be maintained.35 Judgment for a plaintiff should not be for a greater amount than the petition authorizes, but the plaintiff has the option of taking the property or the amount of the judgment, when the judgment conforms to the petition.³

If the jury, after hearing the evidence, shall be satisfied that the property belonged to the defendant at the commencement of the action, or that the defendant was entitled to the possession or had a special interest in the same at that time, they shall find accordingly and shall assess the value of such property or the value of the defendant's right thereto, and any damages for withholding the same which may be just and proper. b. Damages. 

In all cases where the property has been delivered to the plaintiff, and the justice or jury shall find for the defendant, they shall find whether the defendant had the right of property, or the right of possession only, at the commencement of the suit, and if they find either in his favor they shall also find the value of the property, or the value of the possession, and such damages for withholding said property as may be just and proper (Sec. 2569). The form of a judgment for the defendant may follow the form of judgment for plaintiff heretofore set out, except that it should be adapted to the various controlling statutes, and should follow generally the verdict of the jury. 

Sec. 286. Enforcement of Judgment for Plaintiff. 

The plaintiff shall not be required to elect as to whether the defendant shall return and deliver the property or pay the assessed value thereof, until the property is delivered to the constable on the execution and the plaintiff has notice thereof; and if the property shall not be delivered to the constable within ten days after the execution issued, the plaintiff may cause the asesssed value thereof and the damages and costs to be levied of the property of the defendant and his sureties (Sec. 2567).

Sec. 287. Enforcement of Judgment for Defendant. 

If such property shall not be produced and delivered to the constable within ten days after execution issued, the defendant may cause the assessed value thereof and the damages and costs to be levied of the property of the plaintiff's sureties (Sec. 2571). 

Sec. 288. Action and Defenses on Bond When Plaintiff Dismisses 

Suit.

In all cases where the property has been taken and delivered to the plaintiff, or is in his possession, and the proceedings before the justices, or, in case of appeal, in the circuit court, shall be dismissed for the want of jurisdiction, the defendant shall have a right of action upon the bond against the plaintiff and his sureties on such 363

JUSTICE COURTS 

bond. In such action defendant shall have the right to set up as a defense the ownership or the right of possession of the property involved in the original replevin suit, but such defense may only be made where it is made to appear on the trial of such case that the right of possession was in defendant at the date of the bringing of the original replevin suit. (Sec. 2572.) A failure to prosecute a replevin suit to a conclusion constitutes a breach of the bond and warrants suit thereon, although there may have been no judgment in the replevin suit, either for damages or for a return of the property.52 An action will not lie for a breach of the replevin bond until a final determination of the replevin suit.53 A cause of action accrues for a breach of the bond where the property is not returned as the condition of the bond required. 54 Where a cause in replevin has been appealed to the circuit court, action for a breach of the bond is properly brought in the circuit court, as the justice court has not jurisdiction over such a suit.55 A summary judgment cannot be had on a bond where a suit is dismissed for want of jurisdiction, but recourse must be had in a direct action on the bond.56 In an action on a bond where a replevin suit has been dismissed, the defendant may set up as a defense that the ownership and right to possession of the replevied property was in the defendant and that plaintiff was not injured by the taking and detention.57

IV.  A. MISDEMEANORS Sec. 289. Misdemeanors and Felonies Defined and Distinguished. 

Criminal offenses are divided into two general classes, namely, misdemeanors and felonies. The statute defines the term "misdemeanor" as an offense punishable only by fine or imprisonment in

Sec. 290. Jurisdiction and Venue. 

Justices of the peace have always had criminal jurisdiction.59 

But such jurisdiction has been limited to that of trying and convicting offenders for misdemeanors or minor offenses and committing offenders prosecuted for felonies.60 The statute gives justices of the peace concurrent original jurisdiction with the circuit court, coextensive with their respective counties, in all cases of misdemeanors, except in cities having courts exercising exclusive jurisdiction in criminal cases, or as otherwise provided by law, but such prosecutions must be commenced and prosecuted in the township wherein the offense is alleged to have been committed; except where the defendant is authorized to take a change of venue (Sec. 

3414). JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 291. Prosecutions Instituted by Complaint or Information. 

The statute requires that prosecutions for misdemeanors shall be by information (Sec. 3415). When any person has actual knowledge that any offense has been committed that may be prosecuted by information, he may make complaint, verified by his oath or affirmation, before any officer authorized to administer oaths, setting forth the offense, and file the same with the justice of the peace having jurisdiction of the offense, or deliver same to the prosecuting attorney. Whenever the prosecuting attorney has knowledge, information or belief that an offense has been committed, cognizable by a justice of the peace in his county, or shall be informed thereof by complaint made and delivered to him as aforesaid, he shall forthwith file an information with a justice having jurisdiction of the offense, founded upon or accompanied by such complaint. (Sec. 

3415.) Thus a prosecuting attorney may file an information based upon his own knowledge, information or belief, or he may file an information based upon a complaint made by some other person.65 

If a complaint is filed, the prosecuting attorney may, in his discretion, file an information or refuse to do so, or he may ignore the complaint and file an information on his own information and belief. On the other hand, he may file an information charging any offense comprehended by the complaint. If the information is based upon the complaint, such fact must be stated in the information. If there is a complaint, it must either be filed with the justice or delivered to the prosecuting attorney and accompany the information. The information must follow the complaint,"¹ and if not based on the complaint the record should so show." The information cannot be based on both the affidavit and the prose- 66

Sec. 292. Essentials of Complaints. 

Complaints may be made by persons having actual knowledge that an offense has been committed. Any such complaint shall be verified by the oath or affirmation of the person making it before any officer authorized to administer oaths, and shall set forth a statement of the offense charged. The complaint must be filed with the justice of the peace having jurisdiction of the offense, or delivered to the prosecuting attorney. (Sec. 3415.) Technical accuracy in the complaint is not required," and it need not recite that affiant is a competent person.75 It should set forth the offense in plain and concise language,76 and it will be held good if it be made upon the best knowledge and belief of the affiant." But if it is made upon information and belief, it is insufficient,78 as convictions cannot be had upon complaints made by persons having no actual knowledge.79 

Informations based on insufficient complaints must be quashed.80 

If an information is based on a complaint and contains more than one count, there must be a complaint for each count.81

Sec. 296. Arrest Without a Warrant.

The statute provides that if any justice of the peace shall have personal knowledge that any affray or breach of the peace is about to be committed, he shall issue his warrant; and if any such offense is committed, threatened or attempted in his presence, he shall arrest the offender immediately, or cause it to be done; and for this purpose no warrant or process shall be necessary, but the justice may summon to his assistance any sheriff, coroner or constable, and all other persons there present, whose duty it shall be to aid the justice in preserving the peace, arresting and securing the offenders, and all such as obstruct or prevent the justice or any of his assistants in the performance of their duties (Sec. 3419). But it has been held that a justice has no authority to arrest without a warrant upon information derived from another.100 It has also been held that, while a justice of the peace has a right to carry concealed weapons as a conserver of the peace, he has no right to do so because his life has been threatened a short time before.¹

Sec. 297. Filing of Information Must Precede Imprisonment or Trial. 

When any person shall be arrested upon the verbal order of the justice, or upon a warrant issued upon his own knowledge, the person so arrested may be kept in custody for the space of two hours, unless he shall be sooner taken from such custody by virtue of a warrant issued upon an information or complaint under oath, as "Adapted from Form No. 124, III R. S. Mo. 1929, p. 3849. 

100 State vs. May, 142 Mo. 135, 43 S. W. 637. 

¹ State vs. Davis, 284 Mo. 695, 225 S. W. 707. 372

required in other cases; but the person so arrested shall not be confined in jail, nor put upon trial for any offense until he shall be charged therewith by information (Sec. 3420).

When the defendant shall be brought before the justice of the peace, or shall be held in custody, charged by information with any misdemeanor, it shall be the duty of the justice, unless a continuance be granted, forthwith to hear the case (Sec. 3421).

Sec. 298. Witness, How Subpoenaed and Served. 

It shall be the duty of the justice in all cases to summon the injured party as a witness, when he is not present and his presence may be procured; and at the request of the defendant or prosecuting attorney, or prosecuting witness, he shall summon all persons as witnesses whose testimony may be deemed material, and enforce their attendance by attachment, if necessary. In those cases filed by the prosecuting attorney upon information furnished by a prosecuting witness, and where the prosecuting attorney has given a list of the witnesses to be subpoenaed on the part of the State, if the prosecuting witness shall order subpoenas for witnesses in addition to those ordered by the prosecuting attorney, he shall be liable for the costs of all such witnesses not used on a trial of said cause, and it shall be the duty of the justice to tax such prosecuting witness with all costs of subpoenaing, serving and attendance of such witness, and the State nor county shall in nowise be liable for any such costs. (Sec. 3422.)

Either party shall order all his witnesses at one time, and they shall be included in one subpoena; but the justice may, for good cause shown, issue additional subpoenas, and he may, at the request of a party, issue such additional subpoenas at the cost of the party ordering the same (Sec. 3423).

When a cause shall be continued or a change of venue awarded, it shall not be necessary to summon the witnesses again but the justice. shall verbally notify them, or such of them as either party may require, to attend and testify in the case on the day of trial, or before the justice to whom the case shall be sent, which verbal notice shall be as valid as a summons (Sec. 3424). 373

Sec. 299. Continuance and Postponements. 

Upon good cause shown, the justice may postpone the trial of a cause to a day certain; in which case he shall require the defendant to enter into a recognizance with sufficient security, conditioned that he will appear before the justice at the time and place appointed, then and there to answer the charge alleged against him in the information, and not to depart without leave (Sec. 3425).

A motion to postpone the trial on account of the absence of evidence can be made only upon oath or affidavit, showing the materiality of the evidence expected to be obtained, and that due diligence has been used to obtain it, or good excuse for not using such diligence, and where the evidence may be; and if it is for an absent witness the application must conform to and be governed by the provisions of the statutes relative to proceedings for continuances in criminal cases in courts of record (Sec. 3427). It has been held that where a defendant enters into a recognizance for his appearance on a day certain, and on that day appears, and the cause is continued, no new recognizance is required.² 2 'City of St. Louis vs. Young, 235 Mo. 44, 138 S. Sec. 300. Commitment of Defendant.

If the defendant shall fail or refuse to enter into a recognizance, the justice shall commit him to the common jail of the county, or to the calaboose or other prison of the city where the trial is pending, there to remain until the day fixed for the trial of the charge alleged against him (Sec. 3426).

Sec. 301. Change of Venue. 

a. When and for what causes granted.

The defendant shall be entitled to a change of venue if he shall, before the trial of the case is commenced before the justice, or before the jury is sworn, file an affidavit, stating that the justice is prejudiced against him, or is a near relation to the injured party or prosecuting witness, stating in what degree, or interested in the subject of the offense, or is a material witness in the case, or that 'III R. S. Mo. 1929, p. 3850, Form No. 129. 376

the defendant cannot have a fair trial in the township, on account of the bias or prejudice of the inhabitants thereof, as the defendant verily believes (Sec. 3429). b. How completed and to whom certified.

If such affidavit be filed, the change of venue must be allowed, and the justice must immediately transmit all the original papers and a transcript of all his docket entries in the case to the next nearest justice in the township, if there be one, unless the party asking for a change of venue shall, in his affidavit, state that the other justice in the township is a material witness for him, without whose testimony he cannot safely proceed to trial, or that he is near of kin to the injured party or prosecuting witness, stating in what degree, or that he cannot have a fair and impartial trial before such justice in the township, in which case, then to a justice in some other township in the county, or, if the change be allowed on account of the bias or prejudice of the inhabitants of the township, then to a justice in some other township in the county; and the justice to whom such case shall be sent shall proceed forthwith with the same in like manner as if said cause had been originally brought before him. No more than one change of venue in the same case shall be allowed. (Sec. 3430.) 4 It has been held that where there was another justice of the peace in the township where the case was pending, who had been subpoenaed, the justice of the peace before whom defendant was arraigned, exceeded his powers in sending the cause to a justice of the peace of another township on motion for change of venue, and that the latter had no jurisdiction and could be prevented from proceeding by a writ of prohibition. It has also been held that where a felony was committed in a township having four justices of the peace, and defendant's affidavit for change of venue disqualified three of them for bias and prejudice, the case should have been transferred to the fourth justice in the township, and not to a justice in another township in the county." Where a defendant voluntarily appears before the justice to whom the case was awarded 'State ex rel. McGinnis vs. Melton (App.), 31 S. W. (2d) 248. 

Ibid.; State ex rel. Hazel vs. Watkins, 212 Mo. A. 501, 253 S. W. 781. 377

JUSTICE COURTS 

on change of venue, and engages in trial without objection, he cannot thereafter object because the transcript does not affirmatively show that such justice was the next nearest justice." c. Recognizance for change of venue. 

When a change is granted, the justice shall require the defendant to enter into a recognizance with sufficient surety to appear before the justice to whom the case is sent to answer to the same, and in default thereof the defendant shall be conveyed before such justice by the constable to abide the judgment and order of such justice 

(Sec. 3431).

Sec. 302. Plea of Defendant and Docket Entry Thereof. 

The charge made against the defendant shall be distinctly read to him, unless he shall waive the reading of the same, and he must plead orally thereto, either guilty or not guilty, which plea the justice shall enter on his docket (Sec. 3433). Sec. 303. Judgment on Plea of Guilty.

The statute provides that if the defendant shall plead guilty or confess the charge, the justice shall assess the punishment and enter up the proper judgment, and in order thereto he may hear evidence touching the nature of the case, or otherwise ascertain the facts thereof; but in no case shall he accept the plea of the defendant and assess his punishment without giving the injured party notice and an opportunity to be heard (Sec. 3434). The justice does not have to hear evidence from anyone but the injured party,12 and if there is no injured party he may ascertain the facts by hearing evidence or otherwise.18

Sec. 304. Trial. 

a. Practice in circuit court governs. 

14 The statute provides that all misdemeanors before justices of the peace shall be governed by the practice in criminal cases in courts of record, so far as the same may be applicable, and in respect to which no provision is made by statute (Sec. 3446). Thus such trials shall proceed along the same lines as if they were being held in circuit court, the opening statements, the production of evidence, and the arguments by each side being made in the same order and in the same manner. But it has been held that this provision of the statute does not authorize a justice to appoint an elisor, that is, a person to act for an officer who is disqualified to act himself, to act in lieu of the constable.15 An information in a prosecution for a misdemeanor originating in a justice court has been held amendable on appeal in circuit court.16 b. Prosecuting attorney must appear for state. 

The statute requires that a prosecuting attorney of the county shall appear and prosecute all misdemeanors to be tried before any justice of the peace of the county where such prosecutions originate (Sec. 3447). c. Before justice or jury.

The statute provides that after the plea of the defendant has been entered, if he plead not guilty, the defendant or prosecuting witness, or prosecuting attorney, may demand a jury; but if no jury is demanded the case may be tried by the justice (Sec. 3435). d. Jurors, their qualifications and selection.

All jury trials before a justice of the peace shall be by a jury of six men, unless a less number shall be agreed upon. If a jury be

www demanded, the justice shall cause twelve men to be summoned, whose qualifications shall be ascertained or proved as required of jurors in courts of record; and a list of twelve qualified jurors shall be furnished to the parties. The state shall first strike off three names, then the defendant shall strike off three, and the remaining six shall compose the jury, who shall be sworn to try the cause. If the parties do not make all their challenges, the first six names remaining on the list unchallenged shall compose the jury. (Sec. 3436.)

238. FORM OF OATH TO JURY TO TRY CAUSE

The jury shall sit together while they hear the case, and may decide the case in the jury box or retire to some convenient room or 382

place to deliberate upon their verdict, during which time they shall not hold any conversation or communication with anyone upon any matter pertaining to the case (Sec. 3437). 

f. Verdicts. 

The jury shall in all cases assess the punishment prescribed by law for the offense, and designate the same by their verdict, or if they find the defendant guilty and fail to agree upon the punishment, or shall assess any wrong punishment, the justice may assess the punishment by the consent of the parties; but if the parties do not consent, or if the jury fail to agree upon a verdict and are discharged, the justice shall issue his summons for another jury and proceed to try the case again, and, if necessary, may continue the case until another day, and dispose of the defendant as in other cases of continuance (Sec. 3438). Verdicts must be agreed upon by all members of the jury and must be in writing and signed by the foreman 

(Sec. 3439).

Sec. 305. Fines Commuted to Imprisonment. 19.....

When any person shall be unable to pay any fine and costs assessed against him, the justice shall have power, at the request of the defendant, to commute such fine and costs to imprisonment in the county jail for any period of time not exceeding one day's imprisonment for every two dollars of said fine and costs, nor less than one day's imprisonment for every ten dollars of such fine and costs (Sec. 3441). The giving of this power to justices of the peace was not in conflict with the Constitution (Art. 5, Sec. 8) giving the 

Governor power to grant reprieves, commutations and pardons.22

Where a judgment against a defendant has been that he be imprisoned, or where it is necessary to commit the prisoner for nonpayment of fines or costs, the justice must issue a warrant of commitment (Sec. 3443).

Sec. 306. Appeals From Judgments of Conviction. 

The statute authorizes any person convicted before a justice of the peace for any misdemeanor to appeal to the circuit or other court having jurisdiction in criminal cases. To take such appeal a defendant must immediately after judgment is rendered file an affidavit stating that he is aggrieved by the verdict and judgment in the case, and that he does not make his appeal for vexation or delay. He shall also enter into a recognizance in such sum as the justice shall deem proper, with good and sufficient sureties to be approved by the justice, conditioned that the defendant shall appear at the next term and from day to day and term to term thereafter, of the said circuit 

23 Sec. 3442. 

24 Sec. 3443. 386

court, and prosecute his appeal with due diligence to a decision, and obey every order, sentence and judgment, which shall be made in the premises, and not depart the court without leave. In taking such recognizance, the justice shall not consider the judgment of the justice and costs accrued therein in fixing the amount of such recognizance, but shall only require the recognizance to be sufficient to secure the attendance of the applicant at the next term of the circuit court, and such appeal shall operate as a stay of execution thereon until trial of the case anew has been had in the circuit court. Failure to give the recognizance does not prevent the appeal, but the appellant shall remain in custody or be committed to jail until recognizance be given or the appeal determined. Should the bond be given after the defendant has been committed, it must be approved by the sheriff, and when so approved the defendant shall be released by the sheriff or marshal from custody. (Sec. 3448, as amended 

Laws 1931, p. 202.)

A defendant cannot appeal from a plea of guilty,25 but for the purpose of challenging the sufficiency of the information under which he entered a plea of guilty a defendant has the right of appeal.20 The right of appeal is purely statutory, and the statute must be complied with to give the appellate court jurisdiction, unless the statute authorizing appeals is complied with.27 The appeal is perfected by the filing of the affidavit and not by the giving of the bond.28 The word "immediately," as used in the statute, refers to the filing of the affidavit.29 In the absence of satisfactory reasons for delay, affidavit should be filed on the day of the conviction.80 Where a defendant was convicted at ten o'clock at night, the trial lasting that the

The statute directs that when an appeal is taken in misdemeanor cases from judgments of a justice of the peace, all material witnesses shall be required to enter into a recognizance in the sum of Fifty Dollars each, conditioned for their appearance to testify in the cause at the term to which the appeal is returnable (Sec. 3451).

Sec. 308. Transfer of Cause by Appeal.

The statute requires that within three days after the appeal is taken, the justice shall file in the office of the clerk of the court having jurisdiction of the appeal, a copy of the entries on his docket, with the affidavit of appeal and all original papers filed in the case, including the recognizance of the witnesses and of the defendant for his appeal, duly certified by the justice (Sec. 3451). Sec. 309. De Novo Trial in Circuit Court. 

If the appeal has been regularly taken, the case shall be heard on its merits at the first term of the court after the same shall have been filed in the clerk's office, or if said appeal be taken and filed in term, it shall be returnable to and triable at such term, unless for good cause shown the case be continued; and unless otherwise ordered by the court, the costs in both courts shall abide the event of the trial in the circuit or appellate court (Sec. 3452). Misdemeanor cases appealed from justices of the peace are tried de novo in the circuit court as though the case originated there. But on the trial in the circuit court, the scope of the evidence is not limited by the evidence in the justice court.48 Errors committed in the trial in the justice court are immaterial on appeal, such as a failure to arraign the defendant, or failure to specify in the judgment on which of two counts defendant was convicted.50 But if a defendant goes to trial without objection, arraignment is waived."1 49

Sec. 312. Defendant May Be Discharged.

Any defendant committed under a judgment of affirmance rendered in the appellate court for nonpayment of any fine and costs may be discharged from such terms by an order of the court commuting same to a jail sentence on the same basis as in the justice court (Secs. 3455, 3441 and 3442).

Sec. 313. Duties of Officers in Collection of Fines.

Sec. 314. Penalties Against Officers Failing to Discharge Duties. 

Any justice of the peace, clerk, county treasurer, sheriff, coroner, or constable, who shall wilfully neglect or refuse to perform any duty thus enjoined on him, shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor in office, and shall, moreover, pay the sum of fifty dollars; and any person who shall, when summoned to aid in arresting or securing an offender, refuse to give such assistance, shall pay five dollars (Sec. 3458).

Sec. 315. Judgments and Citations on Forfeited Recognizance. 

If the defendant shall neglect to appear for trial or judgment, or upon any other occasion when his presence may be lawfully required, before a justice, according to the condition of his recognizance, the justice must enter the default upon his docket, and the recognizance shall thereupon be adjudged forfeited (Sec. 3459). When judgment of forfeiture shall be entered upon any recognizance, the justice shall issue a citation to the defendant and his sureties in the recognizance, reciting therein that default has been made by the defendant and judgment of forfeiture rendered upon said recognizance, and that unless the defendant and his said sureties appear before such justice at a day and time designated in such citation, and show cause to the contrary, judgment will be entered against them for the full amount of said recognizance, with costs, and execution issued therefor (Sec. 3460).

Such citation shall be served on the defendants therein, as a summons is served in civil cases, at least fifteen days before the return day thereof (Sec. 3462). If any defendants named in such citation are not served in time, the justice may continue the case to a day certain and issue another citation to the parties not served (Sec. 3463).

Sec. 316. Judgment Upon Citation. 

When such citation shall have been served upon the defendants therein, or any of them, the justice shall, unless good cause be shown against it, proceed in a summary manner to render judgment against the defendant and his sureties in said recognizance, or such as are served, for the amount of the same, with costs; and instead of issuing an alias citation to those not served, he may dismiss as to those not served and proceed to final judgment against those served (Sec. 3463).

Sec. 318 Appeals. 

Any defendant against whom such a judgment may be rendered upon a forfeited recognizance may appeal from such judgment, at any time within ten days after the rendition of the judgment, by filing an affidavit stating that he verily believes himself injured and aggrieved by the judgment, and also entering into a recognizance with sufficient sureties, in the form and with the condition required in appeals from justices of the peace in civil cases; and the prosecuting attorney or prosecuting witness may appeal on behalf of the State, on filing an affidavit therefor, without giving recognizance (Sec. 3465).

Sec. 319. Judgments Not Defeated Because of Irregularities. 

No proceeding upon a recognizance shall be defeated, nor shall judgment thereon be prevented or arrested, on account of any defect of form, omission of recital, condition of undertaking therein, neglect of the justice or clerk to note or record the default of any principal or surety at the time or term when such default shall happen, or of any other irregularity, so that it be made to appear from the whole record or proceeding that the defendant was legally in custody, charged with a criminal offense, that he was discharged therefrom by reason of the giving of the recognizance, and that it can be ascertained from the recognizance that the sureties undertook that the defendant should appear before a court or magistrate at a term or time specified for trial (Sec. 3466).87 "State vs. Simmons, 284 Mo. 664, 225 S. JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 320. Jurisdiction. 

B. FELONIES 

A justice of the peace has authority to issue a warrant for and cause the arrest of a person accused of committing a felony by complaint made in writing and upon oath before him (Sec. 3467). If the offense charged is a bailable one, he is authorized to release the person charged upon a satisfactory bond being given for his appearance (Sec. 3468). He is further authorized to commit the offender (Sec. 3467) and to give him a preliminary examination for the purpose of determining whether or not he is guilty as charged or should be discharged (Sec. 3481), and if upon such examination he thinks that the prisoner should be discharged the justice has the right to discharge him (Sec. 3482). 

Sec. 321. Institution of Prosecution for Felony.

When a complaint shall be made in writing and upon oath before a justice of the peace or other magistrate, setting forth that a felony has been committed, and the name of the person accused thereof, it is the duty of such magistrate to issue a warrant reciting the accusation, and commanding the officer to whom it shall be directed to bring him before such justice or magistrate according to law (Sec. 

3467). The first step in the proceeding is the filing of the complaint with the justice, and a warrant should not be issued until such affidavit has been filed." 68

Sec. 322. Warrants, Their Issuance and Service. 

While an officer may arrest on reasonable suspicion without a warrant, ,69 the ordinary procedure before justices of the peace is for the prisoner to be brought before the justice after complaint has been made and a warrant issued. The warrant is issued by the justice after a complaint is filed with him, and the warrant is directed to an officer who is thereby commanded to bring the accused before the justice (Sec. 3467). A warrant thus issued by a justice of the peace may be executed in any part of the county within which the justice 

6 Monson vs. Rouse, 86 Mo. A. 97. "Wehmeyer vs. Mulvihill, 150 Mo. A. 197, 130 S. W. 681. 398

is an officer, unless it is endorsed for the purpose of proceeding against an offender who escapes to another county (Sec. 3469). If the writ is regular and fair on its face and is issued by a court having jurisdiction, the officer who serves the writ is fully protected.70 A prosecuting attorney cannot file an information against a prisoner in such proceeding until he is by the justice bound over to the circuit court." The proceeding before a justice not being a criminal prosecution, the complaint for a warrant should not be measured by the same rules applied to informations and indictments.72 A writ of habeas corpus ad prosequendum from the circuit court to the warden of the penitentiary is equivalent to a warrant for arrest, and involves no question of conflicting or territorial jurisdiction."

Sec. 323. Proceedings Where Offender Escapes to Another 

County.

If the person against whom any warrant granted by a justice of the peace shall be issued, escape or be in any other county, it shall be the duty of any magistrate authorized to issue a warrant in the county in which such offender may be or is suspected to be, on proof of the handwriting of the magistrate issuing the warrant to endorse his name thereon, and thereupon the offender may be arrested in such county by the officer bringing such warrant, or any officer within the county within which the warrant is so endorsed; and any such warrant may be executed in any county within this State by the officer to whom it is directed, if the clerk of the county court of the county in which the warrant was issued shall endorse upon or annex to the warrant his certificate, with the seal of said court affixed thereto, that the officer who issued such warrant was at the time an acting officer fully authorized to issue the same, and that his signature thereto is genuine (Sec. 3470).

When any person who shall have committed a felony in one county shall escape into another, any magistrate within the county in which such offender may be found may, upon complaint in writing and upon oath being made before him charging such person with such offense, issue his warrant for the apprehension of such offender, and the officer making the arrest shall convey the prisoner to the county in which the offense is charged to have been committed (Sec. 3471). 

It is generally held that a warrant issued by a justice is invalid outside of the county in which the justice resides, unless it is properly endorsed.75

Sec. 324. Place of Holding Preliminary. 

Persons arrested under a warrant for any offense shall, when no provision is otherwise made, be brought before the magistrate who issued the warrant, or if he be absent or his office be vacant, or if he be not authorized to act within the county in which the offense was committed, then before the nearest magistrate in such county; and the warrant by virtue of which the arrest was made, with a proper return endorsed thereon, and signed by the officer or person making the arrest, shall be delivered to such magistrate (Sec. 3472). But a person charged may remove the cause to another justice by change of venue (Sec. 3429), and if a person charged applies for a change of venue before the trial is commenced before the justice in the manner required by statute (Sec. 3429), and the justice refuses to grant the change of venue, mandamus will lie to compel the justice to send the cause to another justice." It has been held that where a felony was committed in a township having four justices of the peace and the defendant's affidavit for a change of venue disqualified three of them for bias and prejudice, the case should have been transferred to the fourth justice in the township, and not to a justice in another township in the county."" 

Sec. 325. Necessity for and Purpose of Preliminary Hearing. 

a. Preliminary unnecessary where proceeding is by indictment. 

The statutes do not require a preliminary hearing to be given a defendant who is indicted by a grand jury, and the courts follow the statute and hold that where the proceeding against a defendant is by indictment he is not entitled to a preliminary examination.78 b. Preliminary necessary where proceeding is by information. 

A preliminary examination must be given an accused charged with committing a felony where the proceeding is instituted against him by information." The right to such an examination is statutory, and, since the statute confines the right to those charged of felonies 

76 State ex rel. Hazel vs. Watkins, 212 Mo. A. 501, 253 S. W. 781; State vs. 

Brumley, 53 Mo. A. 126. "State ex rel. Hazel vs. Watkins, 212 Mo. A. 501, 253 S. W. 781. 

78 State vs. Sanders (Sup.), 4 S. W. (2d) 813; State vs. Burlison, 315 Mo. 232, 285 S. W. 712. 

State vs. Teague, 190 Mo. A. 280, 176 S. W. 250. 401

JUSTICE COURTS 

by information only, the right cannot be extended beyond such statutory limitations.80 Formerly, preliminary examinations were required only in capital cases. 81 The information charging an accused need not allege that a preliminary examination has been held, for in any case a failure to accord the accused a preliminary examination is not jurisdictional but only goes to the regularity of the proceedings.82 Thus the jurisdiction of the circuit court to try a defendant charged with a felony cannot be defeated merely by a record showing that a preliminary examination had not been accorded the accused.88 c. Purpose of preliminary hearing.

The law providing for preliminary hearings was framed to serve a dual purpose, the first of which was to accord persons charged with felony the privilege at the outset of the prosecution to have a hearing, to the end that groundless or vindictive prosecutions might not be continued, and the second of which was to preserve the evidence against a defendant and enable the State to have the witnesses enter into a recognizance to appear before the court having jurisdiction to finally try the cause.84 It is an expedient to prevent a suspected person from escaping, and to preserve the evidence and keep the witnesses within the control of the State.85 A preliminary examination is in no sense a trial, in that the guilt or innocence of the accused is not thereby generally determined, but it is a course of procedure authorized whereby a possible abuse of power may be prevented, and the accused discharged or held to answer, as the facts warrant.86

Sec. 328. Consequence of Failure to Appear for Preliminary Hearing. 

If the person recognized does not appear before the magistrate according to the condition of such recognizance, the magistrate shall record the default, but such default may be set aside by the magistrate on the appearance of the prisoner and, for good cause shown, at any time to which the examination may be continued by said magistrate; and in case such default be not set aside, as aforesaid, the magistrate shall certify the recognizance, with a record of such default, to the court having cognizance of the offense charged against the person so recognized, and like proceedings shall be had thereon as upon breach of condition of a recognizance for appearance before said court (Sec. 3475).

Sec. 329. Preliminary Hearing. 

a. Justice may call in an associate.

The statute authorizes any magistrate to whom any complaint is made, or before whom any prisoner shall be brought, to associate with himself any other magistrate of the same county, and the powers and duties imposed by law upon any magistrate may in such case be executed by the two so associated. If there should be a difference of opinion between the two magistrates on any question, the decision of the one before whom the case was first pending and before an associate was called in shall prevail (Sec. 3491). b. Reading of complaint and giving prisoner opportunity to consult counsel.

The statute requires the magistrate to inform the prisoner strictly of the charge made against him and read to him the complaint, if requested to do so, and allow the prisoner reasonable time to advise with his counsel and for that purpose to send for counsel, if he require it (Sec. 3477). The statutory provision giving a defendant reasonable time to advise with counsel is in conformity with the constitutional provisions that in criminal prosecutions the accused shall have the right to appeal and defend in person and by counsel (Art. 2, Sec. 21). The right must be observed. If a defendant is not represented by counsel or given time to procure the attendance of his witnesses after the original complaint against him has been dismissed and a new proceeding is instituted, his preliminary examination is illegal.100 

c. Order of conducting trial. 

The statute provides that the order of conducting the trial or hearing, with respect to the introduction of the evidence and the examination of witnesses, shall be the same as govern in the trial of causes in courts of record, as far as practicable (Sec. 3479). "State ex rel. Cave vs. Tincher, 258 Mo. 1, 166 S. W. 1028; State vs. Page, 21 

Mo. 257; State vs. Jones, 12 Mo. A. 93. 

100 State vs. McNeal, 304 Mo. 119, 262 S. W. 1025. 405

JUSTICE COURTS d. Exclusion of witnesses. 

While any witness for or against the prisoner is under examination, the magistrate may exclude from the place in which such examination is had all witnesses who have not been examined, and he may cause the witnesses to be kept separate and prevented from conversing with each other, until they shall have been examined (Sec. 3478). e. Submission of evidence by State.

The statute requires the justice to proceed as soon as may be to examine the complainant and witnesses produced in support of the prosecution, on oath, in the presence of the prisoner, in regard to the offense charged, and other matters connected with such charge which the magistrate may deem pertinent (Sec. 3473). If the defendant waives the preliminary examination, it is not necessary for the State to produce any evidence, and the justice may immediately bind the defendant over to the circuit court. f. Evidence by prisoner.

The statute gives the prisoner the option to be sworn and examined as a witness in his behalf, and to produce witnesses in his be half. If the prisoner elects to testify himself or produce witnesses in his behalf, they must be sworn and examined under the restrictions applicable to the examination of defendants in the trial of criminal cases. (Sec. 3481.) Ordinarily, of course, a defendant does not testify or produce the testimony of witnesses in his behalf, unless he hopes thereby to prevail upon the justice to discharge him. g. Adjournment of cause.

The statute provides that a magistrate may adjourn an examination of a prisoner pending before himself from time to time as occasion requires, not exceeding ten days at one time, and to the same or any different place in the county, as he deems necessary. Such adjournment may be allowed on the motion of the prisoner. During such adjournment the prisoner shall be committed, if the offense with which he is charged is not bailable, otherwise he may give a bond for his appearance. (Sec. 3474.) 406

Sec. 330. Preservation of Testimony in Homicide Hearings. 

8 The statute provides that in all cases of homicide, but in no other, the evidence given by the several witnesses shall be reduced to writing by the magistrate or under his direction and signed by the witnesses respectively (Sec. 3480). In preliminary hearings a justice is the sole judge of the competency and weight of the evidence, in the absence of fraud or arbitrary conduct.¹ A nonresident witness's testimony at a preliminary examination, not signed by him and certified by the justice, has been held inadmissible.2 In a second prosecution for homicide after a mistrial, it was held error to permit the introduction in evidence of unsigned testimony of a witness given at the first trial who was since deceased. The transcript of testimony at a preliminary hearing may be introduced when the witness is out of the jurisdiction of the court. By entering into an agreement that in the absence of the official stenographer another stenographer should take the testimony and that the original transcript should be delivered to the attorney for the State and an exact carbon thereof to the attorney for the defendant, the defendant thereby waived compliance with the statute authorizing the preservation of testimony in homicide cases. If the deponent is unable to sign his own name, it has been held that his signature by another at his request was in legal effect his own signature. It has been held that where a prisoner was committed to jail for failure to furnish the recognizance required by the statute, the court in a habeas corpus proceeding could not review the competency or sufficiency of evidence introduced at a preliminary hearing." Testimony taken down in shorthand at a preliminary hearing, after being transcribed and signed by witnesses only before examining magistrate's successor, was held a sufficient compliance with the statute to authorize its introduction in evidence.Ⓡ 'Ex parte Cloud (App.), 18 S. JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 331. In Preliminary Hearing Justice Does Not Exercise Judicial Power. 

While a preliminary hearing is a proceeding in the nature of a trial conducted before a judicial tribunal, and according to judicial methods and procedure, it is generally held that when a justice of the peace holds a preliminary hearing he does not exercise judicial power." In a preliminary examination the justice does not act in the capacity of the court. He does not determine the question of the guilt or innocence of the accused. His conclusion is not a judgment, and if he makes no records on his docket of the proceedings on the 'State ex rel. Board of Education of City of St. Louis vs. Nast, 209 Mo. 708, 108 S. W. 563. 

The discussion of this point in the foregoing case is significant: "We concede that the power or authority conferred by this act is in its nature judicial. The justice of the peace is called upon to exercise judgment and discretion. He is to judge of the sufficiency of the affidavit on which the warrant of arrest is founded. 

He must determine upon the evidence adduced against the prisoner whether there is reasonable ground of suspicion against him so as to require that he should be put upon trial for the offense; and he is to imprison or take bail for the appearance of the party at court to abide his trial. But, although such authority involves in its exercise judicial functions, we are very clear it does not fall within the meaning of 'judicial power' in the sense in which that term is used in the third article of the Constitution. It is manifest, we think, that by the term 'judicial power' is here meant that power with which the courts are to be clothed for the purpose of the trial and determining of causes. commitment is not such an act of judicial power as requires that it should be exercised by courts or judges within the meaning of the third article of the Constitution. By judicial power is there meant such regular and permanent duties as belong to courts and judges in the ordinary and popular signification of the words. A justice of the peace or any other person designated by the act of Congress may be authorized to commit, although they cannot be required or compelled to do so. The magistrate in exercising this jurisdiction appears to act, not judicially but ministerially; at least he does not put forth 'judicial power,' within the meaning of the Constitution of the United States. Cer- tainly the conclusion of the committing magistrate in no sense partakes of a judgment; for, whether held over or discharged, it is no bar to a further prosecution by the state. . . . As said by the Supreme Court of Alabama, the fact that some of the duties devolving upon the examining magistrate partake of a judicial character does not bring them within the grant of the judicial power of the state and constitute the said court or the judge thereof one of the courts in which the judicial power is vested by the Constitution.'' ... 408

preliminary hearing, the accused cannot complain if he has in fact had such hearing."

Sec. 332. Discharge of Prisoner. 

The statute authorizes the magistrate to discharge the prisoner if, upon the examination of the whole matter, it appears to the magistrate either that no offense has been committed by any person, or that there is no probable cause for charging the prisoner therewith (Sec. 

3482). The prisoner's discharge has been held prima facie evidence of want of probable cause.11 But the discharge of a prisoner is not a bar to further prosecution by the State for the same offense under an indictment returned by a grand jury.12 This does not mean, however, that a prosecuting attorney may, upon the discharge of a defendant after a preliminary hearing, file an information against the same defendant in circuit court for the same offense, for, although such practice has been resorted to, it is now definitely settled that a prosecuting attorney is without authority to file an information charging a felony in the absence of a finding by a magistrate that a felony has been committed and that there is probable cause to believe the prisoner guilty thereof.¹ 18 

Sec. 333. Prisoner May Be Bound Over to Circuit Court. 

A justice of the peace on a preliminary hearing is empowered either to discharge the prisoner, as already stated, or to bind him over to the circuit court. Sec. 335. Order Committing Prisoner. 

If the offense is not bailable or a sufficient bail is not offered, the justice shall order the prisoner committed to the jail of the county in which he is to be tried, and to remain until he is discharged by due course of law (Sec. 3487). When the prisoner is committed to jail for a bailable offense, the justice must endorse on the warrant of commitment the sum on which bail was required (Sec. 3488). Sec. 337. Pursuit and Arrest of Felon. 

The statute provides that whenever any felony shall be committed, and the offender attempt to escape, public notice thereof shall be immediately given, at all places near where the same was committed, and pursuit shall be forthwith made after the offender by sheriffs, coroners and constables, and all others who shall be thereto required by any such officers; and the offender may be arrested by any such officer or his assistants without warrant (Sec. 3492).

When any person shall be so pursued and arrested, he shall be immediately taken before some magistrate authorized to act under the provisions of the law, who shall proceed thereon in the same manner as if the prisoner had been arrested on a warrant (Sec. 

Every sheriff, marshal, coroner, constable or police officer who shall fail or refuse to pursue and arrest any offender, as required by the preceding provisions, shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor, and shall be punished by a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year, or by both such fine and imprisonment (Sec. 3494).

A justice of the peace is without authority to appoint a special constable to serve a warrant in a case of felony." .35 If a peace officer acts without a warrant it must be upon a reasonable suspicion." 

Either a policeman or a town marshal may make an arrest.³7 The statute authorizes officers in making arrests in criminal actions to break open any outer or inner door or window of a dwelling house, or other building, or other enclosure, if, after notice of his office and purpose, he be refused admittance (Sec. 3499).

Whenever the county court of any county in this State, or any two judges thereof in vacation, shall be satisfied that any felony has been committed in said county, such court or judges may, at their discretion, offer a standing reward of not exceeding five hundred dollars for the apprehension and arrest of the person or persons committing the same, which reward shall be paid out of the county "State vs. Julian, 25 Mo. Sec. 338. Defendant May Be Admitted to Bail After Commitment.

Whenever any person shall be committed to jail on a warrant of commitment by any magistrate for a bailable offense, the recognizance, with proper security, may be taken by the court or judge of the court having criminal jurisdiction, and in case of the absence of the judge of such court having criminal jurisdiction from the county, such recognizance may be taken by any judge or justice of the county court, or any judge of a court of record (Sec. 3495). A justice of the peace has no authority to admit a prisoner to bail after committing him to prison, but where the justice fixes the amount of the bail a sheriff may take the bond." Where the bond is taken by a court of record it will be presumed that the necessary preliminary steps were taken.¹ 40 39 Whenever any prisoner shall be let to bail by any court, it shall be the duty of the clerk of the court by which the prisoner was bailed immediately to transmit the recognizance taken by such court to the clerk of the court in which the party bailed is required to appear (Sec. 3496).

Whenever any prisoner shall be let to bail by any officer out of such court, such officer shall immediately cause the recognizance taken by him to be filed with the clerk of the court in which the prisoner is recognized to appear (Sec. 3497). The clerk's duty is to transmit the bond and not merely authenticate the act by his signature. C. MISCELLANEOUS PROCEEDINGS OF A CRIMINAL NATURE 1. Proceedings to Preserve the Peace. 

Sec. 339.

Jurisdiction of a  

Justices of the peace within their respective counties have power and jurisdiction to cause to be kept all laws made for the preservation of the public peace, to issue process for the apprehension of persons charged with criminal offenses, and hold them to bail; require persons to give security to keep the peace, and to execute the powers and duties conferred upon them in relation thereto. Other officers similarly empowered are, the judges of the Supreme Court, throughout the State; judges of the courts of record, within their respective jurisdictions; judges of the county courts, within their respective counties; the mayors and police judges of incorporated cities and towns, within the limits of their respective corporations. (Sec. 3401.) 

Sec. 340. Institution of Proceeding for Peace Bond. 

a. Where affray is committed in presence of magistrate.

Every person who, in the presence of any magistrate heretofore named, or of any court of record, shall make an affray, or threaten to kill or beat another or to commit any offense against his person or property, and all persons who, in the presence of such court or magistrate, shall contend with hot and angry words, may be ordered by such magistrate or court, without any other proof or trial, to give security to keep the peace, and in case of failure or refusal so to do, he may be committed to prison until such security is given (Sec. 3407). b. Upon verified written complaint.

Whenever complaint shall be made in writing, and upon oath, to any such magistrate, that any person has threatened or is about to commit any offense against the person or property of another speci- 417

JUSTICE COURTS 

fied, it shall be the duty of the magistrate to issue a warrant under his hand reciting the complaint and commanding the officer to whom it is directed forthwith to apprehend the person so complained of, and bring him before such magistrate. Such a proceeding is not strictly criminal but is in the nature of a proceeding to prevent the commission of a crime. A person required to give peace bond cannot, therefore, be imprisoned for nonpayment of costs.48

Sec. 341. Trial Before Magistrate. 

Upon such person's being brought before such magistrate, it shall be the duty of the magistrate to summon all witnesses which either party may require, and cause the matters charged in the complaint to be inquired into by a jury of six competent men. If the jury find that there is good reason to fear the commission of the offense charged, then they shall render a verdict of guilty against the defendant, and the magistrate shall thereupon require the defendant to enter into a recognizance, in such sum, not exceeding one thousand dollars, as he shall direct, with one or more sufficient sureties, conditioned that said defendant will keep the peace toward the people of the State, and particularly toward the complainant, for such time as shall be specified in said recognizance, which shall not be less than three months nor more than one year from the date thereof; and the defendant shall be liable for costs, as in other cases of conviction. (Sec. 3403.) The duties of a justice in hearing such proceedings are ministerial, and a justice may be enforced to perform such duties by mandamus. One who is required to give a bond to keep the peace cannot be imprisoned for nonpayment of costs adjudged against him.45 44 

Sec. 342. If Required, Party Must Give Bond or Be Committed. 

If such recognizance be given, the party complained of shall be discharged, but if he fail or refuse to find surety, it shall be the duty of the magistrate to commit him to prison until he find the same, specifying in the warrant the cause of commitment and the sum in which security was required (Sec. 3404).

Any person committed for not finding surety of the peace may be discharged by any magistrate authorized to bind to the peace, within the county, upon giving such security as was originally required of such person, but after thirty days' actual imprisonment the defendant may be released upon his own recognizance, if unable to find security (Sec. 3405). JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 343. Recognizance Must Be Deposited in Circuit Clerk's Office. 

Every recognizance to keep the peace, taken by any magistrate pursuant to any other statute requiring such recognizance, shall be transmitted by such magistrate to the clerk of the proper court of the county, on or before the first day of the term of such court next to be holden after taking the same (Sec. 3406).46

Sec. 344. Prosecution for Breaking Recognizance. 

No recognizance to keep the peace shall be deemed to be broken unless the principal in such recognizance be convicted of some offense amounting, in judgment of law, to a breach of such recognizance (Sec. 3408). Whenever evidence of such conviction shall be produced to the court in which the recognizance is filed or taken, it shall be the duty of the court to order such recognizance to be prosecuted, and the prosecuting attorney shall proceed thereon accordingly (Sec. 3409).

In the action on such recognizance the offense stated in the record of conviction may be assigned as a breach, and such record shall be conclusive evidence of the matters therein stated (Sec. 3410). 

Sec. 345. Appeals. 

Any person convicted in such proceedings to preserve the peace may take an appeal from the judgment of the justice to the court having jurisdiction of the appeal, if he shall, on the day of the rendition of the verdict, file an affidavit stating that he verily believes himself aggrieved by the verdict and judgment, and shall also enter into a recognizance, to be approved by the justice, in a sum not to exceed one thousand dollars, with sufficient sureties, conditioned that he will, during the pendency of the appeal, keep the peace toward the people of this State, and particularly toward the complainant, and that he will appear to answer the charges against him at the next term of court having jurisdiction thereof (Sec. 3411). 

State vs. Emnitz, 27 Mo. 521. 420

If the judgment of the justice shall be affirmed, or if, upon a trial in the court to which the appeal is taken, the defendant shall be convicted, the court shall require a new recognizance in a sum not exceeding one thousand dollars, for such time as shall appear necessary, not exceeding one year, and render judgment against the defendant for all costs in the case (Sec. 3412). When any person shall have taken such appeal, and fails to appear, the court shall forfeit his recognizance, and order it to be prosecuted, unless reasonable excuse for the default be shown (Sec. 3413). 

2. Search Warrants. 

Sec. 346. Constitutional Provisions Govern. 

The Constitution provides that the people shall be secure in their persons, papers, homes and effects, from unreasonable searches and seizures; and no warrant to search any place, or seize any person or thing, shall issue without describing the place to be searched, or the person or thing to be seized, as nearly as may be; nor without probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation reduced to writ ing (Art. 2, Sec. 11). The Constitution of the United States pro vides that the right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no warrants shall issue but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized (Amendment 4, Const. of the United States). Under these constitutional provisions it is held that the restrictions contained in these provisions are upon the powers of government, and that they are not meant to serve as a restraint on the unauthorized acts of individuals. Furthermore, it is generally held that the Fourth 

Amendment to the Constitution of the United States is a restriction upon the Federal Government, and not upon the State Governments. 48 "State vs. Wagner (Sup.), 279 S. W. 23; State vs. Lock, 302 Mo. 400, 259 

S. W. 116; State vs. Pomeroy, 130 Mo. 489, 32 S. W. 1002. "State vs Bowenkamp (Sup.), 39 S. W. (2d) 753; State vs. Cook (Sup.), 18 

S. W. (2d) 58; State vs. Rebasti, 306 Mo. 336, 267 S. W. 858. 421

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 347. Grounds for Issuance of Search Warrant. 

a. Complaint of property stolen or embezzled. 

Before an officer authorized to issue process for the apprehension of offenders can issue a search warrant, there must be filed with him a complaint in which the complainant on oath and in writing charges that personal property has been stolen or embezzled (Sec. 3769). 

The complaint must state that the complainant suspects that such property is concealed in some particular house or place (Sec. 3769). b. Reasonable grounds for suspicion.

After such complaint is filed with such magistrate, he must determine whether to proceed further, and if he is satisfied that there is reasonable ground for suspicion that the alleged stolen property is concealed in the particular house or place alleged, he may issue the search warrant (Sec. 3769). The question as to whether there is a reasonable ground for such suspicion is a judicial question.4 .49 It is not necessary for the justice to take testimony when a complaint and application for a search warrant is presented to him,50 although, if the justice desires, he may supplement the affidavit with testimony as to the allegations in the affidavit. All that is required by the statute is that the complaint be made in writing and on oath, and that the magistrate be satisfied that there is reasonable ground for suspicion, and where this appears it is proper for the warrant to issue.5 52

Sec. 349. 

Requisites of Warrant. a. Complaint and reasonable warrant for suspicion. 

The issuance of the search warrant must be preceded by the filing of a complaint in writing, under oath, containing the allegetions required by statute, and the justice must be satisfied that there is reasonable ground for suspicion (Sec. 3769). b. Form of search warrant.

Such warrant shall be directed to the sheriff of the county, or to any constable of the township, and shall command him to search the place where such property is suspected to be concealed, in the daytime, which place shall be designated and the property particularly described in such warrant, and to bring such property before the magistrate issuing the warrant (Sec. 3770). 

c. Description of property. 

Where the search warrant is for the purpose of searching premises on which stolen or embezzled property is suspected to be concealed, the premises must be designated and the stolen or embezzled property particularly described in the warrant (Sec. 3770). The description of the premises to be searched should identify such premises with such certainty that a mistake may not ensue.58 

Where such premises are sufficiently described for identification purposes, the warrant is held good.50 The statute further requires that a search warrant shall describe the place to be searched or the things to be seized, as nearly as may be, and direct the officers seizing the same to seize such articles and bring them before the judge or justice issuing the warrant. Sec. 351. Disposition of Stolen Property. 

When property alleged to have been stolen, purloined, embezzled or obtained by false pretenses, or to have been obtained in any of the modes specified in the article concerning offenses against public and private property, shall come into the custody of any sheriff, coroner, constable, marshal, or any person authorized to perform the duties of such officers, he shall hold the same subject to the order of the court or officer authorized to direct the disposition thereof (Sec. 

3774). Upon receiving satisfactory proof of the title of any owner of such property, the magistrate who shall take the examination of the person accused of having property stolen, purloined, embezzled or obtained under false pretenses, may order the same to be delivered to such owner, on his paying the reasonable and necessary expenses incurred in the preservation of such property, to be certified by such magistrate, which order shall entitle the owner to demand and receive such property (Sec. 3775). If such property come into the custody of a justice of the peace or other magistrate, upon satisfactory proof of the title of any owner thereof, it shall be delivered to him on the payment of the necessary expenses incurred in the preservation thereof, to be certified by such magistrate (Sec. 3776). If such property shall not have been delivered to the

Sec. 352. Proceedings for Restitution or Reparation in Damages. 

In all cases of conviction of felony, the party convicted shall restore the property stolen or destroyed, or make reparation in damages therefor. The court in which such conviction may be had, if applied to at the same term in which the sentence was pronounced, by petition, verified by affidavit, may order restitution or give judgment against the convict for reparation in damages, and enforce the collection of the same by execution or other process. (Sec. 3781.)

On motion for restitution or reparation, the court shall cause the prisoner to be set within the bar, and demand of him if he has any defense to make to the motion; and if the convict consent to such restitution or reparation in damages, the court shall give judgment accordingly, if the damages are agreed; otherwise a jury shall be impaneled to try the facts and ascertain the amount and value of the property or assess the damages, as the case may be. A failure to pursue the remedy hereby given shall not deprive the party aggrieved of his civil action for the injury sustained. The party injured shall have a lien on the estate of the criminal from the time of his arrest, subject to any lien granted by law to the State. (Sec. 3782.) 428

Sec. 353. Defendant Must Have Notice of Date of Hearing. 

The judge or justice issuing the warrant shall set a day, not less than five days nor more than twenty days after the date of such service and seizure, for determining whether such property is the kind of property mentioned that may be seized, and shall order the officer having such property in charge to retain possession of the same until after such hearing. Written notice of the date and place of such hearing shall be given, at least five days before such date, by posting a copy of such notice in a conspicuous place upon the premises in which such property is seized, and by delivering a copy of such notice to any person claiming an interest in such property, whose name may be known to the person making the complaint or to the officer issuing or serving such warrant, or leaving the same at the usual place of abode of such person with any member of his family or household above the age of fifteen years. Such notice shall be signed by the justice or judge or by the clerk of the court of such judge. (Sec. 3785.)

Sec. 354. Disposition of Property After Hearing. 

The owner or owners of such property may appear at such hearing and defend against the charges as to the nature and use of the property so seized, and such judge or justice shall determine, from the evidence produced at such hearing, whether the property is the kind of property hereinbefore mentioned (Sec. 3786).

If the judge or justice hearing such cause shall determine that the property or articles are of the kind hereinbefore mentioned, he shall cause the same to be publicly destroyed, by burning or otherwise, and if he find that such property is not of the kind mentioned he shall order the same returned to its owner. If it appear that it may be necessary to use such articles or property as evidence in any criminal prosecution, the judge or justice shall order the officer having possession of them to retain such possession until such necessity no longer exists, and they shall neither be destroyed nor returned to the owner until they are no longer needed as such evidence. (Sec. 3787.) 429
