Sec. 355.

Prosecution and Punishment. 

But such proceedings shall not prevent the prosecution and punishment, under the criminal laws, of any person guilty of having in his possession or custody or keeping, making, publishing, selling, giving away, circulating, distributing, or otherwise using or disposing of any of the articles heretofore mentioned, contrary to law. 

Nothing in such procedure shall be construed to affect the seizure and disposition, under any law or proceeding, of any other property not herein described. (Sec. 3788.)

Sec. 356. Duty of Officer in Handling Prisoners. 

Every officer or other person, who shall have arrested or have in his custody, under the authority of the law of this state, any prisoner who is to be conveyed from one county to another, may carry such prisoner through such parts of any county as shall be in the ordinary route of travel from the place where such prisoner shall have been arrested to the place where he is to be conveyed and delivered, under the process or authority by which such prisoner shall have been arrested or is detained (Sec. 3791).

The officer or person having such prisoner in charge shall not be liable to arrest on civil process while on his route; and he shall have the like power to require any person to aid in securing such prisoner and retaking him if he escape as sheriffs or other officers have in their own county; and a refusal or neglect to render such aid shall be an offense punishable in the same manner as for disobedience to a summons to assist in the execution of process (Sec. 3792).

The jailer of every county through which such prisoner may be taken is required to receive and safely keep such prisoner in the jail of which he has charge, when thereto requested by the officer or person having lawful charge of such prisoner, and to redeliver him on demand of such officer or person (Sec. 3793).

V.  A. JUSTICES IN TOWNSHIPS OF 75,000 To 150,000 INHABITANTS Sec. 357. Number, Salary and Bonds of Justices. 

In all townships containing 75,000 to 150,000 inhabitants according to the last United States decennial census, at the general election 430

in the year 1934, and every four years thereafter, there shall be elected three justices of the peace and each shall receive a salary of two thousand dollars per annum, payable monthly out of the treasury of the county in which he is elected (Sec. 2366, as amended Laws 

1933, p. 214). The statute authorizing the number and salary of justices in such townships has been held constitutional.68 

Each justice of the peace shall, before entering upon the duties of his office, give bond to the State of Missouri, with two good and sufficient sureties, residents of the county, in the penal sum of two thousand dollars, conditioned that he will account for and pay to the proper officer all the money received by him by virtue of his office; said bond to be approved by the county court, or the clerk in vacation, and if taken by the clerk in vacation it shall be approved or rejected by the court at the next term (Sec. 2367).

Whenever any surety shall die, remove from the county, or become insolvent, or when from any other cause the county court shall have reason to believe that the sureties to a justice's bond are likely to become, or have become, insufficient, the court shall require the justice, at a time to be fixed, to show why a new bond shall not be required, and, unless cause to the contrary be shown, the justice of the peace shall be required within a given time to give a new bond; and in default thereof the office shall be vacant, which shall be filled as now provided by law for filling vacancies in office of the justice of the peace (Sec. 2368). Any such county shall sue for and recover all sums of money payable into the treasury thereof by any justice of the peace, and the sureties on his official bond shall be liable therefor 

(Sec. 2371). 

Sec. 358. County Shall Provide Justices With Offices and Clerk. 

Said county shall provide proper offices for said justice courts and for the proper care of the same, and shall provide light, heat, proper books of accounts, dockets, and printed forms of writs, and stationery, and whatever else may be deemed necessary by the county court of said county, for the proper conduct and the business of such court, including a clerk thereof, to be designated by the justice, at a salary of seventy-five dollars per month, payable at the end of each month, out of the treasury of such county (Sec. 2372). 

Forgrave vs. Buchanan Co., 282 Mo. 599, 222 8. W. 755. 431

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 359. Justices Required to Pay Fees Into County Treasury. 

Each justice of the peace shall pay over all fees collected for his services to the treasurer of the county in which he is elected, every thirty days, accompanied by a statement thereof sworn to by him, and all other costs collected by said justice of the peace shall be paid by him every thirty days, accompanied by like sworn statement, to the constable of his district, who shall be responsible for the same and pay over the same to the parties entitled thereto, as is now required by law in cases of costs collected by or paid to said constable (Sec. 2369).

Sec. 360. Penalty for Failure to Perform Duty. 

Upon failure or neglect of any justice of the peace to comply with the provisions of the law applicable to him, within five days from the time provided for paying over said costs and filing the statement he is required to file, he shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and shall forfeit his salary for and during such time as he fails to make such statement as required by law. Should he further fail and neglect to pay over said costs and file said statement for a period of thirty days from the time required for same, he shall forfeit all his right and claim to said office. (Sec. 2370.)

B. JUSTICES AND CONSTABLES IN TOWNSHIPS OF 200,000 To 400,000 INHABITANTS Sec. 361. Jurisdiction of Justices. 

In townships containing 200,000 to 400,000 inhabitants, justices of the peace have original jurisdiction of all actions and proceedings for the recovery of money, whether such action be founded upon contract, tort, or account, or upon a bond or undertaking given in any civil action or proceeding, or for a penalty or forfeiture given by any statute of this State, when the sum demanded, exclusive of the interest and costs, does not exceed $500.00 (Sec. 2373). Every such justice has original jurisdiction coextensive with the county in which he is elected, except in landlord and tenant cases and in cases 432

of forcible entry and detainer and of unlawful detainer, which shall be brought before a justice of the peace in the township where the property to be affected is situated (Sec. 2374). Thus a justice of the peace has jurisdiction of all replevin suits coextensive with the county, but does not have jurisdiction in unlawful detainer unless property is located in township where suit is brought.65 

Such justices of the peace shall have original jurisdiction for the recovery of specific personal property when the value of the property sought to be recovered, and the damages claimed for the taking or detention and for injuries thereto, shall not exceed in the aggregate $500.00; they shall have original jurisdiction in all actions. brought to enforce mechanic's liens, as provided by law; for enforcing such liens in the circuit court, when the amount of balance claimed to be due does not exceed $500.00; and in all suits between landlords and tenants for rents or for possession of lands and tenements, when the amount of rent claimed shall not exceed $500.00; and in all cases of unlawful or forcible entry or detainer, and shall have jurisdiction in attachment proceedings, and to enforce boarding house keepers' liens, and liens for keeping horses and other animals, to an amount not in excess of $500.00. They shall have all the powers and jurisdiction in civil and criminal cases now conferred by law on justices of the peace, not in conflict with the provisions of the statutes pertaining to townships now under consideration. All provisions of law pertaining to civil and criminal cases, now applicable to justices of the peace and the practice and procedure in their courts, are applicable in all respects to justices here under consideration, if not in conflict with the provisions of the statutes especially applicable to justices in such townships. (Sec. 2375.) It has been held that in a complaint in an unlawful detainer action before a justice of the peace in townships with a population between 200,000 and 400,000, a failure to allege that lands involved were situated within the township, rendered all the proceedings in the cause void, so that neither the first justice nor the justice to whom the cause was transferred, nor the circuit court to which judgment was appealed, acquired jurisdiction." "Altergott vs. O'Connor, 6 S. W. (2d) 1012, 222 Mo. A. 852. 

65 Ellsworth vs. Wilhelm (App.), 186 S. W. 1128. "State ex rel. Brown vs. Bird (App.), 73 S. W. (2d) 821. 433

JUSTICE COURTS Sec. 362. Salaries, Clerks and Place of Keeping Offices. 

a. Salaries. 

In all such townships each justice of the peace of each district shall receive a salary of twenty-five hundred dollars per annum, payable monthly out of the treasury of the county in which he is elected (Sec. 2376). b. Appointment of clerk.

Each justice of the peace shall appoint a clerk of such court to hold office during the pleasure of said justice, with a salary of one hundred and fifty dollars per month, to be paid out of the treasury of the county in which such court shall be located, at the end of each month. Such appointment shall be in writing, signed by the justice, and shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the circuit court having jurisdiction in such county. The justice may at any time remove such clerk and appoint another in his stead. (Sec. 2388 as amended 

Laws 1933, p. 209.) Under this statutory provision, a county is authorized to lease room for court room for justice." c. Must keep offices within district.

The justices elected in such townships shall keep their offices and hold their courts within the districts for which they were respectively elected, which shall be designated in the commission; and such justices so elected or appointed shall exercise the powers and perform the duties throughout their townships prescribed by law in relation to other justices of the peace; and whenever any such justice shall remove his office or place of holding his court out of the district for which he was elected or appointed, he shall be deemed to have vacated his office, and he shall thereupon proceed as provided by law in case of removal from the township, and such vacancy may be filled as provided by law for filling such vacancies in other cases (Sec. 

2381, as amended Laws 1933, p. 209).

Sec. 363. Acceptance and Oath of Office. 

Every person who receives a commission of election as justice of the peace shall, within thirty days thereafter, and before entering 67 " Ebert vs. Jackson County (Sup.), 70 S. W. (2d) 918. 434

upon the discharge of his duties, take the oath prescribed by the Constitution of this State, and an oath that he will faithfully demean himself in office, and shall file his commission in the office of the clerk of the circuit court of said county, together with the oath required endorsed thereon, to be recorded in the office of the clerk of the circuit court, which shall be deemed an acceptance of such election; and in case of his failure to do so, it shall be deemed a refusal thereof (Sec. 2377, as amended Laws 1933, p. 209). 

Sec. 364. Clerks, Their Bonds, Statements, Duties and Salaries. 

Every clerk, within ten days after his appointment, shall give bond to the State, with two good and sufficient securities, residents of said county, in the penal sum of two thousand dollars, conditioned that he will pay all money received by him by virtue of his office, and in every respect discharge all his duties as such clerk according to law. 

The said bond shall be approved as now provided by law in case of bonds of constables; and all other provisions of law relating to requirement of new bond, discharge of sureties on old bond, and suits on bonds, and summary proceedings in cases of constables and their sureties, shall be applicable to said clerks and their sureties in like manner. (Sec. 2378, as amended Laws 1933, p. 209.)

All fees and costs collected in said courts not paid to or collected by the constables or their deputies, shall be paid to and received by said clerks, and in no instance paid to or received by said justices; said clerks shall pay over all fees collected for services of the justice to the treasurer of said county every thirty days, accompanied by a statement thereof, sworn to by them, and all other costs collected by said clerks shall be paid by them every thirty days, accompanied by a like sworn statement, to the constables of the respective districts, who shall be responsible for the same, and pay over the same to the parties entitled thereto, as now required by law in case of costs collected by or paid to said constables (Sec. 2379, as amended Laws 

1933, p. 209).

The clerks of said justices of the peace shall keep accurate books, in which shall be entered full, complete itemized accounts of all fees and costs taxed or collected in said courts by said clerks, which books shall at all times be open for inspection by the treasurer of such county, or any agent appointed by such county for that purpose, and 435

shall perform all clerical and ministerial duties now imposed by law on justices of the peace (Sec. 2380 as amended Laws 1933, p. 209). 

Sec. 365. Constables, Their Salaries, Bonds, Duties and Liabilities. 

The constable elected in such townships shall receive one hundred and fifty dollars per month, payable at the end of each month, out of the treasury of such county, and also a commission of two and onehalf per cent on all collections made by him (Sec. 2382). 

Every constable shall have power to appoint one deputy, with pay, who shall take the same oath of office as the constable, for whose conduct he shall be answerable. Such appointment shall be in writing and shall be endorsed "approved" by the justice of the peace of the district for which he shall have been appointed, and shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the county court. Such deputy shall receive a salary of one hundred and twenty-five dollars per month, to be paid in like manner as herein provided for the payment of constables. He may be removed at the pleasure of the constable appointing him, or his successor in office, and in case of vacancy in such office of deputy constable the constable may fill such vacancy as in case of original appointment. The constable shall give bond to the State as now required by law, shall have and exercise the same authority as now had and exercised, perform the same duties, and be subject to the same liabilities and responsibilities which now attach to the office of constable. (Sec. 2383.)

The constable shall keep accurate books in which shall be entered full, complete, itemized accounts for all costs and fees, commissions and emoluments charged and collected, and shall pay over all such fees, commissions and emoluments collected and received by him, to the parties entitled thereto. All constable's fees and sums remaining in his hands uncalled for by those entitled thereto for the period of sixty days shall be paid over to the county treasurer, accompanied by a statement thereof, sworn to by him, showing the amount and to whom the uncalled-for fees belong. (Sec. 2384.)

The county treasurer shall hold such fees for the period of six months, with authority to pay over the same to the parties entitled thereto when called for; all sums remaining in his hands uncalled for, after the said period of six months, shall be paid into the public school fund of the county (Sec. 2385). 436

If any constable fail to make and file such a statement with said county treasurer as required, the justice of the district shall issue a citation to such constable, requiring him to make and file such statement on or before a day named in such citation, and after service of such citation if he fail to make and file such statement as required by the justice, the justice may, by attachment, compel the attendance of such constable, and, if necessary, commit him to jail until he make and file such statement (Sec. 2386).

Any such county may sue for and recover all sums of money payable into the treasury thereof by any constable or justice of the peace, and the sureties of their official bond shall be liable therefor (Sec. 2387).

Sec. 366. Change of Venue. 

Each party shall be entitled to a change of venue in any civil cause pending before a justice of the peace if he shall, before a jury is ordered summoned by the justice or trial begun before the justice, file an affidavit that the justice is a material witness for him or of kin to either party, stating the degree of relationship, or that he cannot have a fair or impartial trial before such justice because of the bias and prejudice of such justice, which affidavit may be made by the party to the suit, or his agent or attorney (Sec. 2389). It has been held that the courts will take judicial notice that Kaw Township, in Jackson County, is a township coming within the provisions of the statutes here under discussion, for change of venue purposes.68 

Upon the filing of a change of venue in due time, the justice must allow the change of venue and note same on his docket, and shall on the day said cause shall be set for trial transmit the original papers and a transcript of all his docket entries to some other justice in the township and publicly adjourn the trial of said cause to the court of said justice to a day certain, not exceeding five days, and no further notice to the parties shall be necessary (Sec. 2390).

No more than one change of venue shall be allowed the same party, in any case (Sec. 2391). A justice may transfer any case to some other justice in the township, but no cost shall be charged for so doing and said transfer shall be made publicly on the day on which said cause shall be set and transfer shall be made in the manner provided 

State ex rel. Hart vs. Mazuch (App.), 68 S. W. (2d) 923. 437

JUSTICE COURTS 

for changes of venue (Sec. 2392). When any party to a cause demand a jury, the justice may require said party to deposit a sum sufficient to pay the fees of the jurors in said cause, and if the issues be found in favor of such party he shall have judgment against the other party for such costs (Sec. 2393). The right to change of venue being statutory, it has been held that the general law respecting change of venue in justice court is inapplicable to Kaw Township, Jackson County.69

C. JUSTICES AND CONSTABLES IN CITIES WITH 300,000 INHABITANTS

Sec. 367. Number, Election and Salaries. 

The statute provides that in all cities of 300,000 inhabitants or more there shall be elected, on the general election day, every four years, one justice of the peace and one constable for each district in such cities (Sec. 2394). For the first 100,000 of population in such cities there shall be five districts; and there shall be an additional district for every additional 100,000, and for every fractional part of 100,000 exceeding 50,000 of population. For the purpose of determining the population, the last general census of the United States of America shall be taken as a basis. (Sec. 2395.) This act pertaining to such officers has been held constitutional." If there is no election, or if a person elected fails to qualify, the justice in office holds his office until the next regular term.71 

Each of said justices shall receive a salary of three thousand dollars per annum, payable monthly, to be paid out of the treasury of the city in which they are elected (Sec. 2406). 

Sec. 368.

Division Into Districts. 

The judges of the probate court, criminal court, criminal court of correction, and of the circuit court, or a majority thereof, in all such cities, shall, six months prior to the general election of 1894, divide their respective cities into districts upon the basis of population

In justice court districts of which the business shall have exceeded two thousand two hundred cases in any successive twelve months, there shall be two justice courts, to which there shall be elected, in the manner provided for the election of justices generally in such cities, except as hereinafter pointed out, two justices of the peace and two constables, said justices to have jurisdiction, powers and to receive the same salaries as other justices; and said constables shall perform all the duties and have the powers, and shall give the same bond and receive the same salaries, as provided for other constables in such cities (Sec. 2407).

Sec. 370. Where Offices Are Kept, Vacancies and How Filled.

Sec. 371. Eligibility, Qualifications and Laws Applicable. 

No person shall be eligible to the office of justice of the peace who is not a citizen of the United States, and who shall not have been an inhabitant of this State and a resident of the city in which he is elected for twelve months next preceding his election (Sec. 2400). 

Every person who receives a commission of election as justice of the peace or constable shall, within thirty days thereafter, and before entering upon the discharge of his duties, take the oath prescribed by the Constitution of this State, and an oath that he will faithfully demean himself in office, and shall file his commission in the office of the clerk of the circuit court of said city, together with the oath herein required endorsed thereon, to be recorded in the office of the clerk of the circuit court, which shall be deemed an acceptance of such election; and in case of his failure to do so, it shall be deemed a refusal thereof (Sec. 2402).

All laws now or hereafter in force, concerning justices of the peace and constables, applicable to townships, shall be applicable to the districts of said justices and constables in such cities, except where inconsistent with the other provisions hereof (Sec. 2399).

Sec. 372. 

Jurisdiction. 

The said justices of the peace shall have original jurisdiction of all actions and proceedings for the recovery of money, whether such action be founded upon contract, tort or account, or upon a bond or undertaking given in any civil action or proceeding, or upon special tax bills, or for a penalty or forfeiture given by any statute of this State, when the sum demanded, exclusive of interest and costs, does not exceed seven hundred and fifty dollars (Sec. 2403).

Sec. 373. Clerks, Their Appointment, Salary and Bond.

Such appointment shall be in writing, signed by the justice, and shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the circuit court having jurisdiction in such city. The justice may at any time remove such clerk and appoint another in his stead. (Sec. 2409.) 

Every clerk, within ten days after his appointment, shall give bond to the State, with two good and sufficient securities, residents of the said city, in the penal sum of two thousand dollars, conditional that he will pay all money received by him by virtue of his office, and in every respect discharge all his duties as such clerk according to law. The said bond shall be approved as now provided by law in case of bonds of constables; and all other provisions of law relating to requirement of new bond, discharge of sureties on old bond, and suits on bonds, and summary proceedings in cases of constables and their sureties, shall be applicable to said clerks and their sureties in like manner. Sec. 376. Deputy Constables. 

Every constable shall have power to appoint deputies not to exceed two in number, for whose conduct he shall be answerable, and such appointments shall be in writing and shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the circuit court having jurisdiction (Sec. 2418).

Such deputies shall receive a salary of one hundred twenty-five dollars per month, to be paid out of the treasury of the city, in like manner as provided herein in case of constables. They may be removed at the pleasure of the constable appointing them, or his successor in office, and in case of vacancy in said office of deputy constables, the constable may fill the vacancy, with the approval of the justice, as in case of original appointment. (Sec 2419.)

If any constable or clerk fail to make and file such statement with said city treasurer, the justice of the district shall issue a citation to such constable or clerk requiring him to make and file such statement on or before a day to be named in such citation, and such citation may be served upon such constable or clerk in order; and if such constable or clerk, after service of such citation, fail to make and file such statement, as required by such justice, the justice may, by attachment, compel the attendance of such constable or clerk, and, if necessary, commit him to jail until he make and file such statement (Sec. 2414). In the City of St. Louis, the duties and services required by Chapter 79, Revised Statutes of 1929, of the county clerk shall be per- 444

formed by the register of said city, and those required to be performed by the county court shall be performed by the mayor of said city, except in case of a tie or contested election, which shall be tried in the circuit court; and, so far as applicable, said city shall be considered as a county; and likewise a district in said city shall be held to be the same as township in said chapter (Sec. 2421). 

Sec. 379. Quarters for, Furnished by City. 

The municipal assembly of said city shall provide proper rooms and offices for said justices' courts, and their clerks and constables, in their respective districts, and for the proper care of the same, and shall provide heat, light, proper books of account, dockets and printed forms of writs, and stationery, and whatsoever else may be necessary for the proper conduct of the business of such courts (Sec. 2420).

Sec. 380. Jury Service. 

In any cause pending before a justice of the peace in such cities, no person shall be eligible to sit as a juror unless he has the same qualifications as prescribed for jurors in the circuit court of such cities, and no person shall be permitted to serve as a juror in such cities before any justice of the peace more than once each year (Sec. 2422).

It shall be the duty of the clerk in each court of a justice of the peace in such cities to record in a book suitably headed and ruled, the name of each juror serving in such court, arranged under the proper letter of the alphabet, together with the number and street of his residence and the date of his service (Sec. 2423).

Sec. 381. Changes of Venue. 

Upon the filing of an affidavit for a change of venue in the manner provided in proceedings before justices generally in any justice court in such cities, the justice must allow the change of venue, noting the fact in his docket, and shall forthwith transmit all papers and a transcript of all his docket entries in the case, to some convenient justice in the district, if there be one, unless the party ask- 445

JUSTICE COURTS 

ing for a change of venue shall, in his affidavit, state that the other justice in the district is a material witness for him, without whose testimony he cannot safely proceed to trial, or that he is near of kin to either party, stating in what degree, or that he cannot have a fair or impartial trial before such justice, or if there be no justice in the district, in which case, then to a justice in some other district in the city, or if the change be allowed on account of the bias and prejudice of the inhabitants of the district, then to a justice of some other district in the city; and the justice by whom such change of venue is allowed shall, on the day and at the hour at which said cause is called for trial, publicly adjourn the trial of said cause to a day certain, not exceeding ten days, to the court of said justice to whom he shall transmit forthwith all the original papers and a transcript of his docket entries in the case, and no further notice to the party shall be necessary.

When such affidavit for change of venue shall be filed, the justice shall have no further jurisdiction in the cause except to grant such change of venue, and, on the day said cause shall be set for trial, to transmit all the papers, together with said transcript, to such other justice and to publicly adjourn the trial of said cause before such other justice to a day certain. (Sec. 2424.)

The justice to whom the cause is sent shall, when he becomes possessed of the cause, forthwith cause same to be placed upon his docket and shall set the same for trial and shall call the same for trial on the day to which said cause shall have been publicly adjourned by the justice transmitting said cause, and shall proceed with said cause in all other respects as if it had been originally commenced before him; but it shall not be necessary to cause the parties to be notified of the setting of the same for trial (Sec. 2425). 446

I. STATUS AS JUDICIAL INSTITUTIONS Section 382. Origin and Evolution. 

The term "county courts" was first applied to a specific class of courts that were created in Missouri during the territorial era.¹ 

Though these courts were short-lived, they appear to represent, both 'By an act approved January 4, 1815, the Territorial Legislature of Missouri established in each county a county court composed of the justices of the peace of such counties, three of whom constituted a quorum. These courts were given power formerly exercised by the courts of common pleas and relating to the supervision of public roads and highways, matters pertaining to taxation, elections, the care of the poor, and other cases which were of "the concerns of the county." 

T. L., Chap. 125, pp. 345-350. 'By an act approved January 21, 1816, county courts were abolished and their duties transferred to the circuit courts. T. L., Chap. 159, pp. 444-449. 451

COUNTY COURTS 

in name and functions, the germ of the idea underlying the present county courts of the State. The transaction of county business seems to have been first made the function of what was known as the Court of Quarter Sessions in Missouri in 1804. This court took its name from and had similar jurisdiction to the ancient Court of Quarter Sessions of England. The Constitution of 1820 provided for the establishment in each county of inferior tribunals for the transaction of all county business and probate business." The Constitution of 

1865 provided for the establishment in each county of inferior tribunals to be known as county courts for the transaction of all county business. It vested in such courts and "such other tribunals, inferior to the circuit courts as the General Assembly may establish,' all matters pertaining to probate business and such other jurisdiction as may be conferred by law. By the Constitution of 1875 it was provided that "in each county there shall be a county court, which shall be a court of record, and shall have jurisdiction to transact all county and such other business as may be prescribed by law.' 

From the time of the first Constitution of Missouri until the adoption of the present Constitution the functions of the county court were of both administrative and judicial character, such courts having both the powers they now possess and also having extensive probate 

T. L., Chap. 4, pp. 34-41; Chap. 20, pp. 69-78.

It had been transplanted to America through the colony of Virginia and carried to Missouri during the western movement principally through Kentucky. Later, local government in this state was modified somewhat by the introduction of certain features of the county-township government of Pennsylvania which had been carried westward through Ohio and Indiana. The present county court, for instance, is organized on substantially the same basis as the board of commissioners in those states. The sys- tems of town and township-county government, developed in Massachusetts and New York respectively, had practically no influence on local government in Missouri. The New York township-supervisor type of county board was tried in 

1872 and 1874 in some half dozen counties. It had been entirely abandoned by 1875.''

Sec. 383. Creation and Character of Existing County Courts. 

Following the adoption of the Constitution of 1875, the General Assembly of Missouri passed an act approved April 27, 1877, by which county courts were established in all of the counties of the State, which courts have continued with only slight changes as to functions since that time.10 The county court as it now exists has been deprived of some of the most important judicial functions it formerly exercised, the Constitution of 1875 having taken from it probate powers, and, although it has extensive judicial powers, it is more of an administrative than a judicial agency of government.11 In this respect it differs materially from the chief agency of government in control of county business in many of the other states where such agencies are generally known as Boards of County Commissioners.12 'On this point see Bradshaw, "The Missouri County Court'' pp. 25-26, 41-46, 65-76; Fairlie & Kneier "County Government and Administration'' pp. 3-26, 107-130. 'Laws Mo. 1877, pp. 226-229. 

10 The existing statutes applicable to the composition, powers and organization of the county courts are embraced in Art. 4, Chap. 9, R. S. Mo. 1929, Secs. 20722094. "Bradshaw, "The Missouri County Court" p. 26 says, “Since 1877, the title 'board of commissioners' or 'board of supervisors' would have been more appropriate than 'county court' for the chief administrative body of the county. But apparently there was no desire or agitation to change the name at that time. 

Probably the transition from a court exercising important judicial functions to one whose principal duties were administrative in nature came about so gradually that contemporaries did not realize what was happening. Moreover it is not likely that many people distinguished between administrative and judicial functions until a later date. At any rate the framers of the constitution of 

1875 did not change its name, though they adopted a provision which relieved the county court in all counties of its most important judicial function, viz. probate jurisdiction. It is also significant that the constitution of 1875 provides for the county court in the article on the Judicial Department instead of the one on Counties, Cities, and Towns where it logically belongs. It is in the latter article that a person unfamiliar with the history of county government in Missouri would expect to find the provisions establishing the chief administrative and supervisory board of the county." 

137 R. C. L. 936-947. 453

COUNTY COURTS Sec. 384. Vested With Judicial Powers by Constitution. 

County courts are among the judicial bodies of the State in which the Constitution has vested the judicial powers of the State as to matters of law and equity (Art. 6, Sec. 1). A pronounced sentiment for diverting the administrative head of the county business of judicial power and creating a county court exercising judicial functions only was expressed but defeated in the Constitutional Convention of 1922-23.13 

Sec. 385. Courts of Record.

County courts are among those courts that are by statute made courts of record and required to keep just and faithful records of their proceedings (Sec. 1826). As courts of record they must speak through their records, and they have inherent powers to supply entries in their records nunc pro tunc.¹4 

II. JUDGES, THEIR QUALIFICATIONS, ELECTION AND POWERS Sec. 386. Court Consists of Three Judges. 

The Constitution provides that the county court shall consist of one or more judges, not exceeding three, of whom the probate judge 13 Journal and Debates of the Constitutional Convention of Missouri, 1922-23. "State ex rel. Chaney vs. Grinstead, 314 Mo. 55, 282 S. W. 715; Henry County vs. Salmon, 201 Mo. 136, 100 S. W. 20; Cummings vs. Brown, 181 Mo. 711, 81 

S. W. 158; Medlin vs. Platte County, 8 Mo. 235.

The importance of having this general rule applicable to courts of record extend to county courts was explained by Lamm, J., in the case of Henry County vs. Salmon, supra, as follows: "The inherent power of a court of record to sup ply entries nunc pro tune which have been omitted through the misprision of its clerk, where sufficient data exist in the clerk's office, ought not to be gainsaid. 

This power does not depend on statute, but is a necessary incident to the juris diction of every court of record—inasmuch as, by a presumption of law, the record imports verity, therefore, it is essential to the administration of justice that records should speak the very truth they are held to import. The confusion and distress that would arise from the denial of this sensible power to a county court, whereby the business affairs of the county would be left at the mercy of the caprice, wiles, slips, lapses, or other inadvertences of a clerk, are apparent."' 454

JUDGES, THEIR QUALIFICATIONS, ELECTION AND POWERS 

may be one, as may be provided by law (Art. 6, Sec. 36). The statute provides that the county court shall be composed of three members, to be styled the judges of the county court, of whom the probate judge may be one (Sec. 2072). Of these three judges one serves as presiding judge and is elected from the county at large (Sec. 2073). 

The other judges are known as associate judges, who represent the districts in the county from which they are elected (Sec. 2073). 

Sec. 387. Qualifications. 

Every judge of the county court must have attained the age of 24 years and have been a citizen of the United States five years, and a resident of the county in which he may be elected for one year next preceding his election (Sec. 1824). A county judge need not be learned in the law, and in fact lawyers are rarely elected to positions on these courts.15

Sec. 388. Quorum. 

A majority of the judges of the county court constitutes a quorum to do business (Sec. 2091).

Sec. 389. Election of, and Terms of Office. 

a. Presiding judge.

The presiding judge is elected from the county at large for a term of four years and until his successor is duly elected and qualified. 

He takes office on the first day of January next after his election. 

b. Associate judges.

For the purpose of electing associate judges of the county court each county is divided into two districts of contiguous territory as nearly equal in population as practicable without dividing municipal townships (Sec. 2072). An associate judge is elected from each of such districts every two years, and holds his office until his successor is duly elected and qualified. Associate judges take their offices also on the first day of January next after their election. (Sec. 2073.) 

15 Bradshaw, "The Missouri County Court" p. 28. 455

COUNTY COURTS Sec. 390. Disqualification of County Judges. 

No judge of any county court shall, directly or indirectly, become a party to any contract to which his county is a party, or act as any road or bridge commissioner, either general or special, or keeper of any poor person, or act as director in any railroad company in which such county or any township, part of a township, city or incorporated town or village therein, is a stockholder, or act as agent for the subscription of any stock voted to any railroad by any county or subdivision thereof (Sec. 2089). He cannot sit on the trial or determination of a case in which he is interested, or where he is related to either party, or where he shall have been of counsel (Sec. 1848). He cannot be taken as surety for any guardian or curator of a minor (Sec. 391) or an insane person (Sec. 460), or as surety on any official bond that may be given by any officer in the State (Sec. 2847). Nor is a judge of the county court permitted to borrow, either directly or indirectly, for his own use, any school money or county money or money over which he may have any control as a judge of the county court, nor become a security for any person who may borrow any such money (Sec. 2081). The penalty that may attach where a county judge violated statutory provisions placing limitations upon his powers, is in some cases severe (Secs. 2081, 2090).

Sec. 391. Powers. 

Each judge of the county court is a conservator of the peace throughout his county (Sec. 2080). Such judges have authority to administer oaths and affirmations to witnesses appearing in proceedings before them and to administer oaths and take affidavits within their respective jurisdictions (Secs. 1720, 1721), and to administer any oath relating to the assessment of property for taxes (Sec. 9758).

Judges of the county court serve as members of the county board of equalization (Sec. 9811). Any judge of the county court, as any justice of the peace or judge or justice of a court of record, may hold inquests and perform the duties enjoined on coroners, when the regular coroner is unable to serve (Sec. 11624). County judges are exempt from jury service (Sec. 8748). Each of such judges is entitled to have a copy of the journals of each of the houses of the General Assembly (Sec. 673). Any judge of a county court when he is 456

the only member in attendance at any session of the court has authority to adjourn the court from day to day (Sec. 2091). 

Sec. 392. Vacancies.

When a vacancy shall occur in the office of judge of the county court, such vacancy shall at once be certified by the clerk of the court to the Governor, who shall fill such vacancy as provided by law. (Art. 6, Sec. 32; Sec. 2075.)

Sec. 393. Probate Judge May Act as Judge of County Court. 

The Constitution (Art. 6, Sec. 35) and the statute (Sec. 2072) pro vide that the probate judge may be one of the judges of the county court. It is further provided by statute that whenever, by reason of sickness, absence from the county or other preventing cause, the judges of the county court of any county, or a majority of them, shall not be able to hold any regular term of court, then the judge of the probate court of such county shall hold said term of court, and for the time he shall hold the same shall receive the same compensation as a judge of the county court, to be paid in the same manner; but such probate judge shall not have the power to levy any taxes except those necessary for ordinary expenditures (Sec. 2052).

III. JURISDICTION, FUNCTIONS AND POWERS 

Sec. 394. As Provided by the Constitution.

The Constitution provides that the county court of each county shall have jurisdiction to transact all county and such other business as may be prescribed by law (Art. 6, Sec. 36).

Sec. 395. As Fixed by Statute. 

a. Of an administrative or supervisory nature.

While the principal administrative or supervisory functions of the county court are thus prescribed by the Constitution, the Legislature has specified the particular matters of a general nature over which the county courts have been given jurisdiction. Among the various 457

COUNTY COURTS 

duties and functions assigned by the Legislature to the county courts, and related to those prescribed by the Constitution, are, the power to exercise control and management of the real and personal property belonging to the county, and power to purchase, levy or receive by donation any property for the use of the county; to sell and cause to be conveyed any real estate, goods, or chattels belonging to the county, appropriate the proceeds of such sale to the use of the county, and to audit and settle all demands against the county (Sec. 2078). When not otherwise provided by law, the county court has power to award process and cause to be brought before it every person it deems necessary to examine, whether parties or witnesses, and to examine every person on oath or affirmation, touching any matter in controversy before the court (Sec. 2077). The Legislature has also authorized the county courts to have a supervisory control over certain kinds of cemeteries (Secs. 14053-14072), the drainage of land for agricul tural or sanitary purposes without the organization of drainage districts (Secs. 10865-10876), the organization of levee districts (Secs. 

10958-11013), the organization of drainage districts for the drainage of lands (Secs. 10809-10863), proceedings to vacate streets in certain cities, towns and villages (Secs. 7165, 7166), and for the creation of sanitary sewer districts in cities of 300,000 inhabitants and counties adjoining same (Secs. 10886-10901). These courts are also authorized to issue ferry licenses and grant permits for keeping and operating ferries, landings and wharves (Secs. 14198-14219), issue peddlers' licenses (Sec. 13316), incorporate cities and towns (Sec. 6095), preserve the public peace (Secs. 2080-3401), audit, adjust and settle all accounts to which the county is a party (Sec. 12162), and to supervise the support of the county poor (Secs. 12953-12967). These courts are given extensive powers of supervision and conrol over county roads and bridges, special road districts and various miscellaneous public activities (Secs. 7825-8203). They also have broad powers for the assessment of property for taxation purposes and providing revenue and supervising the use of same (Secs. 9742-10164).

Recently, they have been granted power and directed to operate the county business upon a strictly business basis by what is known as the county budget law, which is applicable to counties having a population of 50,000 inhabitants, or less. (Laws, 1933, p. 340.) In the performance of some of their statutory duties as administrative or 458

TE Das supervisory agencies it has been observed that county courts also exercise legislative powers.18 b. Of a strictly judicial nature.

County courts have been given jurisdiction over matters that are strictly of a judicial nature, including the right to conduct inquiries as to the sanity of a person (Sec. 8636) or a judge of the probate court (Sec. 452), the right, under certain conditions, to hear applications for and grant writs of habeas corpus (Secs. 1427, 1429), the power, under certain circumstances, to grant injunctions (Secs. 

1497, 1498), and the power to punish for contempt (Sec. 1864). c. Of a mixed supervisory and judicial nature.

The Legislature has also given to the county courts jurisdiction that is of both an administrative and judicial nature, such as, that of selecting persons for service on petit juries and grand juries in the circuit court or other courts with civil or criminal jurisdiction (Secs. 

8754-8758). The jurisdiction exercised by the county courts in taking land for use as public highways and for other public or private purposes, and the manner in which such jurisdiction is exercised, are of both an administrative and judicial nature.¹7 d. Various miscellaneous powers. 

The foregoing classification of the kinds of powers given county courts does not at all include the many different specific matters over which county courts have been assigned powers. The Legislature has given to these courts power over a large number of various miscellaneous subjects. The jurisdiction to transact all county business, therefore, is of constitutional origin and is exclusive, although it has been held that the State may appoint other agencies for the transaction of county business in particular cases. 22 Jurisdiction of particular matters in connection with the transaction of county business is of exclusive statutory origin and limitation.23

c. Judicial powers. 

49 County courts also exercise extensive judicial powers. As has been heretofore indicated it is not always easy to classify the powers of the county court, inasmuch as the exercise of a single function involves the use of different kinds of powers. Thus it has been held that the power exercised by such courts in providing for the levying of taxation upon special improvement districts is legislative power, while their power to hear and determine allegations of erroneous assessment or mistakes in assessments for taxes has been held judicial in character.50 And, while the right to appeal is given those whose claims against a county court are rejected, such rights are not based on the fact that the court acts judicially in such cases, but because of the special statute authorizing such appeals (Sec. 2088). These courts have been held to exercise judicial powers when they render judgment by default and order an execution against a collector.52 

The whole subject of the character of power exercised by a county court in a given instance is one on which the courts have not always spoken with clarity and uniformity, largely because of the varied functions the court exercises.58 51 "Birmingham Drainage District vs. Chicago, etc., Railway Co., 274 Mo. 140, 202 S. PLEADINGS, JUDGMENTS AND APPEALS Sec. 399. Implied Powers. 

While a county court cannot exercise any powers except those expressly conferred by the Constitution or statute, it has been held that such courts may exercise not only the powers expressly conferred but also such other powers as may be fairly and necessarily implied from those expressly granted." Thus where the law required the appointment of an agent for the transaction of county business to be made by order of record in the county court, a contract made by an agent acting under a verbal appointment that was subsequently ratified and approved by order of the county court was held binding on the principle of implication, 55 and where a statute authorized a county to provide proper offices for justices courts, same has been held to impliedly authorize a county to lease a room for a courtroom for a justice.50 

IV. PLEADINGS, JUDGMENTS AND APPEALS Sec. 400. Pleadings Are Generally Informal. 

A large part of the business conducted in the county court is of such nature that formal pleadings are not necessary. The general rule is that in the ordinary proceedings in the county courts, legal rules of pleading do not apply." But this general rule is probably vs. Glaves, 268 Mo. 100, 186 S. W. 685; McGhee vs. Walsh, 249 Mo. 266, 155 S. W. 445. "Ebert vs. Jackson County (Sup.), 70 S. W. (2d) 918. "Walker vs. Linn County, 72 Mo. 650. 

50 Ebert vs. Jackson County (Sup.), 70 S. W. (2d) 918. 

57 This rule and the reason for it was stated in the case of Sublett vs. Nelson, Adm'r., 38 Mo. 487, 1. c. 488, as follows: "" The strict legal rules of pleading have never been applied to proceedings in county courts. The law provides that county courts shall hear and determine in all demands in a summary way, without the form of pleading. ; and the same rules of procedure must govern in the trial in the Circuit Court when the cause comes up on appeal from the inferior tribunal. The practice in the County Court is purposely so framed that parties can attend to their own business in ordinary matters, and the decisions should be so rendered as to subserve the ends of justice according to the evidence, without regard to technical precision in pleading. The law has pointed out and adopted a summary mode of proceeding for the convenience of the people, and to apply the doctrine of variance with the strictness here contended for would make it a snare to entrap the unwary." 467

applicable only to those proceedings where the court acts in a ministerial or administrative capacity.

Sec. 401. Pleadings Must Conform With Statutes. 

In those instances where the court acts strictly in a judicial capacity and where the statute requires that petitions must set out certain facts, such petitions must be drawn so as to include the facts the statute requires to be stated. Thus a petition to establish a public road must conform with the requirements of the statute in order to give the court jurisdiction in such case. (Sec. 7827.) The same is true with regard to petitions for the incorporation of cities and towns (Secs. 6095, 7091), petitions for disincorporating cities and towns (Sec. 7144) and petitions for vacating streets (Sec. 7165). In all of such cases, where the statutes prescribe a particular procedure and make the validity of the proceeding to depend upon whether such procedure is followed, it is one of the functions of the county court to determine whether or not a petition is sufficient before it can assume jurisdiction of a case based on such petition.58 Thus, in the practice before the county court, it is always important, in those cases where the court is not concerned with ministerial or administrative matters, to observe the same careful rules relative to pleadings as obtain in circuit courts.

Sec. 402. Judgments of, Not Subject to Collateral Attack. 

While county courts are courts of inferior rank, the judgments of such courts are as conclusive collaterally as if rendered by a circuit court.59 The general rule is that in a collateral attack upon a domestic judgment of a court of general jurisdiction the record thereof imports absolute verity and every reasonable presumption is indulged to support the judgment. And this general rule applies to judgments of county courts entered while such courts are acting within the scope of their general authority.1 Therefore, orders and

PROCEDURE IN EXERCISE OF STRICTLY JUDICIAL FUNCTIONS Sec. 407. Inquiry as to Sanity of Poor Person, How Instituted. 

The power to conduct an inquiry as to the sanity of a poor person may be exercised at the instance of a citizen residing in the county. 

The proceeding is initiated when any citizen interested files with the clerk of the county court a statement in writing alleging that the person to be proceeded against is insane, that he has not estate sufficient to support him at a state hospital, and is a resident of the county where the proceeding is instituted. The statement should give the names of two persons residing in the county, who can testify as to the facts alleged, one of which persons shall be a reputable physician." If the person alleged to be insane is dangerous to the safety of the community by being at large, that additional fact should be set forth in the written statement.91

B. HABEAS CORPUS Sec. 409. Power to Issue Writs. 

The statutes authorize any court of record in term time, and any judge of such court in vacation, to hear applications for and grant writs of habeas corpus (Secs. 1427, 1429). But this power to issue writs of habeas corpus can be exercised by county courts, or judges thereof in vacation, only when it shall appear that such relief has not been sought from and refused by a superior court or officer (Sec. 

1493), and when it shall appear that the judge of the circuit court of the county in which the applicant is held in custody is not in the county at the time of the application (Sec. 1494). Under this statutory authority it has been held that a judge of a county court in vacation may issue a writ of habeas corpus and pass upon the application of petitioner for discharge. If a judge of the county court should undertake to grant a writ of habeas corpus when he had no jurisdiction to do so he could be prevented from granting the writ by pro hibition or his action reversed on a certiorari proceeding. On the other hand if a judge of the county court has jurisdiction to discharge a prisoner in a habeas corpus proceeding and erroneously grants the discharge, the decision is not subject to review by an ap- Sec. 8647 R. S. Mo. 1929. C. INJUNCTIONS Sec. 410. Power to Grant. 

Express power to grant injunctions is lodged in county courts. 

The court as a whole, or any two judges thereof in vacation, may grant injunctions (Sec. 1497), provided that the applicant shall produce satisfactory evidence that there is not then any circuit court in session nor any judge thereof within the county where the application is made. When a preliminary injunction is granted by two judges of the county court, it is not necessary that the order show that evidence was produced that the circuit court of the county was not in session and that the judge thereof was not in the county at the time of granting the injunction.10 The power to grant injunctions is exercised rarely by county courts and their judges, and is not thought to be a proper function of existing county courts.¹¹ 

Sec. 411. Procedure. 

Procedure for the granting of injunctions by county courts generally should follow that prevailing in the circuit courts.12

It has been held that in the exercise of such power county courts cannot go beyond the limit of the authority expressly given by the statute or necessarily implied from a power conferred.18 The county court may commit to jail any person who shall refuse to answer any lawful question in an investigation made by the court of any acts to which the county is a party (Sec. 12162). The power to punish for contempt is rarely exercised but it is a wholesome power, and, even without the authority of the statute, such courts would probably have the authority to punish for contempt on the general principle that since such courts are vested with judicial authority the power to compel the observance of decorum in the presence of the court and due respect and obedience to its process, orders and judgments naturally inheres in such power.¹4 

Sec. 413. Procedure in Contempt Proceedings. 

The power to punish for contempt is granted by the statute to all courts of record and the procedure governing such actions follows that ordinarily prevailing in circuit courts. Where such proceedings are for constructive contempt, that is, contempt committed out of the presence of the court,15 it is the general rule that the affidavit initiating the proceedings must show on its face sufficient facts to constitute contempt.16. This general rule applies when the proceedings are had in county courts where presumptions and intendments will not be indulged in order to sustain a conviction for contempt of court. But the guilt of contempt must appear from the facts stated in the affidavit on which the proceedings are instituted and cannot be shown by mere statements of conclusions and inferences.¹7

VI. PROCEDURE IN SPECIAL CASES Sec. 414. Generally. 

In a necessarily limited treatise on practice and procedure in courts and other government agencies acting in a judicial or quasijudicial capacity, it is impractical, if not impossible, even to outline the various steps in the proceedings in all cases that may arise in county courts. It has been shown how extensive are the powers of these courts, and over what a broad and varied range of subjects and subject matter their jurisdiction extends. It will be observed that in a large number of instances the statutes mark out and in meticulous detail prescribe the various things that shall be done in each class of the cases which may be brought in county courts. Instead of attempting to set out and discuss here the extensive statutory provisions governing each class of the special cases that county courts may hear, we shall select some of the subjects over which county courts exercise a large degree of supervisory and judicial control and discuss the various steps in the procedure in such special cases. The relation of county courts to the subjects selected is somewhat typical of that which they have with other subjects not specially covered in this work, and it is believed that the procedure herein discussed may be helpful and suggestive for that prescribed for other subjects which space forbids that we here attempt to cover. 

A. COUNTY COURTS AND ROADS Sec. 415. Control of Roads Exercised by County Courts. 

Perhaps no statutory law in Missouri has been changed more frequently and is more complex and ambiguous than the law pertaining to roads.18 Until 1921 the county courts practically had complete "In Holloway vs. Howell County, (1912) 249 Mo. 601, l. c. 609, 144 S. W. 860,

Lamm, J., speaking for the Supreme Court of Missouri, said: 'We pause long enough to remark there is a precept that every man is presumed to know the law. But should not that precept be amended so as to read, every man is presumed to know the law, except the road law? Certain it is that in some of its features it is a tangled skein of incongruities and ambiguities, if not absurdities. 

Some of its provisions overlap. They do not make a neat joint with cognate sections, and the law needs scientific revision. It would be a bold court that did not approach the road laws of Missouri with questioning eye and modest degree of doubt." 479

COUNTY COURTS 

control and supervision of all public roads in the State. With the adoption of what is generally known as the Centennial Road Law,¹º a part of that control, especially as it applies to state and national highways, passed from the county courts to other state and national agencies. To the extent that local self-government, as it applies to roads, still prevails, however, the county courts, with other political subdivisions or municipalities, such as common road districts and special road districts and township boards, in those counties having township organizations, and the agencies created by them, such as the County Highway Commission 20 and the County Highway Engineer (Secs. 8006-8023), retain general control over roads.

Sec. 416. Proceedings for Opening a Public Road, Initiated How. 

Public roads are required to be not less than thirty feet in width.21 

Applications for the establishment of all public roads, except State roads, are made by petition to the county court. Such petition must be signed by at least twelve freeholders of the township through which the proposed road may run, three of whom shall be of the immediate neighborhood. The petition shall specify the proposed beginning, course and termination of the proposed road, and shall be accompanied by the names of all persons owning land through which said road shall run, with the amount of damages, if any, claimed by them, so far as estimated, and also the names of those who are willing to give the right of way for said proposed road. If the proposed road begins or terminates on or runs along a boundary between the county wherein the petition is filed and an adjoining county, any or all of the petitioners for such road may be freeholders of such adjoining county and of the township or townships thereof through which the proposed road may run, or in which it may begin or terminate.22

Under the statutes authorizing county courts to establish public roads, it has been held that these courts have exclusive original jurisdiction to open and establish new roads and to settle, in the first instance, all questions relating to practicability, necessity, public utility, and damages connected therewith.23 The petition need not show on its face that twelve of its signers are freeholders, but it must be signed by twelve freeholders, and proof that the signers are freeholders must be made to the court or shown of record in the proceedings, otherwise the case will be dismissed in circuit court.24 The petition should describe the land owned by each person over which the proposed road is to be located, but it has been held that if several defendants are joined in any proceeding to open a road across certain described lands and judgments are entered for all defendants it will be presumed that they owned the land jointly.25 Those named as trustees and beneficiaries in a deed of trust on land crossed by the proposed road are not considered owners and need not be listed in the petition.26 It is necessary that the proposed beginning and termination of the road be stated with definiteness in the petition.27 It is sufficient if the petition shall be accompanied by the names of all resident land owners through whose land the proposed road runs, if such names are on a map filed with the petition.28 Even though the petition should not contain the names of the persons owning the land through which the proposed road runs, it has been held that the court is not thereby prevented from assuming jurisdiction, where such petition recited that it was accompanied by the names of the owners of the lands through which the road runs and the judgment of the county court recited that such was a fact.29 But an order establishing a road was held void, where it was signed by eight persons instead of twelve.30 The general rule is that the filing of a petition setting out the facts as required to be shown by statute is jurisdictional, and unless such petition is filed, meeting all the statutory requirements, 23 Parsons vs. Wilcox, 206 Mo. A. 603, 227 S. W. 620.

The term "freeholder" is defined by Ballentine as follows: "A person who owns lands in fee, or for life, or for some indeterminate period. He must have title to the property, and not simply a contingent or an expectant estate, or a right of occupancy, or a privilege, with power to prevent alienation or incumbrance by the holder of the legal title."

COUNTY COURTS Sec. 419. The Giving of Notice Jurisdictional. 

The giving of the notice in the manner prescribed is a prerequisite to the jurisdiction of the county court.32 The record of the county court must show affirmatively that the notices were posted in the manner prescribed by the statute. It is not necessary that the petitioners sign the notice. Where copies of the petition were posted as notices, it has been held that the notice is sufficient, although the form of notice heretofore set out is recommended. Where the last day of the required twenty days included the first day of the term, the notice was held sufficient.86

At such hearing the petitioners and the remonstrants have the right to produce witnesses on the questions as to the public necessity, practicability, and probable damages, if any, to the owner of the lands through which it is proposed to establish such road, and the expenses of establishing and building same, including bridges and culverts therein.41 After a hearing of these issues the court may find that the facts do not justify establishing the road at the expense of the county or of the petitioners. Sec. 421. Where the Right-of-Way Given. 

Within the time prescribed by the order made upon the county highway engineer, this officer should file his report with the clerk of the court. With the report he should also file all relinquishments, deeds, and plats of the proposed road or parts thereof. These relinquishments, deeds and plats should be preserved in the office of the county clerk as public records. All deeds should be filed and recorded in the office of the recorder of the county. (Sec. 7829.) If this report shows that the right-of-way has been secured and the deeds therefor filed, or that the damages claimed do not exceed the amount offered by the court or deposited by the petitioners, or both, the court shall order the road established (Sec. 7829).

Sec. 422. Where Land Owners Refuse to Relinquish Right of Way. 

If it appears that any person through whose lands the proposed road shall run has failed or refused to relinquish the right of way, and is not willing to take the amount of damages offered him by the court or petitioners or both, the court may, if it appears that said proposed road is of such great public utility as to warrant the establishment of the same, appoint, by order of record, three disinterested commissioners to view the premises, hear complaints and assess damages. These commissioners must be freeholders of the county, and they must not be kin within the fourth degree of consanguinity to any of the parties asking damages on account of the establishment of said road, or to any of the petitioners therefor. The court, by proper order, must make the appointment, designating the time when the commissioners shall meet, and giving such instructions relative to their proceedings as may aid them in complying with the law and performing their duties as commissioners.44

Sec. 423. Proceedings of Commissioners. 

The commissioners must be disinterested freeholders.45 They should estimate the damages as of the date of the appropriation of the land. They should observe the usual and ordinary rules applicable in fixing damages in condemnation cases.47 Two of the three commissioners may make a valid report (Sec. 7830).48

The proper procedure is for the clerk to make up and certify a copy of the order appointing the commissioners and deliver same with the other papers in the proceedings to the commissioners at the time the commissioners meet in compliance with the order of the court, which time must be not more than ten days from the date of their appointment (Sec. 7830). At that time the commissioners are required to take an oath that they will faithfully perform their duties (Sec. 7830).

Sec. 424. Proceedings Where No Exceptions Are Filed. 

The report of the commissioners in writing must be filed within 5 days after they have completed a view of the land. If no exceptions are filed within 10 days after the report is filed the court may then order the road established and opened (Sec. 7830). Such order may be made at the first sitting of the court after the expiration of 10 days following the filing of the report of the commissioners (Sec. 7832). The court is not compelled to make the order opening the road. If, under the report of the commissioners, damages are due to the owners of the lands across which the road runs, the court has the option to pay such damages or to refuse to pay same. If the court refuses to pay the damages the petitioners may pay them, and when the damages are paid, the court must make the order that the road be established. (Sec. 7832.) The court may be compelled by writ of mandamus to order the road opened,19 where all requirements of the statute are met. But since the county court has the option to pay the damages as shown by the report of the commissioners, or to refuse to pay such damages, a judgment in favor of the landowner and against the county or the petitioners is erroneous.50 If a judgment is entered establishing a road, it is not subject to collateral attack.51 The form of the order opening and establishing a road where no exceptions are filed may follow generally the form heretofore set out 52 with the additional findings based on the report of the commissioners. 

Sec. 425. Exceptions to Report of Commissioners. 

Any party in interest, including guardians of minors and insane persons affected by the proceedings, petitioners and the county, may ❤ State ex rel. Cornelius vs. McClanahan, 221 Mo. A. 399, 278 S. W. 88. 

50 Galbraith vs. Prentice, 109 Mo. A. 498, 84 S. W. 997. " New Madrid County vs. Phillips, 125 Mo. 61, 28 S. W. 321. "See Form 267. 495

COUNTY COURTS 

file exceptions to the report of the commissioners at any time within ten days after such report has been filed. Such exceptions should set out the grounds upon which the exceptors feel aggrieved by the report of the commissioners. If the exceptions are filed within ten days after the report is filed, the county clerk shall immediately thereupon make up a complete transcript of the records of the county court in said proceedings, and transmit the same, together with the original files, to the clerk of the circuit court of the county wherein the proceeding is pending. (Sec. 7831.) The circuit clerk shall file and docket said cause, and the same shall be triable at the same term, or the next regular or adjourned term of said court, after ten days after the filing of the exceptions (Sec. 7831).

Sec. 426. Appeals. 

In proceedings to establish roads the statutory method of appeal is by the filing of exceptions to the report of commissioners (Sec. 

7831). If no such exceptions are filed, the county court retains jurisdiction for making final disposition of the case (Sec. 7832).

Appeals in cases to establish roads can only be taken by the filing of a remonstrance in accordance with the applicable provisions of the statute (Sec. 7831), the general statute authorizing appeals to the circuit courts from judgments and orders of the county court (Sec. 

1938) not being applicable to such cases. 53 If the county court makes an order refusing to open the proposed road there can be no appeal from such order.54 Where all landowners relinquish the right of way and do not claim damages and the road is opened by the county court, an appeal should be denied.55 If the landowner is not satisfied with the report of the commissioners, his remedy is by appeal and this remedy must be pursued by the filing of exceptions, for if such remedy is not pursued by the landowner, he cannot later bring a suit in equity to vacate the proceedings,56 nor to enjoin same. The statute does not contemplate that an order of 57

The appeal carries the entire case to the circuit court where the cause is heard and determined anew as other causes therein, except that no commissioners are appointed by the circuit court, and six qualified jurors may constitute a jury for the trial of the question of damages in said cause (Sec. 7831). Upon the trial the circuit court shall determine and declare by its judgment whether the road shall be established, and at whose expense, and such judgment is final (Sec. 7831). To the extent that the circuit court on appeal may determine the question of the public necessity for the road, the original jurisdiction of the county court to determine that question is not exclusive. 50 While the circuit court is considering the case anew on appeal, it has the right to correct the errors made by the county court in a description of the road, where the error was patent on the record.60 The judgment of the circuit court in a case thus appealed from the county court is final, the statute providing that such judgment shall not be reviewed on appeal, nor on a writ of error (Sec. 7831). But this does not apply to appeals from judgments of the circuit court vacating public roads, since in such proceedings appeals are specifically allowed by the statute.61 A judgment refusing to open a road at the request of petitioners is not a bar to subsequent proceedings for the same purpose, and applications for a new road may be made from time to time even though former applications have been denied.62 59

Any landowner who shall fail or refuse to open said road within the time specified in the judgment shall be deemed guilty of obstructing a public highway and punished accordingly. (Sec. 7834.)

Sec. 428. Alternate Method for Establishing Public Road. 

The statutes authorize the establishment, location, relocation, widening and changing of public roads and empower the county court to condemn land and material therefor by an alternate method differing in several material respects from that heretofore discussed (Secs. 7840-7841).68 Under this statutory authority it is not necessary that the county court delay the establishment of a road until parties interested therein start a proceeding therefor by filing a petition before the county court, but such proceeding may be initiated by the court acting upon its own motion. The stat ute provides that when a county court finds that a public necessity exists for the establishment or change of a public road, it shall in the same order by which it declares the existence of such public necessity, direct the county highway engineer to survey, mark out and describe the property to be taken and the lands across or upon which said proposed public road will run, or the area, dimensions, description and location of any other property to be taken. After a map and a report of the proceedings of the highway engineer are filed in the office of the county clerk in accordance with such order, the court is required to cause notice of the proceeding to be given in a newspaper of general circulation in the county of the proposed taking. Within twenty days after the last day of the publication of such notice, interested parties are required to file claims for damages. And if no such claims are filed within that time the court is authorized to enter upon and appropriate the lands taken for the road or other property condemned. If any claim for damages is filed, such claim shall be heard on the first day of any regular or adjourned term of the county court after the expiration of the period for the filing of claims. If the county court and the land or property owners are unable to agree on the amount of the damages, the county court shall make an order reciting such fact, and cause a copy of same to be delivered to the judge of the circuit court of that county, and a transcript of the record and the original files in said cause shall be transmitted by the county clerk to the circuit clerk of the county. 

Upon receipt of the copy of the order of the county court by the circuit judge, the circuit court, or the judges thereof in vacation, shall make an order setting the cause for hearing within fifteen days. ties as quasi municipal corporations, and the county court is made the agent through which the power is to be exercised. Whenever the county court is of the opinion that public necessity exists for the establishment of a public road, regardless of the source of its information or of the considerations that may move it thereto, it may by an order of record so declare, and direct the county highway engineer to survey, mark out, and describe the road, etc. No antecedent or preliminary steps are necessary to give it jurisdiction to take these proceedings. 

This section of the road law was plainly intended to invest the county court with the power to establish and open public roads whenever and wherever public necessity requires it, without waiting upon the tardy and uncertain action of individual landowners or communities.'' 500

The court or judge in vacation shall cause to be empaneled a jury of six freeholders not interested in the matter or of kin to any member of the county court, or to any landowner in interest. Such jury is required to view the land or other property and hear the evidence and determine the question of damages under the direction of the court or judge. Five of such jury concurring may return a verdict, and in case of a disagreement another jury may be empaneled. But the public necessity for taking such property shall in nowise be inquired into by the circuit court, and the judgment of the circuit court, or judge thereof in vacation, shall not be reviewed on appeal or by writ of error. (Sec. 7840.)
