I. ORIGIN AND EVOLUTION 

Sec. 479. Definitions.

The term "probate courts" refers to a distinct classification of courts in Missouri, the primary duties of which are those of determining, directing and supervising probate matters,² or the business of administering estates. These courts operate largely, if not entirely, within the sphere of a distinctive and independent branch of the law known as probate law. The meaning of the word "probate," as it is known in American Law, has been broadened by its use in connection with the class of courts it describes, and the varied and extensive functions performed by such courts.* 3 

Sec. 480. Probate Courts Are Distinctly American.

Probate courts have no precise counterpart in the English Judicial System after which so much of our judicial structure was 'Defined by Ballentine, pp. 1021-1022, as "distinct tribunals for the establishment of wills and the administration of the estates of men dying either with or without wills. Such tribunals are variously called prerogative courts, probate courts, surrogate courts, orphans' courts, etc., and occasionally there have been added to their functions the guardianship of infants and the control of their property, the allotment of dower and other powers related more or less to the general subject." * The term "probate matters" is defined by Ballentine, p. 1022, as ´´the settlement of estates, including the granting of letters testamentary or of administration, the collection of assets, allowance of claims, payment of debts, the sale of real estate if necessary for that purpose, and the distribution of the property to those entitled thereto by the laws of descent or by the will." "In common understanding-as distinct and clearly defined a branch of the law as is criminal law or corporation law, and in popular signification, including all matters of which probate courts generally have jurisdiction, among which are estates of deceased persons." Ballentine, p. 1022. 

4 The word "probate" is said by Ballentine, p. 1021, to have "originally meant merely 'relating to proof' and later 'relating to the proof of wills,' but in the American law it is now a general name or term used to include all matters of which probate courts have jurisdiction, which in many states are the estates of deceased persons and of persons under guardianship." 570

ORIGIN AND EVOLUTION 

6 5 fashioned. To these courts have been assigned duties and in them have been vested jurisdiction and powers which were formerly held and exercised by a number of different kinds of courts. Under the English System, the business now transacted by our probate courts was originally transacted by the King's Courts of Common Law, known as the county courts. The administration of estates of deceased persons was later conceived to be a religious function, and the business incident thereto was released to the clergy as a part of their spiritual duties, so that, to a large extent, these duties came to be performed by the courts known in the English Judiciary as the Ecclesiastical Courts. Subsequently various phases of the work incident to the administration of estates of deceased persons and of minors came to be handled by different courts, some of these duties being assigned to the chancery courts' and others to the ecclesiastical courts. But the law governing administration of estates, now sometimes referred to as probate law, has its origin in remote antiquity. Some of it, such as the law of inheritance and the law pertaining to testamentary disposition of property, has been in use among the Hebrews, the Greeks, the Romans, and the Anglo- Saxons, from time immemorial. A large part of the law pertaining to descents and distribution, inheritance, wills, and the processes of administering estates, has been taken over by us from our English ancestors and now prevails in the probate courts of America. 

Our probate courts, however, have been assigned jurisdiction that is so nearly confined to probate matters exclusively, and the proceedings in these courts have been made so simple and uniform, that the probate courts in our judicial system occupy a unique position that is characteristically and distinctly American." 5 

3 Blackstone, 95.

Ecclesiastical courts were those courts presided over by members of the clergy. As said by Ballentine, p. 421, in the American states the ecclesiastical courts were not made a part of the judicial system.

Sec. 481. Evolution of Probate Courts in Missouri. 

a. During the territorial period.

11 By an organic act of the Congress of the United States, approved March 26, 1804, it was provided that the executive power vested in the Governor of Indiana territory should be exercised in the District of Louisiana and it was directed that the District of Louisiana be divided into districts by the Governor under the direction of the 

President.10 By a similar act of Congress, approved March 3, 1805, the Governor of Louisiana territory, of which Missouri was a part, was directed to proceed from time to time as circumstances required to lay out districts subject to such alterations as were necessary." 

In October, 1804, the Territorial Legislature of Missouri, consisting of the Governor and Judges of the Indiana territory, passed an act providing that there should be one judge of probate in each district, whose duty it would be to take the proof of last wills and testaments and to grant letters testamentary and letters of administration and attend to all matters pertaining to the probate office, except the rendering of definite sentences and final decrees. 

Such probate judge was required to hold four sessions each year, one at St. Charles for the St. Charles district, another at St. Louis for the St. Louis district, a third at Ste. Genevieve for the Ste. Genevieve district, with no places designated for holding such court in either the Cape Girardeau or New Madrid districts. Final decrees could only be rendered by the probate judge and two justices of the court of common pleas, called by him to sit with him and assist in contested matters or cases requiring final decrees.12 The probate judge was required to file wills and testaments and make entries of the granting of letters testamentary and of administration, and preserve bonds, inventories, accounts, and papers necessary to be perpetuated.

In 1807 an act was passed directing the method for probating wills and relating also to descents and distribution, this being the first statutory enactment in Missouri relative to the administration of

By an act approved January 7, 1825, the provisions of the Constitution relative to the establishment of probate courts were carried into effect.23 This act provided that the 

Governor appoint in each county a judge of the probate court and it gave probate courts exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases concerning the administration of estates of deceased persons and minors.

During the period from 1835 to 1877 the practice of enacting special legislation was freely indulged in in Missouri, and special acts of the Legislature were passed creating probate courts in more than half of the counties of the State and defining their jurisdiction and limiting their powers. During that period and under this special legislation, probate jurisdiction over most of the matters which probate courts now handle was given to the probate courts created by such act either exclusively or concurrently with other courts, such as courts of common pleas. 

c. Under the Constitution of 1865. 

The Constitution of 1865 did not materially alter the position of probate courts created under special acts of the Legislature. It established district courts 24 and gave them appellate jurisdiction. from final judgments of all inferior courts except probate and county courts. It also established inferior tribunals known as county courts in each county and provided that "in such courts, or in such other tribunals inferior to the circuit courts as the General Assembly may establish, shall be vested the jurisdiction of all matters appertaining to probate business, to granting letters testamentary and of administration, and to settling the accounts of executors, administrators and guardians, and to the appointment

of guardians, and such other jurisdiction as may be conferred by law."25 After the adoption of the Constitution of 1865, creation of probate courts by special act continued, and the courts already established under previous acts continued to function and to transact the regular probate business. 

d. Under the Constitution of 1875. 

The Constitution of 1875 recognized probate courts as a distinct classification of courts in our judicial system and made provision for the uniformity of their organization, powers and functions.26 

The Constitution provided: "The General Assembly shall establish in every county a probate court, which shall be a court of record, and consist of one judge, who shall be elected. Said court shall have jurisdiction over all matters pertaining to probate business, to granting letters testamentary and of administration, the appointment of guardians and curators of minors and persons of unsound mind, settling the accounts of executors, administrators, curators and guardians; and the sale or leasing of land by administrators, curators and guardians; and also jurisdiction over all matters relating to apprentices: Provided, that until the General Assembly shall provide by law for a uniform system of probate courts, the jurisdiction of probate courts heretofore established shall remain as now provided by law."27 It further provided: "Probate courts shall be uniform in their organization, jurisdiction, duties and practice, except that a separate clerk may be provided for, or the judge may be required to act ex officio, as his own clerk.'' 28 

Following the adoption of the Constitution of 1875, and conforming to its provisions relative to the establishment of a uniform system of probate courts in the State, the Legislature in 1877 passed an act providing for the establishment of a probate court as a court of record and consisting of one judge in the City of St. Louis and in every county in the State. This act provided that judges of the courts be elected at the regular popular elections held every four years, and it prescribed the jurisdiction of the court and the powers

The probate courts established in each county under that act have had a continuous existence since that time, and the jurisdiction and powers exercised by such courts and the procedure therein have been and continue uniform throughout the State. 

Sec. 482, Nature and Character of Probate Courts. 

a. Courts of record.

By virtue of a provision of the Constitution (Art. 6, Sec. 34) and the statutes (Sec. 1826), probate courts are courts of record and must keep just and faithful records of their proceedings. Being courts of record, they speak only through their records,30 in conformity with the general rule that their records are the only evidence of their official acts. 81 b. Courts having seals.

Each of these courts, like all other courts of record, is required by statute to keep a seal (Sec. 1827). c. Not inferior in strict sense.

While probate courts are inferior in the sense that certain of their judgments may be appealed from to the circuit court, in the strict legal meaning of the term they are not inferior courts but have a general original jurisdiction over certain definite subject matters, and as to these matters their judgments and findings are as conclusive and binding as the judgments of any other courts of general jurisdiction.32 They are distinguishable from inferior courts, such 

20 Laws 1877, p. 229. 

3º Farris vs. Burchard, 242 Mo. 1, 145 S. W. 825. 

31 Cunio vs. Franklin County, 315 Mo. 405, 285 S. W. 1007.

As was said in 7 R. C. L. 1018 and quoted in said case: "The acts of a court of record are known by its records alone, and cannot be established by parol testimony." 

See also State ex rel. Chaney vs. Grinstead, 314 Mo. 55, 282 S. W. 715.

II. ORGANIZATION AND ADMINISTRATION A. IN PROBATE COURTS GENERALLY Sec. 483. Number of Courts and Judges. 

In accordance with the provisions of the Constitution of 1875 (Art. 6, Secs. 34, 35), the Legislature established a probate court consisting of one judge, in the City of St. Louis and in every county in the State (Laws 1877, p. 229, Sec. 2045). The Probate 

Court of Jackson County was established by separate act (Laws 1871, p. 116, Sec. 14814), and the judge of the Criminal Court of 

Jackson County was made ex officio judge of said court, and the clerk of the Criminal Court of Jackson County was made ex officio clerk of the probate court (Sec. 14815). The Criminal Court of

Jackson County was abolished in 1921 (Laws 1921, p. 220), and the juisdiction of that court was vested in the Circuit Court of Jackson County and the powers and duties of the clerk were transferred to the clerk of the Circuit Court of Jackson County. The Cape 

Girardeau Court of Common Pleas has concurrent original juris diction with the Probate Court of Cape Girardeau County (Sec. 

"This distinction was stated in Johnson vs. Beazley, 65 Mo. 250, 1. c. 262, as follows: "The distinction is not between courts whose proceedings are, and proceedings are not, according to the course of the common law; but between courts of record which have, and, in the particular case, exercise their general original jurisdiction, and courts not of record courts of record, which have a limited and special jurisdiction, and courts of record having original general jurisdiction, but which, in the particular case, exercise a limited jurisdiction, not within the scope of their general jurisdiction"; and in the same case, 1. c. 256, as follows: "The jurisdiction of probate courts is not, like that of justices of the peace, confined to special cases in which the jurisdiction must appear, but their jurisdiction pertaining to wills and administrators is general. The subjects of their jurisdiction are clearly defined, and any action of theirs outside of such subjects would be of no force or validity, and the same may be said of the circuit court; but their action, on subjects exclusively and originally confided to them, is entitled to the same weight as that of any other court of record.'' 577

14501). Through these courts and the judges who preside over them, the probate business of Missouri is transacted. 

Sec. 484. Terms and Places of Holding Court. 

Probate courts are required to hold four terms annually, commencing on the second Monday of February, May, August and November, and they may hold special and adjourned terms at any time when required (Sec. 2050). But in those counties in which courts for the transaction of probate business are now held in more than one place, the terms of courts shall be held at the times and places as designated by law. Said courts may alter the time for holding their stated terms, giving notice thereof in such manner as to them shall seem expedient. (Sec. 2050.) It has been held that the judge of a probate court cannot, without previous order to adjourn during term time, call a term of his court in vacation, except in those cases where he is given such power by the statutes. Nor is his power in that respect enlarged by the provisions of the statute authorizing the holding of special and adjourned terms at any time when required. Where court adjourns to a day prior to beginning of the next regular term, the adjourned session is not a special term, but only a continuation of the regular term.95 In the absence of a contrary showing, the presumption is that a special term was properly and lawfully held.86 34

Sec. 486. Seal and Supplies. 

The law requires every probate court to have a seal of office, of some suitable device, the expense of which, and the necessary expense incurred by said court for books, stationery, furniture, fuel and other necessaries, shall be paid by the county (Sec. 2056). By virtue of this statutory requirement, it has been held that probate judges may purchase necessary furniture without first getting an order from the county court, and the county must pay for same. 

The words "other necessaries" used in the statute have been held to include postage stamps, and janitor and telephone service.40 39 38

In the City of St. Louis.

Before entering upon the discharge of his duties, such clerk must make and subscribe an oath before the city register that he will support the Constitution of the United States and of the State of Missouri, and that he will faithfully discharge all the duties of the office of probate clerk.

The municipal assembly in such city is authorized and empowered to provide by ordinance for the orderly transaction of business between such clerk and the treasurer of such city, and for the payment of such clerk, deputies and assistants (Sec. 2066). d. In counties having from 80,000 to 150,000 population. 

In counties having a population of from 80,000 to 150,000, wherein circuit courts are held in two or more places, the judge of the probate court may appoint one clerk at a salary of nine hundred dollars per year, paid in the same way as the salary of the probate judge in such counties (Sec. 11875).

B. PROBATE COURT IN JACKSON COUNTY Sec. 488. Terms of Court. 

There are eight terms of the Probate Court of Jackson County held annually, four terms of which are held at Independence, beginning on the second Monday in February, May, September and November, and four terms in Kansas City, beginning on the third 

Monday in February, May, September and November (Sec. 14816).

Sec. 489. Offices Both at Independence and Kansas City. 

The clerk of said court, who is allowed the same fees as allowed for similar services to clerks of the county courts transacting pro- 581

PROBATE COURTS 

bate business (Sec. 14817), is required to keep two offices for the transaction of business relating to said court, one at Independence and the other at Kansas City, and all records and proceedings and all papers filed relating to the business of the court in Kansas City shall be kept in the Kansas City office, while all records and proceedings and papers filed relating to the business of the court in Independence shall be kept in the Independence office, and a duplicate seal of the court shall be provided by the clerk, which shall be kept by said clerk at his office in Kansas City (Sec. 14818).

Sec. 490. The Granting of Letters. 

Letters testamentary and of administration on the estates of all decedents whose mansion house or place of abode was at the time of their deaths in either Kaw or Westport Townships, shall be granted by the court, or the clerk thereof in vacation, at the City of Kansas, and all orders, settlements, trials and other proceedings had therein shall be had, done and kept of record in the office of said clerk at the said City of Kansas. If the deceased had no mansion house or place of abode at the time of his death, and he be possessed of lands lying in either of said townships of Kaw or Westport, letters shall be granted by said court, or the clerk thereof in vacation, at the said City of Kansas; if the deceased had no mansion house or place of abode and died in the County of Jackson, not being possessed of lands in said county, letters may be granted either at Independence or the City of Kansas; if he died without this State, leaving a mansion house or place of abode, or lands in this State, but leaving personal property in the County of Jackson, then letters must be granted at either Independence or the City of Kansas, and in all other cases not provided for by this section such letters shall be granted by the court, or the clerk thereof, as provided by law, at Independence, and all guardians or curators for minors, who reside in Kaw or Westport Townships, shall be appointed by the probate court at Kansas City. (Sec. 14819.) 

Sec. 491. Sales of Real Estate.

The records and papers appertaining to the business of said court at Kansas City shall be kept at that place, and all public sales of 582

real estate by order of said court at that place, if made in Jackson County, shall be made at the court house door in said city, while said court or some other court of record, established by the laws of this State, is in session in said city (Sec. 14820). All public sales of real estate situated in Jackson County made by order of said court at its session in Independence, shall be made at the court house door in said town, and while said court or some other court of record is in session thereat (Sec. 14822).

Sec. 492. Transfer of Hearings. 

In all cases where it may be by the said court deemed advisable, or to the interest of the party or parties to any proceeding or controversy therein, it may by order, entered of record, remove and transfer the hearing of such proceeding or controversy either from Independence to the City of Kansas, or from the City of Kansas to Independence, and said cause, proceeding or controversy shall be proceeded with to final settlement or conclusion at the place to which it may be removed, and a transcript of all proceedings had in relation thereto, before such removal, together with the original papers, shall be forwarded to the office of the clerk at the place to which such cause, proceeding or controversy shall be sent for final determination (Sec. 14823).

Sec. 493. Appeals. 

All appeals taken from the court at Kansas City are taken to the circuit court of Jackson County (Sec. 14824).

III..JUDGES, THEIR QUALIFICATIONS, DUTIES AND COMPENSATION Sec. 494. Election, Term of Office, and Vacancies. 

The Constitution requires that the General Assembly establish in each county a probate court consisting of one judge, who shall be elected (Art. 6, Sec. 34). The statute directs that a probate judge of each county be elected by the qualified voters therein every four years, except where some other method therefor is fixed by law. 

Such judges are elected at the general election held every four years and on those years when a President of the United States is 583

PROBATE COURTS 

not elected. (Sec. 2047.) In case of a tie, a special election is held, called by proclamation of the Governor (Secs. 10176 and 10177). 

All contested elections for judge of the probate court of the City of St. Louis are heard and determined by the circuit court of that city (Sec. 10378). Following their election, probate judges are commissioned by the Governor and are required to take the oath prescribed by the Constitution for all officers. Such judges enter upon the discharge of their duties on the first day of January following their election and continue in office for four years and until their successors are duly elected and qualified. In case any judgeelect dies before he qualifies, the office thereby becomes vacant from and after the date on which such judge-elect is required to qualify. (Sec. 2047.) When a vacancy occurs, the clerk of the circuit court of the county is required to certify the fact to the Governor, who must fill the vacancy by appointing some eligible person to the office, and the person thus appointed, when qualified, continues in office until the next general election, when a successor must be elected for the unexpired term (Sec. 2048).

Sec. 495. Qualifications. 

To be eligible for judge of the probate court, a person must have attained the age of twenty-four years, and must have been a citizen of the United States five years and a resident of the county in which he may be elected for one year next preceding his election (Sec. 1824). A probate judge is not required to be learned in the law. Every person elected probate judge must be commissioned by the Governor, and the judge elected holds his office until his successor is elected and qualified. (Sec. 1824.) Within thirty days after the receipt of his commission, and before entering upon the duties of his office, each probate judge must take the oath prescribed by the Constitution of this State, and a certificate of having taken such oath must be endorsed upon his commission (Sec. 1825). 

Sec. 496. Special Probate Judge May Be Elected by Attorneys of the Court.

Whenever the judge of probate, from any cause, shall be unable to hold any term or part of a term of court, the attorneys of the 584

court who are present, but not less in number than five, may elect one of their members then in attendance, having the qualifications of a judge of probate, to hold the court for the occasion, or to hold the court for a part of a term (Sec. 2067). It has been held that jurisdiction of a special judge of probate terminated with the end of service at the term of court to which he was elected, but a probate court's jurisdiction over an application for the distribution of a decedent's estate did not cease therewith.41

The election shall be held by the clerk of the court, if there be one; if not, by the sheriff of the county. And in the event of a tie, the clerk, if there be one, or, if not, the sheriff of the county, shall cast the deciding vote. The clerk of the court, if there be one, if not, the sheriff of the county, shall enter the proceedings of such election on the probate records of that day; and the special judge shall, before entering upon the discharge of his duties, take and subscribe the same oath that the judge of probate is required to take, which oath shall be filed with the records of such court. (Sec. 2068.) 

If the person first elected to act as special judge fails or refuses to act, or cannot properly preside, another election shall be held, in like manner as the first election, from time to time, until a suitable attorney is chosen who can and will preside (Sec. 2069). 

Sec. 497. Special Judge May Be Appointed by Governor. 

Whenever the judge of probate, from any cause, shall be unable to hold any term of court, or shall be unable to discharge his duties from continued sickness or mental or physical inability, the Governor, upon the certificate of such judge, or upon satisfactory proof of such fact, shall have power to appoint some suitable person, a resident of the county possessing the qualifications of a probate judge, to discharge the duties of the office, and to hold probate court in such county during the existence of the inability of the regular judge; and the judge so appointed, during the period he shall act, shall possess the same powers, take and subscribe to the same oath, and be liable to the same responsibilities, as the regular judge of said court, and receive the same compensation during such time. After the appointment of such special judge, he shall con- "State ex rel. Gott vs. Fidelity & Deposit Co., 317 Mo. 1078, 298 S. W. 83. 585

PROBATE COURTS 

tinue to act as such until the Governor shall be satisfied by competent evidence that the regular judge is competent in all respects to act as judge, and until the Governor is thus satisfied, the regular judge shall have no power to act. (Sec. 2071.) The attorney thus elected shall, during the period he shall act, have power to solemnize marriages, administer oaths and affirmations, take acknowledgments to deeds, and all of the other powers, and be liable to all of the responsibilities of the judge of probate, and shall receive for his services the same fees as the judge of probate is entitled to receive for similar services (Sec. 2070).

Sec. 498. Disqualifications of Probate Judges. 

Because of the nature of his office, a probate judge is disqualified, by provisions of the statute, from acting as an executor or administrator (Sec. 6), as guardian or surety for guardians of minors (Secs. 391, 2053), as guardian or surety for guardians of insane persons (Secs. 460, 2053), or as surety in any official bond given by any officer in this State (Sec. 2847). He is exempt from jury service (Sec. 8748). While a judge of probate may practice law in courts besides his own, he cannot sit in a case in which he is interested, in which he may have been counsel or a material witness, or related to either party, or in the determination of any cause or proceeding in the administration and settlement of any estate of which he is or has been executor, administrator, guardian or curator, when any party in interest shall object in writing, verified by affidavit (Secs. 1848, 2053), and he cannot, under any circumstances, practice in his own court, under any pretense whatever (Sec. 1860). 

He is prohibited from having any partner practicing in the court of which he is judge (Secs. 1862, 2053). A probate judge is prohibited from witnessing any will or making any settlement for any administrator, executor, guardian or curator, over which his court has jurisdiction (Sec. 2053).

Sec. 499. Powers and Duties. 

a. Conservators of the peace.

A judge of the probate court is a conservator of the peace and has been granted by statute power to issue such writs as may be neces- 586

sary in the exercise of his jurisdiction according to the usage and principles of law, and may let to bail any party indicted for a bailable offense in the county in which the indictment is pending (Sec. 2051).42 b. To hold county court.

Whenever, by reason of sickness, absence from the county, or other preventing cause, the judges of the county court of any county, or a majority of them, shall not be able to hold any regular term of the county court, then the judge of the probate court of such county shall hold such term of the county court (Sec. 2052). When this occurs, the probate judge receives the same compensation as the judge of the county court, but while acting as judge of the county court a probate judge does not have power to levy taxes of any kind, except those necessary for ordinary county expenditures (Art. 6, Sec. 36; Sec. 2052). c. To punish for contempts. 

Probate courts have power to enforce obedience to their orders, rules, judgments and decrees, and may issue attachments for contempt offered them or their process, and may fine and imprison such offenders in the same manner as circuit courts may do in like cases (Sec. 2060).48 

d. Miscellaneous powers. 

In addition to their judicial functions, probate judges have varied miscellaneous powers. A probate judge is authorized to take affidavits (Secs. 1720, 1721), administer oaths (Secs. 1720, 9758), act ex officio as his own clerk (Sec. 2049), appoint a separate clerk (Sec. 2049), take bail in certain cases (Secs. 2051, 3401), issue 44 "Ex Parte Webers, 275 Mo. 677, 205 S. Sec. 500. Guilty of Misdemeanor, When. 

If the judge or clerk of probate shall knowingly and wilfully do any act prohibited by law, or omit or refuse to perform any act, service or duty required of him by law, he shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor in office, and, on conviction thereof, shall be removed from office, and be subject to suit for damages by any person who may be injured by such act (Sec. 2055). 

Sec. 501. Compensation of Judges.

And every probate judge shall, within thirty days after the expiration of each and every year of his term of office, file for record with the clerk of the circuit court having jurisdiction in said county, a statement, verified by his affidavit, containing a full account of all fees collected and amounts expended for clerk hire, by or for such probate judge, during such year, specifying the respective amounts collected, from whom, and dates when collected, and the respective amounts paid for clerk hire, to whom, and dates when paid; and within three months after the expiration of his term of office he shall file for record with said clerk of the circuit court a statement, verified by his affidavit, of all fees which accrued but were not collected during his term of office, specifying the names of the parties from whom due, the amounts due, on account of what services rendered, and the date of accrual. 

Every probate judge shall, before collecting or being authorized to collect any fees whatsoever, give a good and sufficient bond in a penal sum which in counties of less than 150,000 inhabitants shall be equal to the compensation of a circuit judge in such county, and which in counties of over 150,000 inhabitants shall be in a penal sum of double such compensation of a circuit judge in such county; every which bond shall have good and sufficient sureties, to be approved by the said clerk of the circuit court having jurisdiction 591

PROBATE COURTS 

in such county, and shall be filed with such clerk, and which bond shall be renewed within twenty days after notification by the said clerk upon his being satisfied that said bond, or the sureties, or any of them, is or are, or have become, insufficient, and failure to renew such bond shall, until the same be furnished, suspend the authority of the judge so in default to collect any fees; every said bond shall run to the State, and may be sued upon by any corporation or person in interest, and shall be conditioned upon the faithful performance by said probate judge of all the duties imposed by law, and the prompt filing of such statements as are required by law, and the payments in full, promptly when due, into the county treasury, of each and every one of the amounts to the extent and in the manner required by law. For all the purposes of the statute pertaining to probate judges, the City of St. Louis shall be considered as a county. (Sec. 11782.)

IV.  Sec. 502. The Constitution. 

A. SOURCES 

Probate courts are among the tribunals in which judicial power is vested by the Constitution (Art. 6, Sec. 1). The Constitution not only directed the General Assembly to establish a probate court in each county (Art. 6, Sec. 34), but it also provided that such courts be uniform in their organization, jurisdiction, duties and practice (Art. 6, Sec. 35), and it commanded that such courts have jurisdiction over all matters pertaining to probate business, to granting letters testamentary and of administration, the appointment of guardians and curators of minors and persons of unsound mind, settling the accounts of executors, administrators, curators and guardians; and the sale or leasing of lands by administrators, curators, and guardians; and also jurisdiction over all matters relating to ap prentices (Art. 6, Sec. 34). Thus, the jurisdiction and powers of probate courts are directly derived from the organic law, the Constitution.45 

45 7 R. C. L. 1030; Jones vs. Peterson (Sup.), 72 S. W. (2d) 76. 592

des 

Sec. 503. The Statute. 

It will be observed that the Constitution did not "establish" probate courts, but it directed the Legislature to establish them, and it commanded that in establishing such courts they be made uniform in organization, jurisdiction, duties and practice. These provisions of the Constitution relative to the creation of probate courts were not self-enforcing, but they required legislation to carry them into effect.48 As to the jurisdiction of these courts, however, the Constitution was more specific. As heretofore stated, the Constitution set out, in general terms, the subject matter over which probate courts should have jurisdiction. When the General Assembly passed an act to enforce the provisions of the Constitution relative to probate courts, it included a provision defining the jurisdiction of such courts in the exact language of the Constitution. To that provision it added that the judges of probate court shall have power to solemnize marriages (Sec. 2046).47 The General Assembly has conferred other powers on probate courts or the judges thereof not specified by the Constitution,48 but in the granting of such additional powers it is generally held that the Legislature cannot go beyond the scope of the subject matter over which the Constitution provides that probate courts shall have jurisdiction.¹º

Sec. 504. Inherent and Implied Powers.

Sec. 505. Legislature Cannot Enlarge Powers. 

Much has been written by the courts of this State on the question as to whether or not the Legislature may enlarge the powers vested in probate courts by the Constitution, and not all that has been written can be easily reconciled. In approaching the subject, it is well to keep in mind some well-established principles as to constitutional limitations upon legislative authority, among which are: 

First, that the Constitution is not a grant of power to the Legislature, but is a limitation on legislative authority; 57 second, the legislative power is the sovereign power of the people, and, subject to the constitutional limitations thereon made either expressly or by necessary implication, is vested in the General Assembly; 58 or, as is sometimes stated, the power of the Legislature to enact laws is subject to the limitations of the Constitution, whether such limitations be expressed by prohibitory clauses or by affirmative provisions relating to the particular subject, both methods of restriction being equally binding on the law-making power, and no valid law may be enacted by the Legislature which contravenes either; 59 third, the Legislature may pass any law upon any subject not forbidden by the State or Federal Constitution; 60 fourth, where the

Constitution makes no provision for enlarging the jurisdiction granted by it to a particular class of courts, the Legislature cannot enlarge the jurisdiction of such courts. 61

It will be observed that the Constitution does not specifically prohibit the Legislature from passing any acts granting powers to probate courts beyond the sphere of the powers expressly granted by the Constitution. And, following the statement of a fundamental principle of constitutional limitations by a well-known authority, that "the inhibition of a Constitution may be either express or implied; that is, the Constitution may expressly prohibit any act of the Legislature, or the Constitution, by its inherent terms, may of necessity prohibit certain acts of the Legislature by reason of inherent conflict which would arise by the terms of the Constitution and the power claimed in favor of the Legislature," 62 the Supreme Court has held that, since Article 6, Section 34, of the Constitution names the subjects over which probate courts shall have jurisdiction, this amounts to a prohibition against the Legislature's extending the jurisdiction of such courts over subjects not specified in the Constitution. Since its decision that the Legislature does not have the power to enlarge the jurisdiction of probate courts beyond that specified by the Constitution, the Supreme Court has adhered generally to that doctrine. Earlier cases expressed a doctrine not altogether reconcilable with this.65 However, the results of the decisions

B. NATURE AND EXTENT 1. Jurisdiction Denied. 

Sec. 506. Common Law. 

Probate courts are not common-law courts, and do not have common-law jurisdiction." But, while probate courts are denied common-law jurisdiction, they may, in the exercise of their regular functions, apply common-law principles.72

Sec. 508. Habeas Corpus. 

Statutes authorizing the issuance of writs of habeas corpus from an early date provided that application for such writs may be made "to some court of record in term, or a judge thereof in vacation" (Secs. 1426-1427)." In an early decision by the Supreme Court it was held that, by virtue of such statutes, probate courts could issue writs of habeas corpus.78 This appeared to be the clear purpose of the statutes authorizing the issuance of writs of habeas corpus (Secs. 1426-1427). Sec. 509. Title Controversies. 

Although in the subject matter with which probate courts deal, land titles are frequently involved, jurisdiction to determine title to real estate is denied probate courts. Original jurisdiction of actions to determine title to real estate is vested exclusively in cir cuit courts by the Constitution (Art. 6, Sec. 22).84 The power to determine real estate title controversies not having been vested in probate courts, such courts cannot entertain an action to determine title either as a suit in equity or in ejectment.85 The same rule applies to personal property title, it having been held that a probate court does not have jurisdiction to try the question as to whether specific personal property claimed by an administrator actually belonged to the estate of deceased,80 nor jurisdiction to determine adverse claims to either real or personal property in the hands of an administrator.87 But this should be read in connection with the law pertaining to proceedings to discover assets or determine the validity of gifts, where probate courts are held to have the right to determine who is entitled to property.88 Except in such proceedings, however, it is uniformly held that probate courts do not have jurisdiction to decide title controveries.89 If, in the administration of an estate involving real estate, a question arises as to the title, and it appears to the probate court that there are adverse claimants asserting claims against such real estate, it is the uniform policy by the Constitution. The statute, therefore, in so far as it attempts to include probate courts is violative of the Constitution (Section 34 of Article 6) and void." "This section of the Constitution, among other things, provides: ". . . circuit courts shall have exclusive original jurisdiction in all civil cases not otherwise provided for.'

Sec. 510. Equity.

In England, equity or chancery courts exercise jurisdiction concurrent with ecclesiastical courts over many of the matters involved in the administration of estates. This practice naturally evolved as a part of their system. But in America the tendency has been to segregate completely the administration of estates and other probate business and to assign jurisdiction thereof to probate courts.92 Missouri is one of those states that has gone farthest among the states in the American Union in thus segregating probate business from other branches of the law and giving probate courts original power and exclusive jurisdiction over such business. The result is that, under our system, the courts exercising chancery powers and having the right to grant relief in equity have been almost completely divested of all powers pertaining to the administration of estates and the transaction of probate business, jurisdiction over such matters having been by our Constitution and statutes vested almost exclusively in probate courts.93 

Chancery courts, or courts having the right to grant relief in equity, are permitted to take jurisdiction of particular questions incident to the administration of estates or involving probate business only when the constitutional or statutory power of probate "⁰ Trent's Administrator vs. Trent, 24 Mo. 307; Valle vs. Bryan, 19 Mo. 423;

Because jurisdiction over probate business has been vested in probate courts by the Constitution and statutes, which do not authorize such courts to exercise jurisdiction of an equitable nature, and because the business of such courts is of an entirely different nature from that of courts exercising chancery powers, it is generally held that probate courts do not have jurisdiction to hear and determine equity cases, or try issues of a purely equitable nature, or grant equitable relief.95

PROBATE COURTS Sec. 512. Appeals Where Probate Court Had No Jurisdiction. 

On an appeal from a judgment in a proceeding originating in a probate court, the circuit court only acquires jurisdiction of the subject matter over which the probate court had jurisdiction in the first instance.18 In disposing of such appeal, the circuit court may determine every question of law and fact which was properly before the probate court and from the determination of which an appeal was taken, but the jurisdiction of the circuit court on such appeal does not extend further.19 Though a circuit court may exercise chancery powers and has original equity jurisdiction, such court cannot exercise chancery powers or invoke equity jurisdiction in an appeal from a probate court, because the probate court is denied such jurisdiction and powers, and in determining such appeal the circuit court cannot exercise jurisdiction originally denied the probate court.20 

2. Original and Exclusive.

Sec. 513. Of Matters Pertaining to Probate Business Generally. 

Under our system of jurisprudence, circuit courts have general original jurisdiction of all actions at law and equity, except those taken out of that jurisdiction by positive law and conferred upon other courts and tribunals.21 Had it not been for provisions of the 

Constitution and statutes, jurisdiction over probate business would have naturally vested in circuit courts incident to the general chancery powers with which such courts are vested. But the Constitution and the statutes have taken out of the jurisdiction of circuit courts probate business and have vested such jurisdiction in probate courts.22 By provision of the Constitution (Art. 6, Sec. 34),

Neither the Constitution nor the statutes provide that such jurisdiction is exclusive, 28 but, except in some particular instances which will be hereinafter referred to, jurisdiction of the matters therein specified is not given to any other courts in our "In some of the earliest decisions holding that the jurisdiction of probate courts over probate matters was exclusive, including those of Dodson vs. Scroggs, 47 Mo. 285; Cones vs. Ward, 47 Mo. 289; Titterington vs. Hooker, 58 Mo. 

593; Pearce vs. Calhoun, 59 Mo. 271; Wernecke vs. Kenyon's Administrator, 66 Mo. 275; Ensworth vs. Curd, 68 Mo. 282; the fact should not be overlooked that the courts were construing the meaning of special acts of the Legislature creating probate courts. From 1840 until the adoption of the Constitution of 1875, the Legislature of Missouri passed a large number of special acts creating probate courts in different counties. In his very excellent thesis on "The Organization of Courts in Missouri" (1915), available only in the Library of the University of Missouri, Mr. Joseph Jackson Gravely, now a member of the St. Louis Bar, estimated that from 1845 to 1865, fifty-four counties in Missouri had obtained special probate courts through this special legislation; that in the same time fourteen counties had in the same way obtained special courts of common pleas, some of which exercised probate jurisdiction; and that in the same period five counties had obtained a special court with both common pleas and probate jurisdiction. (Table I, II and III, between pages 

35 and 36.) Following the adoption of the Constitution of 1865, the practice of creating probate courts by special acts of the Legislature continued, and Mr. Gravely estimated that at different times during the period from 1865 to 

1875, ninety-four counties in Missouri had special probate courts created by special acts of the Legislature; that during the same period twenty-six counties in Missouri had special common pleas courts, and fourteen counties in Missouri had special courts with both probate and common pleas jurisdiction, all created by special acts of the Legislature. As a general rule, the special acts creating such probate courts and courts exercising probate jurisdiction expressly gave such courts exclusive jurisdiction over probate business. For example, see Laws 1845, p. 71, Sec. 4; Laws 1849, p. 436, Sec. 4; Laws 1865, p. 85, Sec. 6; Laws 1870, p. 227, Sec. 11; Laws 1870, pp. 228-229, Sec. 1. In the cases referred to, where the court was called upon to determine whether or not probate courts had exclusive jurisdiction of probate matters, the court in each instance held that by virtue of the provisions of these special acts giving these courts exclusive jurisdiction of probate matters, exclusive jurisdiction was thereby lodged in probate courts. 607

And it is generally held that as to all matters pertaining to probate business, and particularly those items of probate business specified by the Constitution and statute, probate courts have exclusive jurisdiction.24 Except in those rare instances where other courts have been given jurisdiction concurrent with probate courts over certain matters incident to the administration of estates, probate courts are generally held to have exclusive original jurisdiction over all matters pertaining to the administration of estates of deceased persons, minors and lunatics, and all matters pertaining to probate business.25

23 This idea has been expressed in the case of Pearce vs. Calhoun, 59 Mo. 271, 1. c. 274-275, as follows: "Our Probate Courts were established with extensive powers and jurisdictions, for the purpose of doing everything necessary to the full and final administration of an estate. Both real and personal property are under their control for the payment of debts. They possess about the same powers formerly exercised in England by the ecclesiastical and chancery courts. 

They are authorized to collect the assets of the deceased, to allow claims, to direct their payment, and to subject the realty to sale where there is a deficiency of personal property to satisfy creditors, and to make distribution to the parties entitled thereto, and, in general, to do everything essential to the final settlement of the affairs of the deceased, and the claims of creditors against the estate. "With a tribunal clothed with such ample powers, all parties have a sufficient protection and opportunity for the assertion of their rights; at least, if they attempt to proceed otherwise some very strong and satisfactory excuse should be shown for the failure to present the claim in the mode prescribed by law."

The reasoning supporting this doctrine of the exclusive nature of the jurisdiction of probate courts over matters pertaining to probate business, and as against the claims of courts having chancery powers to exercise such jurisdiction, has been well set forth in Matson & May vs. Pearson, 121 Mo. A. 120, 97 S. W. 983, quoted and adopted by the Supreme Court in Scott vs. Royston, 223 Mo. 568, 123 S. W. 454, as follows: "It is determined, and abundantly supported by both principle and authority, that a court of equity will not assume jurisdiction of a claim against an estate of a deceased person until it has been made to appear that the probate court cannot afford the requisite relief. . . . The principle thus announced pervades the entire system of equity 610

the jurisdiction of probate courts over matters pertaining to the administration of estates and probate business is exclusive and jurisprudence and is to the effect that equity interposes only to supply the deficiencies of the law, and therefore, if it appears that a party has an adequate remedy at law, equity will point him to that court for relief and decline to assume jurisdiction. It is suggested, however, that even though the claims presented in the bill be demands against the estate within the meaning of the administration law, and as such cognizable in law courts, this equitable proceeding may be sustained upon the principle that, inasmuch as, under the English rule, courts of chancery assumed jurisdiction in nearly or about all manner of instances with respect to estates of deceased persons and the administration thereof, and that the doctrine is firmly established to the effect that, whenever chancery once had and entertained jurisdiction, such jurisdiction continues, and the subsequent grant of remedy at law will not oust the court of equity of its jurisdiction in the premises unless the equitable remedy is extinguished by direct and positive prohibitory provisions in the statute conferring such remedy at law. There is no doubt but such is the rule which obtains with us and elsewhere. . . . Now it appears that in England the subject of the settlement and disposition of estates of deceased persons is, or was, a matter over which the ecclesiastical and chancery courts, to a very large extent, exercised what seemed to be a concurrent jurisdiction, and it is pointed out in the history of that jurisprudence that the courts of chancery so lightly esteemed the proceedings of the ecclesiastical courts with respect to matters of administration that they did not hesitate to take the subject from them, etc.; but, upon examination of the authorities, the reason for the exercise of this jurisdiction by the courts of chancery is discovered to be that the chancery courts asserted the prerogative on account of the inadequacy of the powers and infirmities of the ecclesiastical courts to meet the exigencies presented and to render complete justice to all concerned. So we ascertain the true ground upon which chancery courts assumed jurisdiction in these cases to be, either, that the remedy at law did not exist at all, or was not 'full, adequate, and complete.' . . . And indeed this was but the application of the same ancient principle of equity jurisprudence heretofore adverted to. It has been pointedly decided, however, by our Supreme Court, that the reason on which equity interposed in matters of administration in the old days does not obtain with us, and that the principle suggested has no application in view of our statutes with respect to administration. It is pointed out that they are so full and complete, abounding with apt and pertinent provisions to administer full, complete, and adequate relief at law, and that their provisions are so ample with respect to matters of administration, that they amount to an exclusion, in fact, of the chancery jurisdiction asserted, unless there be some fact or facts involved which renders the case one where adequate relief at law cannot be had.' 

See also Seibert vs. Harden (Sup.), 8 S. W. (2d) 905, wherein the same language was quoted and approved. 611

Sec. 515. Proceedings to Discover Assets. 

Proceedings to discover concealed, embezzled or wrongfully withheld assets of a deceased person are considered incident, or involving matters pertaining, to probate business, and statutes authorizing such proceedings by probate courts (Secs. 63-67) are generally held to vest such courts with exclusive jurisdiction of such proceedings.37 In such proceedings, unless some purely equitable ground is stated for the determination of title to property claimed for the estate, probate courts have exclusive jurisdiction to determine whether there has been any property concealed, or embezzled, or otherwise wrongfully withheld from the assets of the estate.88 Thus, where a suit was brought in the circuit court by the heirs of a deceased person against the widow and administratrix of the deceased, charging that she had failed to make a true and correct inventory and appraisement and had not faithfully accounted for the assets of the estate as was required by law, but had converted to her own use a large amount of property belonging to the estate, a demurrer was properly sustained on the ground that the suit was one to discover assets, and, since the statute commits only to probate courts jurisdiction to entertain such proceedings, the circuit court had no jurisdiction.39 Such proceedings are "actions" wherein the parties are entitled to a jury trial as in any other lawsuit, our statutes authorizing such proceedings being different in that regard from statutes of a similar nature in other states,¹º and probate courts are generally held to have exclusive jurisdiction thereof where no strictly equitable issue is involved." Sec. 516. Proceedings to Determine Validity of Gifts or Transfers by Deceased.

Contrary to the general rule that probate courts do not have jurisdiction to determine title controversies, it is now generally held that probate courts have exclusive original jurisdiction, not only of actions to discover assets, which involve the determination of rights to property, but also of actions and proceedings to determine the validity of claims to property withheld from the administrator or heirs of a deceased person and based upon a gift of same by deceased, or of a transfer thereof by deceased in payment for services, or on some other similar claim.45 Proceedings of this nature are closely akin to, and are governed by the same statutes as, proceedings to discover assets. Such proceedings may, and ordinarily do, originate by an administrator or interested party filing an affidavit in probate court charging that a widow or some relative or donee of a deceased person is withholding from the estate property that belonged to the deceased at the time of his death. If the person against whom such proceeding is instituted claims the title to the property by gift of the deceased or otherwise, the probate court. alone has jurisdiction to try the title.46 While this question has been one about which there has been much controversy, resulting in inharmonious decisions,47 the rule is now definitely established that in 43

Sec. 517. Sale of Real Estate to Pay Debts and Legacies. 

On the same principles heretofore stated, it is generally held that probate courts have original exclusive jurisdiction over proceedings for the sale of real estate to pay the debts and legacies of a deceased person. Thus, it is said that the statutes authorizing such sales (Secs. 142-181) furnish a full, adequate and complete method within themselves for such sales and, until such method is exhausted, no other court has jurisdiction of the subject matter.52 And on the same theory it has been held that the probate court has exclusive jurisdiction to order a sale of the homestead of a deceased husband leaving a widow and collateral heirs only to pay the legallyestablished debts,58 and that the circuit court has no jurisdiction of a suit to sell real estate of a decedent alleged to have been charged with the payment of a legacy, since the exclusive jurisdiction to make such sale is in the probate court.54

3. Concurrent With Other Courts. 

Sec. 519. Circuit Courts-Demands Against Estates. 

The circuit court has jurisdiction concurrent with probate courts over proceedings to determine and allow claims against the estate of a deceased person (Secs. 189, 190). Presentation and allowance of such claims in either court are sufficient if done in compliance with the statutes.57 In order for this rule to apply as to claims allowed by the circuit court, however, the circuit court must exercise original jurisdiction in the allowance of such claims, for it has been held that the allowance of a claim by a circuit court on an appeal from a justice court was insufficient, because in such instance the jurisdiction of the circuit court was derived, whereas the statute contemplates that in the allowance of such claim in a circuit court that court must exercise original and not derivative jurisdiction.58 

The statutes vesting circuit courts with jurisdiction concurrent with probate courts to hear and allow demands which clearly pertain to probate business are not violative of the Constitution. The 

Constitution vested circuit courts with such concurrent jurisdiction ❝ Woerther vs. Miller, 13 Mo. A. 567. In this case the circuit court, upon stipulation of the parties, entered an order setting out a widow's dower in personalty. The court of appeals reversed the case, saying: "If this could be done, the greatest confusion would be introduced into the administration of estates, and the circuit court, in ignorance of the condition of the estate, might make a peremptory order of distribution conflicting with that which, on final settlement, and in view of all the facts, the probate court would be bound by law to make."

And it has been held that, under that provision of the Constitution, the Legislature properly authorized the retention of the practice, that had prevailed long prior to the adoption of the Constitution, of permitting claims against the estates of deceased persons to be filed and allowed in circuit courts.59 Thus, it has been held that either the probate court or the circuit court may exercise jurisdiction of an action to recover by reason of administrator's breach of an agreement for the sale of mortgaged property and payment of the proceeds to the mortgagee.60 Likewise, either a circuit court or a probate court has jurisdiction of an action to recover for legal services rendered an estate at the instance of an administrator.61 

Decisions holding the contrary 62 have been disapproved and are not the law.63 Where the purpose of the action is to have a trust established, which is purely of an equitable nature, the probate court does not have jurisdiction, nor does the limitation statute of the administration law apply to bar such claim. With this exception, however, it is now generally held that claims or demands 64

V. PROCEDURE Sec. 521. What Law Governs. 

Probate courts, in the exercise of their jurisdiction, are governed by the statutes in relation to administration, to guardians and curators of minors and persons of unsound mind, to apprentices, and such laws as are enacted from time to time defining and limiting the practice in such courts (Sec. 2058). All probate courts and the clerks thereof are governed in all things by the provisions of the statutes governing the administration of estates of deceased persons, so far as they may be applicable to their jurisdiction and duties (Sec. 295). In other words, in the exercise of their constitutional and statutory powers, probate courts are governed by what are generally known as the laws of administration. 

Sec. 522. Laws of Administration a Separate Code. 

Probate courts are not governed by the same rules that obtain in circuit courts, and the pleadings and practice in probate courts are not according to the Code of Civil Procedure. Proceedings in probate courts are governed by the laws of administration, and the chapter of the statutes on administration, which comprises probate law in Missouri, is a code unto itself." Taken altogether, procedure 

70 Sidwell vs. Kaster, 289 Mo. 174, 232 S. W. 1005; Painter vs. Painter, 206 

Mo. A. 312, 228 S. W. 538. "In re Jarboe's Estate, 227 Mo. 59, 127 S. W. 26, 1. c. 36. In his dissenting opinion in that case Chief Justice Valliant said: "The law governing probate courts and directing their course of procedure is a chapter in itself, and contains all the judicial power that the court is possessed of, except, of course, such powers as are necessarily inferred from the powers expressly given and necessary to the full execution of those express powers, and except also such powers as are expressly given in other statutes. The chapter headed 'Administration' contains all the powers, except as elsewhere in the statutes expressly conferred, that the probate court may exercise; it is a code of laws in itself. Many of the provisions in that chapter, prescribed for the exercise of the jurisdiction of the probate courts, would be entirely unnecessary if the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure applied. But the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply to probate courts; it applies to circuit courts and courts of limited jurisdiction, exercising within their limits the same kind of juris- ... 620

Sec. 523. Pleadings. 

a. Generally.

There is no code governing pleadings in the probate courts in Missouri. In each proceeding where pleadings are required, the statutes prescribe what matters must be set out in the pleadings. 

In such cases the provisions of the statutes must be complied with. 

The character of the pleadings required in each separate proceeding will be hereinafter discussed in connection with the other subject matter involved in such proceeding. b. In actions or demands against estates. 

In the presentation of demands against estates, the general rule is that formal pleadings are not required, either in the probate court or on appeal to the circuit court." This rule is based upon the statute (Sec. 198), which provides that demands against estates shall be heard in a summary manner "without the form of pleading." By this provision of the statute, the established practice of informality has been conserved. Neither the statute nor the rule diction that circuit courts exercise; for example, courts of common pleas and the like."' It is believed that this is in accordance with both the trend of the decisions and administrative practice.''

74 In Guthrie vs. Fields (App.), 299 S. W. 141, 1. c. 143, the court said: "The strict legal rules of pleading are not applicable to proceedings in probate courts. 

The law provides that probate courts shall hear and determine all demands in a summary way, without the form of pleading. The practice in the probate courts is purposely so framed that parties can attend to their own business in ordinary matters, and the decisions should be so rendered as to subserve the ends of justice according to the evidence, without regard to technical precision in pleading. The law has pointed out and adopted a summary mode of proceeding for the convenience of the people, and to apply the rules of pleading with the strictness here contended for would make of them a snare to entrap the unwary." 621

Process issued by probate courts, like that of other courts, may be served in the ordinary manner, and when there is no sheriff or other ministerial officer qualified to act, or where they are interested or prejudiced, the judge or clerk in vacation may appoint one or more persons to execute process of such court and perform any other duty of such officer (Sec. 1845). 

Sec. 525. Docket. 

It is made the duty of the clerk of every court of record, including probate courts, before the commencement of each term of court, to make out two dockets of all causes in which an issue of fact is to be tried and arrange such causes upon the docket in the same order in which they stand in the course of proceeding, setting a proper proportion for each day (Sec. 1829). One of such dockets is known as the "court docket," the other as the "bar docket," and are arranged appropriately, with spaces for the names of attorneys, and brief statements of the orders and judgments of the court in the respective cases (Sec. 1830). Every clerk who shall neglect or refuse to make out such dockets, according to law, shall be fined by the court in any sum not exceeding one hundred dollars for every such offense (Sec. 1831).

The statute further requires the probate court to keep a docket in which must be entered, at least thirty days before each regular term, the names of all guardians and curators whose settlements are due each term, and shall designate in such docket the particular day of "Ex parte Zorn, 241 Mo. 267, 145 S. Such docket must be published for three weeks in some newspaper published in the county, if there be one, and the cost thereof shall be divided by the whole number of cases docketed, and taxed against each estate in proportion to the amount ascertained by such division as the part of such estate in such cost. Sec. 526.

Trials. 

Trials in probate courts are generally of a summary nature, and, except in those instances where the statute authorizes trial by jury, are before the court. Where the statutes authorize trials by jury, such trials must be held according to such provisions of the statutes, as such statutes direct probate courts to try causes in the way thus specified, and in no other way.84 Jury trials are authorized by statute in hearings of demands against estates (Sec. 200), or demands and set-offs (Secs. 201-202), in the determination of the issues raised in proceedings to discover assets (Sec. 66), in actions for waste (Sec. 276), in actions to admeasure dower (Secs. 344, 347-349), and, of course, in suits to contest wills in circuit courts the statute provides that either party may require a jury (Sec. 

537). In will contest cases, the parties would be entitled to a jury regardless of statutory provisions therefor, inasmuch as they are actions at law.85 But in other actions and proceedings in probate courts, where the statutes do not authorize jury trials, such as in the hearing of exceptions to a final account of a guardian," controversies growing out of final settlements and concerning the widow's rights to the personalty,87 proceedings for the removal of administrators,88 the hearing of issues raised by objections to items contained in the final settlement of an administrator,80 the parties

Conclusive against collateral attack.

The orders, judgments and decrees of probate courts are as free from collateral attack as those of any other court, unless it affirmatively appears in some portion of the entire record that the steps. necessary to acquire jurisdiction were not taken.96 Thus, a judgment of a probate court admitting a foreign will to probate is conclusive against collateral attack,97 as is an order appointing a person other than the widow of a deceased person as administrator, even though the record did not show a renunciation of the right to administer by the widow; 98 or orders authorizing and approving sales of a minor's interest in real estate; or an order adjudging a person insane and appointing a guardian for such person.100 c. Judgments probating wills not subject to attack in equity. 

Notwithstanding the general rule that orders, judgments and decrees of probate courts generally are subject to direct attack in courts of equity on the ground of mistake or fraud, judgments admitting wills to probate are immune from attack in courts of equity. 

The admission of a will to probate is a judicial act not open to collateral attack. When a judgment is entered admitting a will to probate, such judgment is binding on all the world, and is not subject even to a direct attack in a court of equity for any reason.¹ A

I. PRELIMINARY QUESTIONS, PARTIES AND DISTINCTIONS A. PURPOSE, NECESSITY AND AVOIDANCE OF ADMINISTRATION Sec. 528. Purpose and Desirability of Administration. 

The immediate purpose served by the administration of an estate of a deceased person is that of using his property, where necessary, to pay his legal obligations and distribute the remainder among his heirs, devisees, legatees or distributees, according to their interests, and by the sanction or with the approval of a court having jurisdiction. By the process of administration, creditors are enabled to collect what is due them from the decedent's property, and the heirs or distributees take the remainder free from claims of creditors. Until there has been an administration, whereby the claims of creditors are barred by operation of a statute requiring such claims to be filed within a certain time (Sec. 183, as amended 

Laws 1933, p. 163, Sec. 1), or until the rights of decedent's creditors to sell whatever real estate he may have owned to pay their debts have been extinguished by operation of statute (Secs. 180, 633

181), both the real and personal property of decedent are held subject to the rights which the law gives to decedent's creditors to have same sold and the proceeds thereof applied to the payment of their debts. But the basic purpose of administration lies deeper than this. It involves the right of possession and ownership of property, and the preservation of the peace of society. The law of administration and the method of applying it have been devised to enable the owner of property to perpetuate after his death, in the hands of those of his choice, or, in default of his selection, in the hands of those to whom the law directs that it shall go, the ownership and dominion over such property. That this purpose may be achieved, the judicial arm of the State is raised to direct an orderly process by which the property of a decedent may be used to discharge his obligations and then distributed to those entitled to share in it, without the disturbance, confusion and strife that would ensue among those claiming rights in such property, if no supervision over its distribution were provided. The practice of administering estates for the purpose of keeping the title to property lawfully vested, without disturbance to society, after the owner of the property dies, has grown out of the experience of mankind.¹ 

While our statutes governing administration do not make compulsory the administration of estates, and while in some cases the administration of an estate is wholly unnecessary, ordinarily, when a person dies leaving an estate consisting of more property than the law authorizes the widow, widower or minor children under the age of eighteen years, to take, it is desirable that his estate be administered. 

Sec. 529. Necessity of Administration. 

From an early date, the rule has prevailed in Missouri that the property of every person who dies in this State, whether a citizen or a stranger, is subject to the course of administration provided by our statutes and is regarded as in the custody of the law for the benefit of all persons interested. Unless such property is withdrawn from the custody of the law by some of the methods hereinafter discussed, it remains in such custody, in contemplation of the 

12 Blackstone 490. 2 'Bartlett vs. Hyde, 3 Mo. 490. 634

law, either until there is an administration of the estate or until, by the operation of some statute, it is withdrawn from such custody because it is no longer subject to be used for the payment of the debts of decedent. While such property is in the custody of the law, certain persons are given prior rights to appear in court, have themselves appointed as administrators of such estate, and compel an administration thereof (Sec. 7), and if such persons do not apply for letters of administration and open the administration of the estate of such decedent, the probate court, or judge, or clerk in vacation, may, upon motion of any person interested, and by the use of a citation, either compel such person to appear and administer or, in case of his default, appoint some other suitable person (Sec. 8). Under the power granted them by statute, any creditors of a decedent may thus appear and not only compel an administration (Sec. 8) but also cause both the personal and the real property of the decedent to be sold to pay the debts of the decedent (Secs. 

112, 113, 146). If the deceased person left a will, the will must be probated to be effective, and letters testamentary must be issued before the executor can enter upon his duties of administering the estate under the will (Secs. 528, 568). And if a person dies, and his heirs cannot agree to a distribution of his estate, regardless of whether he left any debts owing, without the aid of an administration, the court will require that the property be turned over to an administrator.*

Sec. 530. Vesting of Title of Decedent's Property. 

The question as to whether an administration of decedent's estate is indispensable often depends upon how title to his property vests upon his death. The general rule is that the legal title to personal property of a person who dies intestate vests in his administrator, who, as long as the administration continues, holds same as trustee for the purpose of paying lawful debts against the estate, if any, or who serves as a conduit for the transfer of such title; while the equitable title in such personal property vests immediately in the heirs and distributees of decedent, subject to being divested when 

11 R. C. L. 27. 'Meyer vs. Nischwitz, 198 Mo. A. 101, 199 S. W. 744. 635

the property is used by the administrator for the payment of claims against the estate. This is the general rule that prevails in other jurisdictions. Since the legal title to the personal property of a decedent vests in his administrator, the heirs of the decedent cannot obtain the part due them except through the administrator in the regular course of administration and after the debts of the decedent have been paid." Any action to recover personal property belonging to the decedent, or enforce rights therein, must be brought and prosecuted by the administrator, and cannot be maintained by the heirs. And this is true even though it is shown by the heir bringing the suit that the administrator had neglected and refused to sue," and even though the heir be the sole distributee of the estate.10 When the administration of an estate is closed and the trust under which the administrator held is thereby terminated, the title to any undisposed of assets in the hands of the administrator immediately vests in the heirs and distributees, who thereafter hold both the legal and equitable title of such personal property.¹¹ 

When a person owning real estate dies, the legal and equitable title to such real estate passes to and vests instantly in the heirs or devisees, subject to the right of the administrator or executor to "Wass vs. Hammontree (Sup.), 77 S. Sec. 531. Administration Unnecessary, When. 

While the law favors, and in many instances requires, the administration of estates of deceased persons, there are cases where, because of the practical operation of the statutes or rules of law generally recognized, administration of estates becomes unnecessary. Thus, if an unmarried minor having a guardian or curator, dies intestate, leaving no debts, but being possessed of property, a separate administration of his estate is made unnecessary by provision of the statutes (Secs. 427, 428). If a husband and wife own property, the title to which is vested in them as tenants by the entirety, and one of them, who owns no other property whatever, dies, title to the entirety property vests in the survivor, and it would appear that an administration of the estate of the one who dies would be unnecessary, regardless of whether such deceased owed any debts.14 Where a deceased person leaves no debts owing by him, and his heirs, legatees or distributees are all of lawful age, and they, by common consent and without the exercise of fraud or mistake, make a distribution of the personal assets of the deceased among themselves, they may thereby dispense with an administration.15 "Wass vs. Hammontree (Sup.), 77 S. Such a division of the property of a decedent by his heirs or distributees is known as a domestic partition,16 or domestic distribution.
