Sec. 533. Testamentary Direction to Avoid Administration 

Invalid.

Persons unacquainted with the conflicts that arise from an attempt to dispose of their estates without administration, and who have an aversion for courts and court procedure, sometimes try to 643

avoid having their estates administered, and it is not uncommon for testators who have not received legal advice to provide, by their wills, that there be no administration of their estates or no probate of their wills. Testamentary provisions of this character are held contrary to public policy and void.31 When a will containing provisions of this kind is discovered following the death of a testator, it may be offered for probate, and, when probated, will be carried into effect in all respects except as to such void provisions, which will be ignored.32

B. PARTIES AND THEIR POWERS Sec. 534. Generally. 

The term "parties," as ordinarily used in law, refers to persons who are directly interested, or claim an interest, in the subject matter of an action, and who may prosecute, defend and control proceedings of an action and appeal from a judgment rendered therein. The administration of estates, and proceedings relating thereto in probate courts, are not actions, and they involve parties having different designations and serving purposes unlike parties in civil and criminal actions. These proceedings are not governed by the General Code of Civil Procedure, and have little relation or 

31 State ex rel. Welch vs. Morrison, 244 Mo. 193, 148 S. W. 907; Sevier vs. 

Woodson, 205 Mo. 202, 104 S. W. 1; Southworth vs. Southworth, 173 Mo. 59, 73 S. W. 129.

A typical testamentary expression of this character is found in the will involved in Sevier vs. Woodson, supra, which, among other things, provided: “I will and direct that my son, as executor and heir as aforesaid, manage and control my estate, hold and divide the same without going into court or taking letters testamentary. In holding this provision of the will void, the court (104 

S. W. 1. c. 4) said: "This expresses the preconceived notion of the testator that by an obiter in his will, he could overturn the statutes of the state on the subject of administration of estates. In this the testator was wrong. Such a provision is in our judgment violative of public policy, and violative of public policy as expressed by the statutes of this state. The testator has no inherent right to keep his estate from the courts given jurisdiction to administer the same. To declare such a policy would be a very dangerous precedent. We therefore hold this paragraph void and of no effect." · • 

State ex rel. Welch vs. Morrison, 244 Mo. 193, 148 S. W. 907; Southworth vs. Southworth, 173 Mo. 59, 73 S. W. 129. 

20 R. C. L. 662; Ballentine, 936. 644

similarity to criminal procedure. The Code provisions applicable to parties to actions have little from which we can borrow in a consideration of parties to probate proceedings. In the special code governing administration proceedings, there is no separate or special place given to a consideration of parties, and yet, a consideration of the various parties to probate proceedings involves a wholly different nomenclature from that of the same subject in any other field of the law. It is not new, but the terms as applied to parties known in administration proceedings have come down to us from antiquity, and the place they serve, the functions they perform, and the rights and liabilities vested in and attached to them are, to a large degree, the same under our statutes as under the common law, the chancery law, and the ecclesiastical law, from which so much of our probate law, or law pertaining to the administration of estates, was derived. 

1. Decedents. 

Sec. 535. Relation to the Proceedings. 

Obviously, a deceased person is not, and cannot be made, a party to a court proceeding, but his estate and his obligations constitute the entire subject matter of administration proceedings in probate court. Moreover, the acts of a person prior to his death, particularly with regard to the disposition, or failure to make disposition, of his property must be taken into account and, to some extent, control the proceedings. Thus, while a decedent is not a party to the proceeding for the administration of his estate, in the sense that a litigant is a party to a civil suit, the interest that was his before his death constitutes the whole subject matter of the proceeding, and his acts while living largely determine the course the proceedings take for the administration of his estate. Therefore, the relation which the decedent, though dead, has to probate proceedings, is of the most intimate and inseparable nature. 

Sec. 536. Intestate. 

A person who dies without leaving a valid will disposing of his property is usually referred to as an intestate. The term is one of 34 34 

Ballentine, 678. 645

long use.35 The estate of an intestate is administered and his assets, after his debts and the costs of administration, and inheritance taxes if any, are paid, are distributed to his heirs under the law of descent and distribution, without regard to any wishes he may have had for the final disposition of his affairs. The law of administration, including the law of descent and distribution, supplies the wishes the decedent failed to express. Our laws of descent and distribution, which govern the estates of intestates, are based upon the English common law.37 Under the early common law, the estate of an intestate was administered with little regard for what the decedent may have done with the property had he made testamentary disposition of it. But in the course of centuries of experience there evolved the law of descent and distribution, the underlying purpose of which is to carry into effect what one may naturally presume were the wishes of the ancestor relative to the use and succession of his property had he made testamentary disposition of it." 98 

Sec. 537. Testator.

2. Personal Representatives of Decedents. 

Sec. 538. Who Are Personal Representatives of Decedent. 

While executors and administrators of the estates of deceased persons are sometimes referred to as trustees of decedents' creditors, or as standing in the relation with the creditors and heirs of deceased persons as trustees, they are generally known as the personal representatives of decedents.42 These personal representatives of the deceased, under our statutes, whether known as general or as some kind of special executors or administrators, bear the same name and are vested with similar, and to a large degree identical, powers as personal representatives known to the common law.

Sec. 541. Administrator.

An administrator is a person officially appointed by a probate court to take charge of, manage and settle the estate of a deceased person. Persons appointed administrators, in all cases where the decedent died intestate, receive, as evidence of their authority to serve, what are known as general letters of administration, and such persons are sometimes referred to as general administrators.61 

Our statutes do not define the term "administrator" but recognize and provide for the position, so that when an administrator is re-

64 The terms "executor" and "administrator" are sometimes used interchangeably to refer to the person acting officially as personal representative of a decedent, although, from a strictly legal standpoint, the terms are not synonymous.63 Blackstone observes that as to the office and duties of executors and administrators they are in general very much the same, except in three things, namely: 

First, that the executor must carry out the direction of a will, while an administrator is not required to do so, unless he acts as administrator with the will annexed; second, that an executor may do many acts before he proves the will, but an administrator may do nothing until letters of administration are issued; 65 third, that the executor derives his power from the will and not from the probate, while the administrator owes his powers entirely to the appointment under which he serves. While the functions of executors and administrators are practically the same, the source from which their powers are derived and the manner by which they perform their duties differ, in that an administrator who does not serve with a will annexed derives his power solely from his appointment, and must perform his duties solely in accordance with the law of the State and the order of the court under whose supervision he operates; whereas, an executor derives his power both from the will by which he is appointed and from the laws of the State under which he must execute the trust vested in him by the will, and in the performance

Sec. 543. Administrator With the Will Annexed. 

will as

Under our statutes, if the person or persons named in executor or executors refuse to act, or be disqualified, and some other person is appointed in his or their stead to administer the estate according to the terms of the will, such person is known as an administrator with the will annexed (Sec. 11). This is the same kind of special administrator that has been long known under the English law and referred to by the Latin expression adopted because it described the chief distinguishing characteristic of such special administrator. The name and function of the position is one of several borrowed by our statutes on administration from the English system, all of which were mentioned, described and distinguished by Blackstone."

Sec. 544. Administrator of Goods Unadministered. 

Our statutes provide that when a will has been proved and letters thereon have been granted, and the will is thereafter set aside and such letters revoked and other letters are granted of the goods unadministered, the latter person to whom such letters are granted is known as an administrator of goods unadministered, or an administrator de bonis non. The statute also provides that if all executors or administrators of an estate die or resign, or their letters are revoked, or if, after final settlement and the discharge of an executor or administrator, unadministered assets of the estate are discovered, letters shall be granted thereon to some qualified person, who is also

known as an administrator de bonis non. (Sec. 47.) Such special kind of administrator recognized by our statutes is one that has also been long known to the law.68 

Sec. 545. Administrator Pending Litigation. 

Our statutes provide that when an action is filed to contest a will which has been admitted to probate, and it appears that the executor named in the will has an interest adverse to the contestants of the will, the court may, in its discretion, grant letters of administration to some disinterested person or corporation to administer the estate until the termination of the will contest. Such person is known as an administrator pendente lite. (Sec. 14.) Such special administrator recognized by our statutes is one whose position has also been known in the law from antiquity.69 

Sec. 546. Administrator During the Minority or Absence of Executor.

Under our statutes, if an executor named in the will is a minor, or is absent from the State, special letters of administration are granted during the minority or absence to some other person. Such special administrator is known as an administrator during minority or absence. (Sec. 13.) Special administrators of this kind were regularly used under similar circumstances under the English law, except that under that law a person could serve as an executor after he reached the age of seventeen years. 70

Sec. 547. Administrator ad Litem. 

An administrator ad litem is a special administrator appointed to represent the estate when the executor or administrator regularly serving is adversely interested." Under our statutes, where an administrator or executor files a claim against the estate for which he is serving as executor or administrator, and there is no coexecutor or coadministrator, the court is required to appoint some suitable person to appear and manage the defense against such claim (Sec. 

203). Or if such executor or administrator holds a bond or other instrument of writing against the testator or intestate for the conveyance of real estate which was not completed by the testator or intestate in his lifetime, and there is no coexecutor or coadministrator, and if such administrator or executor files his petition for the enforcement of such bond or instrument, the court is required to appoint some suitable person to appear and manage the defense on the part of those interested (Sec. 177). The person thus appointed in each instance is known as administrator ad litem. During the period for which he serves he has the same power and responsibilities as the ordinary administrator or executor.72 

Sec. 548. Public Administrators. 

In every county in the State and in the City of St. Louis there is a public administrator (Sec. 296, as amended Laws 1933, p. 165). 

Such officers are county officials. They are not parties to all probate proceedings, but the statute sets out those cases in which they are required to take charge and serve as personal representatives of decedents in the administration of estates (Secs. 299, 300). A public administrator is not allowed to retain the office and choose for himself which of the duties of office required of him to be performed he shall undertake and which he shall reject.78 He cannot choose only lucrative estates and reject those which offer no hope of pecuniary compensation." 3. Beneficiaries. 

Sec. 549. Creditors. 

Ordinarily, creditors of the deceased are not parties to administration proceedings, except in the proceedings to have their claims or demands against the estate allowed and paid (Secs. 182-212). 

But, while they are not nominally parties, one of the principal purposes of administration is that creditors' interests may be protected and their claims paid out of the assets," so that actually creditors are parties to the entire proceedings for the administration of a deceased person's estate against which they have unpaid claims. In case of the failure of the persons having a right to administer to appear and obtain letters of administration, a creditor may himself appear before the probate court and see that there is an administration (Sec. 8).78 This was the practice under the English law." Notices required by law to be published by executors or administrators of the granting of letters (Sec. 75) and of final settlement (Sec. 230) are both addressed to and are for the protection of creditors. Creditors may file affidavits to compel the executor or administrator to give a new bond (Sec. 27). They may personally make application for the sale of real estate to pay debts (Sec. 146), or to reserve personal property and have real estate sold to pay debts (Sec. 157), when the executor or administrator does not apply for authority to exercise such power. They also have the right to inquire into the final settlement of an executor or administrator when they think he has not made just account of the assets in his hands (Secs. 274, 275). 

Sec. 550. Widow, Widower and Minor Children.

Where the decedent leaves a widow, widower, or minor children, 75 State ex rel. Russell vs. Mueller (Sup.), 60 S. W. (2d) 48. 

76 Infra, Chapter 6, X. 

77 Ante, Sec. 528. 

78 Rozell vs. Harmon, 29 Mo. A. 569, 103 Mo. 339, 15 S. W. 432. "In 2 Blackstone, 505, it is said that "if none of the kindred will take out administration, a creditor may, by custom, do it." 655

they all have either vested or contingent interests in the property of the decedent, and, whether they are nominally joined in the administration proceedings or not, they are parties, nevertheless, and their interests must be protected. Thus, they are entitled to priority in administering on the estate (Sec. 7), and the widow, widower, or minor children under the age of eighteen years of age, have the right to apply for an order that letters of administration be refused and all the property delivered to them (Sec. 2), the right of homestead (Secs. 612, 613), and provisions necessary for their sustenance for twelve months (Sec. 106). The widow and widower also have absolute property interests in certain property (Sec. 106) and the right to have other property sold and the assets thereof paid them in lieu of provisions that are not on hand (Sec. 107, as amended Laws 1933, p. 164), additional personal property (Sec. 

108), quarantine rights (Sec. 338), dower in the realty (Secs. 318, 321, 322), and various other rights.

Sec. 551. Heirs, Devisees and Legatees. 

"Heirs' are those persons whom the law appoints to succeed to the property of a deceased person, and in whom absolute title to his real estate vests at his death, and in whom equitable title to personal property vests, subject to the payment of the debts of decedent. 

They may be lineal heirs of the decedent, such as children or grandchildren, or they may be collateral heirs, such as father, mother, brothers, sisters, or other next of kin. If the deceased leaves a will, his property is distributed to those who are named as beneficiaries therein, according to the provisions of the testamentary document, and after his debts are paid. If the deceased person dies intestate, his property is distributed according to the statutes on descent and distribution. (Secs. 306-317.) In all cases where such heirs have any interest in the estate of their decedent, they are actually parties to the proceedings for the administration of the estate. In the strict legal sense, the term "devisee" refers to a person to whom real estate is given by a provision of a will, while the term "legatee" refers to a person who is given personal property by a testator through his will. The land or interest a devisee receives is called a devise, while the personalty which a lega- 1 656

tee receives is known as a bequest. In proceedings for the administration of estates of persons who die testate, both their devisees and legatees are interested, and, though they may not be actually named, are, nevertheless, parties to the proceedings. Under our statutes, because of their interest, they would have the right to compel administration (Sec. 8). 

4. Evidence of Authority. 

Sec. 552. Letters of Administration. 

When a probate court, or judge or clerk in vacation, appoints a person to act as administrator of an estate of a decedent, a document, signed by the judge or clerk and attested by the seal of the court, is issued to the person appointed as evidence of his official authority to act. Such document issued to an administrator of an estate of a person dying intestate, or to some special administrator, is known as letters of administration. Letters of administration may be granted by the probate court while it is in session, or by the judge or the clerk if the court is in vacation (Sec. 1), to such person or persons applying therefor who may be entitled to priority in administering (Sec. 7), or who may be deemed by the court or judge or clerk suitable persons to administer (Secs. 7, 8, 9). Such letters should be kept by the administrator for use against anyone who may challenge his authority, but if the letters should become lost or destroyed, or if by oversight of the parties letters should not be issued, the right of the administrator to act is not at all questionable, for it has been held that an order appointing an administrator, together with the bond and oath given by the administrator, is sufficient though letters evidencing the appointment are not actually issued.8 80

Sec. 553. Letters Testamentary. 

Letters testamentary is a document issued by a probate court to a person, persons or corporation named in a will as executor, and who has been found by the court to be qualified to serve in that capacity. Such document represents the fact that the testator has named such person, persons or corporation as his executor, and that the court has confirmed the appointment by issuing letters. Letters testamentary are evidence of the authority of the executor to act in that capacity in the proceeding in the probate court for the administration of the estate of the testator. (Sec. 11.)

II.  A. JURISDICTION AND VENUE Sec. 554. Authority to Grant Letters. 

Authority to grant letters testamentary or of administration is vested by statute in the probate court, or the judge or clerk thereof in vacation, subject to the confirmation or rejection of the court (Sec. 1). Such authority is original and exclusive, no other courts, officers or persons having such power.88 When this power is properly exercised and an administrator is appointed, the order making the appointment is final, as no appeal lies from an order appointing an administrator,84 or from an order refusing to appoint.85 If the court is in session when letters are issued, the letters should be iscued by the court. If the court is not in session, either the judge or the clerk may issue the letters. If letters are granted by the clerk, they should be issued in his name, as a deputy clerk cannot grant letters in his name.88 But it has been held that where letters purporting to be granted by the proper authority are in due form and under seal of the court issuing them, but are not signed, they are voidable for want of mere formality, but are not void.87 An order appointing an administrator and granting letters is not sub-

Sec. 555. Confirmation of Vacation Order Granting Letters. 

In all cases where letters are granted in vacation, it is the duty of the clerk to present to the court, at the next succeeding term, all such letters as may have been granted in vacation, and, after the court has confirmed or rejected the same, the clerk must enter on the record the action of the court thereon (Sec. 3). Unless and until letters issued in vacation are rejected by the court, they are valid,⁹1 and when the court confirms letters issued in vacation the order of confirmation relates back to the original issuance of the letters and makes the letters valid ab initio.92 

Sec. 556. Where Letters Must Be Granted. 

The statute provides that letters testamentary and of administration shall be granted in the county in which the mansion house or place of abode of the deceased is situated. If he had no mansion house or place of abode at the time of his death, and be possessed of lands, letters shall be granted in the county in which the land or the greater part thereof lies. If the deceased had no mansion house or place of abode, and was not possessed of lands, letters may be granted in the county in which he died, or where the greater part of his estate may be. If he died out of the State, leaving no mansion house, place of abode or lands in this State, such letters may be granted in any county. (Sec. 4.) All orders, settlements, trials and other proceedings contemplated by the statute must be had or made in the county in which the letters testamentary or of administration were granted (Sec. 5). B. RIGHT TO LETTERS ON ESTATE OF INTESTATE Sec. 557. Persons Disqualified From Receiving Letters. 

The statute provides that no judge or clerk of any probate court, in his own county, or his deputy, and no male or female person under twenty-one years of age, or of unsound mind, shall be executor or administrator. No executor of an executor, in consequence thereof, shall be executor of the first testator. (Sec. 6.) Also, nonresidents are specifically disqualified by statute from receiving letters testamentary or of administration; and if letters are granted to an executor or administrator who becomes a nonresident, the court shall, upon proof thereof, and after due notice to such executor or administrator, revoke his letters (Sec. 10). Removal or nonresidence only disqualifies a person from acting as administrator or executor, and in order for the disqualification to become effective an order of revocation must be made.98 And in a proceeding against 94

Sec. 558. Origin of Statutory Control of Right to Administer. 

The right to receive letters of administration on the estate of an intestate is not inherent, but wholly statutory, as no such right existed at common law. The origin of our statutes granting such right is found in early statutory engraftments by Parliament upon the ancient common law. At common law, when a man died intestate, the King was entitled to seize upon his goods as the parens patriae, or general trustee of the kingdom. The power was exercised through the King's ministers of justice. The royal prerogative was granted as a franchise to many lords of manors, and others, who, from that day until modern times, exercised a prescriptive right to grant administration on their intestate tenants. Subsequently, the crown vested the right to administer estates on the prelates of the church, on the theory that the conscience of spiritual men should lead them to deal more fairly with the estates of intestates. Under this system, when a man died intestate, title to his property vested in the ordinary, or judge of the ecclesiastical court, and the prelates, in the disposition of the assets of such estates, were held accountable only to God and themselves for their conduct. Unsavory abuses arose, which led to the enactment of an early statute (13 Edward I, ch. 19) which required that the ordinary pay the debts of the intestate. While this statutory check upon the abuses incident to the administration of estates by the ordinaries was a measure of relief to creditors, the abuses in the administration of the remainder of the assets of deceased persons continued until, by another statute (31 Edward III, ch. 11), ordinaries were required to depute the nearest and most lawful friends of deceased persons to administer their goods. This statute was said to be the origin of the present-day statutory administrator. 

Under this statute, which made the nearest and most lawful friend of the intestate the person entitled to administration, it became the custom to appoint those of the next blood of the deceased as administrators. Under a later statute (21 Henry VIII, ch. 5), Walker's Estate vs. Walker, 1 Mo. A. 404. 665

the power of the ordinary was enlarged so as to permit him to grant administration either to the widow, or to the next of kin, or to both of them, at his own discretion, and where there were two or more persons in the same degree of kindred the ordinary had the power to select whichever one he preferred.100 The result of this statutory regulation of the right to administer was to secure for the descendants of decedents, in the order of the nearness of their relationship, the right to manage, under the order of court, the administration of the estates of their deceased ancestors.¹ 

Sec. 559. Statute Vests Prior Rights to Administer in Those Nearest in Relationship. 

Missouri, as other states, has adopted the principle of the English system of statutory control of the right to letters of administration, 100 

2 Blackstone, 494-496; 11 R. C. L. 34; Leakey Adm. vs. Maupin, 10 Mo. 368. 

12 Blackstone, 504-505, thus summarizes the result of the statutory control of the question of the right to administer: "In consequence of which we may observe; 1. That the ordinary is compellable to grant administration of the goods and chattels of the wife, to the husband, or his representatives: and of the husband's effects, to the widow, or next of kin; but he may grant it to either, or both, at his discretion. 2. That, among the kindred, those are to be preferred that are the nearest in degree to the intestate; but, of persons in equal degree, the ordinary may take which he pleases. 3. That this nearness or propinquity of degree shall be reckoned according to the computation of the civilians; 

And therefore in the first place the children, or (on failure of children) the parents of the deceased, are entitled to the administration: both which are indeed in the first degree; but with us the children are allowed the preference. Then follow brothers, grandfathers, uncles or nephews (and the females of each class respectively), and lastly, cousins. 4. The half blood is admitted to the administration as well as the whole; for they are of the kindred of the intestate, and only excluded from inheritance of land on feodal reasons. Therefore the brother of the half blood shall exclude the uncle of the whole blood; and the ordinary may grant administration to the sister of the half, or the brother of the whole blood, at his own discretion. 5. If none of the kindred will take out administration, a creditor may, by custom, do it. 6. And, lastly, the ordinary may, in defect of all these, commit administration (as he might have done before the statute of Edward III), to such discreet person as he approves of . . "" This crystallization of the English law, out of centuries of experience, not only regarding the right to administer on estates but also governing descents, forms the skeleton, if not the flesh and blood, of the body of our law on the same subjects. ... 666

namely, that those nearest in relationship and interest have priority to the right to letters of administration on the estate of an intestate. Accordingly, our statute provides that if a married man dies, his widow shall have the prior right to serve as administratrix of his estate, and if a married woman dies, her husband shall have prior right to serve as administrator. If a husband or wife does not survive the intestate, those next in order of priority to serve as administrator, and the order in which their rights appear, are those entitled to distribution of the estate, or one or more of them, as the court or judge or clerk in vacation shall believe will best manage and preserve the estate; but if the court or judge in vacation should believe no one of the persons given prior right to administer is a competent and suitable person, some other person than those mentioned may be appointed. (Sec. 7.) That part of the statute authorizing the court or judge to use his discretion in determining whether or not the persons given priority are competent and suitable persons and to select some other person was first added to the statute in 1917 (Laws 1917, p. 93). Prior to that time the statute did not authorize the court to exercise discretion in appointing persons as administrators out of the groups given preference, but its provisions were mandatory, and a person given prior right to administer under same could, by mandamus, compel the court to appoint him.2

Sec. 560. Right of Surviving Husband or Wife. 

In line with ancient statutory provisions, our statute gives first right to letters to the surviving husband or wife, and does not provide, as statutes in some states, that such right is forfeited by a remarriage. Under our statute, a divorced wife could not claim the first right to letters, as she would not be the surviving wife. But a woman claiming to be a widow of the deceased by virtue of what is sometimes called a common-law marriage would have the right to letters if she could show such marriage relationship prior to the 'Sec. 15 R. But the statute abolishing For one to claim the right to letters of administration as a common law wife, it would be necessary for her to show that her relationship with the deceased during his lifetime was such as would constitute her a wife under the rules governing common law marriages. Such marriages were improperly named common law marriages, because they are a strictly American invention, and under the Common Law of England marriages without religious solemnnization were expressly repudiated. The frequency of the marriage relationship between parties where no legal marriage ceremony had been performed existing in pioneer America brought forth a legal recognition of what came to be known as common law marriages. A woman claiming the right to letters of administration based upon a common law marriage would have to bring herself within the rules generally recognized as governing such marriages, and which are stated in 38 C. J. 1316, as follows: 

"To constitute a marriage valid at common law, that is in the absence of a statute otherwise specifically providing, it is not necessary that it should be solemnized in any particular form or with any particular rite or ceremony. All that is required is that there should be an actual and mutual agreement to enter into a matrimonial relation, permanent and exclusive of all others, between parties capable in law of making such a contract, consummated by their cohabitation as man and wife or their mutual assumption openly of marital duties and obligations. "In accordance with the rule obtaining in respect of marriages generally, the consent of the parties is essential to the constitution of the common-law marriage. The absence of such consent renders the relations of the parties meretricious, but where there is consent, the law will create the marriage status, regardless of what the parties believed to be the effect of their agreement . . . "Although the rule is otherwise as to ceremonial marriages, the common-law marriage requires an assumption by the parties of the rights and duties of the marital relation, in order to establish the existence and reality of the alleged consent thereto. That is to say, there must be a cohabitation of the parties, matrimonial in nature, professed and open, such as will create some public recognition that their intentions were matrimonial. "In the absence of the requisite cohabitation by the parties evidence that copulation has taken place may be necessary to establish the sufficiency of the consent. "A common-law marriage may come into being: (1) Where the parties in tend to enter into an informal marriage; (2) where the parties intend to contract a formal marriage, but a requisite formality is wanting; (3) where the parties intended to contract a valid marriage, but an impediment or incapacity existed which has subsequently been removed. "" . . . There must, however, be a clear and sufficient promise or agreement, which must be acted upon by the parties, although it is not always necessary 668

Therefore, regardless of the statute abolishing commonlaw marriages, if a woman claimed the right to letters of administration, based upon a common-law marriage consummated prior to the adoption of the statute, it would appear that she would have the right to compel the court to grant her such letters. The right to administer being a valuable one,' and that right being first awarded to the surviving spouse of the deceased, unless a widow is prohibited from acting by some rule of law or by some disqualifying statutory provision (such as those contained in Sec. 6), the probate court should appoint her as administratrix, and this though she is shown to be a person that is improvident, wasteful, of immoral character, and devoid of appreciation of the value of money,⁹ and though it is charged that the marriage between her and deceased was during his last illness, when he was not mentally capable of understanding the marriage ceremony." 10 that they should hold themselves out to the public as husband and wife. Although the relations of the parties were at first illicit, this does not prevent them from afterward contracting a valid common-law marriage.'' 'Randazzo vs. Randazzo (App.), 236 S. W. 1061.

The recognition of so-called common-law marriages by the courts of this State has been uniform and undisputed. What constitutes such marriages under our law was stated in the case of Randazzo vs. Randazzo, supra, as follows: "The foundation of a common-law marriage is the contract entered into by the parties, and to establish such marriage there must be not only reputation and cohabitation as a sequence thereto, but it must be shown that there was a contract through word by which the man agrees to take the woman as his wife, and the woman agrees to take the man as her husband. . . . In other words, it is not enough, of course, that they live together, but their minds must become united. Such a contract must be followed by marital cohabitation; that is to say, the parties must live together in fact as man and wife to such an extent and in such manner as will produce the reputation that they are married.'' 

Other cases in Missouri in which such marriages have been considered and discussed, are: Topper vs. Perry, 197 Mo. 531, 95 S. W. 203; State vs. Hansbrough, 181 Mo. 348, 80 S. W. 900; Adair vs. Mette, 156 Mo. 496, 57 S. W. 551;

Sec. 561. Next of Kin. 

If the deceased person left no husband or wife surviving, those next entitled to preference in receiving letters of administration are those who are entitled to distribution of the estate, or next of kin of the deceased, the statute leaving to the court the right to select one or more of such next of kin (Sec. 7). The statute designates those who are entitled to inherit and who are entitled to letters of administration in the following order: First, decedent's children or their descendants; second, decedent's father, mother, brothers and sisters and their descendants; third, the husband or wife or the grandfather, grandmother, uncles and aunts and their descendants; fourth, the great-grandfathers, great-grandmothers and their descendants; and so on, in other cases, without end passing to the nearest lineal ancestors and their children and their descendants (Sec. 306). Since the statute gives to the next of kin or the distributees the right to administer, such persons are entitled to letters of administration where there is no surviving husband or wife, and this right is subject only to the discretion given by the statute to the probate court or judge to say whether or not such person was a competent and suitable person to serve as administrator (Sec. 7).11 

A distributee given such right cannot be compelled to share the right with some other person appointed as coadministrator, as that would be a withdrawal by the court of the right granted by the statute to such distributee, and this will not be permitted, for the appointment of the one the statute designates as entitled to appointment indicates that the court has decided that such person is a competent and suitable person.12 The courts in this State have not determined, as against the claims of all who may be entitled to letters, just which ones have the superior right in contests with each other, so that in those cases where persons are entitled to distribution it must be assumed, until the courts have spoken to the contrary, that any person next of kin, actual or assumed, near or remote, would have the right to letters of administration as against a stranger,18 unless the court, in its discretion, found him to be in- "State ex rel. Fansher vs. Guinotte, 58 S. W. (2d) 1005, 227 Mo. A. 902. 

12 Ibid. 

13 In Re Graves' Estate (App.), 73 S. W. (2d) 844. 670

competent and unsuitable, just as the statute says (Sec. 7). Thus, an adopted child should have the right to letters of administration (Sec. 14079), as should a descendant of the half-blood (Sec. 309), because each of them is interested and is entitled to distribution. 

The statute has arranged the order in which next of kin succeed to the right to letters and should, in all cases, control where there is a contest.14 

Sec. 562. Strangers.

Neither a stranger in blood, nor a volunteer, nor any other person not entitled to distribution out of the estate of a decedent, has any right to letters of administration.15 The right to receive letters of administration being one that is regulated solely by statute,16 and the statute not giving that right to a stranger (Sec. 8),17 strangers in blood and volunteers have no right to letters of administration, and where they are granted letters within the time when parties having the right to letters may be awarded same, such letters are void.18

Sec. 563. Right to Letters as Controlled by Judicial Discretion. 

The most recent Missouri statutory regulation of the right to administer is that which gives probate courts authority to determine whether those to whom the statute gives prior rights to administer are competent and suitable persons (Sec. 7). This statutory power is similar to that granted by 21 Henry VIII, ch. 5.19 Prior to this addition to the statute, the statutory right to administer was

If, in appointing some other person, the probate court finds the persons named by the statute incompetent and unsuitable, it thereby exercises judicial discretion which the statute authorizes, and the person to whom it has denied letters cannot compel such court to appoint him, for no other court has the power to use the mandamus writ against a court rightfully exercising judicial discretion.27 But if a probate court fails to follow the statute when a person entitled to letters applies for same, and unlawfully appoints another as coadministrator with applicant, thus showing by the appointment of applicant that she was, in the opinion of the court, a competent person to serve, the order of the court appointing a coadministrator and thus denying the person to whom the statutes give the right to administer the right to serve alone, is illegal and void, and mandamus will lie to compel the probate court to revoke the order and issue letters to the applicant alone. 28 It was true be-

311. FORM OF ORDER HOLDING PERSON HAVING RIGHT TO LETTERS IS INCOMPETENT AND UNSUITABLE 

Now is presented the application of ...., widow of ............, deceased, for letters of administration upon said estate, and and ....., heirs of deceased, and entitled to distribution of said estate, also appearing and objecting to the granting of such letters, evidence is heard on the question of the competency and suitableness of applicant as administrator of such estate, and after the hearing of evidence offered by applicant and evidence offered against her, and having duly considered all questions relating thereto, the court finds that widow of............, deceased, is not a competent or suitable person to act as administratrix of said estate, and that it would not be to the best interests of said estate that she be appointed. It is now therefore ordered and adjudged that the application of deceased, be and the same is hereby denied, and she is hereby declared a person incompetent and unsuitable to act as administratrix of said estate, and the court finding that would be a competent and suitable person to act as administrator, it is now hereby ordered and adjudged that letters of administration be issued to the said.... and his bond as administrator is hereby fixed at $ -" widow of mus was used. After the exercise of such judicial discretion and the adjudication of the question of the fitness or competency of the person authorized by statute to serve, it then became the duty of the court under the statute to appoint that person and no other. The duty of the court to appoint such person was thus made mandatory by the statute, and for failure of the probate court to follow the course required of it by statute, which course only required the specific act of issuing letters to the person entitled by statute to and found suitable for same (a ministerial function), mandamus was properly used.

Sec. 564. Effect of Delay on Right to Administer. 

Delay on the part of those having the right to letters to make application therefor does not have the effect of immediately forfeiting such right. However, if none of the persons entitled to administer applies for letters within thirty days after the death of the deceased, the statute provides that, on motion of any person interested, the court or judge or clerk may issue citation to such persons to appear and qualify for administration, giving at least five days' time for that purpose. If the person cited fails to administer within the time appointed, letters may be granted to any person whom the court or judge or clerk in vacation may deem most suitable. (Sec. 8.) Thus, within the thirty-day period following the death of the deceased, the court cannot appoint some person other than than those entitled to letters under the statute, unless, either the persons entitled appear and apply for letters and after a hearing the court finds them incompetent or unsuitable (Sec. 7),30 or such persons are shown to be nonresidents (Sec. 9), or are otherwise disqualified by statute (Sec. 6), or renounce their right to letters (Sec. 9). Absent such circumstances or conditions, the right to administer is not interfered with during the thirty-day period following the death of decedent, and it has been held that any order appointing another within thirty-five days after the death of the decedent, such period being the thirty days given for the appearance of those having the right to letters and five days for notice following the expiration of thirty days, is void,³¹ even though the persons entitled to administer by virtue of being sole distributees are all minors.82

Sec. 565. Letters Prematurely and Improvidently Granted, How 

Revoked.

When the probate court has, within thirty-five days following the death of a deceased person, improvidently granted letters of administration to a stranger, when others entitled to letters are not cited to appear and administer and are not found unsuitable or incompe- 

Ante, Secs. 561 and 563. 30 

Pikey vs. Riles (App.), 20 S. W. (2d) 550. 

22 In Re Allen's Estate, 307 Mo. 674, 271 S. W. 755. 675

tent to administer, such letters should be revoked by the order of the court granting them, upon the application of persons entitled to administer under the statute. The order making such appointment or granting such letters, being void, may be set aside at a subsequent term of the court or at any time within three years.³¹ 

An order revoking letters in such case need not await an application by the party entitled to administer, but the court improvidently making the appointment may, under its inherent powers, revoke the letters previously issued and the order making the appointment ex mero motu.35 Such order of revocation made by the court of its own motion can be made where no positive rule of law forbids it and even though no statute authorizes it.30

C. RIGHT TO LETTERS ON ESTATE OF TESTATOR Sec. 566. Who May Serve as Executors. 

At common law, all persons capable of making wills were qualified to serve as executors, and even some persons not authorized to make wills could qualify as executors, such as unmarried women and infants.87 Under our statutes, testators are free to name persons of their own selection executors, but the statute disqualifies certain persons from acting, even though they may be appointed executors by will.38 Subject, however, to the statutory regulations providing for the disqualification of certain persons to act as executors on account of minority, insanity, official position in the probate court (Sec. 6), or nonresidence (Sec. 9), a testator may name 

37 2 Blackstone, 503; 11 R. C. L. 43.

The statute (Sec. 6) heretofore referred to as disqualifying certain persons from acting as administrators also disqualifies persons to serve as executors on the same grounds. 678

any competent person as the executor of his will, and have reasonable assurance of the fact that such person will execute the will if he survives the testator and some disqualification does not intervene. Corporations, being artificial persons, may serve as executors where, under the statutes regulating them, they are authorized to serve as such.39 Corporations in Missouri generally are not authorized to serve as executors, and national banks are not permitted to serve in such capacity, but a Missouri trust company or merged trust companies, by provision of the statutes, are authorized to serve either as executors, administrators, guardians or curators (Secs. 5421, 5423, 5463, 5470-5471),40 provided that when they are authorized to act as executors the will appointing them must show by a recital therein or by a certificate or codicil attached thereto that at or before the execution of said will the testator had advice in relation thereto from someone not under salary of such trust company (Sec. 5426). Prior to 1919, a married woman could not act as executrix or as administratrix," but this statutory disqualification was removed 42 and since that time a married woman has the right to serve as executrix or administratrix (Sec. 6). 

Sec. 567. Named Executors. 

The right of an executor named in a will to letters testamentary is absolute unless such right is removed by some statutory provision disqualifiying him. Such executor may expressly renounce his rights to serve as executor, either by his own direct acts, such as by antenuptial contract whereby the right to serve as executrix was expressly renounced as a part of the consideration for the marriage, or by his conduct in pais,¹5 and so long as he has not re- 44 "Where a will contest is filed and an administrator pendente lite is appointed, the statute provides that a corporation may serve as such administrator pendente lite (Sec. 14).

But the fact that one has been named as executor in a will does not give him the unconditional right to serve, because that right depends also upon whether or not he is disqualified from serving by the operation of some statute, or is able to qualify after his appointment has been confirmed; or is considered by the probate court a suitable person to execute the will.48 The statute expressly vests the probate court or the judge in vacation with authority to determine whether the persons named in the will as executors are incompetent, unsuitable or improper to execute the will (Sec. 7), and if, under the provisions of the statute, persons named as executors claim interests hostile to their trust as executors, the probate court may, within its statutory authority, refuse to grant letters testamentary to such persons, on the ground that they are not suitable to execute the trust.49

Sec. 568. Next of Kin and Distributees. 

If the testator does not appoint anyone as executor by his will, or if the named executor does not survive the testator, or if the person named as executor refuses to act or is otherwise disqualified, then the next of kin or distributees of deceased, or the persons that have the right to letters of administration where there is no will, may apply for and receive letters of administration with the will annexed. The statute provides that if a part of the persons appointed executors refuse to act, or be disqualified, the letters shall be granted to the other persons appointed therein. If all such persons refuse to act, or be disqualified, letters of administration shall be granted to the persons to whom administration would have been granted if there had been no will, unless it shall be shown, to the satisfaction of the court or the judge in vacation, that the person "State ex rel. The right of such next of kin or distributees to letters of administration with the will annexed is contingent upon the disqualification, refusal or death of the named executor or executors. 

Sec. 569. Judicial Control of Right to Letters on Estate of Testator. 

The statutes give the probate court and the judge thereof in vacation extensive control over the right to letters on the estate of a deceased testator. Such court or judge in vacation not only has the right to determine whether or not persons named as executors are suitable, competent or proper to execute the will (Sec. 11), but, having determined such fact, the court or judge in vacation also has the right to appoint such persons as would have been entitled to letters of administration had no will been made (Sec. 11), the right to grant letters to some other person during the time of the minority or absence of the named executor (Sec. 10), and the right to determine whether or not the executor is interested when a will contest is filed (Sec. 14). In case a suit is filed to contest a will, the filing of the suit does not have the effect, as formerly, of disqualifying the executor and making necessary the appointment of an administrator pendente lite.50 Under the existing statute (Laws, 1925, p. 100; Sec. 14), the court or judge in vacation may permit the executor named in the will to continue serving after a will contest is filed, if such executor is not found interested, and if, after a hearing, the court or judge finds such executor is interested, some disinterested person or corporation, in the discretion of the court, may be named by the court as executor (Sec. 14). And where there was a contest of a will in which the executor was a legatee, it was held that the appointment of an administrator pendente lite was discretionary with the probate court, and where this discretion is not abused a circuit court or appellate court will not on appeal disturb the appointment.51

Sec. 21 R. S. 1909; Sec. 13 R. S. 1919.

D. RENUNCIATION OR WAIVER OF RIGHT TO ADMINISTER 

Sec. 570. Waiver by Failure to Assert Right.

If persons entitled to receive letters of administration fail to assert such rights within thirty days after the death of decedent, or fail to appear and qualify for administration after being cited by the court to appear, their rights to letters of administration are thereby defeated, because of their indifference (Sec. 8).52 The statute disqualifies nonresidents from serving as executors, but, since residence is a question of intention and may be acquired for the purpose of qualifying for letters,53 a nonresident executor will waive his right to serve by failing to establish his residence where he could qualify (Sec. 9).

Sec. 571. Voluntary Renunciation. 

The statute provides that letters testamentary and of administration may at any time be granted to any person deemed suitable, if the person or persons entitled to preference file their renunciation, in writing, with the clerk of the court (Sec. 9). The statutory provision is mandatory, and an order appointing an administrator twelve days after the death of the deceased, and before one having the right to administer files his renunciation as required by the statute, was held void.54 Where, a few days before an executor named in a will started on an extended journey and wrote the probate court that he had just learned that he had been appointed as executor and would be gone about two months, during which time he presumed no administrator would be necessary, his letter could not be construed as a renunciation.55 But if those entitled to letters file a written waiver in compliance with the statute, their rights to administer are thereby lost, and the court can appoint any other suitable person.56 Such renunciation, however, cannot be made conditional upon the appointment of one of their selection, for the "State ex rel. E. APPLICATIONS, ORDERS AND LETTERS Sec. 572. Requisites of Application for Letters and Oath. 

a. By general administrators.

No formal petition for letters is necessary, but the statute requires the applicant to file a formal affidavit at the time he makes application for letters, in which affidavit he must state, to the best of his knowledge and belief, the names and places of residence of the widow and heirs of the deceased; that the deceased died without a will, giving as near as may be the date of the death of the decedent; that he will make a perfect inventory and faithfully administer all the estate of the deceased and pay the debts, as far as the assets will extend, and the law directs, and account for and pay all assets which shall come into his possession or knowledge (Sec. 15). The proceedings for the appointment of a representative of the deceased is a proceeding in rem.00 Letters are granted on an ex parte application and without previous notice to anyone, and such letters, when issued to an administrator, are evidence that the proper steps were taken to procure the appointment.¹

Parties desiring to object on the ground that it did not affirmatively appear that the administrator made the required affidavit must do so in the probate court, as such objections cannot be made in a collateral suit.62 But since the proceeding for the appointment is in rem, the finding by the court as to the place of residence of the deceased is not res judicata in a subsequent collateral action between the parties, unless the issue is raised in the second proceeding for the purpose of attacking the title of the administrator to his office. 63 b. By special administrators. The statute requires a similar affidavit, with such variation as the case may require, for administrators of goods remaining unadministered, and by administrators during the time of the contest about a will, or the minority or absence of an executor (Sec. 16). If facts do State ex rel. Gott vs. Fidelity & Deposit Co., 317 Mo. 1078, 298 S. W. 83. 61 Ibid. 

62 State ex rel. Gott vs. Fidelity & Deposit Co., 317 Mo. 1078, 298 S. W. 83; 

McIntyre vs. St. Louis & S. F. Railway Co., 286 Mo. 234, 227 S. W. 1047; Macey vs. Stark, 116 Mo. 481, 21 S. W. 1088. 

State ex rel. Gott vs. Fidelity & Deposit Co., 317 Mo. 1078, 298 S. W. 83. 684

have been given to the probate court sufficient to show jurisdiction to appoint an administrator de bonis non, and the appointment has been regularly made, it is generally held that same cannot be attacked in a collateral proceeding; 64 but if the appointment is coram non judice and void, the validity of the appointment can be collaterally attacked.65 c. By executors and administrators with the will annexed. 

Where the deceased left a will appointing an executor, the first step required of the executor in opening the administration of the estate is to produce and prove the will and have same admitted to probate and his appointment made by the will confirmed by the probate court. Such will may be proved and admitted to probate in the manner hereinafter discussed.66 The statute does not require the executor to file a written application for letters, as such letters are granted to the persons appointed by will after the probate of the will, unless the person appointed is found incompetent, unsuitable or improper (Sec. 11). But the statute does provide that every administrator with the will annexed, and every executor, at the time letters are granted to him, shall make an affidavit that he will make a perfect inventory of the estate and faithfully execute the last will of the testator, pay the debts and legacies as far as the assets will extend and the law directs, render just accounts, and faithfully perform all things required by law touching such executorship or administration; also he shall make an affidavit, or supply the affidavit of some other person knowing the facts, stating, to the best of the knowledge and belief of the affiant, the names and places of residence of the widow and heirs of the deceased testator, and the date of his death, and the place of his death (Sec. 17).

Sec. 573. Notice. 

In the ordinary course of a proceeding on application for letters by those entitled to administer on the estate of a deceased person, notice to others than those applying for letters, or those entitled to administer under the law, is not required by statute to be given before letters are issued. The proceeding on the application is ex parte. When the court is presented with an application by a person or persons shown to be entitled to letters, immediate determination of the question of the fitness or suitableness of the person applying may be made without delay such as would be occasioned by serving parties with notice. It has been held that where a nonresident died testate leaving property in this State upon which his wife and executors were disqualified to administer by reason of nonresidence, and the brother of the deceased, who was a legatee under the will, thereupon became a resident of this State and applied for letters of administration, the brother having a prior right to administer on the property in this State, it was not necessary to give notice of his application to the others interested in the estate.69

Sec. 574. Order Issuing Letters. 

The statute makes no specific requirement for the court to enter an order appointing an administrator or confirming the appointment of an executor.70 However, such appointment involves a judicial determination of, or the exercise of judicial discretion as to, a number of matters, such as the jurisdiction of the court, the competency and suitableness of the persons given preference to letters, whether the persons authorized to administer are disqualified be- "State ex rel. Gott vs. Fidelity & Deposit Co., 317 Mo. 1078, 298 S. W. 83. Ibid. 

Stevens vs. Larwill, 110 Mo. A. 140, 84 S. W. 113.

TO Ibid. 

688

cause of nonresidence, insanity, minority or other statutory disqualifications, and a number of other questions which the statute requires the court to decide in different cases incident to the issuance of letters. While it will be presumed that all things were done by the court required of it by statute in making the appointment, in the absence of evidence to the contrary," a formal order appointing an administrator, or confirming the appointment of an executor, and issuing letters of administration or testamentary, should always be entered at the time the action is taken,72 especially in view of the general rule that actions and orders of a probate court are not binding or effective unless shown of record." The court must first of all determine whether or not it has jurisdiction of the proposed proceeding to administer the estate and whether or not venue lies in the county where the application is made, and since these jurisdictional questions are involved in and must be determined by the court in granting letters, the order of the appointment should recite the decision of the court as to its jurisdiction." A trial or formal hearing to determine these questions is not required by statute, but the determination thereof is left to the discretion of the court with the power to remove where the court later finds that its action was invalid or its appointees disqualified (Secs. 10, 40, 43).75

Sec. 575. Issuance, Recording and Use of Letters. 

As a necessary step in opening the administration of an estate, the probate court or judge or clerk thereof in vacation must issue 691

letters to the person appointed as administrator or executor. The forms for such letters are prescribed by statute and have been heretofore set out.76 The original letters should be issued and delivered to the executor or administrator. Before delivering such letters, however, the clerk of the court must record same in a well-bound book kept for that purpose, and the clerk must certify on the letters that they have been recorded. (Sec. 34.) If any clerk deliver such letters without recording the same, he may be fined by the court, and shall forfeit to the party injured double the damages occasioned by such default (Sec. 35). Possession of letters by the administrator or executor is evidence of their delivery." Such letters, or copies of the record thereof, duly certified under the seal of the proper court, are admissible as evidence (Sec. 36). A copy of the record showing the granting of letters has been held sufficient as evidence, without the production of the letters.78 

F. COMPELLING ADMINISTRATION 

Sec. 576. Who May Compel Administration. 

If a testator dies and the executor named in the will does not offer to prove the will or have same admitted to probate, any devisee, legatee, creditor or other person interested in the estate may take such steps as may be necessary to produce and prove said will and have same admitted to probate.79 If the persons entitled to priority in administering on the estate of an intestate do not appear within the time required by statute, any person interested may appear before the probate court and ask that such persons be cited to appear and qualify for administration. Thus, if no one appears and applies for letters of administration, and a creditor of the deceased finds that the estate is being improperly used, he may, after the expiration of thirty days following the death of the deceased, file a motion with the probate court asking that citation be issued to the persons entitled to administer. (Sec. 8.)

G. BONDS Sec. 578. Required of Executors and Administrators. 

The statute requires the court or judge or clerk in vacation to take a bond of the persons to whom letters of administration are 694

granted, with two or more sufficient securities, resident in the county, to the State of Missouri, in such amount as the court or judge or clerk shall deem sufficient, not less than double the amount of the personal estate (Sec. 18). A similar bond, with such variation as the case may require, must be given by all executors or administrators with the will annexed or of the goods remaining unadministered, and by all administrators during the time of contest about a will, or the minority or absence of an executor (Sec. 

20). Since the statute authorizes the allowance to executors and administrators in their settlements of a disbursement to cover a reasonable cost for a surety company bond, if the court deems it just and proper under all the circumstances connected with the estate to allow cost of such bond (Sec. 221), bonds of administrators or executors signed by a surety company are generally accepted in compliance with the statutory requirements for bonds. Except where wills expressly provide that no bond shall be given by the executor, and except where the executor is a trust company having deposited with the State the necessary securities to qualify it to serve as executor without giving bond (Sec. 5423), the filing of a sufficient bond by the administrator or executor is a necessary prerequisite to his right to letters, and an essential qualification for service as representative of the deceased.80 It is generally held that the statutes requiring bonds contemplate the filing of the bond upon the issuance of letters, all being part of one transaction, and the one depending on the other.81

The bond of an executor or a general administrator or that of any special administrator may follow the form of bonds generally, but the conditions thereof are prescribed by statute, and are: That if

Sec. 580. Persons Disqualified as Sureties. 

The statute disqualifies judges of the Probate Court, sheriffs, marshals, clerks of courts, deputy clerks of courts, and attorneys-atlaw from acting as sureties on bonds required of administrators and executors (Sec. 21), but it has been held that this statutory provision is directory only, and that the signing of an administrator's bond by an attorney as one of the sureties does not render the bond void. 82 

Sec. 581. Duties of Judge and Clerk in Taking Original and in

Requiring New Bonds. 

The statute requires the court or judge or clerk in vacation to take special care to take as securities on all official bonds men who are solvent and sufficient and who are not bound in too many other bonds. The applicant or persons offered as his securities may be examined on oath by the court or judge or clerk in vacation, and testimony may be taken to enable the court or judge or clerk to determine the sufficiency or insufficiency of the bond. Such bonds must be signed and executed in the presence of the court, judge or "State ex rel. Howell County vs. Findley, 101 Mo. 368, 14 S. W. 111; Hicks vs. Chouteau, 12 Mo. 341. 697

clerk, or acknowledged before some officer authorized to take acknowledgments of deeds, who shall certify to the same. It is the duty of the probate judge annually to examine all bonds of executors and administrators, guardians, and curators on file in his said office, and if, upon examination thereof, he shall have good reason to believe that any security has become a nonresident of the State or county, or has died or become insolvent, the judge thereupon shall make an order that said executor or administrator give another bond to the satisfaction of said judge or court, five days' previous notice of such intended order first having been given to said executor or administrator; and upon failure to give such bond within ten days after such order shall be made, the judge may make an order revoking his or her letters, and his or her authority from that time shall cease. (Sec. 22.) The clerk is required to record in a well-bound book kept for that purpose all bonds given by executors and administrators, preserve the originals in regular files, and present all such as are taken in vacation to the court at the next session (Sec. 23). The court is required to approve or reject the bonds taken in vacation, and the clerk must enter such approval or rejection on the record, and endorse the bond accordingly (Sec. 

24). If the bond is rejected, the court must order the executor or administrator to give another bond, with sufficient security; and if he fail to give such bond within such time as the court shall direct, his letters shall thenceforth be deemed to be revoked (Sec. 25). If a bond of an executor or administrator is rejected, it shall be valid. until such new bond be given, notwithstanding its rejection by the court (Sec. 26), and same will be held valid, though not approved. 8

Sec. 582. Liability on Bonds. 

to act as ad- 84 The bond of an executor or administrator is binding as against the principal and sureties for all acts of the principal from the time the bond is taken and approved until the principal is discharged." 

Such bond covers all acts of the administrator or executor, and serves as security against anyone's sustaining loss as a result of the breach of any official duty by the principal (Sec. 19). A bond of this character from which was omitted the given name of the deceased was held valid where such bond referred to the letters of administration and such letters contained the complete name of the deceased; and such letters were admissible to remove the ambiguity.85 It is not essential to the validity of the bond that it be approved by the probate judge.86 Since the statute is mandatory as to the conditions to be inserted (Sec. 19), such conditions should always be stated in the exact language of the statute; but it has been held that if the conditions do not follow the exact wording of the statute, but embrace the meaning of the conditions set out by the statute, the bond should not be held invalid.87 Nor will the bond be held invalid for including provisions not required by the statute, as such provisions will be rejected as surplusage and the bond held valid as to the other provisions.88 After an administrator gives one bond and subsequently, of his own volition, gives another with different sureties, it is not necessary to the validity of the last bond that it be approved by the Probate Court. Sec. 585. Publication of Notice of Letters. 

The judge or clerk of the court granting letters must, within ten days after the date letters are granted, cause same to be published in some newspaper published in the county where letters of administration have been granted, and if no paper is published in such county then in a paper published in any other county in the State nearest to the county where such letters of administration have been granted, once a week for two consecutive weeks in all counties or cities having over six hundred thousand inhabitants at the last preceding Federal census, and in all other counties once a week for four consecutive weeks. If, for any cause, such notice shall not have been so published for the first time within ten days after the date of the granting of such letters, the term of six months and the term of one year mentioned in such notice shall begin to run from the date of the first publication of said notice. Where publication 703

of such notice is made in a daily newspaper, publication for each week after the first shall fall on the corresponding day of the week as did the first publication. (Sec. 75.)

The statute requiring the giving of notice, prescribing the contents thereof and governing the time and place and effect of publication thereof has been frequently changed, so that cases construing such statute should always be read with the particular provisions of the statute in mind which were in effect at the time such cases were decided."

Sec. 586. Proof of Publication of Notice Must Be Filed. 

Every executor and administrator must file in the office of the clerk of the Probate Court the affidavit of the publisher or editor of the paper in which such executor or administrator shall publish such notice, within ten days after the same shall be made, with a copy of such advertisement annexed, stating the number and date of the papers in which the same was published (Sec. 76). 

Sec. 587. Proof of Publication Evidence When Recorded. 

The clerk of said court must carefully file and preserve such affidavit and the affidavits of the publication of other notices required by law in the administration of estates in his office and must record the same in a book to be kept by him for that purpose (Secs. 76, 77). 

The affidavit of the publisher or editor, so filed and recorded, or a certified copy of the record thereof, shall be received in evidence in all courts of this State (Sec. 78).

Notary Public.

The purpose of publication of notice of the granting of letters is to give creditors notice that their claims against a deceased person must be presented to the representative of the deceased in the course of 7 

Cunningham vs. Kinnerk (App.), 74 S. W. (2d) 1107. 705

the administration of the decedent's estate and within a certain fixed time or they will be barred from collecting their claims out of the assets of such estate. Since the proceeding appointing an administrator or executor and granting letters of authority to proceed with the administration of an estate involves the taking of the property of the deceased, notice to those having claims against the former owner of such property is a constitutional requirement. 

Notice is published not only to protect creditors and see that their right to collect their claims out of the assets of the deceased person is conserved, but also to hasten the administration of estates by setting in operation a special statute of limitations, to the end that the assets of the estate may be turned over to the persons beneficially interested as early as possible. The limitation statute begins to run when there is proper publication, notwithstanding a clerical error in the jurat of the affidavit of the publisher.10 The statutory mode of proof of notice does not exclude other competent evidence.¹ 

Responsibility for the publication of the notice is placed directly upon the judge or clerk, who is required by the statute to have such notice signed by the administrator or executor (Sec. 75).¹

Sec. 590. Notice Where There Are No Known Heirs. 

When an intestate has left no known heirs, the administrator shall also publish a notice once a week for six consecutive weeks, in at least two newspapers, containing the name of the intestate, the description of his person, the time and place of his death, the place of his nativity, if known, and the appraised amount of his estate. 

Where publication of such notice is made in a daily newspaper, publication for each week after the first shall fall on the corresponding day of the week as did the first publication. (Sec. 80.) 

The purpose of this notice is to bring the fact of the intestate's death, and the administration of his estate, to the attention of any heirs the deceased may have and who are unknown where his estate is administered, to the end that the constitutional guaranty that no person shall be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law, may be preserved.20 It has been held that an order of distribution made at a time other than first or final settlement, without publication of notice, is void as to an unknown distributee. 

Where, notwithstanding identity of heirs was doubtful, certain persons were, on ex parte hearing without notice, awarded legacy to heirs, judgment was void except as to them.2 21

INVENTORIES AND APPRAISEMENTS IV. INVENTORIES AND APPRAISEMENTS Sec. 591. Executor or Administrator Shall Take Charge of Property. 

Immediately after letters are granted, it becomes the duty of the executor or administrator to collect and take into possession the goods, chattels, money, books, papers and evidences of debt or of title to any real or personal property, except the property reserved as the absolute property of the widow (Sec. 57). Prior to that time he has absolutely no power to intermeddle with the property or affairs of the decedent, and even after he receives his letters he should be accompanied by witnesses appointed by the court when he makes an inventory thereof (Sec. 62). As heretofore seen, legal title to personal property of the deceased immediately vests in the administrator or executor, while the title to the real estate vests in the heirs subject to the right of the administrator or executor to take charge of, manage and sell same for the purpose of paying debts and legacies.22 Since title to personal property vests in the administrator, it is his duty to take possession of same,23 and a failure on his part to inventory and collect accounts which he knows to be due justifies his removal.24 If an executor finds personal property in the safe deposit vault of deceased, it is his duty to take possession of it for the estate, and if he takes possession thereof in good faith he should be protected from personal liability.25 The power of an administrator to take charge of property does not extend beyond the boundaries of the State, and an administrator should not inventory property belonging to the deceased and located in another state.26 But where an owner at the time of his death is a nonresident, title to personalty vests in the administrator appointed in this State,27 and the foreign domiciliary administrator cannot maintain a suit here for same, because he has no title to the 22
