Sec. 592. Purpose, Operation and Use of Inventory and 

Appraisement.

All parties interested in an estate have the right to know of what it consists, its value, how it is used, and how it is disposed of. For the purpose of making this information available, and for having some basis upon which to determine whether the administrator disposes of the property to the advantage of the estate and accounts for the assets that he takes into his possession, the law requires an inventory and appraisement to be made and filed.29 The inventory and the appraisement and the qualifying oaths, affidavits and certificates of the witnesses, appraisers and the administrator are very properly required to be incorporated in a single document (Sec. 73). Both the court and the executor or administrator should exercise the utmost care and precaution in seeing that the law is followed in selecting witnesses and appraisers, in seeing that the witnesses and appraisers properly perform their duties and in seeing that an accurate inventory and appraisement is made of all the deceased's assets. The statute now requires that all of the real and personal property of decedent be both inventoried and appraised, and the result thereof shown in a single instrument. Unless another appraisement is ordered by the court, the appraisement thus made at the opening of the administration is accepted as proof of the value of the property appraised for the purpose of assessing the State inheritance tax, and as the assessed value required in sales of real estate during the course of the administration. (Sec. 58.) 

The proceeding is a sensible one, as it is quite as desirable and more economical, although not compulsory, that three men act both as

Inventories and appraisements are admissible in evidence under the statute, although they are not conclusive for or against an executor or administrator, other evidence being admissible to vary the effect thereof (Sec. 74). But it has been held that an appraisement of stock in a corporation is not, as between the administrator and the distributees, the prima facie value of the stock at the time of the appraisal.30 Where an executor submitted a final settlement of his administration, knowing that some of his own personal property was mixed with that of the testatrix, and the settlement had become the judgment of the Probate Court, it has been held that such settlement must stand until set aside in a proceeding for that purpose; so that in an action by a husband to have declared his ownership of one-half of his deceased wife's estate, evidence that his own personal property was mixed with that of the deceased wife in the inventory of her estate was inadmissible. 8: 81 

Sec. 593. Witnesses to Inventory and Appraisement. 

a. Qualifications. 

At the time of appointing an executor or administrator, the court or judge or clerk in vacation is required by statute to name three persons as witnesses to accompany and aid the administrator in making an inventory and appraisement of the personal property of the deceased (Sec. 61). These witnesses must be responsible householders of the vicinity of the last abode of the deceased. They must be disinterested and of no kin to the administrator or executor. (Sec. 61.) b. Appointment and duties.

While these witnesses are appointed by the court or judge or clerk, ordinarily the appointing officer confers with the executor or 

Moffit vs. Hereford, 132 Mo. 513, 34 S. W. 252. "Lynch vs. Jones (Sup.), 247 S. W. 123. 711

administrator concerning those to be appointed, as the witnesses should be both congenial to the personal representative of the deceased with whom they are required to do their work, and competent to perform the duties required of them by law. It is the duty of witnesses to aid the administrator or executor in opening and examining the papers, money and other property of the deceased and in making an inventory thereof, and to appraise all personal property required by law to be appraised. If they fail to attend, the court or judge or clerk thereof in vacation must appoint others in their stead, so that three witnesses shall be present to attend the proceeding before it shall be lawful for the executor or administrator to open or examine such papers, money or other property by virtue of his appointment. (Sec. 61.) c. Fees.

The statute provides that every witness to the inventory and every appraiser shall receive three dollars per day for his attendance; also such further sum as the court may allow where expert advice or such services are required to be rendered by the witness or appraiser (Sec. 72). The men selected to aid the administrator in making the inventory and appraisement may serve in the dual capacity of witnesses and appraisers, thus saving the estate from paying double fees for performing what may be made a single service. Additional fees over those authorized by statute should not be paid by the administrator except with the approval of the court. When the administrator pays the witnesses and appraisers, he should take from them a receipt, which he must file with his settlement as for all other sums he expends.

Sec. 594. Penalty for Proceeding Without Witnesses. 

The statute provides that if any administrator or executor opens or examines the papers, money or other property of the deceased without the publicity and attestation provided by the administration statutes, he shall forfeit and pay to the person entitled to the estate a sum not exceeding five thousand dollars, to be recovered by civil action instituted in the name of the State to the use of the 712

parties entitled to the estate, in the circuit court of the county wherein letters of administration or testamentary were granted 

Sec. 595. Requisites of Inventory and Appraisement. 

a. Real estate and personal property. 

In preparing and filing the inventory and appraisement, the administrator or executor should follow the provisions of the statute which require that the administrator or executor make an inventory and appraisement, in one written instrument, of all the real and personal estate of the deceased, describing the quantity, situation and title of the real estate, and appraise each parcel thereof at its fair cash value, also describing the books and papers, the debts due or to become due to the deceased, the names of the debtors, the date of the contract, the amount of the interest due thereon to date of the death of the deceased, the rate of interest, and such further description as will render it a perfect inventory of the estate; also an appraisement of all personal property inventoried, except evidences of debt having a fixed value. Such appraisement, when verified, shall be accepted, unless another appraisement be ordered by the court, as proof of the value of the property appraised, for the purpose of assessing the State inheritance tax, and as the assessed value required in sale of real estate. (Sec. 58.) All of decedent's property must be inventoried and appraised.82 The inventory must include the real as well as the personal property, and if the administrator collects rents without an order of court he must account for same. Debts due from the executor must be inventoried as other debts.4 The inventory should include money coming into the executor's hands after the death of the testator and before the letters were granted. It should include a leasehold interest, regardless of the term of the lease; but the dower interest 36 "In Re Van Fossen (App.), 13 S. W. (2d) 1076.

Before entering on their duties, the witnesses to the inventory and the appraisers are required to make an affidavit stating that they are not interested nor of kin to any person interested in the estate as heir or devisee, and that they will, to the best of their ability, view and appraise the property to them produced, except evidences of debt having a fixed value (Sec. 69). This oath may be administered to the witnesses and appraisers by the executor or administrator, as the statute specially empowers the latter officers to administer such oaths (Sec. 68). The oaths should be attached to and made a part of the inventory and appraisement (Sec. 73). c. Oath of executor or administrator. 

The statute requires that the administrator shall annex to the inventory and appraisement an affidavit stating that it is a full description of all the money, goods, chattels and estate, real and personal, books, papers and evidences of debt and title of the deceased, and of all debts due and becoming due, so far as he can ascertain them, and an appraisement of all the property subject to appraisement, and that he was not in debt or bound in any contract to the deceased at the time of his death, except as stated in the inventory and appraisement (Sec. 59).

Sec. 596. Additional Inventory. 

If, after making the first inventory and appraisement, any other real or personal estate of the deceased comes to his possession or knowledge, the administrator or executor shall file a similar additional inventory and appraisement thereof (Sec. 60). At any time before the final settlement, the Probate Court has jurisdiction to compel the administrator to inventory any property of the estate which has been overlooked or omitted. Proceeds of insurance policy on life of a deceased member of a copartnership have been held to be assets of his estate, and should be inventoried."¹

Sec. 597. When Inventory and Appraisement Must Be Filed and 

Recorded. 

The statute requires that the inventory, appraisement and affidavits be filed in the office of the clerk of the probate court within 30 days after letters are granted, and that same must be duly recorded by the clerk in a well-bound book to be kept by him for that purpose (Sec. 71). The statute is mandatory, and it should always be strictly complied with. If, within the time allowed for filing the original inventory and appraisement, property belonging to the decedent has not come to the attention of the administrator or executor, the property thus omitted can be included in an additional inventory which may be filed at any time before a final settlement of the estate.12

V. THE PROBATE OF WILLS Sec. 598. Introductory Note. 

The general subject of wills is hereinafter discussed in this part of this work. 48 Since the probate of a will is a necessary step in the administration of the estate of a person dying testate, we shall here consider only that part of the subject of wills which has to do with the opening of the administration of the estate of a deceased testator, namely, the procedure by which wills are proven and admitted to probate. And, preliminary to that discussion, we shall consider the "Walter vs. Ford, 74 Mo. 195. "Post, Chapter 6, XII. 719

nature and kinds of wills, the necessity of probating wills in order for them to be effective, and the place and manner of proving wills. 

Sec. 599. Nature and Kinds of Wills. 

a. Definition of "will" and "testament."

A will is a declaration made with such formalities as are required by law, by which a living person expresses his intention or wishes as to what shall be done after his death relative to the disposition of his property and affairs. A testament is the same thing as a will, and is always similarly defined. It has been said that at one time a testator disposed of his personal property by a testament and his real estate by a will, but, if such distinctions ever obtained, they no longer exist.46 The words are now held to be synonymous and are generally used interchangeably." Both by express statutory declaration (Sec. 

564) and by the statutory rules enacted in aid of statutory construction (Sec. 655), the term "will" includes the term "testament." b. Written wills.

There are two general classifications of wills known to the law, namely, written wills and verbal or nuncupative wills. Written wills are those which are committed to writing, either in the handwriting of the testator, in which case they are sometimes referred to as holographic 18 or olographic 10 wills, or by a scrivener or other person engaged by the testator to prepare his will in accordance with the usual formalities of law required for written wills. 48 "Ballentine, 1365; 2 Blackstone, 449-500; 28 R. C. L. 58; Kelley (5th ed.) pp. 2-3; Starks vs. Lincoln, 316 Mo. 483, 291 S. W. 132. 

45 Blackstone translated what he called the old Roman lawyers' definition of "testament" thus: "The legal declaration of a man's intentions, which he wills to be performed after his death," and added that their definition was much better than their etymology. 2 Blackstone, 499-500; see also Ballentine, 1276. 

Compton vs. McMahan, 19 Mo. A. 494, l. c. 505. 46 

47 Ibid. 

48 28 R. C. L. 161. 49 Holographic or olographic wills are not recognized by the Missouri statutes, but in Harvy vs. Chouteau, 14 Mo. 587, 1. c. 588, the court referred to a will written in the testator's handwriting and not witnessed as an olographic testament, saying: "The olographic will is thus called because written throughout in the handwriting of the testator."' 720

c. Codicils. 

A codicil is an addition or supplement to, and a qualification of, a will." 

50 It has been called a "little will-made in reference to some former will, and commonly designed to enlarge, limit or modify" the original will and bring it down to the date of the codicil.5¹ 

It may also be either written or nuncupative. 52 By statute in Missouri, the term "will" includes codicil (Secs. 564, 655). d. Nuncupative wills.

A nuncupative will is an oral declaration by a testator in extremis, that is, in his last illness, before a sufficient number of witnesses, and subsequently reduced to writing by another than the testator.53 

When the art of writing was less practiced, nuncupative wills were favored by the law, so that under the early common law of England, nuncupative wills were as valid as written wills.54 The practice of fraud in connection with the proof of such wills made it necessary for the enactment of extensive statutory restrictions governing the probating of such wills (Secs. 541-544).55 These rigid statutory restrictions have resulted in an almost complete elimination of the practice of testamentary disposition by nuncupative wills.56

Sec. 600. Will Must Be Probated to Be Effective. 60 61 A will differs from most documents which pass title, in that it does not become effective at the time it is executed. 57 During the life of a testator, his will is ordinarily kept among his valuable papers, is subject to revocation by him, is static and inoperative, and is known as an ambulatory instrument.58 Immediately upon the death of the testator, rights of property vest according to the provisions of the will, subject to the probate of the will and the administration of the estate.50

But in order for a will to take effect and for its terms to become operative, it must be probated. At common law a person could assert title to real estate derived from a provision in a will, although the will had never been proved, and it has been said that the same rule obtains in some jurisdictions in this country. But the general rule is that a will cannot be given in evidence as the foundation of a right or title to property unless it is probated. However, it has been observed by the Supreme Court of Missouri that our statutes do not expressly postpone the vesting of title sufficient to support a conveyance in a devise under a will until such will is probated, and that our statute (Sec. 1681), by implication, recognizes the operative effect of unproved wills in those cases where there is cupative wills, by so numerous a train of requisites, that the thing itself has fallen into disuse; and is hardly ever heard of, but in the only instance where favor ought to be shewn to it, when the testator is surprised by sudden and violent sickness. The testamentary words must be spoken with an intent to bequeath, not any loose idle discourse in his illness; for he must require the bystanders to bear witness of such his intention: the will must be made at home, or among his family or friends, unless by unavoidable accidents; to prevent impositions from strangers: it must be in his last sickness; for, if he recovers, he may alter his dispositions, and has time to make a written will: it must not be proved at too long a distance from the testator's death, lest the words should escape the memory of the witnesses; nor yet too hastily and without notice, lest the family of the testator should be put to inconvenience, or surprised.''

Sec. 601. Partially Invalid Will May Be Probated. 

There is no middle ground in the procedure for probating a will, by which a will may be partially probated and partially rejected. 

The only question for determination when the will is offered for probate is whether it was the will of the testator. If the instrument offered is found to be the testator's will, it is entitled to be admitted to probate, although its provisions are invalid and cannot be carried into effect. The acts of proving the will and ordering that the will be admitted to probate do not have the effect of establishing the validity of the provisions of the will. And, though an earlier decision in this State announced the doctrine that portions of a will may be admitted to probate and other parts of the same instrument rejected, the case announcing such doctrine has been overruled and the rule established that if the document offered for probate is found to be the testator's will, it should be admitted to probate, even though it is partially or altogether invalid."7 A will containing invalid provisions or provisions impossible of performance should not, therefore, be withheld from probate, and should not be rejected when 66

Sec. 602. Where Will Must Be Probated. 

The statute specifically states where a will must be probated. If the testator has a mansion house or known place of abode in any county, his will must be there proved. If he has no place of residence, and devises lands, his will must be proved in the county where any part of the lands lie. If he has no place of residence and devises no lands, the will must be probated in the county in which the testator dies. If the testator dies out of the State, his will may, in that event, be proved in any county in the State. (Sec. 530.) The residence or domicile of the testator at the time of the making of the will does not control in ascertaining where the will must be proved." But the domicile of a testator at the time of his death is material in determining the county in which the will must be probated. And if a person makes a will in another State and later removes to Missouri, where he is domiciled at the time of his death, his will must be admitted to probate where he died, and not where he lived when he made the will.72 Where a will is deposited in a probate court, that court has jurisdiction of the proceedings relative thereto, and the probate court of another county cannot subsequently proceed to probate the will, and if it does, it can be ousted of jurisdiction by prohi-

Sec. 603. Authority to Admit or Reject Wills. 

The statute vests the probate court, or the judge or clerk thereof in vacation, subject to the confirmation or rejection by the court, with authority to take proof of last wills and of the date of the death of testators (Sec. 528), and to grant letters testamentary (Sec. 1). As the jurisdiction vested in probate courts to grant letters testamentary has been held exclusive and original," so also jurisdiction vested in probate courts to take proof of wills has been held exclusive and original.76 Judgments of probate courts admitting wills to probate are final and cannot be either directly attacked in equity for any reason," or collaterally attacked in any court.78 If the probate court is in session in term time, proof of wills must be made to the court. 

If the court is in vacation, proof of wills may be made either to the judge or the clerk. If the will is proved in vacation, the probate thereof is not complete until it is confirmed by the court in term time." Thus, it is said that the act of the clerk in admitting the will to probate in vacation is conditional and of no effect unless confirmed by the probate court.80 And, while it has been frequently held that the probating of a will is a judicial act and that the proof of the will

Sec. 605. Production of Will for Probate. 

The statute does not directly place upon anyone the obligation to produce the will of a testator and offer same for probate. But it does authorize the probate court, when satisfactorily informed that any person has in his possession the will of any testator, and such person refuses to produce the same for probate, to summon such person and compel him by attachment to produce the will (Sec. 568), thus indirectly placing upon the person having possession of the will the duty to produce it for probate. Any person interested in an estate of a testator whose will has been suppressed or withheld from probate, may report the circumstance to the probate court and obtain the aid of the statute in getting the will produced. 86 Ordinarily, a testator's will at the time of his death falls into the hands of those who have custody of his other papers and property, and those having such custody should produce the will for probate. If the executor named in the will desires to accept the appointment, he should proceed with the probating of the will, for this is one of the duties incident to administration which an executor should perform, and one which at common law he was required to perform.87 If such executor does not desire to accept the appointment, he may voluntarily appear before the probate court and resign or renounce his right to letters (Sec. 9). If the executor is dead or disqualified, parties interested in the estate may obtain possession of the will and offer same for probate or compel its production in the manner heretofore men-

Sec. 606. Limitation Upon Probate of Will. 

Prior to 1921 there was no limitation upon the time within which a will could be probated in Missouri, nor was there any statutory provision invalidating a will that was not probated.90 Under the law then existing, the courts recognized conveyances of real estate by will where such wills were not probated until long after the testator's death. But in 1921, the Legislature amended the statute providing for the granting or rejection of a certificate of a will under which no proof can now be taken of any will and no certificate of probate of a will issued unless such will is presented to the probate court, or judge or clerk thereof in vacation, within one year from the date of the first publication of the notice of granting letters testamentary or of administration that may have been granted by any probate court in the State of Missouri, on the estate of the testator, or named in such will so presented (Sec. 531).92 As to limitations upon the proof of nuncupative wills, the statute provides that proof of such

Sec. 607. Methods of Proving Wills. 

Our statutory requirements for establishing wills are based upon the two methods existing at common law for proving wills, namely, proof in common form, and proof in solemn form. Proof of wills by either method is said to be in the nature of a proceeding in rem.' a. In common form. 98 A will is proved in common form when the executor or some person having possession of the will produces it before the probate court or judge or clerk in vacation for the purpose of having same probated, and shows by statements of the attesting witnesses that same is the testator's will. In such proceeding, the presence of other interested parties is not required. This is the usual proceeding for probating a written will under the statutes of this State in our probate courts. (Secs. 532-536.) Such proceeding is ex parte, no process being necessary." When proof of a will is thus made, the court or judge or clerk hearing same may immediately either admit or reject the will and grant a certificate showing the action thereon (Sec. 531). Such action is provisional, that is, it may be conclusive, or it may be only conditional, depending upon whether or not interested parties exercise their statutory right to appear within one year and contest the validity of the will or the action of the court in rejecting the will (Sec. 537). At common law, when a will was admitted to probate in common form, any person having an interest therein could appear at any time within thirty years and compel the executor to prove the will in solemn form. And, even after proof of the will in solemn form before the ecclesiastical courts, parties claiming an interest in real estate could contest the validity of the will, as ecclesiastical courts "Watson vs. Alderson, 146 Mo. 333, 48 S. W. 478; Harris vs. Hays, 53 Mo. 

90; Garvin's Adm. vs. Williams, 50 Mo. 206. "42 Blackstone, 508; 28 R. C. L. 367; Kelley, 49; Watson vs. Alderson, 146 

Mo. 333, 48 S. W. 478. 

95 State ex rel. Mitchell vs. Gideon (App.), 237 S. W. 220. 

96 Watson vs. Alderson, 146 Mo. 333, 48 S. W. 478. 729

were held not to have jurisdiction over real estate. Our statutes providing for the proof of wills in common form and granting the right thereafter to parties interested within one year to contest the validity of the will were designed for the purpose of making judgments probating wills conclusive and at the same time preserve for interested parties the right to contest such judgments.98 Thus, when a will is proved in common form, the parties are bound by the judgment admitting the will to probate or rejecting it, unless they desire to contest the validity of the will or the order rejecting it, and if they do not contest the validity of the will within one year after the date of the probate or rejection, they are concluded by such judgment (Secs. 537, 539).99 b. In solemn form.

The common law method of proving a will in solemn form was in the nature of that provided by our statute for contesting wills. Such method of proving wills was referred to as proof of wills per testes, or by witnesses. This form of proof was resorted to when the validity of the will was disputed.100 By this method, any parties interested in the will are authorized to contest its validity, in which case the attesting witnesses of the will and others may be called to prove the instrument (Secs. 537, 540). This method of proving wills is final and conclusive. The proceeding for the proof of a will by this method is in fact a continuance of the original proceeding, a will contest proceeding not being an appeal but a revival of the same matter in the circuit court originally passed upon by the probate court. In will contest proceedings, the proponents of the will are required, as in the first instance in the probate court, to make proof of due execution of the will, and that the testator was of sound mind 1

Sec. 608. Proof of Written Will by Resident Witnesses. 

When attesting witnesses of a testator's will reside in the county where proof of the will must be made, such witnesses should appear before the court, if in term time, and before the judge or clerk if in vacation, and testify as to whether or not the instrument offered was the will which the testator signed in their presence and whether or not the testator was of sound mind at the time he signed his will. 

Such testimony must be reduced to writing, signed by the witnesses and certified by the clerk. (Sec. 536.) Ordinarily, this is all done on forms kept on hand in the office of the probate judge for the purpose, and, after such forms are completed, the will is attached thereto, the certificate of probate appended (Sec. 531), the affidavit of the executor or other person as to the date, place of death and widow and heirs of testator made (Sec. 17), the attesting certificate of the clerk attached (Secs. 546, 547), and the whole filed and recorded in the office of the probate court within thirty days after probate, in which office the original is permanently kept (Sec. 545), and if the testator devised real estate, a copy of the will must be certified by the clerk and recorded in the recorder's office in each county where the lands are situated, within six months after probate (Sec. 548). There follows a form of will, proof of such will, certificate of probate of will, affidavit as to the date, place of death and widow and heirs of testator, and the attesting certificate of the clerk, all of which may be used as a basis for proof of will and getting same probated, filed and recorded, as required by law.

Sec. 610. Proof Where But One Witness Is Available. 

A will must be in writing and signed by the testator, or by some person, by his direction, in his presence. It must be attested by two or more competent witnesses subscribing their names to the will in the presence of the testator. (Sec. 519.) If the witnesses to a will are competent when they sign as witnesses, the fact that they may subsequently become incompetent has no effect on the validity of the will. But if a witness to a will becomes insane or dies, or his residence is unknown at the time of the death of the testator, it is necessary to take proof of the handwriting of both the testator and the dead, insane or unavailable witness, and of such other circumstances as would be sufficient to prove such will on a trial at common law (Sec. 534). The statute (Sec. 519) requiring the testator to sign his will in the presence of two attesting witnesses being mandatory, and the statute (Sec. 534) making it necessary to prove the handwriting of both the testator and of any dead, insane or unavailable witnesses being the only authority under which wills can be proved when any witness becomes insane, or dies, or his residence is unknown, it is impossible to probate a will when only one witness is available, without proving the testator's handwriting and the handwriting of the other witness who is dead, insane or whose residence is unknown. And, while the attesting clause on the will is not indispensable, proof of the will by the testimony of only one of the 'Holmes vs. Holloman, 121 Mo. 535. 8 

Ray vs. Walker, 293 Mo. 447, 240 S. W. 187. 

'German Evangelical Bethel Church of Concordia vs. Reith (Sup.), 39 S. W. 

(2d) 1057. 736

subscribing witnesses, without a showing of what became of the other, or proof of his handwriting if he is dead, insane or unheard-of, as well as proof of the handwriting of the testator, is insufficient.10 

Thus, when only one witness is available, his proof may be taken in the same manner as if both were present, or, if he is outside the county, his proof may be taken by commission. Proof may then be made by others who knew the signatures of the testator and the other attesting witness.

If proof is made of the will by one available witness whose proof is taken either before the court or the judge or clerk in vacation, or by commission, the certificate of such proof, or the commission and the return showing proof by such living witness, must be attached to the will; and, in addition, there must be attached a certificate of proof of the handwriting of the testator and of the other witness who must be shown to be dead. If the surviving witness to the will knows the signatures of the testator and the other witness, he may be permitted to make proof thereof, as the statute does not disqualify him for making such proof. But, since the statute requires proof of the will to be made by at least two subscribing witnesses, it is the better practice, where only one of such witnesses survives and is competent, to have proof of the signature of the other witness to the will, and perhaps also of the signature of the testator, to be made by some person or persons other than the competent surviving witness to the will. If proof of the signature of the deceased, insane or unheard-of witness cannot be made by the same person who makes proof of the signature of the testator, such proof can be taken separately and certified as it is made. Such proof may be made in open court or before the judge or clerk in vacation, and the forms here set out can be adapted to suit the circumstances under which such proof is made. 

If proof is taken of one witness only, and the will is improperly admitted to probate upon such inadequate proof, the remedy is by a direct proceeding against the will, as the order admitting the will to probate is like the judgment of any other court of competent jurisdiction. It may be based upon insufficient proof, as it would be in such event, but it is a judgment, and cannot be impeached collaterally." 

Sec. 611. Proof Where There Are More Than Two Witnesses. 

The statute requires the will of a testator to be attested by two or more subscribing witnesses (Sec. 519). Wills are usually attested by only two witnesses, for this is sufficient under the statute. Occasionally, however, a will is signed by more than two witnesses. In such instances, should proof of the will be made by all such witnesses, or if two of such witnesses are available and the other subscribing "Dilworth vs. Rice, 48 Mo. 124. 738

witnesses are dead or unavailable, should proof be made of the will by more than the two available witnesses? Language in the nature of dicta has been used indicating that all the attesting witnesses of a will must give proof of the will or be accounted for. 12 But this cannot be said to be the prevailing rule.13 Nor is the rule that prevails as to the proof of the execution of a will in solemn form or in will contest cases controlling in proceedings to prove wills in common form. 

In will contest cases, it is generally held that the execution of the will may be proved by one of the subscribing witnesses and that both are "Thus, in Odenwaelder vs. Schorr, 8 Mo. A. 458, it was said: "The rule, both in this country and England is that the party propounding the will must produce all the witnesses, make them his, and give the contestants the benefits of cross examination if these witnesses are alive and in a condition to give evidence; and that the court, generally, will not decree the establishment of the will, unless the devisee has called all the subscribing witnesses, or has accounted for their absence.''

But in the case where this language is used, the will was attested by only two witnesses, one of whom had sworn adversely to the will, and the court called attention to the fact that "our statute requires two witnesses only." The language used in the Odenwaelder vs. Schorr case was quoted by the Supreme 

Court in the case of Craig vs. Craig, 156 Mo. 358, 56 S. W. 1097, similar on the facts. 

13 In the case of Lorts vs. Wash, 175 Mo. 487, 75 S. W. 95, the court distinguished the rule in the Craig case thus: "While the general rule is announced in Craig vs. Craig, supra, that all the subscribing witnesses should be introduced, it does not follow that a failure to introduce them would constitute error. That rule is announced as a suggestion of the appropriate method of procedure in cases of this character. On the other hand, the rule is well-settled that all that is required of those claiming under the will is to make out a prima facie case. Judge Black, in Norton vs. Paxton, 110 Mo., l. c. 462, 19 S. W. 807, in speaking of the method of procedure, announced this very plain and simple rule. He says: 'It is sufficient for those who claim under the will to make out a prima facie case in the first instance. 

There is a presumption that every adult person is compos mentis, but the presumption is one of fact only. It may be that the production of a will, reasonable on its face, with proof of due execution and attestation, and that the testator was of full age, will make out a prima facie case on the part of the proponents, thus giving full force to the presumption, though the usual course is to offer some evidence of mental capacity. The parties claiming under the will having made out a prima facie case, the contestants must bring forward their evidence. But it does not follow from all this that the burden of proof shifts. It remains with those claiming under the will.' It was not absolutely essential to introduce all the witnesses attesting the execution of this will.'' 739

not necessary for that purpose.14 Nor does the rule that a lost will may be established by the testimony of only one of the subscribing witnesses that he signed and saw the other sign 15 control in proof of wills generally in common form. In the proof of wills in common form in the first instance, the court or officer before whom the proof is made must be satisfied that the instrument offered for probate was the testator's will. If the court or officer is satisfied from the proof of two of the subscribing witnesses that the instrument is the testator's will, no further proof would appear necessary under the terms of the statute, even though there were additional subscribing witnesses. But if proof by two such attesting witnesses is not sufficient to satisfy the court or officer before whom same is made, then it would appear that such court or officer would have the right to require proof by the other attesting witnesses. 

Sec. 612. Proof Where All Witnesses Are Unavailable. 

Where all the subscribing witnesses are dead, insane or their residences are unknown, so that the court or clerk is satisfied that none of them can be produced as witnesses, the court or clerk shall take and receive such proof of the handwriting of the testator and subscribing witnesses to the will, and of such other facts and circumstances as would be sufficient to prove such will in a trial at law (Sec. 535). 

Where all subscribing witnesses are dead, the proof cannot be shown by the attesting witnesses that testator was of sound mind when he made, published and declared his will, as it is required to be made by such subscribing witnesses where they are available and testify. 

Thus, the statute has authorized the court or officer taking the proof to go beyond the proof of signatures of the testator and witnesses, if necessary, to determine whether the will produced is the will of the testator, and take proof of such other facts and circumstances as would be sufficient to prove such will in a trial at law. Since the formal execution of the will, and the possession of mental capacity

Sec. 613. Proof Where Testator's Name Was Signed by Another. 

The statute requires that written wills be signed by the testator, or by some person, by his direction, in his presence (Sec. 519). This statutory provision is mandatory, and if not complied with, the will is void.20 If a testator does not sign his name to his will, in order for 

20 McGee vs. Porter, 14 Mo. 611. 742

the will to be valid, it must be signed by some other person at the testator's request and in his presence.21 The testator's name, either in his own handwriting or in that of someone else by his direction, must be attached to the will.22 It is sufficient if the testator sign by mark, if his signature is attached at his direction, but, in any case, the governing statutory provisions must be complied with,23 or the instrument cannot be established as a valid will.24 Where testator signs by mark, the statute does not require that proof of the testator's signature be made, and it is sufficient if the proof of such will be in the usual form with the additional proof that the testator's name was signed on the will by some person by his direction and in his presence.

Sec. 614. Proof of Nuncupative Wills. 

Clerk.

No nuncupative will shall be good when the estate bequeathed exceeds the value of two hundred dollars; nor unless the same be proved by two witnesses, who were present at the making thereof; nor unless it be proved that the testator, at the time of pronouncing the same, did bid some person present to bear witness that such was his will, or to that effect; nor unless such nuncupative will was made at the time of the last sickness, and at the dwelling house of the deceased, or where he had been residing for the space of ten days or more, except where such person was taken sick from home, and died before his return. (Sec. 541.) No probate of any nuncupative will shall be granted for fourteen days after the death of the testator, nor shall any nuncupative will be at any time proved unless the testamentary words, or the substance thereof, be first committed to writing and a citation issued, accompanied with a copy thereof, to call the widow or next of kin of the deceased, that they may contest the probate of such will if they think proper (Sec. 544). Sec. 615. Proof of Lost Will. 

A will that has been lost, or a part of such will, may be proved and established after the death of the testator, if it can be shown that such will had not been revoked prior to the testator's death.20 If it is known that a decedent made a will prior to his death which cannot be found after his death, and it also appears that the testator did not intend to revoke such will, the lost instrument may be established and probated as the last will of the deceased, either by a copy of the will, if there is one in existence, 27 or by other secondary evidence of the contents thereof, such as the testimony of the subscribing witnesses.28 Such will may be established upon the proof of only one of the subscribing witnesses.29 Even the death or forgetfulness of the subscribing witnesses to a lost will is not sufficient to prevent the probate thereof, if there is other evidence which will aid in the establishment of the will.30 Thus, where the execution of a lost will is shown, the contents of the will may be established by the testimony of a person other than a subscribing witness, who has seen and read the will and talked with the testator about its contents. 31 In a proceeding to establish a lost will, the testimony of one of three subscribing witnesses may be considered sufficient to uphold the will, 20 McClellan vs. Owens (Sup.), 74 S. Sec. 616. Proof of Codicils. 

It is generally held that a codicil is, in effect, a reaffirmation and re-publication of the original will, modified by the provisions of the codicil and brought down to the date of the codicil, so that the original will and codicil may be construed and read together as one 749

instrument. 

Under our statute, the word "will" includes codicil, so that if a codicil is offered for probate, it must be proved with the same formalities as a will. It has been held that where a codicil is proven, and it refers to a will, the proof of the codicil amounts to a proof of the will, so that the will is not required to be separately proved.42 Where an original will and codicil were written on the same sheet of paper, and to this the probate judge attached a certificate that the judge had examined the instrument and heard the evidence of the subscribing witnesses and adjudged the same to be the will of the testator, it was held that the probate court admitted the whole will to probate, including the codicil.43

Sec. 617. Certificate and Order of Probate or Rejection. 

It is the duty of the court or judge or clerk in vacation to receive immediately the proof of a will exhibited for probate and grant a certificate of probate, if the instrument offered for probate is found to be the will of testator, or a certificate of rejection, if the will is rejected (Sec. 531). Such certificate should be attached to the will and recorded by the clerk of the probate court within thirty days after probate (Sec. 545). But, in addition to issuing a certificate of probate or rejection, the probate court, or judge or clerk thereof, should enter on the judgment record of the probate court an order or judgment showing the proceedings and the action of the court at the conclusion thereof. Such order and judgment is entirely distinct from the evidence upon which the judgment is pronounced and the certificate of admission to probate or rejection. The judgment as shown by the court record represents the action of the court on the issues raised upon the presentation of the will for probate. The certificate of probate or rejection evidences the action of the court. 

The order or judgment admitting the will to probate or rejecting it represents the performance of a judicial act, and such decree is binding on all the world.45 Such judgment, however, is not final or conclusive as to the construction of the will or the validity of particular testamentary provisions contained therein.46

Sec. 618. Recording of Wills. 

The statute requires that all wills be recorded by the clerk of the probate court in a book kept for that purpose, within thirty days after probate, and that the originals be carefully filed in his office (Sec. 545). If lands are devised by will, a copy of such will must be recorded in the recorder's office in the county where the land is situated, and if the lands are situated in different counties, a copy of such will must be recorded in the recorder's office in each county within six months after probate (Sec. 548). It will be observed that the statutes requiring the recording of wills do not require the recording of the proof thereof. This is unfortunate, especially in those instances where title to real estate is involved, for a will that devises real estate is a muniment of title and the stability of such title de- 755

pends upon whether or not the will is probated. A mere recording of the will in the office of the probate court as required by statute (Sec. 545) and a recording of a copy thereof in the recorder's office (Sec. 548) does not provide sufficient evidence upon which to base title, although it has been held that when the will has been recorded in the probate records, it is presumed to have been first probated, for it is a breach of duty, both on the part of the probate judge and the probate clerk, to permit a will to be recorded unless it has been first. admitted to probate. However, titles based on presumptions are not sufficiently secure, and where a will only is recorded in the probate records and a copy thereof is recorded in the recorder's office, in compliance with all that the statutes require, the only way by which a title examiner can assure himself of the fact that title is good is to examine the complete records of the proceedings on the will in the office of the probate court. Thus it is held that the statute requiring the recording of a copy of a will devising real estate in the recorder's office (Sec. 548) is merely directory.48 A failure to record the will in the recorder's office in compliance with the provisions of the statute will not defeat the title, for even a recorded copy of the will is not conclusive evidence that the title passed by the will.19 Even though the statute does not require it, the will recorded in the probate court and the copy recorded in the recorder's office should each have attached to it a copy of the proceedings on the will, showing the proof of the will, the affidavit as to the place and date of testator's "Hartwell vs. Parks, 240 Mo. 537, 144 S. W. 793. 48 

Simpson vs. Lehmann (Sup.), 219 S. W. 608; Nichols vs. Hobbs (Sup.), 197 

S. W. 258; Wolf vs. Brown, 142 Mo. 612, 44 S. W. 733; Rodney vs. McLaughlin, 97 Mo. 426, 9 S. W. 726; Lewis vs. City of St. Louis, 4 Mo. A. 563; 3 Mo. A. 582. 

As was stated in Nichols vs. Hobbs (Sup.), 197 S. W. 258: "Section 566 (now Sec. 548) does not provide for filing in the recorder's office the proof of the will, nor that such record shall impart notice and be admissible in evidence, so that, if one examining a title should find a will recorded there, he would have no evidence that it had been properly probated or that it had any force or effect. . . . He would have to go to the probate court and find the judgment of that court admitting it to probate, and in examining the judgment in this case he would have found the will was not correctly recorded in the recorder's office. While the record of a will in the recorder's office as provided by Section 566 may be admissible in evidence for some purposes, it does not protect a purchaser relying upon the provisions of a will as recorded. Accordingly, it has been held that Section 566 is merely directory." 756

death, his widow and heirs, and a certificate showing the admission of the will to probate, all certified by the clerk of the court.50 

Sec. 619. Operation and Effect of the Probated Will. 

54 While a will vests title in the property disposed of by its terms immediately upon the death of the testator, this title is contingent, first, upon the will being admitted to probate,52 and, second, upon no contest of the will being filed, or, if a contest is filed, upon the will being finally established at the end of the litigation. The probate of the will is the crucial test of its vitality and validity in vesting title to real estate in a devisee.58 The judgment admitting the will to probate, when it becomes final, is binding on all the world and cannot be attacked collaterally. The judgment is not final until the time fixed by statute, within which a suit to contest the will may be filed, has expired. Any conveyance of title based upon interests passing by the will may be nullified by a judgment invalidating the will. Where a will has been probated, it is presumed that the court found that the testator signed the will and that witnesses also signed in the presence of the testator.55 The judgment admitting the will to probate is a binding judgment until vacated in the manner allowed by law.58 The probate of a will will be presumed from the fact that it has been recorded.57 But an unprobated will is not admissible to show the title intended to be passed thereby.58 

Wills admitted to probate, together with the orders of the court admitting same, if recorded and certified by the clerk of the court and attested by his seal of office, may be read as evidence without any further proof of such will (Sec. 546). The record of any will made, admitted to probate and recorded, together with the exemplification of such record by the clerk of the probate court, in whose custody

(Continued in Volume II) I.  Sec. 620. General Scope of Powers and Duties of Administrators and Executors.

After the appointment of an administrator or executor, such representative of the decedent is empowered, by virtue of his appointment and the provisions of the law, to do all things necessary to administer completely the estate as the law requires, and subject only to the supervisory control of the probate court. His general 763

duties embrace all those tasks the performance of which are necessary for a complete administration of an estate. After the estate of a decedent is opened in the manner heretofore discussed, by the appointment of an administrator or executor, his qualification and acceptance and the issuance of letters as an evidence of his authority to act, and after he has prepared and filed his inventory and appraisement of the estate and published notice of his appointment, the further duties of the administrator or executor require the performance of the following tasks which shall be hereafter discussed in the order named: (1) Collection and preservation of the assets of the decedent; (2) the management and sale of decedent's property so that same may be as speedily as possible reduced to cash and used for the payment of debts, claims, legacies and charges against the estate, and the balance distributed to descendants or distributees; (3) assignment and setting out to widow, widower and minor children such parts of the property of the deceased as the statutes require to be set off to them; (4) the allowance and classification of demands against the estate of the decedent; (5) the payment of debts and legacies; (6) the ascertainment and payment of inheritance taxes due the State of Missouri and the United States; (7) the making of settlements whereby the administrator or executor accounts for all money, funds or property received by him and the manner in which same was used, and the distribution of the remainder according to the terms of the will or the applicable provisions of the law; (8) the adjustment of the administration proceedings to conditions that interfere with or disrupt the original administration, such as the death, resignation or removal of the administrator or executor; (9) the ad- 

It is noticeable that in the course of time the necessary steps for a complete administration of an estate do not materially change. In tracing the steps necessary for administering an estate and discussing the powers and duties of executors and administrators relative thereto, Blackstone said that these steps and the powers and duties of administrators and executors include: (1) The burial of the deceased in a manner suitable to the estate which he leaves behind him; (2) proof of the will of the deceased and securing letters on the estate; (3) preparation and filing of an inventory of the estate of deceased; (4) collection of all goods and chattels belonging to the deceased and converting same as speedily as possible into cash; (5) payment of the debts of the deceased under the rules of priority established by law; (6) payment of the legacies in accordance with the terms of the will; (7) the payment of the surplus or residuum to the next of kin of the deceased.

A. RIGHTS IN PROPERTY 

1. Real Estate.

Sec. 621. At Common Law Absolute Title Descended to Heirs. 

At common law, title to the real estate of a decedent vested immediately upon his death in his heirs. His personal representative took no interest or rights therein, and could not, with or without an order of court, lay his hands on the real estate, or exercise any control over same, at any time during the process of administration. 

Only in those instances where a testator by his will gave to his executor some measure of authority or control over his real estate was a personal representative of a deceased person allowed any privileges whatever in the use of real estate as a part of his rights or duties in administering the estate. If the real estate had been specially charged with the payment of some obligation of a creditor, it could be taken for the discharge of the obligation after the debtor's death, but unless real estate of a decedent had been specially charged by him in his lifetime with the payment of some debt no creditor could proceed against the lands of a deceased person for the satisfaction of the obligations of the decedent. The only remedy, if any, of such creditor, was against the heirs in whom title and right to the possession of the real estate vested. The sale or use of real estate by the personal representative for the payment of general claims of creditors was wholly unknown to the common law.² 

Sec. 622. Statutory Modification of Common Law Rule. 

Prior to the enactment of any statutes on the subject, the tendency in this country was to subject the real estate of a decedent to sale for

And, from the time of the passage of the first law on administration in Missouri, in the early territorial period, personal representatives of decedents have had the statutory power to sell real estate to pay the debts or legacies of deceased upon order of the probate court (Sec. 142, et seq.). This statutory power vested in the personal representative, subject to the order of court to sell real estate to pay debts, has been broadened, so that, even though there may be a sufficient amount of personal property on hand to pay debts, the personal representative may, upon order of court, reserve such personal property and sell the real estate for the payment of debts (Sec. 157). By an act passed July 4, 1807, by the Territorial Legislature of Missouri (Territorial Laws, Ch. 39, Sec. 56, pp. 138-139), it was provided that an administrator, upon being authorized by the court, could sell or mortgage the real estate of decedent for the purpose of paying his debts and maintaining, educating and improving the residence of his children. In 1815 the administrator was given similar power by a new statute (Territorial Laws, Ch. 143, Sec. 58, p. 414). In 1816 this act was amended so that executors in wills of testators were empowered to sell real estate for the payment of debts of the testator in all cases where such power was not given by the will (Territorial Laws, Ch. 

158, Sec. 9, p. 443). This statutory authority granted to a personal representative of a decedent to sell real estate to pay debts continued in effect until after Missouri's admission as a state, when, by an act approved 1825 (1 R. S. 

1825, Sec. 40, pp. 106-107), it was provided that "where there are not sufficient personal estate and effects charged with the payment of the debts of any testator or intestate, it shall be the duty of the executor or administrator to make application to the court of probate of the proper county, in which his letters were granted, by petition, setting forth the facts, and praying that an order or decree may be made for the sale of any real estate of the testator or intestate, the sale of which is not provided for by will, or so much thereof as shall be necessary for the payment of the debts of the deceased. . . . This act further provided that if application for the sale of real estate to pay debts was not made by the administrator such sales could be had upon application of any creditor of deceased, and the act prescribed procedure for the sale, very similar to that in use today.

This statutory provision has also come down to us from an early period. 

In 1 R. S. 1825, pp. 107-108, it was provided that: "If any executor or administrator or other person interested in any estate, shall deem it necessary, advantageous, or expedient, that any part of the personal estate of their testator or intestate be reserved, and real estate sold for the payment of debts, he or they may make application for that purpose to the court of probate, . . and praying that the whole, or any part, of the personal estate be reserved, and the real estate be sold for the payment of debts.

the statute, in the nature of liens against the real estate of deceased (Sec. 306). The personal representative may also lease the real estate and collect the rents therefrom for the purpose of raising money with which to pay debts (Sec. 130). And when the heirs do not take charge, or their whereabouts are unknown, the personal representative may take charge of and manage decedent's real estate (Sec. 131), repair and care for same (Sec. 132), and if decedent has not completed paying the purchase price for his real estate, the personal representative may pay the remaining part of such unpaid purchase price out of the assets in his hands (Sec. 134). He may also redeem mortgaged real estate out of personal assets (Sec. 139). 

In the exercise of such statutory authority over real estate, the personal representative is always subject both to the directions contained in the will of a testator, and to the orders of the probate court. The power granted by statute to the personal representative is generally held to be in derogation of the common law, and the representative must be restrained to the performance of such powers only as are expressly given, and in the manner by which the statutes direct." 

Sec. 623. Title Vests in Heirs Subject to Statutory Powers of Representative. 

The giving of these rather extensive statutory powers to administrators and executors has not resulted in a change in the rule as to the vesting of title of a decedent. The rule still obtains that immediately upon the death of a person title to his real estate vests in his heirs.10 But it is a burdened and contingent title. These statutory powers vested in administrators and executors, the exercise of which are contingent upon the order of the probate court, are only naked rights.11 Of these rights it has been said that they do not rise to the dignity of title in real estate. 12 And yet, the essence of title may be entirely consumed by the exercise of such rights. But until the probate court directs the personal representative to take charge of the real estate for the purpose of exercising some of the statutory rights vested in him, the right to the possession of the real estate, as well as the responsibility of defending the title to same, is in the heirs or devisees alone.13 However, this does not mean that the personal representative must remain unconcerned about or exercise an indifferent attitude toward the real estate of the decedent. At the very outset of his official duties he is required to inventory and appraise all the real estate of the decedent (Sec. 58), and if it appears that the real estate is not being properly managed by the heirs or devisees or that the income from same will be needed or the proceeds of sale thereof required for the payment of debts, he may, in the manner hereinafter discussed, apply to the court and, after proper authority is granted, take immediate charge of, manage, control, rent or sell same.

Sec. 629. Representative Required to Take Charge of Assets. 

For the purpose of protecting the decedent's property, managing and caring for same while in the course of administration, and giving assurance to those interested in his property that it will not be wasted but will be conserved and used as the law directs, the law places the personal representative in the shoes of the decedent, especially as to the personal property.68 The law also authorizes the conversion of real estate into personalty at the hands of the administrator under order of the court and the use of the products therefrom, or the proceeds thereof, to pay the debts of the deceased (Secs. 130181). The statute requires every executor and administrator, immediately after the grant of letters to him, to collect and take into possession the goods, chattels, money, books, papers and evidences of debt or of title to any real or personal estate, except the property reserved as the absolute property of the widow (Sec. 57). He must make an inventory and appraise all of decedent's property, both real and personal (Sec. 58). All assets should, immediately upon the 69 the express wishes of the heirs. His rights as administrator cannot be revoked without the consent of the court. He holds in custodia legis the estate coming into his hands as administrator, therefore, in the strict sense of the word, he is not the agent of the heirs, but is rather the agent of the probate court, whose orders, generally speaking, he must obey." " In Leach vs. Asher, 20 Mo. Sec. 630. Interests in Real Estate. a. Crops.

The statute authorizes an executor or administrator to procure indispensable labor to mature and harvest crops ungathered, belonging to a decedent, until the meeting of court (Sec. 102). And on the application of any person interested, the court may authorize further labor to be performed as the interest of the estate requires, and all sums paid therefor, if approved by the court, shall be allowed as expenses of administration (Sec. 103). It has been held that by these statutes it was intended that the crops or emblements growing on the land of one who dies before they are harvested, should descend as assets to the personal representative." It has also been held that a devise of land carries with it the crops growing upon it, and, since a growing crop is considered a part of the realty, it should pass with the realty under the devise, unless the testator expressed an intent to the contrary." But annual crops, raised by yearly labor and cultivation, are generally regarded as chattels, and are the subject of replevin.72 The rule that growing crops are personal property and go to the personal representative as against his heirs, and that they go to the devisee and not to the executor, existed at common law and remains in effect, except where modified by statute."

b. Rents.

The general rule applicable to rents of a decedent is that those rents that have accrued for the use of real estate prior to the owner's death belong to the administrator, while the rents and profits which accrue after the death of the owner belong to the heirs."4 The statute authorizes the personal representative of the decedent, under order of court, to take possession of the real estate and rent same, and when an order of court is made authorizing the representative to rent the real estate for the payment of debts, he has the right, as against the heirs, to collect the rents and apply them as the law authorizes and the court directs (Sec. 130). If the probate court assumes jurisdiction over a decedent's estate and orders an executor to rent his realty, a subsequent will contest does not oust the probate court of its jurisdiction.75 Nor does the circuit court have jurisdiction to appoint a receiver of a decedent's real estate when a will contest is filed, for the custody of the property is in the probate court.76 If the court directs an administrator to rent the real estate, the administrator is liable for failure to make necessary repairs on same, even though no order of court had been made authorizing him to make such repairs." 

If the administrator fails to obtain an order authorizing him to collect rents, and proceeds to collect rents regardless thereof, it is necessary for him to account in his settlement for the rents he receives,78 for such rents are assets in his hands for which he and the sureties on his bond are liable." Where this occurs, the collection of rents by the administrator is held a wrongful or irregular exercise of a power delegated to him by law, and for the rents thus received he is chargeable individually as a trustee or a trespasser.80 If the court does not authorize the administrator to collect rents, such rents and profits derived from the lands of the decedent belong to the heirs and not to the estate. 81

Leasehold interests.

While title to real estate vests in the heirs subject to the contingent rights of the executor or administrator, a lease of real estate is considered a personal asset, and the right thereto vests in the personal representative, regardless of the length of time the lease has to run.83 

This was the rule at common law and it obtains in nearly all jurisdictions today.84 Even where the statutes provide that a widow shall be given dower in leasehold for twenty years or more, which must be assigned to her as real estate, such leasehold interest, regardless of the statutes, is personal property, and so much thereof as is not given to the widow passes to the administrator as assets of the estate of the lessee.85 The law does not permit an executor to waive the term so as not to be liable upon the promise of the testator to pay annual rent, so long as the executor has assets.86 d. e. The doctrine of relation. 

Title to real estate vests in the heirs and devisees eo instanti upon the death of the testator or intestate.94 And, unless the representative of the decedent takes charge of the real estate under order of court, and leases, manages, controls or sells it by appropriate proceedings, the administrator does not interfere with the title of the heirs or devisees. But, if the representative sells the real estate under order of the court to pay debts, and title in the meantime has remained vested in the heirs or devisees, the purchaser at the sale of the representative takes title by the administrator's or executor's deed. His title is not that of the heirs, but it is that of the decedent. 

The title that the heirs held between the time of the death of the decedent and the conveyance as a result of the sale vanishes, and the purchaser at the administrator's sale takes title as of the time of the death of the decedent, by what is known as the doctrine of relation.95 Under this doctrine, the authority of the administrator to sell the land relates back to the time of the death of the testator or intestate, and the execution of the deed by the administrator to a purchaser at a sale to pay debts passes title as against the heirs and as against any person to whom they may have conveyed. This doctrine is a fiction of law, to prevent injustice and the occurrence of injuries for which there would otherwise be no remedy, and 

94 Ante, Sec. 621. ... 96 

95 The doctrine of relation is stated in Grant vs. Hathaway, 215 Mo. 141, 114 

S. W. 609, 1. c. 611, as follows: "It is well settled that when a person dies the owner of real estate or an interest therein, the title, in the absence of statutory provision to the contrary, descends eo instanti, and vests in the heirs, subject to statutory rights and incidents of ownership that exist at common law, as well as to the right of the administrator to sell the land for the payment of debts against the estate and legacies, provided there be not sufficient personal property to pay them. . In this event, the authority of the administrator to sell the land relates back to the time of the death of the intestate, and all creditors have priority over the heirs, and a sale of the land, in pursuance of an order of the probate court, for the payment of the debts against the estate, and the execution of a deed to the purchaser by the administrator, will pass the title as against the heirs or as against any person to whom they may have conveyed the land; but, until such steps as indicated are taken by the administrator, the title and rights of the heirs remain unaffected and unimpaired.

Sec. 631. Personal Property. 

a. Chattels generally.

The rule at common law, and that now universally recognized, is that title and right to the possession of personal property upon the death of a deceased person vest in his executor or administrator until released by some appropriate proceeding or distributed at the conclusion of administration.98 This general rule applies to all personal property. The statute requiring executors and administrators to take charge of all chattels (Sec. 57) follows and reenforces the common law rule. It is, therefore, the duty of the personal representative of the deceased to take into his hands immediately after his appointment all chattels and personal property of every character, title to which is vested in him by law, and for which he must account to those interested in the estate. b. Money.

Money belonging to the decedent at his death passes to his personal representative, who is required by statute to take possession thereof (Sec. 57). Such money is ordinarily on deposit in a bank, and before the representative can take possession of the deposits of the deceased it is usually necessary for him to file with the bank where the money is on deposit evidence of his authority to take possession of such money. If the deceased left a will, banks usually require that a certified copy of the will and proof thereof and certificate admitting same to probate, and a certified copy of letters testamentary, be filed with the bank. If decedent left no will, the depository bank ordinarily requires that a certified copy of letters of administration be filed, and it may require such other evidence of the authority of the representative as will satisfy the bank that it is taking no risk in turning over the money of the decedent to the administrator. If the money is represented by a certificate of de- " Wilson vs. Wilson, 54 Mo. 213, 1. c. 216; Stagg vs. Green, 47 Mo. 500, 1. c. 502. 

Ante, Secs. 624, 625. 783

posit in a bank, the administrator is entitled to the certificate evidencing the debt of the bank, as it is considered an asset within the meaning of the law directing that the administrator take charge of all assets. Whether the money belonging to an estate shall be kept in a bank as a general deposit, in a safety deposit box or some other safe place, or on the administrator's person, is a matter of judgment and discretion on the part of the administrator, and is of no concern to the probate court on final settlement.100 

c. Notes. 

2 The statute specifically requires the executor or administrator to take into his possession evidences of debt (Sec. 57). If notes are made payable to a husband and wife and one of them dies, title to such notes vests in the survivor, and the administrator of the decedent has no interest therein.¹ A note made payable to the husband or his wife passes, on the decease of the husband, to the wife, who becomes the sole owner thereof as his survivor, and the mere fact that the wife handed the papers of her deceased husband to the administrator, among which was a note made payable to the husband or wife, does not warrant a presumption that the wife surrendered. her right to the note. The weight of authority both in England and America recognizes and enforces the right of survivorship in notes made payable to the husband and wife. All other notes and mortgages securing them must be taken over by the executor or administrator and handled as a part of the assets of the estate. The representative is charged with such notes, and in making the inventory thereof he is required to state the names of the makers, the date of the notes, the amount of the interest due thereon to the date of the death of the deceased, the rate of interest and such further description as will aid in further use thereof (Sec. 58). A note may be assigned by the executor or administrator to creditors, legatees or distributees in discharge of an equal amount of their claims

A judgment is a right to collect money, and title to judgments recovered in favor of a deceased person ordinarily passes to his personal representative, who is entitled to collect same as a part of the assets of the estate. However, the proceeds of a judgment for wrongful death of the decedent are not part of his estate.11 Where a decree awarded alimony in gross to a wife and the wife died, the judgment became a vested property right which survived the wife in favor of her administratrix.12 

f. Insurance. 

If a deceased person had a policy of insurance on his life, payable to his estate, the proceeds thereof pass to the administrator, and immediately after his appointment the executor or administrator should furnish proof of the death of the deceased, and evidence of his authority to act, in order to collect the proceeds due under the policy. It has been held that one having an undivided interest in a paid-up insurance policy of another has a vested interest during the life of the insured and the insurance money is an asset of his estate after the death of the insured and payment by insurer, though he died before the insured.18 Where a certificate of insurance in a fraternal beneficiary association was carried by a person who died, it was held that the only person entitled to the money due under the policy, except upon an order of the probate court dispensing with administration, was the administrator of the estate. 14 But where a policy provided that in case of death the insurance be paid to the "heirs or representatives," it was held that such provisions indicated an intention of the insured to leave the insurance to his heirs or next of kin, and that the court would construe the policy so as to "Willgues vs. Pennsylvania Railroad, 318 Mo. 28, 298 S. C. COLLECTION OF DEBTS, PROSECUTION AND DEFENSE OF ACTIONS Sec. 633. Statutory Authority. 

The statute provides that executors and administrators shall collect all debts and money of every kind due to the deceased, and give receipts and discharges therefor, and shall commence and prosecute all actions which may be maintained and are necessary in the course of his administration, and defend all such as are brought against him (Sec. 94). Executors and administrators are required by statute to prosecute and defend all actions commenced by or against the deceased, at the time of his death, and which might have been prosecuted or maintained by or against such administrator (Sec. 97). 

Executors or administrators, with the approval of the probate court, may, in all cases where they are unable to collect by law, com- 

Jacobs vs. Jacobs, 99 Mo. 427, 12 S. W. 457. 

Scudder vs. Ames, 142 Mo. 187, 43 S. W. 659. " Ibid. "Young vs. Ray (App.), 193 S. W. 608. 790

promise any claim against any debtor of the decedent (Sec. 234).

For all wrongs done to property rights, or interest of another, for which an action might be maintained against the wrongdoer, action may be brought by the person injured, or, after his death, by his executor or administrator, against such wrongdoer, and, after his death, against his executor or administrator, in the same manner and with like effect, in all respects, as actions founded upon contract (Sec. 98). The statute provides that the foregoing provision shall not extend to actions for slander, libel, assault and battery, or false imprisonment, nor to actions on the case for injuries to the person of the plaintiff, or to the person of the testator or intestate of any executor or administrator (Sec. 97).

Sec. 634. Authority to Compromise Claims. 

Prior to 1879, executors and administrators had no special statutory authority authorizing them to compromise claims due or against estates of decedents. However, they were held to have implied authority to compromise claims by virtue of their general power as trustees, and, where they undertook to compromise such claims, their actions were measured by the rule that they must exercise such care and skill as prudent men exercise in the direction and management of their own affairs.33 The courts recognized the rule at common law that, while the executor or administrator, incident to his general powers as the personal representative of the decedent, had power to compromise or settle debts or claims, if the representative accepted less than the full amount due on a debt, it was regarded as waste and he was held answerable for the loss, unless he could show that in compromising or releasing a debt he acted for the benefit of the estate and with fidelity and prudence. And our courts accepted the rule prevailing in other jurisdictions, that, regardless of special statutory authority, executors and administrators have power to compromise debts or disputed claims in favor of or against the estates which they represent, which power inheres in the authority granted by the general statute authorizing representa- "Jacobs vs. Jacobs, 99 Mo. 427, 12 S. W. 457; Merritt vs. Merritt, 62 Mo. 150. "Jacobs vs. Jacobs, 99 Mo. 427, 12 S. W. 457. 791

tives to commence and prosecute actions.35 A special statute now empowers executors and administrators to compromise any claim against any debtor of the decedent which they are unable to collect by law, but this can be done only with the approval of the probate court (Sec. 234).88 Thus, the authority of the executor or administrator to compromise claims upon the approval of the probate court is now unquestioned," and a court of equity will compel the performance of a contract made by an executor of an estate to com- 35 This view was expressed by the Supreme Court of the United States in

Vol. 1, p. 87, Sec. 26) to commence and prosecute actions fairly includes the power to make such reasonable contracts in regard to compensation and the compromising of actions on doubtful claims as the circumstances of particular cases may justify.
