360. FORM OF ADMINISTRATOR'S APPLICATION FOR ORDER AUTHORIZING COMPROMISE OF CLAIM 

Ralph Ray, administrator of the estate of Glen Pars, deceased, represents to the court that, among the assets in his hands and belonging to said estate, there is a note in the sum of $1,500 against Paul Penn, and a deed of trust securing same, on forty acres of real estate, located in ............. County, Missouri, and described as follows: (Here describe); that the administrator has made repeated efforts to collect said note, but without avail, and that he has found that the maker of said note and mortgage is a man advanced in years and is insolvent and has no other property and no income other than that derived from said real estate; that he has carefully investigated the value of said real estate, and is of the opinion that it is not worth more than $750, and that said sum could not be now obtained for it on the market; that Price Penn, a brother of Paul Penn, the owner of said real estate and maker of said note, has agreed to pay $1,000 to the administrator in full payment of said note, and in satisfaction of the deed of trust securing same; that the administrator has made an effort to sell said note and deed of trust to others, but has been unable to find anyone who would pay as much for same as has been offered by the said Price Penn; that it would require additional expense to foreclose the mortgage on said real estate, and, if same were foreclosed, administrator is of the opinion that it would not bring as much as $1,000 at public sale, and that the administrator could not thereafter recover any further amount on the note from the maker or from any other source; that after a careful investigation of all the 

Wayland vs. Pendleton (App.), 73 S. W. (2d) 288. 28 

Mosman vs. Bender, 80 Mo. 579. 793

facts connected with this asset of the estate, this administrator is of the opinion that it is for the best interest of the estate to accept said sum of $1,000 in full payment of said note and deed of trust. 

Wherefore, administrator prays for an order authorizing the administrator to accept from Price Penn the sum of $1,000 in full payment and discharge of the note and mortgage of Paul Penn and approving the compromise of said note on said basis. (Affidavit.) 

Ralph Ray, Administrator. 

361. FORM OF ORDER AUTHORIZING ADMINISTRATOR TO 

COMPROMISE CLAIM 

Now is presented the application of Ralph Ray, administrator of said estate, praying for an order authorizing him to compromise a claim belonging to said estate, based on a note and mortgage in the sum of $1,500, and approving a settlement in full payment of said note and a satisfaction of said mortgage for $1,000, and, after hearing the evidence offered in support of the application, and being fully advised, the court is of the opinion that it would be for the best interests of said estate that the offer of Price Penn, to pay the sum of $1,000 in full settlement and discharge of said note and mortgage, be accepted and the settlement of the administrator therefor approved. It is now, therefore, Ordered by the court that the administrator be and he is hereby authorized and directed to accept the sum of $1,000 in full settlement of said note and mortgage, and that a compromise of said claim on said basis be and the same is hereby approved. 

Sec. 635. Actions Representative Cannot Maintain. 

The statutory authority granted executors and administrators to prosecute actions does not extend to all actions involving the assets or property of the deceased. Actions for the possession of, or in defense of the title to, real estate of the decedent cannot be maintained or urged by the executor or administrator except where such actions or defenses are made necessary by order of the court directing the executor or administrator to take charge of the real estate, for until such order is made such actions are the sole concern of the heirs.40 Thus the administrator or executor cannot maintain an

Sec. 637. Actions Concerning Decedent's Contracts. 

At common law, actions ex contractu of a decedent survived against his executor or administrator." The rule is that where the contract is personal the right to enforce same goes to the representative of the decedent.76 Thus, where a decedent, prior to his death, built a party wall on the line between his real estate and that of the adjoining landowner, under an agreement with the adjoining owner that the latter was to pay half the cost, it was held that the easement for the wall attached to and became a part of the land and was enforceable by the heirs, but that the enforcement of the contract of the adjoining owner to pay his part of the cost of the wall was personal to the decedent and upon his death passed to his administrator." All debts founded upon contracts made with the decedent prior to his death survive, and the right to enforce same is vested in his executor or administrator, who alone has the right to sue for the enforcement thereof.78 Thus, a promise by a seller of corporate stock to repurchase same at the option of the buyer has been held enforceable by the buyer's executor." .79 Thus, also, the right to enforce the collection of a note due the decedent passes to the administrator,80 as does the right to a judgment assigned to decedent before his death.81 But where an antenuptial contract provided that the wife would have the right to bring up the offspring in the Catholic faith, even if she died, it was held that the right of the wife was not a property right that would pass to and be enforceable by her administrators.82

Sec. 638. The Survival of Tort Actions. 

At common law, actions in tort did not survive the death of either the wronged or the wrongdoer.88 This common law rule forbidding the survival of actions ex delicto has been modified by statutes in this 

State (Secs. 98, 99), first enacted in 1835.84 The forerunner of these statutes was the English statute of 4 Edward III, which gave actions against trespassers unpunished at the time of the death of the person trespassed against, and other tort actions, to his executors, and not against them, on the theory that as against the person committing the injury the action dies with him, while as to the person injured the right of action survives.85 Our statutes changed the 

English law in this respect, by giving an action ex delicto both to and against executors and administrators (Secs. 98, 99).86 As originally passed, the statute changing the common law rule as to the survival of actions ex delicto provided that: "For all wrongs done to property, rights, or interest of another, for which an action may be brought by the person injured, or, after his death, by his executor or administrator, against such wrongdoer, and, after his death, against his executor or administrator, in the same manner and with like effect, in all respects, as actions founded upon contract."'87 The courts criticized the punctuation of the original statute and held that the statute was meant to provide for a survival of actions "for all wrongs done to property rights, or interest of another."'88 In conformity with this interpretation placed upon the statute by the courts, same has now been modified as suggested (Sec. 98). The purpose and the general effect of such statute, so "Burg vs. Knox, 67 S. W. (2d) 96, 334 Mo. 329; Bates vs. Sylvester, 205 Mo. 

493, 104 S. W. 73; Vawter vs. Mo. Pac. Ry. Co., 84 Mo. 679; Stanley vs. Bircher, 78 Mo. 245; Toomey vs. Wells, 218 Mo. A. 534, 280 S. W. 441. 

84 R. S. 1835, Secs. 24, 25. 85 'Higgins vs. Breen, 9 Mo. 497. 

8 Bates vs. Sylvester, 205 Mo. 493, 104 S. W. 73; Higgins vs. Breen, 9 Mo. 497. 

87 R. S. 1919, Sec. 97. This section remained as it had been originally enacted in 1835 (R. S. 1835, Sec. 24) down to and including the 1919 Revision. It now appears in the 1929 Revision as the courts say it was originally intended. 

Gilkeson vs. Mo. Pac. Ry. Co., 222 Mo. 173, 121 S. W. 138; Bates vs. Sylvester, 205 Mo. 493, 104 S. W. 73; Vawter vs. Mo. Pac. Ry. Co., 84 Mo. 679; 

Toomey vs. Wells, 218 Mo. A. 534, 280 S. W. 441. 800

far as it affects the survival of actions against executors and administrators, was to put injuries to property rights arising from torts on the same basis as those arising out of contract. Under this statute it has been held that, following the death of a person, rights of action in his favor survived and passed to his executor or administrator for replevin," deceit,91 trespass to real estate committed before the death of the owner,92 injury occurring as a result of refusal to release a mortgage, a false return by a sheriff on an execution, and on a covenant against encumbrances.95 Where a cause of action for damages to realty accrued during the lifetime of a decedent, it descended to his administrator, and not to his heirs.⁹ 

The executor or administrator, and not the heirs or devisees, has a right to recover for a conversion of personalty belonging to the decedent." And as to the right to collect unpaid installments of a judgment for alimony rendered in a decree of divorce, it has been held that, upon the death of the wife in whose favor such judgment was entered, the right to enforce the payment of the alimony survives the wife in favor of her administrator, not merely on the ground that the judgment was based on the husband's tortious acts, but also because the judgment was a vested property right.98

Sec. 640. Actions for Death. 

The rule at common law was that civil actions for the death of a person caused by the torts of another did not survive to any person under any circumstances. This rule was so well known in popular usage that it is now referred to as a maxim. The enactment of the statutes providing for the survival of actions for torts against property rights and interest heretofore discussed (Secs. 98, 99) did not have the effect of providing for the survival of causes of action for death after the death of either the wronged or the wrongdoer."

These statutes were declaratory of the common law.10 Thus, after the enactment of such statutes, the administrator of a decedent whose death was caused by the torts of another could not maintain an action for damages for the death of the decedent, because the

* In Davis vs. Morgan, 97 Mo. 79, 10 S. W. 881, Sherwood, J., thus referred to the Latin expression, actio personalis moritur cum persona, as a maxim representing the common law rule. 

In 1 R. C. L. 29, and in Ballentine, 25, 26, it is pointed out that this rule or maxim used by Sherwood, J., standing alone, is inaccurate. As translated from the Latin, the expression used is: A personal action dies with the person. But as stated in 1 R. C. L. 29, and as repeated in Ballentine: "A more restricted meaning must, therefore, be given to the rule or maxim stated above, and it is this: if an injury is done either to the person or property of another, for which damages only may be recovered in satisfaction, the action dies with the person to whom or by whom the wrong has been done."

statutes providing for the survival of tort actions in behalf of the administrator were held to refer to actions concerning property rights or interest only, and did not include actions by the administrator for damages for the death of his intestate.¹¹ While these sections of the statutes (Secs. 98, 99) have been referred to as the "pioneer sections" in the progress of Missouri legislation for the removal of the common law limitation of death upon causes of action,12 the statutes actually providing for the survival of causes of action for death were first enacted in 1855, as a part of what is known as the Damage Act.18 These statutes embodied the principal provisions of the English Statute known as Lord Campbell's Act, passed in 1846, authorizing the prosecution of a cause of action for death caused by a wrongful or negligent act. As originally passed, the Damage Act did not provide for a recovery, by the personal representatives of the decedents, of damages for death, but causes of action for such damages survived only to the persons authorized by such act to bring suit therefor.14 These were: First, the husband or wife of the deceased; second, if there was no husband or wife, or if he or she failed to sue within six months after the death, then by the minor child or children of the deceased; third, if such deceased be a minor and unmarried, then by the father and mother, or if either of them be dead then by the survivor. D. PROCEEDINGS TO DISCOVER ASSETS 

Sec. 641. Nature of Proceeding.

A proceeding to discover assets belonging to the estate of a deceased person is a summary proceeding devised not merely to discover assets but also to expedite the administration of estates by affording a new and special remedy for collecting assets.20 The proceeding is statutory and the procedure therefor is governed by special statutory provisions (Secs. 63-67). The proceeding authorized by the statute is an action within the meaning of the law, in which there is a moving party, an adverse party, and issues requiring the decision 16 Laws Mo. 1911, p. 205, which added to the act authorizing recovery of damages for death the following provision: "If there be no husband, wife, minor child or minor children, natural born or adopted as hereinbefore indicated, or if the deceased be an unmarried minor and there be no father or mother, then in such case suit may be instituted and recovery had by the administrator or executor of the deceased and the amount recovered shall be distributed according to the laws of descent, • • 

17 Burg vs. Knox, 67 S. W. (2d) 96, 334 Mo. 329, and other cases cited in this section, Notes 8 and 11. 

18 Bates vs. Sylvester, 205 Mo. 493, 104 S. W. 73; Strode vs. St. Louis Transit 

Co., 197 Mo. 616, 95 S. W. 851; Hennesy vs. Bavarian Brewing Co., 145 Mo. 104, 46 S. W. 966; Miller vs. Mo. Pac. Ry. Co., 109 Mo. 350, 19 S. W. 58; Gray vs. 

McDonald, 104 Mo. 303, 16 S. W. 398; White vs. Maxey, 64 Mo. 552; Procter vs. Hann. & St. Joe. Ry. Co., 64 Mo. 112. 19 

Post, Chaps. 81 and 82. 

Davis vs. Johnson, 58 S. W. (2d) 746, 332 Mo. 417. 805

of a tribunal vested with jurisdiction to determine the questions involved.21 The purpose of the proceeding is two-fold. It provides for both the discovery and the recovery of assets.22 Not only is title to disputed property tried in such proceeding, but also delivery of such property to the administrator is compelled if it is found to be possessed wrongfully.23 The proceeding cannot be invoked for the purpose of determining issues which are purely equitable in their nature and where the relief demanded is equitable, as an action by a creditor to set aside a transaction whereby the intestate, before his death, returned a note given to him by the defendant for purchase of real estate. 24 But where the executrix of her deceased husband's estate omitted to inventory certain funds which she claimed had been given to her by her husband, an action to determine the validity of the gift by a creditor of the husband should have been brought in the probate court as a proceeding to discover assets, and not originally in the circuit court as a suit in equity to set aside a transfer.2 25

Sec. 642. History of Remedy. 

The existing remedy of those interested in the estate of a deceased person to discover assets believed to belong to the estate of a decedent, try and determine the title to such assets, and compel the delivery of them to the administrator if found to be the property of decedent, evolved from a statutory proceeding which was originally much less comprehensive. The original statute provided that if an executor or administrator, or other person interested in any es- 21

25 Lemp Brewing Co. vs. Steckman, 180 Mo. A. 320, 168 S. W. 226. 806

tate, represented on oath to the probate court that he had good cause to believe, and did believe, that any person had concealed or embezzled any goods, chattels or other property belonging to the estate, the court could require the appearance of such person for an examination on oath for the purpose of discovering such property.20 It was not contemplated by this statute that title or the ownership of assets would be tried. The proceeding was purely ex parte and designed solely as a summary means of discovery.27 

In 1845, the act providing for the remedy was amended, by which amendment the powers of the probate court were enlarged and its authority extended in a manner that is unique in Missouri jurisprudence. By the statute as amended, the probate court was not only authorized to determine rights of property but also, at the instance of either party, to call a jury to try the issues. 28 The statute was again amended in 1855,20 by which amendment the purpose was clearly expressed of providing a method for determining the issue of whether property charged to be concealed or embezzled belonged to the estate or to the person accused of concealment or embezzlement. In 1879, the statutes providing for this remedy were again amended and passed in the same form as they exist today.30 By the amendment of 1879, the procedure was materially modified. Prior to that amendment, the issues were made by the filing of an affidavit charging concealment or embezzlement and the oral answers of the person cited. Under the present statute, the issues are framed by written interrogatories and written answers. 

The issues thus formed may be tried with or without a jury as in ordinary civil actions. Under the statutes as they exist today, the proceeding may be instituted for the purpose of discovering and recovering assets that are concealed, embezzled or otherwise wrongfully withheld. The evolution of this statutory remedy reveals a legislative intent to provide not merely a method of investigating the good faith of a person who detains assets, but to provide also a

remedy by which detained assets can be brought quickly into the course of administration.81

Sec. 643. Jurisdiction. 

As we have heretofore seen, the probate court has exclusive original jurisdiction of proceedings or actions to discover assets," 8,32 and, even though the person against whom the proceeding is instituted claims the title to the property by gift of the deceased or otherwise, the probate court has jurisdiction to try the title to such property incident to its general original jurisdiction over probate matters. But it has been held that a proceeding to discover assets which involves an issue only as to whether or not a transfer of the decedent was in fraud of creditors cannot be originally brought in the probate court.34 However, where a defendant is charged with wrongfully withholding personal property belonging to the estate of his wife and the same is in his possession, an action to recover possession of such property must be brought in the probate court." 

And the grant of power to a probate court in a proceeding for the discovery of assets of an estate grants all incidental authority necessary to make the principal grant effective.86

Sec. 646. 

Process. 

The statute provides that when the affidavit is filed the court may cite the person charged to appear before it and compel such appearance by attachment (Sec. 63). Such citation may be issued by the court or the clerk and served as other process.

Sec. 647. Trial. 

a. Preliminary examination of persons cited. 

When the party cited does not admit the allegations in the affidavit, the statute directs that he be examined under oath, after which other witnesses may be examined both for and against him 812

(Sec. 64). This provision of the statute was retained after the provisions were inserted authorizing the filing of written interrogatories and answers, and, as a step in the proceeding, serves no useful purpose. If the person initiating the proceeding desires to have such examination of the person charged conducted preliminary or auxiliary to the trial of the issues made by the interrogatories and answers, he may do so, but such proceeding would probably serve no useful purpose. 48 

b. Trial by jury. 

The statute provides that the issue upon the interrogatories and answers thereto shall be tried by a jury, or, if neither of the parties requires a jury, by the court in a summary manner. The statute authorizing trial by jury of the issues raised in the proceeding is said to be unlike those statutes governing similar proceedings in the administration of estates in other states.** c. Issues submitted.

In a trial of the issues, evidence as to whether the property was received as a gift from the deceased was held sufficient to take the case to the jury.45 Where the proceeding was against an executor to compel him to inventory and account for his own note to the testatrix, the issue was whether the executor was withholding the note, and the jury could not return a verdict against the executor for the amount of the note with interest. An instruction authorizing the jury to charge defendant with interest at the rate of six per cent, compounded annually, on a note charged to have been withheld by the defendant unlawfully, was erroneous. The issue to be determined is, whether or not the property is concealed, embezzled or wrongfully withheld, and the verdict or judgment determines the title of the property in issue.48

d. Evidence and burden of proof. 

A person claiming the property as a gift of the deceased has the burden of proof in such proceedings.49 If the proceeding is against a widow to discover assets of the husband's estate, she must show title to property superior to that of the estate, and how the property was acquired by her.50 If answers to the interrogatories make a prima facie case, the burden is on the defendants to establish the ownership they claim by proof that is clear, full, unequivocal and convincing.51 If a transfer by a deceased husband to his wife constitutes a gift, the wife must show that it was mutually understood between her and her husband that in making the transfer the husband intended to part with the title to the property, 52 and testimony of a conversation between the widow and the decedent cannot be admitted to determine the issue.52 

Sec. 648. Judgment. 

The statute provides that judgments shall be rendered according to the findings and for costs, and if the person against whom the charge is made is convicted, the court shall compel the delivery of the property detained by attachment of his person for contempt, and the court shall commit him to jail until he comply with the order of the court (Sec. 66). If the proceeding is against the administrator, and the finding is that he has concealed or withheld the property, the judgment should be that he inventory and account for the property unlawfully concealed.54 The provisions of the statute authorizing attachment, as for contempt for refusal to deliver assets, are not violative of the Constitution, prohibiting imprisonment for debt, but such judgment will not be upheld unless the provisions of

By virtue of this statutory authority, it has been held that an administrator may hire and board hands and buy food, if needed to preserve the property, and where such articles have been furnished on credit the person furnishing them may have a claim therefor allowed against the estate.58 An expenditure of money in operating a hotel leased by the decedent until a purchaser could be obtained for the furniture was held justified where it appeared that such a course resulted in the making of a more advantageous sale. And, where the deceased was a cotton factor and had an interest in cotton due to his advancements thereon, it was held that his interest was a valuable one and that his administrator was authorized to continue to exercise the agency powers of the deceased factor as far as necessary to protect his estate.60 Also, an executrix of a deceased building contractor was held to have discharged her official duties properly in carrying on the contract of the decedent with the owner and the materialmen until the next term of court, and this without obtaining an order of court therefor.81 But, even with the aid of an order of court, an administrator cannot perform functions in the execution of his duties that are not authorized by the statute, such as borrow money to complete an unfinished building and execute a trust deed on the premises to secure the payment of same, 62 or complete buildings commenced by the intestate in his lifetime, where the real estate on which the buildings were located descended to the heirs, who took charge of same. 63

Sec. 650. Continuance of Decedent's Business. 

There is no special statutory provision, other than those heretofore quoted (Secs. 102, 103), authorizing an executor or administrator to carry on the business in which his testate or intestate was engaged at the time of his death. However, testators sometimes direct that their executors continue their business after their death, and, even where there is no testamentary direction that business of the decedent be carried on by the executor, the executor or administrator may, in the interest of the estate, continue to operate the decedent's business. In fact, it has been held that, under an order entered by the court authorizing an administrator to sell merchandise at private sale, the administrator may, with the acquiescence of the court and the parties interested, continue the operation of the mercantile business of the decedent.65 But where an administratrix continued to operate the mercantile business of her deceased husband, it was held that she had no authority to bind the estate by purchasing and agreeing to pay for additional goods she bought in the continuance of such business.66 Nor does a surviving partner of a firm of bankers and brokers have power to bind the estate of the deceased partner by new contracts, unless expressly authorized so to do by the deceased, by will or contract. Where a testatrix directed her husband, as executor, to continue her business, and upon her death the probate court directed the husband to continue in charge of the business, it was held that a creditor who sold goods to the executor could recover the price of such goods against the executor personally after the business had become insolvent, where it appeared that the executor derived money from the business sufficient for the payment of the bill.88 Should the executor or administrator be directed to carry on the business of the deceased, in the management of same he is required to exercise such care and diligence as a 67 

Harms vs. Pohlman (App.), 297 S. W. 138. But the decision in this case was based largely on the fact that those interested in the estate acquiesced in the course taken by the administrator, and that the administrator acted with due care in the management of the estate, so that as between him and the distributees the administrator should not be charged with mismanagement. 66

Sec. 651. Representative May Lend Surplus Money. 

The statute provides that if, on the return of the inventory, or at any other time, it shall appear to the satisfaction of the court that there is a surplus of money in the hands of the executor or administrator that will not shortly be required for the expenses of administration or payment of debts, it shall have discretionary power to order him to lend out the money on such terms and for such time as may be deemed best (Sec. 104). But the representative has no authority to lend money belonging to the estate without an order authorizing him so to do, and if he does, he acts at his peril."¹ 

Thus, where an administrator invested the funds of the estate in bonds issued by a religious association and secured by a trust deed constituting a first lien on the church building, without the advice or direction of the court, it was held that he was not entitled to credit in his final settlement for the amount so invested.72

Sec. 652. Other Use of Money Belonging to Estate. 

One of the most important obligations attached to the trust of an executor or administrator is that of properly handling and accounting for the money coming into his hands and belonging to the estate. 

The executor or administrator holds the money belonging to the estate as trustee, and should not use same for any purpose not connected with the administration, unless authorized so to do by the probate court. Usually, the most convenient manner of handling money belonging to the estate is to deposit same in a bank, and, when it is so deposited, it should be placed in a separate account in the name of the administrator. Surety companies usually adopt the safe practice of not only having the administrator deposit the money in the bank in his name as administrator, but also requiring that, before he can draw any money out of the account, a representative of the company must countersign the checks which the administrator writes on the account. Arrangements for this practice are made with the bank where the money is deposited. This course not only makes for greater security for the surety but it also aids the administrator in keeping an exact account of the money deposited and paid out. The money belonging to the estate should not be co-mingled with the money personally belonging to the administrator, and such money should not be invested, lent, nor used, except by order of the probate court. 819

a. Deposits in banks or elsewhere.

The law does not require the administrator to keep the funds belonging to the estate on deposit in a bank. In fact, so long as the administrator accounts for the money in his hands in the manner required by law, it is no concern of the court or others interested whether or not it is kept by the administrator on deposit in a bank or elsewhere. Where an executor invested money of the estate in gold coin and the heirs consented thereto and ratified his actions, it was held that he was not chargeable for losses incurred by the investment. An administrator is not an insurer of the property or money in his hands,75 but is a trustee acting for the benefit of others, and is chargeable with the exercise of such care and skill as prudent men exercise in the management of their affairs. an administrator deposited funds of the estate in a bank of good standing in the community, he was held not responsible for a loss occurring by an unexpected failure of the bank, even though the deposit was in his individual name, it appearing that the bank had knowledge of the fact that the deposit consisted of funds belonging to the estate.76 But the rule is otherwise where the bank had no knowledge of the fact that the deposit consisted of estate funds." 

It has been held that the duties and liabilities of an individual administrator or executor in all material respects are the same as those of the public administrator.78 b. Mingling with own funds. Where The statute does not prohibit the use of funds of an estate by an administrator in his own business, but if an executor or administrator does use funds of the estate for his own private purposes, he is required by statute to pay interest thereon to the estate (Sec. 223). 

At each settlement the probate court is authorized to inquire into the use made of funds belonging to the estate, and compel an ac- "Ante, Sec. 631b; Williams vs. People's Bank of Springfield (App.), 257

Sec. 654. Public Sales of Other Personalty. 

The statute provides that if the perishable goods are not sufficient to pay the debts, the executor or administrator shall, in the same manner, sell other personal estate, until the debts and legacies are all paid; but specific legacies shall not be sold in any case, unless it becomes necessary for the payment of debts. (Sec. 113.) It has been held that where enough money comes into the executor's hands from all sources to pay the legal charges against the estate, neither the necessity nor right to sell the remaining portion of the corpus of the estate, or any part thereof, exists, except such part as may be perishable. The statute provides that, where a person dies leaving a widow or widower or other family, the court has power, if, in its opinion, it will not be prejudicial to creditors and will be advantageous to such widow, widowers or others entitled to distribution in the estate, to order that no more of the personal estate shall be sold than will be sufficient to pay the debts; but the court shall order that good and sufficient security be taken, that the property shall be forthcoming to answer the demand of any creditor or others concerned in the estate. (Sec. 125.) 89

The statute provides that in every public sale the executor or administrator shall employ a competent clerk, not interested nor of kin to any heir or devisee of the estate (Sec. 118). The clerk of the sale shall keep a true account of the sale made, make a list of sales, specifying each article sold, the price, and the name of the purchaser, and shall annex his affidavit to such list, stating that the same is a true account of the sales made by such executor or administrator at the time specified (Sec. 119). c. Conduct of sale.

The statutes make no further requirements as to how the sale shall be conducted, but it is customary for the administrator or executor to conduct such sales in the same manner as public sales are ordinarily conducted, using an auctioneer for the purpose of crying the sale, and in each instance selling each article of personal property to the person bidding the highest price therefor at the auction. The clerk must be present and follow each sale made, and prepare his sale bill thereof in the manner heretofore described. Since the statute requires the clerk of the sale to keep an account thereof and make a list of the sales, specifying each article sold, the price, and the name of the purchaser, it is necessary that each item of personal property be sold by itself in order for the clerk to prepare his sale bill in the manner required of him by law.

Sec. 656. Sale Bill and Use of Same. 

After the clerk prepares an account of the sale, ordinarily known as a sale bill, and attaches his affidavit thereto as required by the statute (Sec. 119), the administrator or executor must file such sale bill in the office of the clerk of the probate court, within thirty days after the sale; and this sale bill must be recorded by the clerk in like manner and with like effect as inventories and appraisements. (Sec. 120.) Such sale bills are not conclusive on the matters to 824

which they relate, but are prima facie evidence thereof.91 The clerk is required at every term of the court to examine all sale bills, as well as all inventories and appraisements, filed since the last term, to see if they have been made and filed according to law. In case he finds any delinquency on the part of an executor or administrator relative thereto, he is authorized to issue such citations as may be necessary to compel compliance with the law. (Sec. 121.)

Sec. 658. Sales of Property Bound by Liens. 

The statute provides that if any personal property shall be bound by the lien of an execution or executions, whether such execution or executions shall have been levied on or not, or shall be bound by the lien of an attachment, at the time of the death of the testator or intestate, the executor or administrator must nevertheless inventory and cause such property to be appraised separate from the other personal property, and report the same to the probate court. If the interest of the estate demands, the probate court may require such property to be redeemed or sold. (Sec. 122.) It has been held that this section refers merely to liens for ordinary debts, and does not exempt a widow from liability for a vendor's claim for the unpaid part of purchase price for personalty.96 A widow was not entitled to take personalty from a vendor's claim for the unpaid part of the price and claim exemption from such liability." If one whose property has been attached and sold by a sheriff dies, his adminis- "Ladd vs. Stephens, 147 Mo. 319, 48 S. W. 915. "Lazonby vs. Smithey, 150 Mo. A. 485, 131 S. W. 708. "Ibid. 827

trator or the attaching creditors may procure an order requiring the sheriff to pay the proceeds of such sale to the administrator." 

The statute provides that the proceeds of the sale of such personal property shall be applied, under the direction of the court: First, where there is but one execution or attachment, to the payment of such execution or attachment; and the residue, if any, shall be assets, to be administered according to law; second, where there is more than one execution or attachment, or both such execution and attachment, the liens whereof are of even date, to the payment of such executions and attachments; and the residue, if any, shall be assets, to be administered according to law; but if such proceeds shall not be sufficient to pay the whole, then in proportion to their respective amounts; third, when there is more than one execution or attachment, or both an execution and attachment, the liens whereof are of uneven dates, and such proceeds shall not be sufficient to pay the whole, to the payment thereof according to their priority of lien. (Sec. 123.)

The provisions of the statutes authorizing the redemption or sale of personal property bound by liens and providing for the application of the proceeds of the sale of such property, are not meant to deprive the widow, widower, or minor children of their benefit of any of the provisions of the statutes applicable to them, nor deprive the demands classed in the first and second subdivisions of Section 182 of their precedence over other demands against the estate of the deceased (Sec. 124).

Sec. 659. Sale of Personalty Not Required, When. 

The statute provides that in all cases where a person dies leaving a widow or widower or other family, the court is authorized, if, in its opinion, it will not be prejudicial to creditors and will be advantageous to such widow, widower, or others entitled to distribution in the estate, to order that no more of the personal estate be sold than will be sufficient to pay the debts; but the court shall order that good and sufficient security shall be taken that the property shall be forthcoming to answer the demand of creditors or others concerned in the estate. (Sec. 125.) The statute authorizes the reserva-

Sec. 660. Care and Management of Personalty Not Sold. 

Where the statute authorizes the reservation of personal property not necessary to be sold to pay debts, the executor or administrator shall make an inventory and appraisement thereof as in other cases, but he shall leave such personal property as is ordered not to be sold in possession of the widow or widower or family of the deceased, who shall use and enjoy the same until the court shall order such property to be administered (Sec. 126). Where property is about to be sold in the vacation of the court, the judge thereof shall have power, upon the petition of the executor or administrator, or any other person interested in the estate, to order the suspension of such sale until the next session of the court (Sec. 127). B. REAL ESTATE 1. Right to Purchase, Lease, Control, Mortgage and Redeem. 

Sec. 661. Administrator May Purchase for Estate. 

The executor or administrator may, when authorized by order of court, purchase real estate at a foreclosure sale of a mortgage, deed of trust, vendor's lien, or other lien held by the decedent as security for the payment of any note, bond, account or other indebtedness belonging to the estate, at a price not exceeding the amount of the debt due the estate. Title to real estate purchased at such foreclosure sale vests in the executor or administrator in trust for the benefit of the creditors or heirs who would have been entitled to the money if such real estate had been redeemed. If the probate court is satisfied that the widow has received the articles or money which she is specially authorized by statute to receive (Secs. 108, 109, 110), and that such real estate will not be needed to pay the debts of the deceased, it must in such order require the executor or administrator to have the deed made to and in the name of the heirs or devisees of the deceased. (Sec. 95.) But if the administrator should purchase mortgaged real estate at a foreclosure sale and pay the purchase price out of the funds of the estate and take title in his own name, he will be deemed to hold same as trustee for those entitled to the estate.³ 

And, under the general rule that when a trustee purchases property with trust funds and takes the title in his own name, he holds same for the beneficiaries of the trust, the land thus acquired by an administrator at a foreclosure sale and paid for with estate funds may be followed in favor of the persons not named in the deed, in proportion to the amount of the interest of each. trator who purchases at a foreclosure sale and takes property in his own name and later dies, an heir of the estate for which the property was purchased may testify as to declarations of the deceased administrator while he was in possession of the land, such declarations being in effect admissions in disparagement of title and competent against him and his widow who claims under him." Where a mortgagor gave two notes, each maturing on a different date, and one mortgage to secure both notes, and the trustee in such mortgage foreclosed same at the request of the owner and holder of the first of such notes to mature, and at such foreclosure sale an administrator of the decedent who held the second note becoming due and secured by such mortgage took no steps to prevent the sale or to require the foreclosure to satisfy both notes, it was held that such administrator could not be heard to say that the sale was one to satisfy both notes and that the note held by him was entitled to priority in the disposition of the proceeds of the sale. Even without the authority of the special statute authorizing the administrator to purchase lands covered by a mortgage belonging to the estate at a foreclosure sale of such mortgage, it was held that where an administrator bought mortgaged property in the interest of the estate there was nothing in the policy of the law prohibiting him from conveying it, and a deed by the administrator conveying the property for the purpose of paying the debts of the intestate was upheld. The court may, upon its own initiative or in response to a petition of the administrator or executor, make the order authorizing the purchase at foreclosure sale. If the administrator or executor applies for the order, the following form may be used and changed to suit the circumstances of the particular case:

Sec. 662. Disposition of Real Estate Purchased for Estate. 

If, at a foreclosure sale under a deed of trust held by the estate, an administrator purchases the real estate and takes a deed to same in the name of the heirs, after an order by the court that same is not needed for satisfying the statutory allowances to the widow or to pay off the debts, such real estate passes to the heirs, and it is not necessary for the administrator to have any further connection with it. But if the real estate purchased at such foreclosure sale is required for the statutory allowances of the widow or to pay the 833

debts, the statute provides that same must be held by the executor or administrator as assets and administered and accounted for as such, and that it may be leased or sold for the payment of debts in the same manner as any real estate of which the deceased person died seized. If such real estate is leased or sold for the payment of debts, it must be so leased or sold upon the order of the probate court and upon the petition filed as is or may be provided for by law in other cases. (Sec. 96.) Even though such real estate may have been bought before the passing of the statute authorizing it, and for a different purpose from that expressed in the statute, if it is paid for by the administrator with funds of the estate it must be sold and accounted for as a part of the process of administration." 

Sec. 663. Administrator May Lease Real Estate. 

8 The statute forbids that an executor or administrator rent or control real estate of the deceased unless the probate court, having jurisdiction, is satisfied that it is necessary to rent same for the payment of debts. But if the court finds that it is necessary to rent the real estate for the payment of debts, an order may be entered of record requiring the executor or administrator to take possession of and rent the same for a period not exceeding one year. At the same time, the court must order the executor or administrator to give bond, to be approved by the court, in double the amount of money that may come into the hands of the administrator under such order. After such order is made, the executor or administrator may prosecute and maintain any action for the recovery of such real estate in the same manner and with like effect as the testator or intestate might have done in his lifetime. 13 In order for an executor or administrator to receive for the estate the benefits derived from an order requiring him to take possession of and rent the premises for the payment of debts, it is first necessary that he acquire possession, and if possession is withheld he may prosecute and maintain ejectment or such other action for possession as the owner might have done in his lifetime (Sec. 130). Sec. 665. Representative May Take Charge of and Manage Real Estate. 

Whenever letters of administration or letters testamentary shall have been granted on an estate and it shall appear to the court or judge in vacation that the decedent died possessed of real estate in the State, and his heirs or legatees have failed to take charge of same, or the identity or whereabouts of such heirs or legatees are unknown, then the court or judge in vacation may, on its or his own motion or that of any party interested, direct the administrator or executor in charge of said estate to take charge of and manage the real estate, until such time as such heirs or legatees shall appear and petition the court to turn over the management of said real estate to them, or until the same shall escheat to the State as is provided by the "escheat act" (Sec. 131). Under this statutory power, a probate court may order an administrator to take control of real estate, notwithstanding the fact that an action is pending to determine right of possession in an ejectment action.24 And ejectment cannot be maintained against an administrator who, under a valid order of the probate court, made under such statutory authority, took control of his decedent's real estate.25 22

Sec. 666. Distinction Between Possession for Lease and to Control and Manage. 

There is no conflict between the statute providing that the administrator may lease the premises for the payment of debts (Sec. 130) and that providing for the administrator to take charge of and manage the real estate when it is neglected or in need of care and attention which it is not receiving from the heirs (Sec. 131). Each of these statutes was designed to serve separate, specific purposes. The purpose of the first was to subject the real estate to the right of the representative to collect rent and apply same on the debts. The purpose of the other was to place the responsibility of controlling and managing real estate needing care and attention which it is not re- 

Infra, Sec. 671. 26 839

ceiving, because of neglect or absence of the heirs, on the representative in charge of the estate.27 

Sec. 667. Administrator May Repair Improvements on Real 

Estate.

The statute provides that when any house, outbuilding, fences, or other improvements on the real estate require repairs, the court may, on the application of any person interested, order the executor or administrator to cause the necessary repairs to be made, whenever such repairs can be done without prejudice to the creditors (Sec. 

132). If the administrator or executor is a proper husbandman and a careful trustee, he will see that the court's attention is called to the fact that improvements on real estate in his hands under order of court need repairs, at any time such repairs should be made. Consequently, improvements on real estate in his hands needing repairs should be authorized upon his application, although the heirs or any person interested may apply for an order directing that such repairs. be made. Such an order can only be made with reference to real estate in the hands of the administrator under authority granted by 

Section 130.28 And the administrator cannot make such repairs without an order of the court.2 29 If he does, he cannot be allowed credit in his settlement for sums spent for repairs. 30 Under the authority granted by the statute (Sec. 132), an administrator cannot erect new buildings on the premises of the deceased.³¹

Sec. 669. Redemption by Administrator of Mortgaged Property. 

The statute provides that, if any person die leaving land encumbered by mortgage or deed of trust, or any lien whatever, or owning any equity of redemption, or leaving mortgaged or pledged any personal property, and not having devised the same or provided for redemption thereof by will, the court shall have power, if, in its judgment, it will promote the interest of the estate and not be prejudicial to the creditors, to order the executor or administrator to redeem the same out of the personal assets of the estate, or to order the sale of other real estate to redeem such land or personal property so encumbered, and also to order the executor or administrator to mortgage or pledge any personal property of the estate in his hands for the purpose of raising and providing the money with which to redeem said premises so encumbered (Sec. 139). If such redemption would injure the estate or creditors, or there would not be assets to redeem such estate after payment of the debts, the court shall order all the right, title and interest of the estate to such property to be sold at public or private sale. Before any sale of real estate shall be made by any executor or administrator under the provisions of Sections 139 and 140, notice of the application for an order directing the sale of such real estate shall be given to all parties interested therein, in the same manner and for the same time as is now provided in case of an application to sell lands of a decedent to pay debts or legacies of such deceased person (Sec. 140). But where a testator placed an encumbrance against his real estate after making his will in which he specifically devised same, it was held that the executor could not pay the amount of the encumbrance from the personal assets of the 843

testator's estate, since the testator expressed no intention in his will that same be done.85 The provision of the statute requiring notice in such cases was first added in 1919 (Laws 1919, p. 101), following a decision by the Supreme Court that notice was necessary.36 

Sec. 670. Foreclosure Sale Under Mortgage, Stayed When. 

The statute provides that, if any person owning real estate on which there is an outstanding deed of trust or mortgage of real estate, or, having pledged or mortgaged personal property with power of sale, shall die, no sale shall take place under said deed of trust or mortgage conveying real estate within nine months after the death of such person, and no sale shall take place of said personal property so mortgaged or pledged within four months after the death of such person (Sec. 141). This statutory provision is in line with other requirements of our statutes regarding the administration of estates, indicating the control and care that the administrator should take of the real estate even when it is mortgaged.37 

Sec. 671. Notice to Persons Interested. 

The executor or administrator cannot take charge of real estate or exercise dominion over same for any purpose except as authorized by statute, and if he is ordered by the court to exercise any authority over real estate not specifically designated by the statute, his acts are invalid and such orders are void.38 The real estate belongs to the heirs and devisees, subject to the lien of creditors, and acts of the administrator exercising rights in real estate owned by the deceased should probably never be committed, even under order of the probate court, until notice has been previously given to those interested therein. Certainly, where the statute requires that notice be given, such as where real estate is sold for the payment of debts (Sec. 144), 35 Gates vs. Rice, 8 S. W. (2d) 614, 320 Mo. 580; Hannibal Trust Co. vs. Elzea, 315 Mo. 485, 286 S. W. 371. 

36 State ex rel. Deems vs. Holtcamp, 245 Mo. 655, 151 S. W. 153. 

St. Louis Natl. Bank vs. Field, 156 Mo. 306, 56 S. W. 1095. 

38 Langston vs. Canterbury, 173 Mo. 122, 73 S. W. 151. 844

or where the decedent's interests in real estate purchased are relin quished (Sec. 138), the giving of notice is indispensable. And because of the character of rights that are involved in any proceeding by which an administrator exercises any control over the real estate of a decedent, such as proceedings to take charge of, lease, purchase or redeem, the safest course would be for the court to make a preliminary order requiring that the administrator give due notice of the proceedings. The publication of notice of the grant of letters is notice to all persons interested of the death of the decedent and the issuance of letters on his estate, from which it necessarily follows that the real estate of decedent is in the custody of the law and subject to whatever control or dominion that may be asserted by the administrator under order of court and as authorized by statute. 

Whether such notice is such due process as would authorize the probate court to order that the administrator take charge of, lease, purchase or redeem the real estate of the deceased, has apparently never been passed on by the courts of this State. Since there has been no direct adjudication of the question in this State, and since the Supreme Court of Missouri has announced principles which indicate a decided disposition to hold that notice is necessary, it would appear best that, before an administrator takes any steps looking toward an * State ex rel. Deems vs. Holtcamp, 245 Mo. 655, 151 S. W. 153. Our organic law ordains that, 'no person shall be deprived of . . . property without due process of law.' 2. Decedent's Contracts to Purchase or Convey. 

Sec. 672. When Administrator May Complete Payment of Pur chase Price.

If any person die having purchased real estate and not having completed the payment nor devised such estate, nor provided for the payment by will, and the completion of such payment would be beneficial to the estate and not injurious to creditors, the executor or administrator, by order of the court, may complete such payment out of the assets in his hands, and such estate shall be disposed of as other real estate (Sec. 134). If the payment due on a contract to purchase is made by the administrator, the deed to the real estate should be made to the heirs of the decedent.41 In order for a person

Sec. 673. Sale of Interest Acquired by Contract.

The statute provides that, if the court believe that, after the payment of debts, there will not be sufficient assets to pay for real estate purchased by the decedent and not paid for in full and not devised by will, and where the will does not provide for the payment of the "Chapman vs. Merritt, 45 Mo. A. 179. 847

balance of such purchase price, the court may order the executor or administrator to sell all the right, title and interest of the deceased therein (Sec. 135). Where no appeal was taken by a residuary legatee of an estate from orders of the probate court allowing the payment of a deed of trust, an assignment of error in allowing payment on a later settlement was held properly overruled.48 A sale of such interest must be ordered only upon petition and notice and in conformity with the statutes governing sales of real estate to pay debts (Sec. 138). For forms to be used in the making of such sales, reference is made to the forms in the proceedings for sales of real estate to pay debts.

Sec. 674. Relinquishment of Interest Acquired by Uncompleted Contract to Purchase. 

If real estate has been purchased by a decedent prior to his death under a contract that is binding on him, but payment of the purchase price thereof has not been completed, if such real estate has been purchased from individuals, the court may, if considered advantageous to the estate, order the same to be relinquished to such individuals on the best terms that can be agreed upon (Sec. 136). 

If such real estate shall have been purchased from any officer authorized by law to sell school lands, the court may, in its discretion, order the same to be relinquished; and in such cases the officer shall be authorized to accept such relinquishment and surrender the obligation of the deceased. (Sec. 137.) The statute provides that the executor or administrator shall be competent to make such relinquishment by deed or to convey to the purchaser all the right, title and interest the testator or intestate had in and to such real estate at the time of his death. But before such relinquishment or sale can be made, notice must be given in the same manner as is required in proceedings to sell real estate to pay debts, and an appraisement must be made in the same manner. (Sec. 138.) If such relinquishment is made under order of court where notice is not given, the proceeding is void. Nor can an order of relinquishment be made 44 "Roloson vs. Riggs, 274 Mo. 522, 203 S. W. 973. "State ex rel. Deems vs. Holtcamp, 245 Mo. 655, 151 S. W. 153. 848

binding on real estate located in another state.45 Forms used in proceedings to sell real estate to pay debts should be used as a basis for the forms required for proceedings for the relinquishment of the interest in real estate acquired by a decedent under a contract where the purchase has not been completed. 

Sec. 675. Vendee May Compel Specific Performance. 

Specific performance is an equitable doctrine having its origin in the common law.46 Probate courts have no equity powers but are authorized to employ equitable principles, and the statutes authorize probate courts to employ the doctrine of specific performance as it applies to contracts to convey real estate made by a decedent in his lifetime (Secs. 169-177). The statute provides that if a testator or intestate shall have entered into a contract in writing for the conveyance of real estate, and shall not have executed the same in his lifetime, nor given power by will to execute the same, the probate court may order the administrator or executor to execute a deed for such real estate (Sec. 169). For the remedy to be available, the contract of the decedent must have been made in writing and must have been signed by him.48 If the contract is made by a minor, who, upon attaining his majority, ratifies the same, it may be specifically enforced against his estate. 49 If an order of specific performance is made, infants, persons of unsound mind, and persons absent from the United States, are authorized by statute, at any time during one year after their disabilities are removed, to appear and file their petition in the circuit court to set aside the order, for fraud or otherwise (Sec. 172). Married women were included among those to whom there was a saving of rights because of disability prior to 1919 (Laws, 1919, p. 102). The same act changed the time within which the action could be brought after disability is removed, from five years to one year. "State Bank of Seneca vs. Morrison, 200 Mo. A. 169, 204 S. Sec. 676. Proceedings for Specific Performance in Probate Court. 

a. Petition and affidavit.

Proceedings for specific performance in the probate court are initiated by the filing of a petition on the part of the vendee in the contract, setting forth the facts and praying that an order be made that the executor or administrator execute specifically the contract made by the decedent with the vendee, by executing to the petitioner a deed for the real estate (Sec. 169). The vendee must annex to his petition an affidavit to the truth thereof and stating that no part of such contract has been satisfied, except as stated in the petition (Sec. 

170). If such affidavit is not annexed to the petition, the probate court is without jurisdiction to grant relief.50 b. Notice.

The statute provides that a notice of such application and a copy of the petition shall be served on the executor or administrator, and also all the heirs or devisees residing, or who may be served, in the county, twenty days before the first day of the term at which it is to be made (Sec. 171). The administrator, as well as the heirs and devisees, must be served.51 All others interested should probably also be notified.52 Certainly, heirs who are nonresidents of the county should have the right to such notice as is ordinarily given persons in like position in other proceedings. The statute makes no provisions for serving them with notice. c. Hearing and order. The statute provides that if the court, after hearing all parties, believes that specific execution of such contract should be made, it shall make an order requiring the executor or administrator to execute such contract specifically (Sec. 172). It is from the effects of such order that the statute saves to infants, persons of unsound mind, and persons absent from the United States, the right to appear within a year following the removal of their disabilities and petition the court to set aside such order. All parties must be heard. 

50 Baldwin vs. Whitcomb, 71 Mo. 651. 52 153. 

McQuitty vs. Wilhite, 218 Mo. 586, 117 S. W. 730. 

Ante, Sec. 671; State ex rel. Deems vs. Holtcamp, 245 Mo. 655, 151 S. W. 850

d. Deed and its effect.

In compliance with the order, the executor must execute and deliver to the petitioner a deed and acknowledge it in open court, conveying the estate according to the order. The deed must contain provisions expressing the saving to infants, persons of unsound mind, and persons absent from the United States. The deed must also state that such persons have the right to petition the court to set aside such order within a year after their disabilities are removed. 

It must also state the date of the order and the court at which it was made. (Sec. 173.) It has been held that if the deed is not acknowledged in open court, as required by statute, it is void.58 The administrator's deed made in compliance with the order of the court is as effectual as if it had been executed by the deceased (Sec. 174). 

It serves to convey only the title held by the deceased.54

Sec. 677. Proceeding May Originate in or Be Removed to Circuit 

Court.

The party entitled to specific performance of a written contract to convey real estate by a person who dies after the contract is exe- 854

cuted, but before the conveyance is made, may file his petition for specific performance in the circuit court of the county in the first instance (Sec. 175). The enforcement of specific performance by a proceeding in the circuit court in the first instance has been suggested as more satisfactory than that by a proceeding in the probate court.55 If the proceeding is first brought in the probate court in the manner heretofore described, the executor or administrator, widow, or any heir or devisee of the estate, may appear and allege that he is unwilling to have the same tried in the probate court, whereupon the probate court is required to certify the proceeding to the circuit court (Sec. 175). Where the proceeding is either certified to the circuit court from the probate court or filed in the circuit court in the first instance, the circuit court shall proceed according to law. 

If it appears to the circuit court that specific execution ought to be made, that court shall give judgment for that purpose in the same manner and with the same reservation as required in cases where such orders are made by the probate court. (Sec. 176.) 

Sec. 678. Proceedings When Administrator Holds Contract for 

Conveyance.

The statute authorizes the enforcement of specific performance only by the surviving party to the contract (Sec. 169). The same remedy is not given the executor or administrator. The statute does provide that if any executor or administrator holds a bond or any other instrument of writing of a testator or intestate for the conveyance of any real estate not completed within the lifetime of such testator or intestate, and for the conveyance of which no power has been given by will or otherwise, the executor or administrator must proceed against his co-executor or co-administrator in the same manner as prescribed in other cases. If there is no such co-executor or co-administrator, he must file his petition setting out the facts, whereupon the court shall appoint some suitable person to appear and manage the defense on the part of those interested. Such person shall have all the powers and perform the same duties as are required of executors or administrators in such cases. (Sec. 177.) "Kelley (5th Ed.), 349, 352. 855

3. Sales Under Power in Will. 

Sec. 679.

Direction of Testator Controls. 

The statute provides that the sale and conveyance of real estate under a will shall be made by the acting executor or administrator with the will annexed, if no other person is appointed by the will for that purpose, or if the person appointed by the will fails or refuses to perform the trust (Sec. 133). A testatrix when making her will was presumed to have known the statute respecting the execution of a testamentary power of sale by the acting administrator.56 

The court will enforce the intention expressed by the testator respecting the sale of real estate as expressed in the will, and will not determine whether he chose wisely or unwisely; 57 and if the testator directs that his real estate be sold, without appointing a person to make the sale, it is generally held that the power of sale inheres in the office of the executor.58 Where the testator directed that his realty be sold as soon as convenient and a fair price could be realized, it was held that the executor should exercise the power to sell within a reasonable time.50 And where a testator directed that, "should my wife prefer to live near a town in this or any other state, the land may be sold," and made the wife executrix, it was held that the testator thereby gave his wife power of sale. 60 All rules for the construction of wills and for carrying them into effect are designed to ascertain and give effect to the testator's intention.61 Where a testator directed that his real estate be sold by his executors, it was held that a deed by one executor was ineffective, because the executors must act jointly.62 If an executor, when a conversion of a testator's real estate into personalty is effected, fails to sell the property converted, it is within the power of the court to order him to make the sale to accomplish the purposes of the will.63

Sec. 680. The Doctrine of Conversion and Right of Reconversion. 

66 Ordinarily, an executor or administrator cannot sell realty to pay debts without an order of the probate court, but if the will directs the executor to sell real estate, such direction controls, and if a testator confers discretionary power of sale by the terms of his will it has been held that a personal trust is thereby created in the executor, independent of the official character of the executor.65 But, instead of directing the sale of real estate for the purpose of paying debts, testators sometimes provide for the sale of lands for the purposes of distribution. A provision directing the executor to sell and convey real estate for the purpose of making distribution to the beneficiaries operates as an equitable conversion of the real estate into personalty. Equitable conversion depends upon the intent of the testator as expressed by the will. In order to effect an equitable conversion, there must be either, first, a positive direction to sell; or, second, an absolute necessity to sell in order to execute the will; or, third, such a blending of real and personal estate by the testator in his will as to manifest his intention expressly or impliedly to create from blended realty and personalty a fund for the purpose of distribution.68 Equitable conversion results where the will develops a necessity to sell real estate in order to distribute pecuniary legacies which are charged upon the real estate. An equitable conversion is said to take effect immediately upon the death of the testator.70

Along with the doctrine of equitable conversion has developed the doctrine of reconversion, under which the devisees under the will elect whether they will take the land rather than the proceeds arising from the sale thereof. This doctrine is based upon the principle that, the conversion being for the sole benefit of the persons to whom the proceeds of the sale of the land are to be paid, such persons are in fact the owners of the property and may, being sui juris, contract concerning it as they may deem proper." Where beneficiaries of a will elect to take land instead of the proceeds, under the principle of reconversion, the executor cannot exercise authority under the will to sell the real estate. 72 A reconversion, however, does not occur unless the election to reconvert is assented to by all the beneficiaries and embraces all their interests.78 Where all the beneficiaries signed an agreement that land be sold at private sale instead of at public auction, as the testator directed, it was held that they elected to take the property as real estate, and partition thereof was permissible." 

Sec. 681. Character of Powers Granted by Will. 

a. Power in the nature of a personal trust. 

Powers of sale conferred by wills have been classified by the courts of this State in two divisions. In the first classification, the power conferred is coupled with a discretion to sell or not sell, as the donee of the power sees fit. Such power is said to create a trust that is personal and independent of the official character of the donee as executor, and may be exercised by him even though he does not qualify as executor. The power survives the final administration of the estate and continues until the purposes of the trust have been accomplished, or until the donee of the power has had a reasonable "Ganahl vs. Ganahl, 19 S. The donee of such power is a fiduciary agent, subject to the control of a court of equity, and such court has the power, upon a proper showing, to terminate the trust, discharge the trustee, and distribute the estate. Upon the death of the person named to exercise the power, a court of equity will appoint a new trustee and clothe him with authority adequate to the duties to be discharged.75 Where a will directed the executor, upon sale of the real estate, to lend one-third of the proceeds thereof on real estate security at the highest obtainable rate of interest and pay the interest annually to the testator's wife during her life, it was held that the trust enjoined upon the executor was a personal trust, calling for discretion, ability and business judgment, and that upon the death of the trustee named the trust should have careful supervision within the powers that may be exercised by a court of equity over trust estates. Where a trust fails because the named trustee cannot administer the trust, a court of equity will appoint a new trustee." A provision in a will directing an executor, "without obtaining an order of court therefor, from time to time, to sell all real estate I may own at my death," was held to contemplate a sale by the executor and a closing of the estate within the period allowed by law for administration, and where the executor proceeded under such will as a trustee rather than as executor, and incurred court costs for a period of thirteen years after final settlement should have been made, it was held that he exceeded his powers and was grossly negligent in handling the estate. 78 b. In such cases, the proceeds of the sale become personal assets of the estate and must be properly administered and distributed as a part of the process of administration.80 This character of power is that conferred by the statute (Sec. 133). If the sale is not made by the named executor, the power inheres in the office, and may be exercised by an administrator de bonis non with the will annexed.81 Where a will provided for sale of land and distribution of the proceeds at the widow's death, it was held that such will imposed an executorial duty which could be properly exercised by an administrator with the will annexed, under the direction and with the approval of the probate court.82 And if the remainder of the estate has been fully administered and final settlement made by the original executor before the happening of an event at which the executor was required by the terms of the will to sell the real estate, it is generally held that an administrator de bonis non with the will annexed may be appointed to carry out the provisions of the will and sell the land, for the reason that such sale is unfinished business connected with the administration, which cannot be attended to until the happening of the contingency named in the will.88 

Sec. 682. Proceedings for Sale Under Will. 

There are no special statutory provisions governing procedure for the sale of real estate under power contained in wills. The manner of conducting such sales depends upon the directions contained in the will. If, by the will, the executor is directed to sell the real es- 79

Where a testator directed his executrix to sell his land as soon as same could be done without sacrifice, and the executrix sold the land to her son at the highest price she had reason to think could be obtained for it without putting it on the market, it was held that she exercised proper prudence in managing the estate and making the sale.87 When real estate is sold under power conferred by will, the proceeds become a trust fund in the executor's hands for payment to the legatees.88 If the will directs that the executor sell without an order of the court, it is not necessary for the executor to obtain such order before making the sale, but if the will provides that the sale be made under order of court, such order must be obtained before the sale is made.89 A plain petition addressed to the court, setting out the facts and referring to the provisions of the will, is all that is necessary. An order made following generally the facts set out in the petition and directing the sale is sufficient. The executor's deed should make proper reference to the power expressed in the will, and if the order of court is first obtained, the deed should also refer to such order and show a compliance with the terms of the will and the order of court. In other respects, it should follow generally the regular forms of deeds of conveyance.

4. Sales for Payment of Debts and Legacies. 

Sec. 683. History, Nature and Purpose of Proceeding. 

Sales of real estate for the payment of debts of a decedent are authorized and governed solely by statute (Secs. 142-168). At common law, unless a decedent specially charged his real estate with debts in his lifetime, his real estate could not be sold to satisfy claims of creditors as a part of the process of administration.90 The common law did not recognize the right or provide the remedy by which a personal representative of a decedent could sell real estate for the payment of debts held by creditors.1 This common law rule grew out of the peculiar manner in which real estate was held under the feudal system, but it completely gave way, under the growth of commerce and trade, to a system for safer security for a creditor against a debtor whose death intervened before his debts were paid.92 From the beginning in this country the common law rule that a decedent's real estate could not be sold for the payment of his debts has been looked upon with disfavor, and in most, if not all, of the states, statutes have been passed authorizing an executor or administrator, under order of court, to sell real estate of a decedent for the purpose of paying his debts or legacies. 98 The sale of the real estate of a decedent for the payment of his debts and legacies has always been authorized by statute in Missouri. By virtue of this statuory authority, conferred upon the personal representative, real estate of an intestate may not only be converted into personalty and the proceeds used to satisfy the claims of the creditors, but creditors are, as well, 00 Ante, Sec. 621; 11 RCL 118, 119. 91

virtually lienholders, for their claims against lands of a decedent are considered liens.95 Sales by administrators for the payment of debts are, therefore, in the nature of proceedings to enforce liens, the administrator or executor in such proceedings standing in a position similar to that of a trustee in the foreclosure of a mortgage lien." 

The right of the creditors to have the decedent's land sold for the payment of debts cannot be defeated by a passive, indifferent, or obstinate executor or administrator. The statute authorizes the creditor himself to set in motion the process by which sales of real estate may be made for the payment of debts (Sec. 146). Such sales may only be made by order (Sec. 145) and subject to approval of (Sec. 164) the probate court. Sales of real estate to pay debts are judicial sales.97 In such sales the officers charged with the responsibility for conducting same must not only enforce the rights of creditors to collect their debts out of the real estate but they must also safeguard the rights of the heirs who are owners of the real estate, or the proceeds thereof after the claims of the creditors have been paid.⁹8 

Sec. 684.

Jurisdiction. 

By provision of the Constitution, probate courts are vested with original jurisdiction of proceedings for the sale of real estate of decedents for the payment of debts (Const., Art. 6, Sec. 34). The general rule is that exclusive jurisdiction of such proceedings is vested in the probate courts, subject to the right of appeal.99 The 95
