same rule applies to the sale of a homestead of a husband for the payment of debts contracted during his lifetime.100 Thus, original proceedings under the statute for the sale of real estate of a decedent to pay his debts must always be brought in the probate court, as the circuit court is without jurisdiction to entertain such proceedings.¹ 

But until proceedings for the sale of real estate under the statutes are instituted, or until the representative of the decedent exercises some statutory control over the real estate, same belongs to the heirs, who may maintain an action to partition the real estate in circuit court, even while the estate is in the process of administration in the probate court.2 Partition proceedings of a decedent's real estate in circuit court, before the final settlement of his estate in the probate court, are authorized by statute, but distribution of the proceeds of partition sales in such proceedings cannot be made until claims against the estate have been fully discharged (Sec. 1558). And if a partition suit is filed in the circuit court, that court thereby acquires jurisdiction of the res and thereafter the probate court cannot entertain a petition for the sale of the same real estate for the payment of debts. Where a suit was instituted in which it was sought to construe a will and determine conflicting claims regarding the rights and title of the executor and other interested parties, and where the defendants in effect asked for partition, it was held that the proceeding was not one for the payment of debts but was a partition suit, and that jurisdiction of same was in the circuit court and not in the probate court. And, after a suit has been brought to contest a will, the executor has no authority to present an application for an order of sale of real estate, and a sale and deed made in a proceeding by him pass no title."

Sec. 685. Parties Authorized to Institute Proceedings. 

The statute authorizing the sale of lands for the payment of debts and legacies authorizes the executor or administrator to start the proceedings by filing a petition in the probate court stating the facts (Sec. 142). But if an administrator begins proceedings to sell real estate and thereafter dies or is removed, his successor may complete the sale. If the executor or administrator does not make application for sale to pay debts, any creditor or other person interested in the estate may make the application, giving twenty days' notice to the executor or administrator. (Sec. 146.) It has been held that one who purchased a judgment against an estate has a right to apply for an order of sale to pay debts, and the right to appeal from the action of the court refusing to make the order. But one who purchased an interest in land from one of the heirs of the decedent is not entitled to make application for a sale of real estate to pay debts, and a sale based on such application is void. 

Sec. 686. Debts for Which Real Estate May Be Sold.

The statute authorizes a sale of real estate of a decedent where his personal estate is insufficient to pay his debts and legacies (Sec. 

142). If there are no debts, the administrator can neither create debts which may be made the basis for the sale, nor ask for a sale for the purpose of paying the costs of administration. The debts for the payment of which a sale may be made must have existed at the time of the death of the decedent.10 The proceeding cannot be maintained for the payment of debts incurred in prosecuting or defending suits concerning the title to lands after the death of the owner;¹¹ nor can the administrator have real estate sold to pay a 11

But the statute authorizes the sale of real estate to pay debts in the nature of judgments which are liens upon the real estate of the deceased (Sec. 182) or mortgage liens (Secs. 182, 189). Sec. 687. Petition for Sale. 

a. Unnecessary, when.

If it appears to the court at the time a settlement is made by the executor or administrator that the personal estate is not sufficient to pay the debts and legacies, the court may order the real estate sold to pay debts, upon its own motion and without the filing of a petition (Sec. 166). And it is generally held that where the proceeding is upon the court's motion the filing of a petition is not necessary.16

Where the proceeding is thus initiated, the settlement stands in lieu of and furnishes the requisite information which a petition, accounts, lists and inventories would otherwise reveal.¹7 b. When filing of is jurisdictional.

In other cases where proceedings are instituted for the sale of real estate to pay debts, they are initiated by the filing of a petition (Secs. 

142, 146, 148, 152, 157). In all of such instances the filing of the petition is held to be jurisdictional.18 The act of filing a petition for an order to sell the real estate to pay debts gives the court jurisdiction of the res.19 If no petition is filed, an order to sell and a sale under such order are void.20 c. Form and allegations of. 

The statute does not prescribe any form for the petition. It only requires that the petitioner state the facts (Sec. 142). Whether the petition is in proper form or sets forth sufficient facts or is accompanied by the proper exhibits, are questions which the court must determine in the exercise of its jurisdiction.21 The allegation of facts showing that the personal estate of the decedent is insufficient to pay his debts and legacies, which is the statutory ground for invoking the remedy (Sec. 142), should appear in the petition, although a failure to state such facts in direct terms, where the facts were undisputed and could be inferred from other allegations in the petition, has been held not to void the proceedings. 22 And proceedings have been upheld where the petition was lost, the contents thereof having been supplied by oral testimony of the attorney who drafted the petition. 23 As against a collateral attack where an order of sale was made, it will be presumed, in the absence of a petition, that everything necessary to confer jurisdiction on the court to make the order, including a finding by the court that the personal assets

This real estate should be particularly described in the petition. A deed based on a sale where neither the petition nor order described the land has been held void.26 But where a petition did not contain a description of the land but such description was set out in an exhibit attached thereto, the proceeding was upheld.27 

d. Prayer. 

The statute requires that the petition shall contain a prayer for the sale of the real estate, or so much thereof as will pay the debts and legacies of the deceased (Sec. 142). The order made in response to the petition must designate whether the sale should be public or private (Sec. 145). Since the order is made in response to the petition, and since the notice given directs attention to the petition, it is always best that the petitioner state in the prayer of the petition whether the land should be sold at public or private sale. 

e. Exhibits. 

The petition must be accompanied by a true account of the administration, a list of debts due to and by the deceased and remaining unpaid, and an inventory of the real estate and of the remaining personal estate, with its appraised value, and all the other assets in the hands of the administrator (Sec. 143). The purpose of these exhibits is to give evidence to the court of the necessity or propriety of the action sought by the petition. 28 Jurisdiction of the court is not defeated because of a failure to file such exhibits with the petition, 24 Harter vs. Petty, 266 Mo. 296, 181 S. The petition and exhibits must be verified by the executor or administrator (Sec. 143). There is no statute of limitations prescribing the time within which an administrator must file a petition for the sale of real estate to pay debts. The courts say that such petition must be filed within a reasonable time.35 The question as to what is a reasonable time depends upon the circumstances and the character of the proceeding in which the question arises. Where the proceeding was delayed eleven years after the administration began, and where the objection was raised in a collateral attack, the delay was held not unreasonable. But where there was a delay for thirteen years and the point was raised in a direct attack by injunction to stop the proceeding, the delay was held unreasonable.38 Likewise, a delay of ten years was held unreasonable where the excuse was that the administrator thought he had sold all the land but later found he had omitted part of it by mistake and then delayed the institution of proceedings to sell two years after the mistake was discovered.39 But where there was no sale for the property because of the homestead claim for the life of the widow and until the minor children reached the age of eighteen years, a delay in making application to sell for a period of eighteen years was held not unreasonable.40

Sec. 688. Service of Notice Indispensable. 

O. L. Cook.

The giving of reasonable notice of an intention by an administrator to assert any right in or control over real estate is a necessary prerequisite to an assertion by him of such right." It has been suggested that, whether or not the statute requires the giving of such notice, reasonable notice is necessary to meet the constitutional requirement of due process.12 But, in addition to the constitutional requirement, the statute governing proceedings for the sale of real estate to pay debts in probate courts specifically provides that when the petition and exhibits are filed the court must order that all persons interested in the estate be notified of the filing of the petition 41 

Ante, Sec. 671. "State ex rel. Deems vs. Holtcamp, 245 Mo. 655, 151 S. W. 153. 874

and exhibits (Sec. 144). The giving of notice of the filing of the petition is held jurisdictional, though not in the sense that by the giving of the notice the court acquires jurisdicton. Jurisdiction of the proceeding and of the res or land is acquired by the court by the filing of the petition. But the giving of notice is jurisdictional in the sense that the court has no jurisdiction to go forward with the proceeding or make an order that the land be sold until notice is given as required by statute. The statute requiring notice is mandatory and essential to further action on the petition by the court.46 

Even though the court has jurisdiction of the res, if the court proceeds to order a sale before such notice is given the proceeding is void. Such proceeding, rendered void for failure to give notice, cannot be validated by a subsequent notice of sale, report of sale, or order approving sale, for, if the notice is not given, all subsequent proceedings are void, as if no order at all had been made.48 The fact that the heirs received the benefit of the proceeds of the sale does not cure the defect caused by the lack of notice.49 Nor can such defect be cured by an order reciting that notice was given, when the record shows that the giving of statutory notice was impossible, the order of sale having been made on the same day the petition was filed.50 

The defect, being jurisdictional, may be raised on an appeal from "Norton vs. Reed, 253 Mo. 236, 161 S. W. 842; Desloge vs. Tucker, 196 Mo.

While it has been held that an order of sale may be made by the court on its own motion, as authorized by statute (Sec. 166), after the filing of any semi-annual and annual settlement, the theory being that such settlements constitute notice,54 the strength of this authority is materially weakened by more recent expressions of the Supreme Court of this State indicating that notice must be given in all cases.55 

Sec. 689. Order of Publication the Basis of Notice. 

The statute provides that when the petition for sale, accounts, lists and inventories are filed, the court shall order that all persons interested in the estate be notified thereof, and, unless the contrary be shown on some day named in the publication, when court will be in session, which date must be at least thirty days after the date of the first newspaper publication containing such order, or thirty days after the posting of handbills of such notice, an order will be made for the sale of the whole or so much of such real estate as will pay the debts of the deceased (Sec. 144). Publication of the notice required to be given may be made either by publication in a newspaper or by the posting of handbills (Sec. 144). The order of publication should so recite. Notice must also be personally served on the heirs or devisees of the deceased who are residents of the county where the administration is had (Sec. 144). The order of publication may con-

Sec. 690. Service by Publication of Order in Newspaper. 

A publication of notice is required by statute, but the statute authorizes alternative methods of publication. If the publication is in a newspaper, the order of publication may be published, but it must be published once a week for four consecutive weeks in some newspaper in the county where the proceeding is had, and so that the day fixed for a hearing on the petition shall be at least thirty days after the date of the first publication. (Sec. 144.) If the publica- 1 877

tion is in a daily newspaper, publication for each week after the first must fall on the corresponding day of the week on which the first publication appeared (Sec. 144). Proof of publication should be made and filed in court. This proof should consist of the publisher's affidavit, form for which has been shown.56 A failure to file proof of publication, however, is not fatal to the proceeding, as evidence that notice was actually published may be supplied from other sources.57 

Nor will the fact that the affidavit of publication was erroneously made out, such as by a failure of the officer taking the affidavit to sign his name thereto, void the proceeding.58

Sec. 691. Service by Publication by Posting Handbills. 

The alternate method of service by publication is that of posting handbills. The statute authorizes the use of this method or the method of publication by publishing notice in a newspaper (Sec. 

144). If the handbill method is used, ten handbills must be put up in ten public places in the county where the proceeding is had, at least thirty days before the date fixed for the hearing on the petition. The statute does not designate a form to be used for the handbills, nor does it direct that copies of the order of publication be used as handbills. It is more convenient, however, to use copies of the order of publication for the handbills, and such order is a type of notice that will serve the intended purpose as well as any other that may be devised. The administrator should post the handbills as required by statute, and as evidence that the statute in this particular has been complied with he should attach his certificate or return showing the posting of the notices to the order of publication, or such other notice as he may use for the purpose, and file same with the other papers in the office of the clerk of the court.

Sec. 692. 64 

Personal Service of Notice. 

All heirs or devisees of the deceased who are residents of the county in which the proceeding is had must be personally served with notice at least ten days before the day of court at which such order of sale is to be made (Sec. 144). In determining who are 'devisees," the court will limit the application of that term to its strict legal meaning and will not require legatees who are residents of the county where the proceeding is had to be personally served with notice.50 On appeal from an order confirming a sale where the only service was by publication and there was nothing to show whether the heirs or devisees were residents of the county, the court will presume that they were not residents, in the absence of a showing that they were personally served. Where the records of a probate sale of real estate to pay debts had been lost, and in a suit brought by the heirs to set aside the administrator's deed some of the resident heirs testified that they had never been personally served with notice of the petition for sale, it was held that the sheriff who served the notice on such heirs should have been permitted to testify that notice was served by him upon such heirs.61 Personal service of a copy of the order of publication is sufficient service on the resident heirs or devisees. Return of the service may be made on a copy of such order or notice as was served on the resident heirs or devisees. 60

Sec. 693. Hearing on Petition. 

The statute contemplates that on the date fixed for a hearing on the petition there shall be a real, and not a perfunctory, hearing. 

The title to real estate is involved. The rights of owners and the holders of liens against the real estate are to be determined as a result of the hearing. It is the duty of the court to examine all the proceedings that have occurred up to that time and determine whether or not the court has jurisdiction to proceed and whether the best interests of the parties involved can be served by ordering a sale. The court should carefully examine the proof of publication and return of the personal service of notice on resident heirs. If notice has not been properly given, either by publication or personal service, that fact should be ascertained and an order refused. It is the duty of the court to hear testimony concerning matters involved in the proceeding. In its discretion the court may examine all parties on oath touching the application for the sale (Sec. 145). 

Parties interested may appear and object to the order.62 A careful compliance by the court with the directions of the statute on the date fixed for the hearing of the petition will serve well to avoid mistakes, errors and omissions that may affect title to the land involved in future years.

Sec. 694. Order of Sale. 

After a hearing on the application, if the court is satisfied that the proceedings are in compliance with the statutes and that the sale should be made, the court shall make an order for the sale of such real estate, or any part thereof, in this State, at public or private sale (Sec. 145). A sale without an order is void. The order of sale in proceedings to sell real estate for the payment of debts occupies the same relation to a sale by an administrator that a judgment or decree does to an execution sale by a sheriff. Where such sales 63 have been held void for lack of an order, it has been held that if the 

63 Blickensderfer vs. Hanna, 231 Mo. 93, 132 S. W. 678. 

Schafer vs. Causey, 76 Mo. 365; Evans vs. Snyder, 64 Mo. 516. 

Evans vs. Snyder, 64 Mo. 516. 880

proceeds of the sale were applied on the debts of the deceased the purchaser was entitled to a lien on the real estate for the purchase money expended and the taxes paid.65 It is not necessary that the court find and state in its order the amount of the debts, since the statute requires only a finding that the personal assets are insufficient to pay the debts.66 Heirs or devisees may appear at the hearing and contest the question as to the insufficiency of the personal estate to pay debts, but if the court finds that the personal estate is insufficient to pay debts the remedy of such parties is by an appeal from the order of sale." If the heirs and devisees have notice of the proceeding and do not appeal from the finding that the personal estate is insufficient to pay the debts, they cannot thereafter raise the point in a collateral proceeding.68 The order should in all cases describe the property to be sold. It has been held that an order which omitted the description was good, since it was based on a petition containing the description. But such authority should never be relied upon to justify neglect to insert the description in the order of sale. If the description is omitted from both the petition and the order of sale, the proceedings are void.70 The petition and order are the basis for the administrator's deed after the sale, and, if the description is omitted from both, the deed subsequently made by the administrator is not only void, even though it contains a correct description, but if the description in the administrator's deed is defective the proceeding is also void. However, if the original order of sale contained a description of the real estate, it has been held that the renewal order need not repeat such description.72 The order should fix the terms of the sale and designate whether the property is to be sold at public or private sale (Sec. 145).

Sec. 695. Appraisement. 

Before any executor or administrator sells any real estate, or interest therein, by order of court, he must, if ordered by the court so to do, have it appraised by three disinterested householders of the county in which the land lies (Sec. 158). If the proceeding for the sale occurs shortly after the administrator files his inventory and appraisement as he is required by law to file in opening the estate,73 а new appraisement for the purposes of sale should properly be dispensed with by a finding and order of the court that such special appraisement is not necessary. This was not true under the old law, where an appraisement under all circumstances was required before a sale. Under the law which required an appraisement under all circumstances, it was held that a sale without the appraisement was an irregularity for which the sale might be set aside in a direct proceeding, but that it did not render such sale void in a collateral proceeding after confirmation by the probate court.75 A special ap- 

73 Ante, Sec. 595. 74 

74 Sec. 157 R. S. 1919; Laws 1921, p. 120. 

75 Noland vs. Barrett, 122 Mo. 181, 26 S. W. 692. 883

praisement for the purposes of sale may be dispensed with by order of the court. The appraisers must be disinterested householders of the county in which the land lies (Sec. 158), and they must make an affidavit that they are, according to the best of their abilities, to view and appraise the estate to them shown. They must view and appraise the real estate and deliver to the executor or administrator a certificate of their appraisement, under their hands. (Sec. 159.) An appraisement certified by two appraisers only has been held sufficient. And where the affidavit of the appraisers was signed by them but their signatures were not attached to the appraisement itself, the appraisement was held good." Nor is an appraisement rendered void by the fact that the administrator takes the affidavit of the appraisers.78 It has also been held that where the description of the land contained in the appraisement is erroneous, the proceeding is not thereby rendered invalid, even though the same erroneous description is copied into the order approving the sale and in the curator's deed.79

Sec. 697. Private Sales.

If the probate court finds that it would be to the best interest of the estate that real estate sold to pay debts should be sold at private sale, an order to that effect should be made (Sec. 145). Such sales cannot be made unless the real estate brings at least three-fourths of its appraised value (Sec. 162). The administrator cannot become the purchaser of such real estate, either directly or indirectly, and all private sales not made in compliance with such statutory provisions are null and void (Sec. 162). In making a private sale an administrator may agree to any terms, not unqualifiedly injurious to the estate or forbidden by law, which might aid in securing a purchaser or which the purchaser might in good faith and under the law require before purchasing.88 If there are two administrators 

87 Noland vs. Barrett, 122 Mo. 181, 26 S. W. 692. 88 

Riley vs. Akin, 45 S. W. (2d) 122, 226 Mo. A. 735. 886

and one attempts to sell the real estate to the other at a private sale, the transaction is void.89 An executor or administrator cannot, directly or indirectly, purchase at his own sale. But a subsequent sale made by a purchaser at an administrator's sale to the administrator does not of itself create a presumption of fraud,¹ even though the sale to the administrator occurred before his final discharge." 

Sec. 698. Report of Sale. 

Within ten days after a sale of real estate to pay debts, the executor or administrator must make a full report of his proceedings, with the certificate of appraisement if a new appraisement is required by the court, and a copy of the advertisement if a public sale, which report must be verified by the affidavit of the executor or administrator that he did not, directly or indirectly, purchase said real estate, or any part thereof or any interest therein, and that he is not interested in the property sold, except as stated in such report. The report of sale must remain on file ten days before being acted upon by the court. (Sec. 163.) An error in the description of the land in the report does not render the sale void. Where the record entry approving the report of sale does not show to whom the sale was made, nor describe the land, but the administrator's deed conveys land which could have been sold, it will be presumed that the report showed that the grantee named in the deed purchased the land at the sale.⁹4 A report of sale made by an administrator after his final settlement has been held void. 95 94

(Name and style of office.) Sec. 699. Objections to Report of Sale. 

Proceedings for the sale of real estate are void if the report of sale is not approved by the court (Sec. 164). The statutory requirement that the report of sale remain on file ten days before being acted upon by the court (Sec. 163) serves a wholesome purpose in the proceeding. It prevents hasty action on the part of the administrator and gives the judge of the court an opportunity to make an independent investigation of the facts connected with the sale and with the entire proceedings, if he desires to make such investigation before acting upon the report. It enables others who may not have 889

had an opportunity to bid on the property at or before the sale to make known to the administrator or the court the fact that, if they had an opportunity, they would pay more for the property than it brought at the sale. Moreover, it gives heirs, devisees, and others interested the opportunity to appear and object to the sale. While the statute makes no provision as to the manner by which objections may be made after the report has been filed and before it has been acted upon by the court, it is clear that the intention in providing for a delay of ten days after the report is filed before action thereon was to allow interested persons the right to appear and object. Such objections may be presented orally before the court, or written objections to the proceedings may be filed. If anything is discovered that indicates the proceedings are erroneous, or that the court does not have jurisdiction, the court should disapprove the report of sale. 

If the sale was privately conducted, special care should be taken to see that the property has not been sacrificed or a sharp bargain made. 

The whole purpose of allowing this interval in the proceedings is to prevent the perpetration of fraud or other wrongs, to protect the interests of the heirs, creditors, purchaser and others interested, in seeing that a proper sale has been made and to secure the most that can be obtained for the property. 

Sec. 700. Order of Disapproval. 

a. Because of inadequate price.

If the sale was held under conditions that prevented the property from bringing as much as could be obtained for it at another sale, it lies within the court's discretion to disapprove the sale and order a new sale (Sec. 164).96 If the real estate was sold at a private sale for only one-half the value of the land, the court should disapprove the sale.97 b. Because of purchase by administrator.

The statute forbids that an administrator or executor purchase directly or indirectly at his own sale (Sec. 162). If it appears to the court, after the report of sale is filed, and before the sale is approved, "Brown vs. Marshall, 241 Mo. 707, 145 S. W. 810.

DT 

Desloge vs. Tucker, 196 Mo. 587, 94 S. W. 283. 890

that the executor or administrator has purchased the real estate, the sale should be disapproved, because such purchase absolutely voids the sale (Secs. 162, 163).⁹8 One administrator cannot sell to his coadministrator." The fact that the sale may be made under a power in the will does not take the case out of the statute prohibiting an executor from purchasing at his own sale.100 The fact that the executor may be prosecuted for making a false affidavit if he purchased at his own sale and falsely reported that he did not do so¹ should not prevent the court from disapproving the sale, if any knowledge comes to him before the report is acted upon that the executor or administrator was the purchaser. The discovery by the court that the administrator or executor purchased at his own sale and an order disapproving the sale will not only save the title to the real estate sold from future attack on that ground but will also save the sureties on the administrator's bond from liability for the administrator's wrongful acts. And while it has been held that an attorney who assisted the administrator in making the inventory and appraisement was not by such employment disqualified from buying the property at a sale thereof under a trust deed, any practice that savors of a purpose by the administrator to profit personally from the sale is not commendable, and both the administrator and the court should take precaution to see that both the letter and the spirit of the statute with regard to such sales are rigidly observed. 2 c. Because of other irregularities.

If the court ordered a special appraisement to be made and none was made before the sale, the sale should be disapproved (Sec. 158).*

If the real estate was sold at public sale and no notice was given

Sec. 701. New Sales and Renewal Orders. 

When, from any cause, no sale is made, and when a report of sale has been disapproved, the court may order a new sale. If a new sale is ordered, the same proceeding shall be had as upon the original order of sale. (Sec. 164.) If a new sale is ordered, the executor or administrator should proceed in accordance with the terms of the new order. It is not necessary that the parties interested be notified again of the proceedings, as the courts in these proceedings apply the general rule that whenever a party is duly summoned into court for a particular purpose he remains in court until that pur- 892

pose has been accomplished, or until he is otherwise discharged according to law.5 Thus, where a sale was set aside by the court on the ground that the price was inadequate, it was held proper for the court to order a resale at a subsequent term without renotifying the parties interested. Where there has been no sale, it is not clear as to whether or not a renewal order of sale should be made from term to term until a sale is actually held and confirmed. Certainly, if the order of sale directed that the sale be held at a certain time and it was not held in accordance with the order, a new sale at a different time should not be made without a new order of sale. And, while sales are sometimes held after the lapse of one or more terms of court following the order of sale and without the original order of sale being renewed or a new order granted, in the absence of a direct judicial approval of such practice it would be best not to follow that course. If an order of sale is made and the administrator fails to make the sale as ordered, the better practice is for the administrator to file a report with the court stating why a sale was not held as directed and requesting that the order be renewed or another order of sale made. This practice would avoid the controversies that are likely to arise if a sale is not held when ordered and no justification therefor appears of record, especially if the administrator undertakes to sell at some time remote from the making of the original order. It has been held that the renewal order of sale need not describe the property if same was described in the original order.

Sec. 702.

Modification of the Order of Sale. 

An order may be made modifying the terms of sale prescribed in the original order. Such sales, being judicial sales and being subject to the orders of the probate court, may be made according to such terms as may be prescribed for them at any time.10 Thus, where it was first ordered that certain real estate be sold at private sale, it was held proper for the court subsequently to modify the original order by directing that the sale be a public sale, instead of a private sale.11 A modification of an original order providing that the land be sold at public sale so as to authorize a private sale has been approved.12 Where a public sale was ordered to be held on a certain day and on that day the sale was adjourned by the administrator until nearly a week later, owing to an unprecedented snowstorm that made it impossible for those interested to appear on the day when the sale was advertised, and the sale was subsequently held on the day to which it was adjourned by the administrator, at which time the property brought a fair price, and the sale was later approved by the probate court, the proceeding was held valid.13 'Brown vs. Marshall, 241 Mo. 707, 145 S. The heirs or interested parties have a right at any time prior to the entry of the order approving and confirming the sale to appear and object to the proceedings.14 By appearing they submit to the jurisdiction of the court. 15 Appearance for the purpose of objecting to the proceeding may be first made in the Supreme Court.16 While notice to heirs residing in the county where the land is located and where the proceedings are had must be given by personal service, for which notice by publication cannot be substituted, so as to give the court jurisdiction of such resident heirs,¹7 the court may acquire jurisdiction of such heirs or interested parties by their voluntary appearance to object to the proceedings.18 Thus, if a resident heir who has not been personally served, and of whom the court has not acquired jurisdiction to order the sale, voluntarily enters his ap-

Sec. 704. Order Approving Sale. 

The statute provides that if the report of sale is approved by the court the sale is valid (Sec. 165). If the sale is not approved, it is void (Sec. 164). The approval of the sale by the court is necessary to complete the act of the sale and to authorize the administrator to make a deed to the purchaser.20 The proper way for the court to express its approval of the sale is by a formal entry of an order approving the sale, although it has been held that the approval of the sale need not necessarily appear by a formal entry if the approval can be gathered from the whole record,21 such as by an acknowledgment of the administrator's deed before the probate judge as ex officio clerk in open court, 22 by a direction to the administrator to make the purchaser a deed, 28 or by a recital in a deed acknowledged before the probate court that the sale had been approved by the court.24

Sec. 705. Effect of Order Approving Sale. 

When a sale by an executor or administrator under order of the court has been regularly approved by the court, an equity in the real estate passes to the purchaser, notwithstanding an irregularity in or an absence of an administrator's deed, and such equity will be enforced in favor of the purchaser if he has complied with the terms of the sale.25 An order approving a sale of real estate is a final judgment, impervious to collateral attack, and is as conclusive as judgments of courts of general jurisdiction. 26 If such order of sale is not appealed from, it becomes a final judgment and is subject to impeachment only by a direct proceeding for that purpose for defects apparent on the face of the record, going to the jurisdiction of the court, or for fraud." Sec. 707. Deed After Administrator's Death,

The statute provides that when any executor or administrator shall remove from this State, resign, or die, or his letters be revoked, after the sale of any real estate and before executing any deed therefor, the purchaser, his heirs, assigns or grantees may petition the court, stating the facts; and if he satisfy the court that the purchase money has been paid, the court shall order the executor or administrator then acting, or, if after final settlement, the sheriff of said county, to execute and acknowledge to the purchaser, his heirs, assigns or grantees, a deed, referring to the petition and order of court, with such other recitals as provided by law, which deed shall be executed accordingly and shall have the effect to all intents and purposes as if made by the executor or administrator who made the sale of such real estate. (Sec. 167.) The probate court is not authorized to appoint an administrator de bonis non to correct a mistake in a deed made by the original administrator, 48 nor can an administrator de bonis non be appointed for the sole purpose of making a deed which his predecessor neglected to make, and a deed made by such specially-appointed administrator is a nullity. Under the provisions of the statute, neither an administrator de donis non nor the sheriff can do anything in the proceeding more than execute a deed, and where an administrator de bonis non was appointed to make a deed based on a sale by the original administrator and in his deed it was not recited that a petition was filed therefor, and where the report of sale was filed by the administrator de bonis non instead of by the original administrator, the proceeding was held void.45 "Grayson vs. Weddle, 63 Mo. 523. 44 "Carey vs. West, 139 Mo. 146, 40 S. W. 661; Long vs. Joplin Mining & Smelting Co., 68 Mo. 422. 

45 Jackson vs. Johnson, 248 Mo. 680, 154 S. W. 759. 1. 901

After final settlement and discharge of the original administrator, such deed can only be made by the sheriff (Sec. 167). 

Sec. 708. Reservation of Personalty and Sale of Real Estate. 

If any executor or administrator, or other person interested in any estate, file a petition setting forth the facts and describing the real and personal estate, and praying that the personal estate may be reserved and real estate be sold for the payment of debts, the same steps shall be taken and the same proceedings and publication had as in proceedings to sell real estate for the payment of debts, and the court may order the whole or any part of the personal estate to be reserved, and the real estate, or any part of it, to be sold at public or private sale (Sec. 157). Proceedings under this statutory authority are far less frequent than ordinary proceedings for the sale of real estate for the payment of debts, owing to the fact that personal property of the estate is usually first exhausted in satisfaction of the debts and claims against the estate before the real estate is resorted to for that purpose. But power to reserve the personalty and sell the real estate as vested by this statutory provision is just as effective as the authority in the first instance to sell the real estate for the payment of debts because the personal estate is insufficient for that purpose.46 Any person interested in the estate may make the application.47 This includes both heirs and creditors.48

(Name, style and seal of office.) Sec. 709. Proceedings Upon Court's Motion. 

The statute provides that if, upon the settlement of accounts of any executor or administrator, it appears that the personal estate is not sufficient to pay the debts and legacies, the court may make such order as it may think necessary for sale of the real estate for that purpose, and such order of sale may be made by the court after the filing of any semiannual or annual settlement, and the sale shall be conducted and the same proceedings had in relation thereto as are provided for the sale of real estate for the payment of debts upon the petition of the executor or administrator, creditor or other person interested (Sec. 166). If the proceeding is initiated by the court upon its own motion, all other steps, except the filing of the petition, accounts, lists and inventories, should be taken, as in a regular sale of real estate to pay debts. The petition, accounts, lists and inventories are held unnecessary where the court initiates the proceeding by its own motion, because the settlement just filed by the executor or administrator stands in lieu of such petition and exhibits and it furnishes such information as the petition and exhibits would otherwise reveal.49 Notice of the proceeding, however, should be given to all parties interested in the same manner as if the proceeding had 

Patee vs. Mowry, 59 Mo. 161. 904

been initiated by the filing of a.petition by the executor, administrator, or other interested party.50

Sec. 710. Proceedings When Real Estate Is Bound by Liens. 

The statute provides that if decedent's real estate is bound by the lien of a judgment or attachment, the executor, administrator or creditor shall state that fact in his petition, the date and amount of the judgment, and the name of the person in whose favor the same was rendered, and the date of the service of the attachment, the amount claimed thereunder, and the name of the person prosecuting the same (Sec. 148). When there is any lien against the real estate, that fact must be stated in the petition to sell, and the nature of the lien must be described. 51 If the real estate is bound by the lien of several judgments or attachments, or both, the executor, administrator or creditor shall state that fact in his petition, the dates and amounts of such judgments, and the dates of serving, the amounts claimed by such attachments, and the names of the persons in whose favor the same were rendered or are prosecuted (Sec. 149). 

The proceeds of the sale of such real estate must be first applied to the payment of such judgments and attachments, according to their priority of lien, and the residue of such proceeds, if any, becomes assets in the hands of the executor or administrator, to be administered according to law (Sec. 150). If the lien of such several judgments or attachments are of even date, and the proceeds of such sale are not sufficient to pay the whole, such proceeds must be applied to the payment of such several judgments or attachments in proportion to their respective amounts (Sec. 151). If such real estate, being or having been bound by the liens of several judgments or attachments, shall have been sold under a junior judgment, the executor or administrator must state in his petition the fact of such sale, the name of the plaintiff in such junior judgment, the name of the purchaser, the dates and amounts of the several judgments and attachments, and the names of the persons in whose favor such several judgments were rendered or such attachments are prosecuted (Sec. 152). The court shall thereupon order that the plaintiff in the 

50 State ex rel. Deems vs. Holtcamp, 245 Mo. 655, 151 S. W. 153. 

51 State to use of Lovell vs. Todd, 57 Mo. 217. 905

judgment under which such real estate was sold, and the purchaser thereof, be notified of the filing of such petition and that, unless good cause to the contrary be shown, on the first day of the next term, an order will be made for the sale of the whole or so much of such real estate as will be sufficient to pay the prior judgments or attachments (Sec. 153). Such notice must be published and served as other notices are required to be published in case of other petitions for the sale of real estate (Sec. 154). The purchaser of such real estate has the privilege of paying such prior judgments at any time within six months from and including the first day of the term of court at which he is notified to appear, or, in case of attachments, within six months after any judgment rendered upon the attachment shall be allowed and classed as provided by law (Sec. 155). If the purchaser of the real estate under such junior judgment fails to pay such prior judgment, or judgment upon prior attachments, or both, within the time prescribed, such real estate must be sold free from the encumbrance of the title derived from the sale under such junior judgment, and the proceeds of such sale shall be disposed of according to such provisions of the law as shall be applicable to the facts of the case (Sec. 156). It has been held that if the personal assets are sufficient to pay the debts, the liens on the real estate should be paid from the personal estate. 52 But if the real estate is encumbered and the personal property is not sufficient to pay debts, the liens must be paid in the order of their priority, regardless of the order of their allowance and classification in probate court.58 A probate court judgment allowing a judgment as a claim against an estate has been held in aid of a former judgment and not destructive of its vitality."

FOREWORD 

There has been no need to revise the forms. The reader should refer to statutory changes from R.S. Mo. 1929 to R.S. 

Mo. 1939 by finding the appropriate section numbers carried forward in the table at the end of the annotations. The important decisions since the publication of the work have been analyzed as briefly as possible, assuming that the reader will consult the decision in the official report or the reporter system.

AMENDMENT OF LAWS 

In 1935 (Session Acts, p. 210, Additional Justices in certain districts) the General Assembly passed an act to be known as Sec. 2136a (now Sec. 2523, R.S. Mo. 1939) of the Revised Statutes providing that in counties where the municipal townships have been or may hereafter be divided into justice of the peace districts, the county court could appoint not to exceed two additional justices of the peace in districts in which the boundary of the municipal township is or may be extended beyond the boundaries of said justice of the peace districts.

In 1935, the General Assembly (Session Acts, p. 217) provided that the probate judges who are elected in counties having 50,000 inhabitants or more, should be learned in the law and prohibiting them from practicing law in any of the courts of the state; containing a proviso applicable only to counties now having or which may hereafter have a population of more than 350,000 and less than 750,000 according to the last federal decennial census, to the effect that the probate judges in such counties are forbidden to practice only in any of the Probate Courts of this State or in a case or proceeding involving an estate in process of administration in the Court to which such judges are elected or appointed during the term of office for which they shall have been elected or appointed. (Now Sec. 2445, R.S. Mo. 1939.)

In 1937 (Session Acts, p. 212), the General Assembly passed an act to be known as Sec. 2373, providing for an increase of the jurisdiction of justices of the peace in civil actions from $500 to $750 in townships of 200,000 and less than 400,000 inhabitants. (Now Sec. 

2759, R.S. Mo., 1939.)

In 1937 (Session Acts, p. 382), the General Assembly passed an act affecting cities of the first class, to be known as Sec. 6294-A (now 

Sec. 6417, R.S. Mo. 1939), providing that within ten days after the bringing of a suit on a special tax bill, plaintiff or plaintiffs shall cause to be filed in the office of the City Engineer a written statement giving a brief description of the tax bill sued upon, and in what court, and against whom such suit shall have been brought, and in the event of failure to file such statement within such time the land described in the tax bill sued on should be free from the lien of the

tax bill and of any judgment in such suit and should not be sold to satisfy such judgment; "provided, however, that failure to file said notice shall not affect or invalidate said lien or judgment as to the interest of any persons made parties to such suit and served with due process therein." (The filing of such statement with the city engineer is applicable alike to actions brought in Circuit or Justice courts.)

In 1939 (Session Acts, p. 334), the General Assembly passed an act repealing the then Section 2143 (R. S. Mo. 1929), which statute provided: "Whenever two or more persons shall have an equal number of votes for justices of the peace for any township, or there is a contested election, the county court shall decide the same." The repealing act was declared to be a revision bill. Its only effect was to repeal an act part of which (giving the county court power to decide who should be justice in case of tie) had been previously declared unconstitutional. (State v. Kramer, 150 Mo. 89, 51 S.W. 716). As the author remarks, the county court still has jurisdiction in an election contest of the office of justice of the peace by virtue of other provisions.

In 1943 (Session Acts, p. 623), the General Assembly repealed Art. 

8 of Chapter 11, pertaining to Justices in townships containing 75,000 and not over 150,000 inhabitants, and enacted other sections with the same numbers, but relating to justices in counties of from 200,000 to 400,000 inhabitants. By that Act of 1943, the pecuniary jurisdiction of such justices was fixed at a maximum of $500, exclusive of interest and costs, in civil actions.

By the new Code of Civil Procedure (Session Acts, 1943), it is provided by Section 23, that: 

"*** the filing of a petition in a court of record, or a statement or account before a court not of record, and suing out of process therein, shall be taken and deemed the commencement of a suit." 

This changes the law as to when suit is begun in the courts of justices of the peace from the time of "delivery of the writ to the constable to be served" to that of "filing a *** statement or account *** and suing out of process therein." This change will be effective as of January 1, 1945.

Sec. 22. 

The test as to whether the complaint against defendant under an ordinance is sufficient is laid down in City of Cape Girardeau v. 

McLain (App.), 61 S.W. (2d) 232, as follows: "*** The complaint in question sets out the ordinance by number, the section it was claimed defendant violated, and is sufficiently AA.M

definite to bar another prosecution for the same offense." Citing 

City of Mexico v. Harris, 115 Mo. A. loc. cit. 711, 92 S.W. 505; City of Moberly v. Kervin (App.), 234 S.W. 514. 

Sec. 31.

That the city has a right of appeal from judgment adverse to it in the prosecution of a defendant for violation of a city ordinance was decided in City of Clayton v. Nemours (App.), 164 S.W. (2d) 935 and the commissioner discusses at length the nature and character of proceedings under ordinances. 

Sec. 37-Note 24.

Burden is upon the city to establish defendant's violation of the ordinance beyond a reasonable doubt. See City of St. Louis v. Stubley (App.), 154 S.W. (2d) 407. In addition to the cases cited in the text on this principle, the case cites King City v. Duncan, 238 Mo. 

513, 142 S.W. 246. 

Sec. 50. 

State v. La Mance, 348 Mo. 484, 154 S.W. (2d) 110.

The rule of law that a court may take judicial notice of an official census does not authorize setting aside the appointment of an additional justice of the peace for a township based on the county court's finding that the township had a population of more than 2,000. 

Sec. 50-Note 25. 

State ex rel Asotsky v. Hicks, 346 Mo. 640, 142 S.W. (2d) 472.

A justice of the peace is not a county officer within the meaning of the statute requiring vacancy in such office to be filled by appointment of the governor. 

Sec. 50-Note 25. 

State v. La Mance, 348 Mo. 484, 154 S.W. (2d) 110.

Appointment to fill vacancy in office of justice of the peace holds only until the next regular election of county officers and then the vacancy is filled for the remainder of a four year term. 

Sec. 58. 

State v. La Mance, 348 Mo. 484, 154 S.W. (2d) 110.

Where county court acted on petitions of citizens of township asking for the appointment of a third justice of the peace, and found as a fact that under the law the township was entitled to have three justices, appointment by county court of third justice made such justice at least a "de facto officer" as respects validity of preliminary hearing held before such justice.

Sec. 59-Note 43. 

State ex rel. Morris Bldg. & Inv. Co. v. Brown, 228 Mo. A. 760, 72 S.W. (2d) 859.

Holds that certifying to a transcript of justice of the peace in a certiorari action against the justice is a ministerial act and not a judicial one and may be performed by the justice's clerk. 

Limits the ruling in prior cases. 

Sec. 60.

Theener v. Kurn, et al. (App.), 132 S.W. (2d) 707. 

Appearance of a railroad company to action in justice court for death or injury to animal by negligence did not confer jurisdiction if the proof in the justice court failed to show that the action was brought in the township where the injury or death occurred or in an adjoining township. 

Sec. 60.

Justice has jurisdiction over suit by State Auditor to recover a sum within the Justice's jurisdiction for delinquent sales tax: 

State ex rel. and to use of Berra v. Sestric, 349 Mo. 182, 159 S.W. (2d) 786.

Sec. 60-Note 46. 

Martindale v. Hall (App.), 132 S.W. (2d) 1041.

The court recognized the principle that a justice of the peace can exercise no powers except those conferred by statute, but held that a liberal construction should be given to statutes concerning their jurisdiction and powers, with a view to effect their object and promote justice. So, in a replevin action, where there was an endorsement on the files before the justice that "this statement, affidavit and bond which was filed and by me approved October 23, 1937, on which bond was signed on wrong line by sureity," and it also appeared in the transcript of the justice's docket, "Statement filed October 23, 1937," the suit was instituted October 23, 1937, although the statement, affidavit and bond on which the case was tried was filed October 25, 1937, that being an amendment of the originals and it was not necessary to show the amendment.

Sec. 60-Note 46. 

State ex rel. and to use of Berra v. Sestric, 159 S.W. (2d) 786, 349 Mo. 182; Martone v. Bryan, 233 Mo. 1249, 130 S.W. (2d) 962; 

Theener v. Kurn (App.), 132 S.W. (2d) 707; Martindale v. Hall (App.), 132 S.W. (2d) 1041.

Sec. 60-Note 50. 

5 

State v. Frank (Sonny) McDaniel, 336 Mo. 656, 80 S.W. (2d) 185, holds that the justice may by leave of circuit court amend the proceedings of the preliminary hearing in a felony case after the transcript has been filed in the circuit court by procuring the signature of a witness to his testimony given at such preliminary hearing and transmit the same to the jailer although he had failed to have such testimony signed and delivered to the jailer at the time of commitment as provided by statute.

Sec. 60-Note 53. 

State v. Frank (Sonny) McDaniel, 336 Mo. 656, 80 S.W. (2d) 185. 

Scheerer v. Waltner, et al., 225 Mo. A. 837, 29 S.W. (2d) 193. 

Sec. 63 (d). 

Barnes Hospital v. Schultz (App.), 90 S.W. (2d) 164.

The hospital by its trustees brought suit in a justice court for services rendered patient. The defendant made an objection to the jurisdiction of the justice on the ground that the litigation involved trust funds or trust property. The court overruled such contention, holding that trustees had a right to bring an action at law; nothing more was involved than the question of debt and no equitable matters were involved. 

Sec. 67.

Section 2553, R.S. Mo. 1939, has been amended by raising jurisdiction from $300 to $500 in counties having 200,000 and less than 400,- 000 inhabitants. See Acts 1943, p. 623. This affects all townships in 

St. Louis County and the new sections are designated as Secs. 2752, 2753, 2754, 2755, 2756, 2757, 2758, 2758A, 2758B, 2758C, 2758D.

Sec. 67. 

The statute relating to jurisdiction in cities of 300,000 and over is somewhat different in its wording than the general statute. The words italicized in the following copy of such section indicate the difference: "The said justices of the peace shall have original jurisdiction of all actions and proceedings for the recovery of money, whether such action be founded upon contract, tort or account, or upon a bond or undertaking given in any civil action or proceeding, or upon special tax bills, or for a penalty or forfeiture given by any statute of this state, when the sum demanded, exclusive of interest and costs, does not exceed seven hundred and fifty dollars."

The Supreme Court in State ex rel Berra v. Sestric, 349 Mo. 182,

159 S.W. (2d) 786, holds that the words "whether such actions be founded upon contract or tort," etc., is not a videlicet restraining the preceding grant of jurisdiction to the character of actions particularly enumerated in the phrase and is sufficient to include a statutory liability for sales tax in a civil action. 

Sec. 67. 

The section of statutes relating to jurisdiction in cities of 300,000 or over should be Sec. 2789 R.S. Mo. 1939 (Sec. 2403, R.S. Mo. 1929).

Sec. 68. 

Where the action is upon a note the principal sum of which is within the jurisdiction of the justice, it is immaterial that the amount of the judgment is in excess of that jurisdiction by reason of the addition of interest, and the execution issued thereon in the circuit court is not void. 

Massey et al. v. Fitzpatrick et al. (Sup.), 175 S.W. (2d) 780. (Citing Sec. 2552, R.S. Mo. 1939; Hoppenbrock v. Dial, 137 Mo. A. 

75, 119 S.W. 496; Williams v. Hannibal & St. Joseph R. Co., 80 Mo. 597.)

Filing an appeal from justice court is now held to enter the appellant's appearance for a trial de novo in the circuit court and service of defective summons or failure to serve summons in the justice court is no longer a ground of quashal or dismissal. The case of Cudahy

Sec. Note 62. 

Replevin Action 

The justice court to which a transcript is sent on change of venue acquires jurisdiction of the parties and the subject matter even though proper notice was never served or posted under Section 2642, R.S. Mo. 1939. 

Standard Electrical Co. v. Lugar (App.), 175 S.W. (2d) 58. 

Cases cited: 

Cullen v. Collison, 110 Mo. A. 174, 80 S.W. 290. 

Hess v. Fox, 140 Mo. A. 437, 124 S.W. 83. 

Sec. 190. 

In Martone v. Bryan, 233 Mo. A. 1249, 130 S.W. (2d) 962 (Wilson & Co., garnishee), the court held that in garnishment upon attachment both the statement and summons of attachment or garnishment must show affirmatively the place where defendant resides and the place where the debt is contracted and the cause of action arose. 

The statement showed that the defendant resided in Kansas and also that the claim was for rent of apartments located in Kansas City, Mo., where the suit was brought. The court refused to infer from this the fact that the debt was contracted and the cause of action arose therein. Held that the justice was without jurisdiction and hence circuit court on appeal was also without jurisdiction. 

Sec. 195-Note 13. 

Vittert v. Melton (App.), 78 S.W. (2d) 467.

The return to the order of publication of the attachment failing to show that the notices were posted twenty days before the day on which defendant was required to appear, the justice acquired no jurisdiction. 

Sec. 200-Note 27. 

State ex rel. and to use of Smith v. Boudreau, 231 Mo. A. 959, 82 S.W. (2d) 129. 

Sec. 213. 

Jurisdiction and venue in unlawful detainer.

Young Women's Christian Ass'n v. La Presto (App.), 169 S.W. 

(2d) 78. 

The complaint in unlawful detainer for property in the City of

St. Louis described it with particularity but did not allege that the property was located in the district of the justice. The defendant

applied for certiorari and the cause was removed to the circuit court. 

In the application for certiorari the defendant stated that the suit was for the recovery of possession of the premises "situated in the said Ninth District of the City of St. Louis, Missouri." 

At the trial in the circuit court a jury was waived and evidence offered and the court made a finding of facts, but there was no evidence offered that the property was located within the district of the justice. Under such circumstances the St. Louis Court of Appeals holds that

The complaint was not fatally defective for failure to allege that such property was within the district where the suit was brought but that such jurisdictional fact should have been shown by the proof and by the judgment, and since such facts did not so appear, the cause was reversed and remanded for another trial. The court found that its opinion and its former opinion in Barry v. Bannerman, 175 Mo. 

A. 142, 157 S.W. 853, are in conflict with the opinion of the Kansas 

City Court of Appeals in the case of State ex rel. Brown v. Bird, 228 Mo. A. 800, 73 S.W. (2d) 821, and ordered the cause certified and transferred to the Supreme Court. (Note: The appellate court evidently considers the matter one of jurisdiction, as it holds that it was not cured by the fact that the application of defendant for certiorari stated that the property was situated in the justice's district.) 

Sec. 215 (d)-Note 45. 

Barber v. Todd et al. (App.), 128 S.W. (2d) 290. 

Sec. 224.

As to title not being involved in unlawful detainer, see Peoples 

Finance Corporation v. Lincoln et al, 345 Mo. 113, 131 S.W. (2d) 520.

Sec. 233-Note 56. 

In a case by the State of Missouri to collect a sales tax, judgment having been obtained in an amount within the pecuniary jurisdiction of the court, the defendant applied to the Circuit Court and obtained a writ of certiorari on the ground that the justice was without jurisdiction, but the court quashed the writ before a return was filed. 

This action was upheld by the Supreme Court. State of Missouri ex rel. Berra v. Sestric, 349 Mo. 182, 159 S.W. (2d) 786. This kind of certiorari, i.e., the usual species of that writ, must be distinguished from the statutory writ in unlawful detainer case. The author remarks as to the writ of certiorari in unlawful detainer: "This proceeding is not one of review"; the whole case is transferred to the circuit court for trial and judgment.

Sec. 402. 

Morris v. Karr, 342 Mo. 179, 114 S.W. (2d) 962.

This was a case where there were exceptions to and appeal from the action of the county court in vacating a portion of a county road and a change of the road at a certain point a few hundred feet before it connected with another highway. The attack was direct, i.e., by appeal, and was grounded on the failure to comply with the statute providing that, "No county court shall order a road established or changed until said proposed road or proposed change has been examined and appoved by the county highway engineer." The circuit court also ordered the portion of road vacated. The Supreme Court held that the approval of the county highway engineer was a condition precedent to the making of the order by the county court and such approval not having been obtained, the order of the county court was "void" because of its failure first to obtain the county highway engineer's approval. The Supreme Court concludes its opinion as follows: "The circuit court therefore had no jurisdiction and its judgment should be reversed."

Since the County Court had obtained jurisdiction by the petition of respondents to vacate or change the road in question, it would seem to have had jurisdiction to proceed to final judgment, however erroneous that judgment might be. However, the Supreme Court was cor-

rect in holding that the statute was mandatory in its requirement to secure approval of the highway engineer before proceeding to vacate or change the road. The circuit court erred in affirming the county court's order, but the circuit court had jurisdiction to determine the matter on appeal and should have reversed the action of the County Court and vacated its order. The opinion of the Supreme Court says, 1.c. (Mo.) 183: "In Sturgeon v. Hampton, 88 Mo. 203, at 213, the rule was early announced which has been generally recognized in this State as follows: 'The county courts are not the general agents of the counties or of the state. Their powers are limited and defined by law. These statutes constitute their warrant of authority. Whenever they step outside of and beyond their statutory authority their acts are void.' 

The court goes on to say that it should go far to uphold the acts of the county court when they are merely irregular, but such acts are not irregularities and are void when made without any warrant or authority in law."

In view of the fact that the Supreme Court holds that failure to secure approval of the County Highway Engineer deprived the County Court of jurisdiction to make an order, then it would seem that the fact of approval by such engineer must of necessity appear in the record of proceedings before the county court and as a part of its order, otherwise the same would be subject to collateral attack. In other words, all facts necessary to the jurisdiction of a court of limited jurisdiction should appear in its record. Local courts and courts of inferior jurisdiction must keep within the prescribed powers of their creation, and where their judgments are called in question, the record should show affirmatively all the facts necessary to give the court jurisdiction both of the subject matter of the suit and the parties to it. See Schell v. Leland, 45 Mo. 289. This rule has been limited, however, to cases where the attack is direct. See State v. 

Corneli (Mo.), 171 S.W. (2d) 687, and the cases cited therein under points (1-4). 

In view of the fact that the result would be practically the same, to-wit, the vacating of the order of the county court, the question is academic so far as the instant case is concerned, but it would perhaps be more proper to say that the county court exceeded its power rather than that it had no jurisdiction since it had general jurisdiction over the subject matter, to-wit, that of changing or vacating roads.

In re Decker's Estate, 348 Mo. 32, 152 S.W. (2d) 104, the Probate

Court had under consideration a proceeding to discover assets against the survivor of a joint bank account and tried the same notwithstanding it involved the right to such account of a survivor who was charged to have fraudulently procured the account to be placed in joint names of himself and deceased. Sec. 512-Note 20. 

Whitworth v. Monahan's Estate (App.), 111 S.W. (2d) 931.

An action originating in the probate court by a claim which alleged in effect that claimant at deceased's request rendered certain services between a certain date and the date of his death; that for said services the deceased agreed to pay claimant as compensation the entire amount of his estate at his death; that under and by virtue of his will said decedent wholly failed to provide for claimant. The claimant then stated that the inventoried value of the estate was a certain sum and that her demand was the same sum. 

Upon the claim being disallowed she appealed to the Circuit Court, where the judgment was affirmed. Upon appeal the appellate court held that the statement showed that the action was upon an express contract and not upon the implied promise to pay the reasonable value of the services; further, it was an action for the specific performance of a contract partially performed and therefore there was no jurisdiction over such a cause in the probate court since the statement itself discloses that it is an action in equity. 

Sec. 512.

In re Ermeling's Estate. Tuttle v. Uncker (Mo. App.), 131 S.W. (2d) 912.

Notes secured by trust deeds, which were executed in favor of guardian and curator of insane person by his (guardian's) wife, and represented improper loan made by guardian and curator to himself from estate funds, should not be canceled by circuit court on appeal

from orders of probate court on exceptions to final settlement, since cancellation of notes would be tantamount to canceling trust deed, which only court of equity could do. 

Sec. 513-Note 25. 

Smith v. St. Louis Union Trust Co., 340 Mo. 979, 104 S.W. (2d) 341.

The provision of a will which grants the executor authority, without approval of the probate court, to sell securities, does not of itself create such executor a trustee so as to give the circuit court jurisdiction of a proceeding to charge the administrator with a loss for the untimely sale of securities. That jurisdiction remains in the probate court unless the action is upon a bond of the executor given for the benefit of that estate; the depositing by a trust company of securities with the finance commissioner to qualify it as administrator and executor generally is not of that character.

Sec. 515-Note 41. 

State ex rel. North St. Louis Trust Co. v. Wolfe, 343 Mo. 580, 122 S.W. (2d) 909. 

A legatee filed an affidavit to discover assets and citation was issued; the respondent appeared and admitted that she had the property described but denied that she wrongfully withheld said property. In the answers to the interrogatories filed it developed that respondent claimed one part of the bonds as an outright gift and a certain remaining $5,000 bond as a gift by deceased in trust for another. 

That other person as cestui qui trust filed suit in the circuit court against the respondent to the interrogatories, and joined the executor. 

The question arose whether the Circuit Court (this being an application for writ of prohibition against said court) could, (1) proceed to try the case at all; (2) whether it had jurisdiction to try the entire matter. The Supreme Court made the preliminary writ permanent, prohibiting respondent from determining the issues in the suit except as to the alleged trust respecting the $5,000 bond, and as to that feature the writ was quashed.

Sec. 519-Note 66. 

Section 5, R.S. Mo. 1929, provides that: "All orders, settlements, trials and other proceedings contemplated by articles one to thirteen, inclusive, of this chapter shall be had or made in the county in which the letters testamentary or of administration were granted." 1 This language would seem to confine proceedings in the circuit court in establishing demands to the circuit court of that county in which the estate is being administered, yet under decisions of the Supreme Court such is not the case. Such suits in the circuit court are governed by the code of civil procedure and may be brought where the plaintiff resides and the defendant, administrator or executor can be served with summons. See State ex rel. Nute v. 

Bruce, 334 Mo. 1107, 70 S.W. (2d) 854; also, Sanders v. Savage, 234

Mo. A. 9, 129 S.W. (2d) 1061. There was a dissent by Judge Ellison in the Supreme Court case. He states that the effect of this construction is to make a suit in the circuit court to establish a demand against the estate of a decedent not a local but a transitory action. 

In view of the decision in Nute v. Bruce, the plaintiff in Sanders v. 

Savage brought a suit in Adair County, where he resided and served the administrator in that county. After judgment was obtained in favor of plaintiff and against the estate, the plaintiff moved for classification in the Putnam County Probate Court, where the estate was in process of administration. The Probate Court refused to classify the judgment on the ground of lack of jurisdiction of the Adair Circuit Court to render the judgment, because real estate belonging to deceased was located in Putnam County and the same would have to be sold to satisfy the judgment. This judgment was approved by the circuit court, but was reversed by the Court of Appeals.

Sec. 523-Note 74. 17 

Murphy v. Pfeifer (App.), 105 S.W. (2d) 39.

Question whether statement of a demand in the probate court was upon express contract and prevented the claimant from recovering upon quantum meruit on appeal to the circuit court was discussed in the above case. The appellate court upheld a recovery for the reasonable value of the services and held that technical precision should not be required of those pleadings or statements filed in the probate court. Such are of a summary character; to apply a strict construction to the rules of pleading therein would make of them a "trap to the unwary." 

Sec. 526-Note 87. 

In re Claus' Estate. 199. 

Sheehan v. Gillespie (Mo. A.), 147 S.W. (2d)

An order by the probate court surcharging certain costs and expenses which were charged by the administrator against the proceeds of the sale of real estate is triable by the court and the administrator is not entitled to a jury trial in the circuit court. It is a purely statutory proceeding originally cognizable before the probate judge alone, and as to which the power which the circuit court. derived on appeal is no greater and no less than that which the probate judge had exercised. In that connection the court cited State ex rel. v. Hostetter, 340 Mo. 965, 104 S.W. (2d) 303; also Ansley v.

Sec. 526. 

In re Helm's Estate (App.), 136 S.W. (2d) 416.

The statute of Missouri authorizes a minor under guardianship by appointment of the Probate Court to choose another guardian after attaining the age of fourteen years. Absent a showing that such person selected by the minor is unfit, the court has no discretion except to appoint the person so chosen. 

In the above case the father was the guardian under appointment of the Probate Court and the ward at the age of twenty chose another person. No question as to the selectee's fitness was raised and the probate court appointed the person chosen by the minor. The circuit court and appellate court both affirmed this action. 

The appellate court held that the denial of appellnat's demand for a jury in the circuit court was not error; neither was it necessary to make a finding of facts. The former guardian's application for jury trial was properly denied since no issue of fact as to fitness or unfitness had been raised. In the light of other decisions it is doubtful

whether a jury trial could be demanded since it is a statutory proceeding, but the court chose not to place its ruling upon that ground. 

The only issue it said was one of law, i.e., whether the ward's selection must be appointed where the question of fitness was not raised. 

Sec. 526-Note 91. 

See In re Claus' Estate. Sheehan v. Gillespie (Mo. A.), 147 S.W. (2d) 199. 

Sec. 527b-Note 96. 

Linville v. Ripley et al., 347 Mo. 95, 146 S.W. (2d) 581; Orchard v. 

Store Co., 225 Mo. 414, 125 S.W. 486, 20 Ann. Cas. 1072. These cases establish that a judgment of the Probate Court is subject to collateral attack where it is shown by the record of that court that an order was obtained without the necessary conditions; thus where an order of sale was obtained by one who was at that time not a creditor. 

The record itself must disclose such lack of jurisdiction. 

Sec. 530-Note 11.

In a In Woolery et al. v. Todd et al. (App.), 139 S.W. (2d) 1005, the testator had devised his personal estate, including a note secured by mortgage to his wife for her life and then to his children. suit by the children after the death of the widow to foreclose the mortgage, it was objected that the personal property belonged to the personal representative for administrative purposes and that he alone could maintain such an action. It was held by the Appellate Court that the legatees could maintain the action and that the appointment of an administrator of the widow for the sole purpose of delivering the note and mortgage was unnecessary since there were no creditors. The court said, 1.c. 1007: "* * The interest of (the widow) in the note in controversy ceased and terminated at her death, and no beneficial interest therein would have passed to her personal representative, if one had been appointed. His sole duty in the premises would have been to deliver the note to the plaintiffs in this case. It would not have been an asset of her estate. It is an elementary rule that neither a court of equity nor a court of law require the doing of a vain and useless thing."
