Sec. 564-Note 31. 

State ex rel. Pryor v. Anderson, 343 Mo. 895, 123 S.W. (2d) 181. (Quashing mandamus (App.), 112 S.W. (2d) 857) holds:

If proof be made that no persons entitled to preference in the right to administer reside in Missouri, the probate court is not required to wait the statutory 30 days after death of intestate, notwithstanding distributees did not file a renunciation of their preferences. 

Sec. 564 Note 31. 

State ex rel. Pryor v. Anderson (App.), 112 S.W. (2d) 857.

Where there are no distributees of an intestate resident of this state and proof of that fact is made, the probate court may appoint the public administrator to take charge of the estate and need not wait for the lapse of time provided by statute for such distributees or any of them to file, and there is no error in the probate court's refusal to revoke appointment of the public administrator even though one of the distributees afterwards becomes a resident. This decision was certified to the Supreme Court; see same case, 343 Mo. 895, 123 S.W. (2d) 181, and was affirmed. The court distinguishes between this case and that where there are resident distributees who are all minors, as in In re Allen's Estate; Cross et al. v. Mullins (Mo.), 271 

S.W. 755, in which it is held that such minors are entitled to the full statutory period on the theory that their guardian might be a suitable person for such appointment and that the statute as to non-residence of the distributees is not applicable. See also, Tittman v. Edwards, 27 Mo. A. 492, which is held not in conflict with the principal case.

In that case a resident was appointed before the public administrator applied and it was held not error to revoke the appointment on application by the public administrator. 

Sec. 569-Note 51. 

Sudekum v. Fasnacht's Estate (App.), 157 S.W. (2d) 264. In this case the executor was devised a piece of real property if he paid $2000 into the estate. A will contest was filed and the respective attorneys upon a hearing to remove the executor agreed that if the executor were present he would testify that he would not pay $2000 to obtain the property. The Circuit Court suspended the executor pending the will contest and the executor appealed. It was contended on appeal that since he had no interest in the estate other than his fee that the order of suspension was not proper. The Court of Appeals held that renunciation of such right to the devise could be made only by some express overt act on the part of the executor and not by some admission or declaration by his attorney. Absent such an act on the part of the executor, he was still a party in interest and the order was affirmed. 

Sec. 582.

In State ex rel. Gnekow v. U. S. Fidelity and Guaranty Co., 349 

Mo. 528, 163 S.W. (2d) 86, the court clarified the liability of sureties in Missouri. The question as to whether surety on administrator's bond should be held liable for property belonging to a third person under the claim by the administrator that it is an estate asset was disposed of in favor of the rule that the surety is liable to the third person to the extent that the assets of the estate are increased by the conversion of such other person's assets. The converse of this rule also holds in this state, viz., that an administrator's bond should be held liable for property belonging to the estate but actually withheld by the administrator to the extent that the assets of the estate are diminished. See the valuable discussion by Judge Hyde, 1.c. 89 (S.W.) et seq. 

Sec. 583. 

Smith v. St. Louis Union Trust Co., 340 Mo. 979, 104 S.W. (2d) 341.

A residuary legatee may sue on administrator's or executor's bond in circuit court before final settlement of the estate, if estate debts have been paid. 

Sec. 583. 

Smith v. St. Louis Union Trust Co., 340 Mo. 979, 104 S.W. (2d) 341.

The corporate trust company had securities on deposit with the 44

227 finance commissioner of Missouri for the purpose of qualifying under the law to act as executor or administrator of estates generally. The plaintiff brought suit against such executor in the circuit court to recover for stocks sold by it which it was alleged were held and not timely sold by which the estate sustained a severe loss. 

The statute, Sec. 281, 1939 (282, 1929) provides that suit may be brought on the bond of any executor or administrator in the name of the state to the use of the injured party for the waste or mismanagement of the estate or other breach of the condition of such bond and the damages assessed thereon, etc.

This section gives the circuit court jurisdiction in suits on such bonds but not otherwise. So where there is no bond in the particular estate, i.e., where the executor is acting without bond, or where, as here, the executor has not given a bond in the particular estate, no suit lies in the circuit court; the Supreme Court holds that the injured person's remedy is on exceptions to the final report for such mismanagement. All such powers which formerly resided in chancery are now by statute relegated to the probate court. The probate court has exclusive jurisdiction of matters pertaining directly to the settle ment of the estate except as to the jurisdiction conferred on circuit courts by statute for suits on the statutory bond of the executor or administrator.

Leach v. Armstrong et al., (App.), 156 S.W. (2d) 959.

While such order would not protect the administrator where the rights of creditors are involved, it will operate by way of waiver or estoppel as against those persons entering into such mutual agreements.

Sec. 624.

A note endorsed and delivered to bank by payee as collateral security for latter's indebtedness to bank was payee's property when she died and became asset of her estate, bank not being absolute owner thereof, but trustee with respect to payee's interest therein. 

Sec. 625 Note 31. 

The text is in error. The case cited, Nye v. U. S. Fidelity & 

Guaranty Co., holds that the personal representative is liable in his official capacity in action either of replevin or conversion in this state where he takes possession of property belonging to another than decedent even though his action is in good faith. See also to same effect State ex rel. Gnekow v. United States Fidelity & Guaranty Co., 150 S.W. (2d) 581.

Sec. 625-Note 32. 

The divorced wife of deceased and his administrator both claimed certain insurance and in action in circuit court by way of interpleader that court awarded the fund to the administrator and the divorced wife appealed without giving bond. The administrator possessed himself of the fund but the appellate court reversed the circuit court (after Certiorari to the Supreme Court). In the meantime the administrator had used a part of the fund for attorney's fees and costs. Held in action against administrator and on the bond that judgment would go for the entire fund. State ex rel. Gnekow v. 

United States Fidelity & Guaranty Co., 150 S.W. (2d) 581.

It became executors' duty to collect note inventoried as asset of deceased's estate after bank to which deceased pledgd it as collateral security for debt, returned it to executors on discovering that deceased's notes evidencing debt were barred by limitation, either by action at law on collateral note or by charging amount thereof against interest in estate devised by deceased to maker, where will did not release or remit latter's debt to deceased.

Sec. 630.

Field v. French's Estate (App.), 106 S.W. (2d) 925.

Under the facts in this case it was held the order of the probate court for executor to take possession of realty disposed of by the will as necessary for the payment of debts was not justified. 

Sec. 630 (d).

Under the statute prior to 1939 the proceeds from the sale of real estate when necessary to pay debts or legacies could not be applied to the expenses of administration. A proviso added to the statute (Sec. 141, R.S. Mo. 1939), provides: "That where real estate is sold to pay debts and legacies the proceeds from the sale thereof may be used when necessary to pay expenses of administration before being applied to the payment of debts and legacies." See as to necessity of debts of deceased as condition to an order of sale. re Claus Estate (App.), 147 S.W. (2d) 199. 

Sec. 630 (d)-Note 89. In 

See, however, In re Foeste's Estate, 153 S.W. (2d) 802, where part of proceeds from sale of real property was applied to widow's statutory allowance. 

Sec. 631. 

Hoshaw v. Fenton, 232 Mo. A. 137, 110 S.W. (2d) 1140.

The deceased undertook to make an assignment of his automobile by an instrument other than the certificate of title; as this is not in accordance with the statute requiring the certificate of ownership to pass between the buyer and seller, the purported transferee had no title either legal or equitable, and the deceased owner's executor was entitled to possession of the automobile and could maintain an action in replevin to recover it.

Under such circumstances the purported vendee could not in the replevin action maintain a counterclaim for services to deceased. His only relief is by way of claim against the estate for such services. 

Since the statute requiring a transfer and delivery of the certificate of ownership is required by statute before any interest in the automobile will pass the case holds that the executor is not a trustee of the legal title for the benefit of the purported purchaser as it is against public policy to recognize any interest either legal or equitable in such automobile without compliance with the statute.

Sec. 631-Note 98. 

Magee v. Pope et al., 234 Mo. A. 191, 112 S.W. (2d) 891. "Where the good will of a business is based solely on the professional skill, personal ability, integrity, high standing, learning and acknowledged repute of the owner, then such good will is not dependent on any particular place or locality. These qualities are not transmissible, and when the owner, who possesses these traits dies, the qualities he possesses, the good will, is 'gone with the wind' if we may use the title of a popular Civil War story." 

The plaintiff succeeded in getting a court of equity to cancel a promissory note given by a physician to the widow of a deceased physician for the good will in the practice of medicine. The court said that even if such good will had survived his death it would be an asset of the estate; but it is evident from the expressions of the court and the authorities cited that the court was of the opinion that no such good will associated with his office survived his death.

Sec. 632-Note 26. 

Metzger v. Metzger (App.), 153 S.W. (2d) 118.

In this case the mother of deceased sought an accounting against his widow for profits of a business carried on by the widow after his death. The court holds that the widow as administratrix could be required to account for such profits in the Probate Court; that under the Constitution and laws of the State the Probate Court had exclusive jurisdiction, and that the Circuit Court was without jurisdiction therein. The court said, 1.c. 121: "It is well established that an administrator who carries on the business of a testator, without an order of court, or engages in business with the funds of the estate, is guilty of a breach of trust and the law charges him with all losses that have been incurred, without allowing him the benefits of any of the profits he may make. *** undoubtedly, the administrator under such circumstances, may be required to account for any profits realized. However, such profits belong to the estate; and in the petition involved herein there is no allegation that there are no creditors of the estate. We are of the opinion that the Probate Court of Jackson County is possessed of the necessary powers and facilities to require such an accounting and, this being so, the 

Circuit Court had no jurisdiction."

27 relating to discovery of assets in the Probate Court. But 'It is a general rule that a probate court has no equitable jurisdiction; no jurisdiction to try issues which are purely equitable in their nature and where the relief demanded is equitable.'" (1.c. 155, S.W.). In this case the deceased during his last illness and in contemplation of death had given a safety deposit box containing certain bonds and certificates of deposit to plaintiff and told her to keep said box and contents and upon his death to divide it equally among herself and her three sisters. This was held to create a question as to trust over which probate court had no jurisdiction. The court refused to entertain the doctrine that the probate court had jurisdiction to determine the question of trust or no trust before the question of establishing and enforcing the same in the circuit court could arise. 

While there were some expressions to the effect that the Probate Court does have such jurisdiction to determine first the question of trust or no trust in North St. Louis Trust Co. v. Wolfe, 343 Mo. 580, 122 S.W. (2d) 909, l.c. 911 (S.W.), they were not approved in the instant case.

Sec. 641-Note 24. 

In re Geel's Estate. Coleman v. Forestner (App.), 143 S.W. (2d) 327.

A joint account in the name of deceased and the survivor under an agreement that deceased was to have the interest during her lifetime as well as a contingent interest in the principal but that it should belong to the survivor is treated as executed upon death of the per son creating it and may be reached by proceeding to discover assets. 

The issue is treated as one at law and not in equity. It would be otherwise if the trust were not executed. 

Sec. 645.

This case deals with a judgment on pleadings after interrogatories and answers filed. Judgment on the pleadings against one of the defendants for a certain sum was reversed by the appellate court. 

That court while holding such judgment proper where no issue was presented for hearing found that there was an issue upon which the defendant was entitled to jury trial and reversed and remanded the case.

Sec. 645-Note 40.

Judgment for plaintiff on pleadings was held improper where answer to interrogatories in effect denied that defendant was at any time in possession of any money belonging to estate. This was held sufficient as a denial. 

Sec. 645 Note 40.

In this case it was held that where the administrator's answer to interrogatories stated that certain envelopes found in decedent's deposit box had been delivered to the persons whose names appeared thereon as directed by order of court based upon a petition filed by the heirs and waivers signed by them, this was sufficient pleading of estoppel to permit the administrator to rely thereon as a defense. 

Sec. 647 (d)-Note 52.

Where a wife had invested funds of husband in corporate stock taken in her own name and placed in safe deposit box in her name to which he had access the probate court could not order a delivery of such stock by her administrator after her death to the husband on the theory that she held such stock as trustee since such became a matter for the circuit court exercising equitable powers to try. In re Main's Estate. Cox et al. v. Main (App.), 152 S.W. (2d) 696.

Sec. 648. 

The judgment of the court in a proceeding to discover assets can only be for the specific personal property discovered and not for its value or for the impressment of a lien thereon; not only that; apparently the probate court is unable to make such order to deliver property so discovered if its ownership comes about on the theory of resulting trust. See In re Main's Estate. Cox et al. v. Main (App.), 152 S.W. (2d) 696. 

Sec. 652.

An interesting case which should be a warning to Executors and 

Administrators is Woodbury v. Connecticut Mutual Life Ins. Co. et al. 

(Mo.), 166 S.W. (2d) 552, 1.c. 556, in which the Court says: "Under the will of his uncle, Charles P. Woodbury was named executor and given full power and discretion to invest the funds of the estate in any manner he might deem proper. The will further provided that, if he should survive appellant and another, each of whom was his elder, he would become the absolute owner of the entire estate. No doubt he felt safe in investing the trust funds in his own name, but

fate decreed that he should meet an accidental death and that appellant should survive him and become the sole owner of the estate. 

Of course, he had no legal right to invest trust funds in his own name and appellant may recover such funds or property wherever she finds them except from an innocent purchaser for value without knowledge or notice."

Sec. 680-Note 73. 

Holmes v. Scott et al., 231 Mo. A. 690, 105 S.W. (2d) 966.

The deceased left land to the defendant for five years, at the end of which period the will directed that the land be sold and the proceeds divided between plaintiff and defendant. 

The plaintiff brought this suit in partition. The defendant had previously executed a deed of trust in the nature of a mortgage upon the land to secure a debt, but now resists partition on the ground that there was by the terms of the will a conversion of the land to personalty. This principle is recognized by the court, but it holds that both parties have elected to reconvert it back to realty, the plaintiff by bringing a partition suit and the defendant by executing a deed of trust upon the property.

The parties did not reconvert by mutual contemporaneous agreement, but this is held not essential. The election to reconvert may be made at different times provided all parties interested have elected to reconvert.

It is also held that the administrator, c.t.a., is not a necessary party to such reconversion. 

Numerous cases are cited upon conversion and reconversion. 

Sec. 684 Note 3. 

In re Adams Estate. Adams et al. v. Meyers (App.), 139 S.W. (2d) 

1037. Where partition suit pending in circuit court at the time of filing of petition for sale of realty to pay debts in probate court was dismissed, and one of defendants in original partition suit afterwards filed another partition suit subsequent to filing of petition in probate court, probate court had jurisdiction. Citing King v. Ayres, 168 Mo. 

250, 67 S.W. 1100. 

Sec. 686 Note 9.

In re Claus' Estate. Sheehan v. Gillespie (App.), 147 S.W. (2d) 199. 

In 1939 the legislature added a proviso to the statute as to sale of real property which authorized the proceeds from the sale of real property to be used to pay the expenses of administration before being applied to the payment of debts and legacies. Of course it is still a

prerequisite to the sale of real property under that provision that the sale be necessary to pay debts and legacies. 

The 1939 provision is not retroactive to estates of persons deceased prior to the date the proviso became effective. In the above case the appellate court held that under the law prior to the 1939 proviso the proceeds from the sale of real property to pay debts and legacies could be used to pay the costs necessarily incident to the sale and no other. The costs of the order of sale could be paid on the theory that it was implied from the power granted. 

Sec. 715. 

Briscoe v. Merchants & Miners Bank (App.), 102 S.W. (2d) 751.

Plaintiff, a widow, sued the bank for the amount on deposit to the credit of her deceased husband. It was contended by the bank that the sum ($72.85) had been paid out at her request to the undertaker for funeral expenses.

The court holds that such sum was a part of her absolute property and right to such credit vested in her immediately upon his death; since she was entitled to it she would be estopped to claim it in the action if the bank paid it out either at her oral or written request. 

Sec. 716. 

Under the statute (Sec. 106, R.S. Mo., 1939) entitling widow to keep as her absolute property family Bible and other books not to exceed value of $200, and household and kitchen furniture not to exceed value of $500, widow is not entitled to $200 cash allowance in lieu of family Bible and other books and $500 cash allowance in lieu of furniture, where such articles are not in existence. See In re 

Evans Estate, Evans v. Moore (K. C. Ct. App.), 165 S.W. (2d) 705.

In re Foeste's Estate. McWilliams v. Foeste (App.), 153 S.W. (2d) 

802. Sec. 733. 

Kay v. Politte et al., 344 Mo. 805, 129 S.W. (2d) 863.

The deceased's debts incurred after he acquired such homestead and not specially charged against such homestead during his life cannot be a charge against such homestead after his death.

Sec. 741. 

Dreckshage v. Dreckshage (Sup.), 176 S.W. (2d) 7.

Where one executes a deed to another and the latter by separate writing makes a written declaration of trust in favor of the grantor, at or about the time of the original conveyance, the grantee in the original deed was not seized of such a beneficial interest as to entitle his wife to dower upon his death. The beneficial interest remained in the grantor.

Testator 13 days before death conveyed the bulk of his estate to trustees, making certain allowances therein for support of his wife.

Sec. 748. 

The right to renounce a gift by will is not confined to the statutory provisions, nor is it confined to widow's election; it is applicable to anyone. A gift to one may be determined by such person to be not beneficial. An important case on this point is Sanders v. Jones et al., 347 Mo. 255, 147 S.W. (2d) 424, where the court recognized the right of a son to renounce a gift of both real and personal property but held it would not be allowed in that case because untimely, having been made fifteen months after death of testator. The court said the ordinary principle of acceptance of the gift would be presumed because beneficial, but if timely renunciation had been made it would go back to the death of testator. The question arose out of the action of attaching creditors, after which attachment, a child of the devisee brought action to determine title in himself as the next in line. 

Sec. 748.

Lee's Summit Building & Loan Assn. v. Cross, 345 Mo. 501, 134 

S.W. (2d) 19.

After renunciation of a will, surviving spouse is entitled to an election to take a child's part in lieu of dower. 

Sec. 748-Note 60. 

A widow is entitled to statutory allowance even if she effectively renounces the will and elects to take a one-half interest in the estate. 

Whether she takes under the will or under the statute she is entitled to the statutory allowances unless the will under which she elects to take expressly provides that the provisions are in lieu of such statutory allowances. The provision of the will that it is in lieu of dower does not deprive her of statutory allowances. In re Wahl's 

Estate. Wahl v. Wahl's Estate (App.), 158 S.W. (2d) 743. 

Sec. 748-Note 69. 

Ferguson v. Long et al., 341 Mo. 182, 107 S.W. (2d) 7.

The provision of the statute as to what shall be done in order to make an election by a widow as to provisions of will in lieu of dower, is mandatory. The statute requires that she must file such election within one year after the first publication of letters granted to administrator. See the citation of authorities in this case and discussion as to what constitutes such filing. 

Sec. 752-Note 18. 

Is there a necessity for election by widow to take one-half of the personal property where the deceased left no children and the will's provisions are in lieu of dower and statutory provisions?

See Nies v. Stone, 232 Mo. A. 1226, 117 S.W. (2d) 407, holding it is not necessary. It is necessary as between the will and dower (i.e., common law dower), but not a prerequisite in order to take as her absolute right one-half of personal property subject to debts. In this case the husband died during pendency of life estate in real property in which he was the remainderman in fee, but the real question was as to the widow's right to a one-half interest in the personal estate without election. The court held she was so entitled and discussed the following cases: (1) Bryant, Adm'r, v. Christian, Adm'r (Mo.), 58 Mo. 98; (2) Perry v. Strawbridge, 209 Mo. 621, 108 S.W. 641, 16 L.R.A.,

N.S., 244, 123 Am. St. Rep. 510, 14 Ann. Cas. 92 (Contains a history of the Missouri law of descent and distribution.); (3) State ex rel. McClintock v. Guinotte, 275 Mo. 298, 204 S.W. 806; (4) Klocke v. Klocke, 276 Mo. 572, 208 S.W. 825; (5) Scott v. Scott, 324 Mo. 1055, 26 S.W. (2d) 598; (6) Von Arb v. Thomas, 163 Mo. 33, 63 S.W. 94; (7) Lynch v. Jones (Mo.), 247 S.W. 123; (8) Hall v. Smith, 103 Mo. 289, 15 S.W. 621; (9) Waters v. Herboth, 178 Mo. 166, 77 S.W. 305; (10) Brown v. Tucker's Estate, 135 Mo. A. 598, 117 S.W. 96. 

Sec. 754. 

Hax v. O'Donnell, 234 Mo. A. 636, 117 S.W. (2d) 667.

In this case a wife endorsed four checks payable to her amounting to $2,045 to her husband and after his death sought to have the sum allowed her under Sec. 325, R.S. Mo. 1939, as personal property which came to the possession of her husband with her written assent. 

The mere endorsement is not such written assent as to give him ownership, as held in the cases cited. The probate court, and the circuit court after it received the case from the probate court after it was certified thereto, chose to treat the application as a claim against the estate and since there was no notice to the executor of the filing thereof it was dismissed. Thereupon, the plaintiff began this action in the circuit court in the first instance as a bill in equity to have the sum set aside to her under that section. 

This was also denied her and the appeal followed. The Court of 

Appeals holds that she should have appealed from the original dismissal; that the probate court has jurisdiction to set aside such property in cases where it is reduced to possession with her written assent and in cases where it is not with her written assent (as in this case) that she might treat it as property held in trust or as a debt.

Sec. 755.

Schuster v. Schuster, 340 Mo. 1110, 104 S.W. (2d) 353.

The statute providing how widow should elect to take one-half of real and personal estate of husband dying without lineal descendants embraced whole procedure of widow's election and is complete within itself.

The statute should be liberally construed. 

Sec. 755. 

Garrett v. Damron et al. (Mo.), 110 S.W. (2d) 1112.

A widower's failure to elect between dower and one-half of real esetate in which wife had vested remainder interest in fee did not waive widower's right to one-half interest, where life tenant was in possession of real estate at time of wife's death, since widower was not then entitled to dower and, therefore, there was nothing on which to elect. 

Sec. 757.

If a deceased spouse dies intestate, it is only necessary for the surviving spouse to make an election by the method required by statute, in order to take an absolute interest subject to debts, and if no such election is made within time specified, surviving spouse is endowed with a one-third interest for life free from debts. Rev. 

Stat. Mo. 1939, Secs. 318, 319, 329. 

Sec. 759 (a). 

In re Flynn's Estate (App.), 142 S.W. (2d) 1069.

Personal representative is not entitled to take credit in settlement for amounts paid for masses for deceased since they are not debts created by the deceased nor can they be classified as costs of administration. 

Sec. 759 (c)-Note 20. 

In re Flynn's Estate (App.), 142 S.W. (2d) 1069. 

Sec. 760-(Limitations). 

In re Jackman's Estate. Flink v. Parcell, 344 Mo. 49, 124 S.W. (2d) 1189.

The filing of a claim cannot be considered as a scire facias to revive a judgment or as a continuance of a scire facias proceeding to revive a judgment brought before death of judgment debtor. 

Where a judgment creditor sued out a scire facias to revive a judgment within ten years of rendition, and made personal service upon

judgment debtor, without any order or judgment of revival ever being made, the creditor was not entitled to maintain a claim against debtor's estate filed more than ten years after rendition of judgment. 

Sec. 760-Notes 60 and 61. 

Broz v. Broz (App.), 132 S.W. (2d) 1039.

No formal pleadings are required in the probate court and the statute of limitations may be interposed as a defense at the hearing without written or formal plea. So also the plaintiff has the privilege of establishing such facts as will take the claim out from the general statutes of limitation.

Sec. 760-Note 63. 

Broz v. Broz (App.), 132 S.W. (2d) 1039. 

Sec. 760 (b). 

Rowe v. Strother et al., 341 Mo. 1149, 111 S.W. (2d) 93.

The above case involved the proper construction of a clause in testatrix' will. The clause was, as follows: "I give, devise and bequeath to my physician and friend, Dr. W. 

G. Rowe, the sum of One thousand dollars for the reason that he has been my physician for years and I never felt as though I had paid him what his services were worth and in addition ot said One thousand dollars, I want my executors to pay him a reasonable sum for his services as my physician. He has not only been my physician but one of my best personal friends in Blue Springs." (Italics ours.)

After the expiration of the statutory period for the filing of demands against the estate the Doctor filed in the probate court a claim for $10,000 which he asserted was the reasonable value of his services which he claimed as a legacy under the will and upon its disallowance an appeal was taken. Claimant offered evidence as to the meaning of the will and to show the intent of the testator. These witnesses testified in the circuit court, but the finding was against the claimant. He sought to have the provision of the will declared a legacy.

The Supreme Court held that it was unambiguous and that claimant could not show by extrinsic evidence that she meant one thing when she had said another. However clearly an intention not expressed in the will may be proved by extrinsic evidence, the rule of law requiring wills to be in writing stands as an insuperable barrier against carrying the intention thus proved into execution. Citing 

28 R.C.L. 243.

In holding that the bequest was the recognition of a debt rather !

than a legacy, the court emphasized certain things as tending to show that, to-wit: (1) That although testatrix made the will a short time before her death, the doctor's services were expected to continue up to the time of her death, which was uncertain. (2) There was no indication by the will as to what amounts, if any, she had previously paid her physician. (3) Although she wanted her executor to pay a reasonable sum for the doctor's services, it was left uncertain as to how the amount was to be determined, as the will did not clothe them with such discretion; or if by the court, the only method was by adjudication of debts against the estate by the filing of a demand in the probate court. 

The uncertainty of the language therefore tended to the conclusion that it was merely the recognition of an unliquidated debt and was not a legacy. The court coming to this conclusion held the claim was barred because not filed in the statutory time. 

Sec. 760 (b). 

Curtin v. Woolley et al. (App.), 114 S.W. (2d) 191.

The mere exhibiting of a demand to the administrator or executor under Sec. 185, R.S. Mo. 1939, without being accompanied by the instrument of writing or account upon which the same is founded or without the notice in writing to the administrator or executor under 

Sec. 194, R.S. Mo. 1939, that he will present the same for allowance at the next regular or adjourned term of the court will not give the probate court jurisdiction and therefore does not toll the statute of limitations.

The court also held that even though the estate be closed without publication of final notice, it would in such case bar the filing of a suit after the one year limitation had passed.

Sec. 760 (b)-Note 96. 

Howard's Estate v. Howe, 344 Mo. 1245, 131 S.W. (2d) 517. 

Sturdy v. Smith (App.), 132 S.W. (2d) 1033.

Sec. 760 (b)-Note 100. 

Sturdy v. Smith (App.), 132 S.W. (2d) 1033. In this case a father conveyed land to his daughter and she agreed to pay her brother the purchase price; thereafter the father died. It was held there was a vendor's lien in favor of the brother which could be foreclosed; that the special statute of limitations on claims was not applicable and that an action in the nature of a foreclosure proceeding would be subject only to the general statute of limitations from the time obligation to pay matured.

Sec. 761 

Liebaart v. Hoehle's Estate (App.), 111 S.W. (2d) 925.

Statutes providing for presentation of demands against estates in probate court and determination thereof summarily and without form of pleading are not to be given a narrow construction or restricted application; the purpose of such statutes is to make it easy for persons not learned in the law to present their demands against estates. 

Sec. 763 (c)-Note 21. 

Liebaart v. Hoehle's Estate (App.), 111 S.W. (2d) 925.

The purpose intended to be accomplished by the statutes for the presentation of demands against estates was to make it easy for persons not learned in the law to present their demands against estates in the probate court and to have them passed upon and determined there as well as on appeal in the circuit court without being held to technical formalities and rules. "Our courts have uniformly given full effect to the plainly evident and laudable legislative purpose by steadfastly refusing to give to the statutes mentioned a narrow construction or restricted application." 

Sec. 763 (e).

St. Louis Fire & Marine Ins. Co. v. Wagoner (App.), 119 S.W. 

(2d) 1007.

The statutory requirement that a claimant against an estate shall file an affidavit or make oath in open court in verification of a demand before the court may allow such demand, is jurisdictional upon the question of right of court to entertain and allow the demand, and if the administrator in such case or someone else file a demand without the claimant appearing and filing affdavit or making oath in open court in verification of the demand an allowance of such demand is void and the court's order that the demand be placed in the fifth class is not res judicata against the claimant. 

It is proper in such case for the claimant to file a petition in the circuit court as a direct proceeding to set aside the allowance, as the irregularity does not appear on the face of the order. In the instant case the petitioner sought to have the order set aside so that it might pursue its suit to impress certain funds in the bank as trust funds to satisfy its claim. 

Sec. 768, Schaefer v. Magel's Estate, 233 Mo. A. 778, 108 S.W. (2d) 608.

Gives a thorough exposition of the statutory limitation as to exhibition, presentation and classification of claims in the probate court.

Sec. 773 (a)-Note 76. 

Smith v. Staley (App.), 156 S.W. (2d) 766. 

Sec. 774 (d). 

Sanders v. Savage, 234 Mo. A. 9, 129 S.W. (2d) 1061. In this case a judgment was rendered on a demand for services in an action brought in the circuit court of a county other than that where the estate was being administered. It was held that the probate court could not refuse to classify the judgment as a claim against the estate where the judgment was regular on its face and there was nothing in the record to indicate any infirmity therein. 

Sec. 774 (d)-Note 98. 

The public administrator is bound by the action of the probate court in this state turning over to the foreign administratrix at the domicile of deceased certain personal property. An action by such public administrator against the foreign administratrix is a collateral attack and cannot be maintained. Such order of the probate court is in accordance with Sheehan v. First National Bank, 346 Mo. 227, 140 S.W. (2d) 1.

Sec. 776-Note 25. 

Section 5, R.S. Mo. 1929, provides: "All orders, settlements, trials and other proceedings contemplated by articles one to thirteen, inclusive, of this chapter shall be had or made in the county in which the letters testamentary or of administration were granted."

This language would seem to confine proceedings in the circuit court in establishing demands to the circuit court of that county in which the estate is being administered, yet under decisions of the Supreme Court such is not the case. Such suits in the circuit court are governed by the code of civil procedure and may be brought where the plaintiff resides and the defendant, administrator or executor can be served with summons. See State ex rel Nute v. 

Bruce, 334 Mo. 1107, 70 S.W. (2d) 854; also, Sanders v. Savage, 234 

Mo. A. 9, 129 S.W. (2d) 1061. There was a dissent by Judge Ellison in the Supreme Court case. He states that the effect of this construction is to make a suit in the circuit court to establish a demand against the estate of a decedent not a local but a transitory action. 

In view of the decision in Nute v. Bruce, the plaintiff in Sanders v. 

Savage brought a suit in Adair County where he resided and served the administrator in that county. After judgment was obtained in favor of plaintiff and against the estate, the plaintiff moved for clas-

sification in the Putnam County Probate Court where the estate was in process of administration. The Probate Court refused to classify the judgment on the ground of lack of jurisdiction to render the judgment because real estate belonging to deceased was located in Putnam County and the same would have to be sold to satisfy the judgment. This judgment was approved by the circuit court but was reversed by the Court of Appeals. 

Sec. 780-Note 73. 

Witte v. Smith (App.), 152 S.W. (2d) 661. 

Hurst v. Hurst's Estate (App.), 151 S.W. (2d) 543 (Board and Lodging).

Sec. 782-Note 36. 

Witte v. Smith (App.), 152 S.W. (2d) 661. 

Hurst v. Hurst's Estate (App.), 151 S.W. (2d) 543 (Board and Lodging).

Sec. 783. 

As to presumption that services to deceased were gratuitous where there is a family relationship; also that such presumption is not conclusive, see: 

Patrick v. Crank (App.), 110 S.W. (2d) 381. 

Liebaart v. Hoehle's Estate (App.), 111 S.W. (2d) 925.

Sec. 784. 

Runnels v. Allen's Adm'r, 169 S.W. (2d) 73 (St. L. Ct. App., 1943).

The deceased was a great-uncle of claimant who sought allowance against estate for services to deceased. An instruction that when one renders valuable services for another, the benefit of which the latter accepts, the law presumes that person for whom services were rendered contracted to pay person performing services the reasonable value thereof, is erroneous. See also Runnels v. Allen, 170 S.W. (2d) 

144, where it is held that whether the law presumes or implies promise or obligation to pay for services rendered depends on nature and relationship of parties, their circumstances in life, and all relevant circumstances. Whether the nephew performed services for his great, uncle under agreement or mutual understanding or intention that sevices should be paid for, was for jury in action against greatuncle's administrator to recover for services. 

Sec. 785.

As to whether services rendered by one not a member of decedent's family were gratuitous, see: 

Weisenborn v. Rutledge, 233 Mo. A. 464, 121 S.W. (2d) 309.

Sec. 785-Note 58. 

Murphy v. Pfeifer (App.), 105 S.W. (2d) 39.

Stranger rendering services to deceased was not presumed to have rendered services gratuitously. 

Sec. 787. 

Murphy v. Pfeifer (App.), 105 S.W. (2d) 39.

A statement filed in the probate court for the reasonable value of services rendered at the special instance and request of deceased for which she promised to pay claimant, then setting out the character and value of said services and the failure to pay any part thereof is sufficient; it was not construed to be a promise to pay a sum certain, and evidence of the reasonable value of such services was proper. 

There is, however, a clear distinction between an express promise to pay for services rendered without setting a price or value thereon, as in the instant case and the case where a sum certain was agreed upon. In the latter case the case does not hold that evidence of reasonable value would be proper. 

Sec. 787. 

Liebaart v. Hoehle's Estate (App.), 111 S.W. (2d) 925.

A plaintiff who seeks to recover for board, lodging and care furnished to her deceased father is not required to prove that she is to be paid a specific amount merely because a demand has been presented in the probate court in a form which named that amount where she merely presents evidence showing that the amount demanded is the reasonable value of such services if she has not alleged nor proven facts showing only an agreement to pay a specific sum.

There is a presumption where a family relation existed that such services were rendered gratuitously, but such presumption is not conclusive. Such presumption affects only the burden of proof. 

Sec. 787. 

In Heathcock v. Wolfe (Mo. App.), 136 S.W. (2d) 105, the claimants were a man and wife with whom it was claimed deceased made an agreement that claimants would move into deceased's house and they were to care for him until his death for the sum of $1,000. Declarations of deceased heard by witnesses (other than claimant) that he would give his house and stock and $1,000 if arrangement could be made with someone to take care of him were held properly admitted. 

Other evidence of a circumstantial character was admitted.

Sec. 790. 

Runnels v. Allen's Administrator, 169 S.W. (2d) 73, St. L. Ct. App., March, 1943.

The rule enabling the client to exclude evidence of his statements to attorney as "privileged communications" does not apply in litigation after client's death between parties all of whom claim under the client but where a party is presenting a claim against the estate, testimony of attorney for deceased would be adverse to the estate and such testimony will not be received over objection by others interested.

Sec. 806 Note 50. 

(General or Specific Legacy) 

See Buder v. Stocke et al., 343 Mo. 506, 121 S.W. (2d) 852

Where will contained numerous legacies of specified amounts of money, without stating how they should be paid, and subsequent paragraph of will provided that, "in the event the funds on hand at the time of my death are not sufficient," executors were empowered to sell a described farm to pay such legacies, the legacies were, nevertheless, general and payable out of general assets when, because of depreciation of value of farm, cash on hand and proceeds of sale of farm proved insufficient.

This the court calls demonstrative legacy which is said to be one payable out of the general assets if the primary fund designated fails in whole or in part. 

Sec. 807-Note 54. 

In Methodist Episcopal Church v. Thomas, 235 Mo. A. 671, 145

S.W. (2d) 157, after giving certain specific bequests of money the testator gave the remainder of his personal estate to T and his wife, -and then added: "I intend this bequest to include all of my livestock and farming implements, all money, notes and mortgages, including the $2400 note I hold on their farm, and all of my life insurance money which is payable to my estate, and any other personal property that I may own at the time of my death." In a suit by the plaintiffs as specific legatees to construe this provision of the will it was held to be a general legacy and not specific, even as to the $2400 note. 

Sec. 808-Note 60.

For annotations on "When legacy is regarded as demonstrative, see: 

73 A.L.R. 1250 (n).

Sec. 823.

In re Bernays' Estate. Bernays et al. v. Major, 344 Mo. 135, 126 

S.W. (2d) 209, 122 A.L.R. 169.

Where will provided that wife's right to income for life should be in lieu of her dower, homestead, allowances, rights of election and other rights in testator's estate, wife by accepting provisions of will waived right to dower and child's share, and amount thereof was not to be included with the $20,000 exemption in computing inheritance tax.

The widow by surrendering her right to dower, allowances, or to a child's part does not become a purchaser of the interest left in the will which by its terms requires an election, and so does not allow her to deduct the value of such statutory interests in addition to the $20,000 allowed her as exempt from inheritance tax. 

Sec. 833.

While the statute creates a personal liability against the Administrator or Executor for the tax, it was said in Sheehan, etc. v. First 

Nat. Bank, 346 Mo. 227, 140 S.W. (2d) 1, 1.c. (S.W.) 4, that the public administrator could not complain after removal of a bank account from a local bank where there was the usual application for such removal by a foreign domiciliary administratrix (under the Statute) on the ground that it was his (public administrator's) duty to collect taxes for the state or city, "since he is neither a tax collector nor charged with any duties with regard to collecting these taxes." 

This may be true so far as that statute is concerned, where he has satisfied the probate court that "all amounts due to this state on account of taxes have been paid"; but a later case shows that ordinarily it is the duty of an executor or administrator to be a tax collector. See State ex rel. Madden v. Sartorius, 349 Mo. 1054, 163 

S.W. (2d) 987. 

Sec. 837.

The tentative additional tax rates and provisions have been changed by the Acts of 1941 and 1942. See Vol. 26, U.S.C.A., Section 

935 (Pocket Part); also Section 811 of the same, as to change in exemptions as to life insurance and other matters. 

Sec. 859-Notes 24, 25, and 26 Where claims are filed and are pending before the court, an order of distribution upon final settlement cannot properly be made. While such order may be attacked collaterally, it may also be attacked by the motion of the claimant creditor to set aside the order. Such motion if made within the term will carry the order approving the

final settlement over and the probate court may at a subsequent term set aside its order approving final settlement. The order of court setting aside the approval of final settlement is not appealable, not being a final order. In re Rohde's Estate, Kuenzler et al. v. Beger (App.), 157 S.W. (2d) 527.

Hanssen v. Karbe, 234 Mo. A. 663, 115 S.W. (2d) 109.

Where notes of testator's son represented advancements, they did not become a part of testator's estate, and commissions were not allowable on them to the executor. 

Sec. 864 (b). 

In re Flynn's Estate (App.), 142 S.W. (2d) 1069.

The executor or administrator is entitled to his commission upon amounts paid out for personal property taxes on the estate. It is not required that an order be made allowing such taxes as a demand against the estate as the statute makes it the duty of the personal representative to pay taxes.

Sec. 864 (b)-Note 4. 

In re Flynn's Estate (App.), 142 S.W. (2d) 1069.

The amount of executor's commission cannot be determined until it is first determined what credits shall be allowed him. 

Sec. 864 (b)-Note 7. 

Where (the) executor with approval of probate court purchased real estate at foreclosure sale under trust deed thereon given to secure repayment of notes belonging to testator's estate and received money from the rents on such real estate or from other sources sufficient to pay all debts so that such real estate was not sold, executor was not entitled as part of his compensation to a commission on the value of such real estate. In re Cohn's Estate. Abrams v. Cohn, et al. (App.), 163 S.W. (2d) 802. 

Sec. 864 (b)-Note 20.

Compensation allowed to one acting in dual capacity as executor and trustee under will, will be that of executor and is allowed in executor's settlement. Estey v. Commerce Trust Co., 333 Mo. 977, 64 

S. W. (2d) 608. Citing Vorderstrasse's Estate v. Haumueller (App.), 266 S.W. 1019, 1.c. 1020. 

Sec. 864 (c).

When an order is made by the Probate Court authorizing administrator to sell real estate for the purpose of paying debts, it is con-

templated that administrator will himself make the sale and not that he employ someone else to perform the duty for him, and if agent is employed, such agent cannot be paid out of funds belonging to the estate. In re Claus' Estate (App.), 167 S.W. (2d) 372. 

Sec. 864 (d).

Where there were no personal assets in the estate and only a parcel of real estate to be sold to pay costs and expenses, the allowance to an attorney was limited to services reasonably necessary in the sale of the real estate. Charge could not be made for both examination of title by lawyer and title company; neither could a charge be made for proceedings to discover assets where it was not connected with such sale; nor could a charge be made for legal services in looking through old files and papers of deceased where that was in the nature of clerical work. In re Claus' Estate. Sheehan, Public 

Admr. v. Gillespie (App.), 167 S.W. (2d) 372. Attorney's fee of $200 was allowed for legal services connected with sale of real estate by 

Public Administrator. 

Sec. 864 (d)-Note 53. 

In re Waters' Estate (App.), 153 S.W. (2d) 774.

An allowance of attorney's fee for services rendered in the administration of the estate without notice to the administrator may be set aside at subsequent term as it is beyond the jurisdiction of the court to make such order without reasonable notice. Such is not a claim and does not require the formalities in the filing of claim but does require reasonable notice. An appeal does not lie from such order setting aside allowance. It is not a final order. 

Sec. 872. 

Proceedings on exceptions to administrator's settlement is an "equitable proceeding" and on appeal reviewing court would hear and determine the matter de novo. Clow's Estate v. Clow (App.), 167 S.W. (2d) 903.

Sec. 872. 

Clow's Estate v. Clow, 167 S.W. (2d) 903 (K. C. Ct. App.).

Exceptions to final settlement is a civil suit within the meaning of the change of venue statute allowing change of venue and such change of venue may be taken from the circuit court after it is certified to that court by the Probate Judge on the ground he is a material witness.

Sec. 872-Notes 12 and 13. 

45 Exceptions may be made to any charge or credit taken by the administrator in any prior settlements at the time when exceptions to final settlement are filed. In re Flynn's Estate (App.), 142 S.W. (2d) 1069.

In re Mills' Estate. 807.

Where exceptions to settlement were filed and part of the exceptions allowed and part overruled and both the administrator and exceptor filed appeals, they constituted cross-appeals where the items overlapped and should be heard as a single appeal in the Circuit Court. See the discussion of Bohling, Commissioner, in the above case, 1.c. 809 et seq. (S.W.). 

Sec. 874.

Exceptions that settlements of administrators are not "in proper form" and are not "just and true accounts" have been considered a generality presenting no specific objections. In re Mills' Estate, Sheehan v. Rudick, 349 Mo. 611, 162 S.W. (2d) 807. See also Hoffmeyer v. Mintert (Mo.), 93 S.W. (2d) 894. 

Sec. 875, Cook v. McCoy (App.), 118 S.W. (2d) 1043.

An heir is not entitled to any part of the estate until there has been an order of final distribution. It is the rule of law in this state that an heir or expectant distributee cannot sue the administrator for his interest until such order has been made, and therefore a creditor of the heir or distributee cannot sue him by way of garnishment, either legal or equitable, until the order of final distribution is made. 

It is only then that the administrator becomes debtor to the distributee or heir; prior to that time the relation of the administrator to such persons is that of personal representative. 

Sec. 889.

Law governing distribution. In re Orth's Estate; Kachel et al. v. 

Wyers, 169 S.W. (2d) 401, the Supreme Court gave effect to the intestacy laws of Germany. The deceased was an unmarried citizen and resident of Germany and had left a will giving her estate to one group of nephews and nieces and excluding others. The will, however, was not presented for probate within the year after grant of letters and the court had held in a previous case in the nature of prohibition that the Probate Court had no jurisdiction to admit it to

probate. See Wyers v. Arnold, 347 Mo. 413, 147 S.W. (2d) 644. It was contended in the present case that the court should give effect to the distribution provided in the will. This contention was denied by the Supreme Court in Kachel v. Wyers. The court holds the 

Prohibition proceeding was an adjudication of this matter, and distribution must be made of the personal estate in accordance with the law of Germany as to descent and distribution. 

Sec. 891 (e). 

In re Knighten's Estate, Knighten v. Gideon, 344 Mo. 246, 125 S.W. (2d) 863.

The will left a specific legacy to a husband who predeceased the testatrix, and she left certain other specific legacies to her cousins who were her next of kin and the residue to charity. Her husband left children by a former marriage and they contended that they were entitled to his share under the statute relating to wills (Sec. 528, R.S. Mo. 1939). The court reaffirms its previous holdings that the words "relatives" "kindred" do not include persons related by affinity and such persons cannot take under the theory that they are entitled as a relative to the share of their ancestor. The court cited the following Missouri cases: 

Bramell v. Adams, 146 Mo. 70, 47 S.W. (2d) 931; 

Union Trust Co. v. Curby, 255 Mo. 393, 164 S.W. 485; 

Rauch v. Metz (Mo.), 212 S.W. 353; 

State ex rel Cowden v. Knight, 338 Mo. 584, 92 S.W. (2d) 610; 

McMenamy v. Kampelmann, 273 Mo. 450, 200 S.W. 1075; 

Jarboe v. Hey, 122 Mo. 341, 26 S.W. 968. 

Sec. 898. 

Crawford v. Arends, et al. (Sup.), 176 S.W. (2d) 1. (Discussion of inheritance by adopted child under deed of adoption under the statute as it existed prior to 1917 and distinguishing the rights under the two acts.)

Sec. 898-Note 19. 

This rule of law must be confined to those adoptions under the law prior to the Act of 1917. Under the present law the adopted child does inherit from ancestors and collateral relatives of the adoptive parents. See McIntyre v. Hardesty, 347 Mo. 805, 149 S.W. (2d) 334. 

Sec. 906. 

Hanssen v. Karbe, 234 Mo. A. 663, 115 S.W. (2d) 109.

A will drawn by an experienced scrivener which directs that cer-

tain loans shall be charged as advancements to the children to whom made, out of their respective shares in his estate, is held to use the term advancement in its technical rather than popular sense or in any such sense as gift. The term advancement is used in the statutes with reference to the estates of intestates which require that the sum so advanced must be brought into hotchpot before dividing the estate into its respective interests. In the case at bar, however, the court holds that before the heir to whom a sum is advanced can receive anything from the estate the other heirs must receive a like sum; interest is to be charged on the sum advanced to the date of death of testator. Giving the will this construction the court held that the executor-trustee should be restrained from foreclosure of a mortgage to secure the indebtedness to the testator; that such indbtedness was no part of the estate; if the one to whom such property was advanced has received more than the other heirs they are without remedy. 

Sec. 908-Note 89 (Advancements).

Taking advancements into account at the time of final distribution. 

See the case of State ex rel Howe v. Hughes, 343 Mo. 827, 123 

S.W. (2d) 105.

Sec. 926 (Partial Distribution). 

State ex rel. Howe v. Hughes, 343 Mo. 827, 123 S.W. (2d) 105.

The failure of the executor to give a claimant against the estate a notice before making partial distribution does not deprive the probate court of jurisdiction to make such an order.

Sec. 957-Note 3. 

Hanssen v. Karbe, 234 Mo. A. 663, 115 S.W. (2d) 109.

The executor would not be ousted from execution of testamentary trust, notwithstanding it had improperly sought to nullify provision of will providing for an advancement where removal of the executor would thwart the wishes of the testator.

Sec. 1014-Note 21. 

The act of a public administrator in taking charge of an estate is subject to review by the probate court, and where that court ordered personal property of a non-resident decedent turned over to the domiciliary administratrix, an attempt by the public administrator in this state to recover such property by action against the foreign administratrix is a collateral attack upon a judgment and cannot be maintained. Sheehan v. First Nat. Bank, 346 Mo. 227, 140 S.W. (2d) 1.

Sec. 1026-Note 73.

The right of minor children to the allowance depends upon their domicile which is that of the deceased, and where he died a resident of another state in which the domiciliary estate is in process of administration, an allowance to the minor children should not be made in this state in which there is an ancillary administration. 

Jaeglin v. Moakley (App.), 151 S.W. (2d) 524. 

Sec. 1029-Note 92. 

The court of the domicile of deceased in administrative proceedings has sole jurisdiction to make allowances to the widow and minor children and the law of the state of deceased's domicile determines the nature and extent of such allowances in the personal estate. 

Jaeglin v. Moakley (App.), 151 S.W. (2d) 524. The ancillary court does not make such allowances, at least in the first instance. The law of the domicile is controlling in such matters. Ibid. 

Sec. 1037-Note 65. 

Where a foreign administrator is the only administrator of the estate in existence he may maintain an action under the Missouri statute for wrongful death in this state, since any recovery therein is not for the benefit of his estate as such, but by the statute such administrator is trustee of an express trust for the kin mentioned in the statute. Demattei v. Missouri-Kansas-Texas R. Co., 345 Mo. 1136, 139 S.W. (2d) 504.

Sec. 1078. 

Blum v. Frost, 234 Mo. A. 695, 116 S.W. (2d) 541. 

Growing crops on land belonging to testator go to devisees of the land and not to the executor.

Sec. 1078-Note 43. 

The question whether the deceased has effectively disposed of or transferred his property during his lifetime is sometimes intimately connected with the question whether property has passed to his heirs or legatees. It arises concretely where the deceased left personal property in safe deposit or other such place marked for someone other than the deceased, but in which there has been no manual or constructive delivery. Thus it was held in State ex rel. Union 

National Bank of Springfield v. Blair (Mo.), 166 S.W. (2d) 1085, that a bond found in the safe deposit box of the deceased bearing the notation: "This $1000 Springfield City Water Company bond, No. M- 4

1638, is the property of George H. Idle" did not convey to Idle either outright or in trust. In other words, neither an equitable or legal interest passed because there was no delivery and the endorsement contains no words of conveyance. Neither does it state that deceased was in possession for Mr. Idle's benefit or express an intention on the part of deceased to become trustee. The Court of Appeals had previously held that while there was no legal transfer the language was sufficient to create a trust, i.e., was indicative that deceased was holding in trust for Idle. This expression is disapproved by the 

Supreme Court, which holds there was neither an outright transfer nor was there a trust created by the endorsement. 

For similar expressions see Napier v. Eigel (Mo.), 164 S.W. (2d) 

908 and the cases therein discussed. 

Palmisciano v. Staltari, et al. (Sup.), 175 S.W. (2d). 793. 

The testator devised and bequeathed all his property to his wife for her sole use during her natural life and after her death directed that if any of it were left it should vest in his living brothers or their heirs, to be divided equally among them. See the commissioner's discussion as to the effect of such provisions on the life estate and remainders. References therein are: 

Burford v. Aldridge, 165 Mo. 419, 63 S.W. 109; (see also) 65 S.W. 720. 

Threlkeld v. Threlkeld, 238 Mo. 459, 141 S.W. 1121. 

Burnet v. Burnet, 244 Mo. 491, 148 S.W. 872.

Consult the annotation in 108 A.L.R. 542, 2 A.L.R. 1243, 27 A.L.R. 

1381, 69 A.L.R. 825.

Masterson v. Masterson, 344 Mo. 1188, 130 S.W. (2d) 629. 

Underwood v. Cave, 176 Mo. 1, 75 S.W. 451.

Sec. 1078-Note 47. 

In Sutorius v. Mayor (Mo.), 170 S.W. (2d) 387, the court held that acts done in ignorance of one's legal rights and without knowledge of facts necessary to a decision do not amount to a binding election to take under will where position of the parties has not changed. 

It was a case where land had been deeded to husband and wife. The husband's will purported to devise part, if not all, of the land as part of his estate. The wife accepted benefits under the will but it was held that although four years had elapsed she was not estopped from asserting her title to the land held by them in entirety even though an audit was required of the estate. See also same case on 

Motion for Rehearing at 171 S.W. (2d) 69.

Sec. 1079.

Roth v. Roth, 340 Mo. 1043, 104 S.W. (2d) 314.

The court recognizes the validity of an agreement by a stepmother to leave half her estate to the stepchildren in consideration of their refraining from bringing action to set aside certain conveyances to their stepmother but also charges the property with a lien in favor of the stepmother to the extent that proceeds of hers from her mother were used to discharge certain incumbrances thereon. 

Sec. 1085. 

Proffer v. Proffer, 342 Mo. 184, 114 S.W. (2d) 1035.

Facts sufficient for jury. 

In this case the court said, 1.c. S.W. (2d) 1042: "We think the facts in the present case stronger than in the 

Smarr and Rex cases. These are outstanding: Testator was unable to understand that he had paid for a load of wood; that he sold corn on credit for 50 cents per bushel, and for 60 cents cash; that he, without trying to collect, traded an $18 note for a $2 pig; and that he paid $95 for a $15 mule. Also it appears measured by the demurrer, that testator had abandoned a long life of honesty, and had on several occasions, as set out, committed petty thefts of the property of his neighbors. These thefts, in view of his former rectitude, were circumstances of substance which the jury had the right to consider in determining the question of testator's mental capacity. 

The court upheld the verdict (for contestant) on the whole record, i.e., held there was substantial evidence to support such a verdict. 

Sec. 1085-Test of Mental Capacity. 

Winn v. Matthews, 235 Mo. A. 337, 137 S.W. (2d) 632, 1.c. (S.W.) 

635. "On the question of the mental capacity required of a testator to make a valid will the courts have spoken as follows: Testator must be mentally capable of understanding the nature of the transaction he is engaged in, that is, disposing of his property to take effect at his death, the general nature and extent of his property (but need not be able, at the instant, to recall to mind the various items that compose his estate, or the names of his various creditors with the amounts owed each), the natural objects of his bounty, and to whom he desires to give it." Citing Hall v. Mercantile Trust Company, 332 

Mo. 802, 59 S.W. (2d) 664, loc. cit. 669; Carl v. Ellis (App.), 110 S.W. (2d) 805, loc. cit. 807, 808; Pulitzer v. Chapman, 337 Mo. 298, 85 

S.W. (2d) 400, loc. cit. 414.

Sec. 1085-Note 33. 

Rex v. Masonic Home of Missouri, 341 Mo. 589, 108 S.W. (2d) 72.

A testator who understands ordinary affairs of life, kind and extent

of his property, what persons are natural objects of his bounty, and that he is giving his property to persons mentioned in will in manner therein stated, is capable of making a will. 

Sec. 1085-Note 33. 

Instruction favorable to proponent; Pulitzer v. Chapman, 337 Mo.

(S.W.) 414, as follows: "The court instructs the jury that soundness of mind, as used in this and other instructions, means no more than the ability to understand and comprehend what one is doing, and the general character of one's property, and the persons who reasonably come within the range of one's bounty, and it is not necessary that one have a perfect and complete understanding of these matters in all their bearings nor be able to deal with intricate and complicated matters, but only that one be able to comprehend and understand the ordinary, as distinguished from the complicated affairs of life."

Sec. 1085-Note 33. 

In the case Pulitzer v. Chapman, 337 Mo. 298, 85 S.W. (2d) 400, l.c. (S.W.) 415, is an instruction favorable to contestant: "That if a person has not mind and memory enough to understand, without the aid of others, the value, nature and extent of her property, the number and names of the persons who are the natural objects of her bounty, their deserts with reference to their conduct and treatment of her, their capacity and necessity, and if she does not have active memory enough to retain all these facts in her mind long enough to prepare her will, she does not have the mental or testamentary capacity required by law to make a valid will." This instruction was criticized by the court as requiring too much of the testator.

As to burden of proof in will contest, see Foster v. Norman, 346

Sec. 1097-Note 23. 

Weaver v. Allison, 340 Mo. 815, 102 S.W. (2d) 884.

In a will contest where the petition avers mental incapacity and undue influence, if the proponent does not offer evidence as to mental capacity of testator, he will not be entitled to judgment establishing the will even though the contestants' evidence is insufficient to establish incapacity or undue influence since the statute requires affirmative proof that the testator was of sound mind in order to prove the will whether in common or solemn form. 

Sec. 1097-Note 25. 

The burden of proof in a will contest remains with the proponent throughout the case, but in the first instance it is incumbent upon him only to make proof of the due execution of the will, i.e., compliance with all the requirements and formalities prescribed by statute, and that the testator was at the time of sound mind. This is

true whether the contest is on the ground of want of mental capacity or not. Foster et al. v. Norman et al., 346 Mo. 850, 143 S.W. (2d) 248, and cases cited under (1) therein. 

Sec. 1098. 

Proffer v. Proffer, 342 Mo. 184, 114 S.W. (2d) 1035.

As to sufficiency or insufficiency of evidence of sickness, old age, and mere eccentricities in determining mental incapacity see the above case. The eccentricities were quite marked, but so long as they are mere eccentricities, while evidence of same is relevant, the courts generally hold they are not sufficient alone to mark the devisor as insane but may be taken into consideration with other facts.

Sec. 1098-Note 38. 

Frank v. Greenhall, 340 Mo. 1228, 105 S.W. (2d) 929.

Evidence held insufficient to show that testator was of unsound mind and possessed of insane delusions when he executed will and codicil thereto.

Sec. 1099. 

Gaume v. Gaume, 340 Mo. 758, 102 S.W. (2d) 636.

It was not contended in this case that testator was not in possession of his mental faculties, which were good, unless he was obsessed by an insane delusion. The evidence reviewed and held not to establish such facts as pleaded. 

Sec. 1099-Note 41. 

Stevens v. Meadows, 340 Mo. 252, 100 S.W. (2d) 281.

Testatrix had on many occasions had altercations with one of her daughters, which arose out of the fact that testatrix did not wish her daughter to receive attentions from her boy friends, although the daughter (now contesting the will) was over thirty years of age. 

The daughter left home and married. It was contended by the counsel for contestant that the mother was suffering from an insane delusion that it was wrong for her children to leave home or associate with the opposite sex and that because of this the alleged will was invalid.

This is not an insane delusion. The court says: "If a testator is capable of reasoning, and does reason to a conclusion that one of the natural objects of his bounty is unworthy of such bounty, and in his judgment, formed without undue influence, such person should not be given a portion of his property, then no jury or tribunal has a right to say to the contrary. Insane delusions

are not the result of reasoning, however erroneous or unjust the result may be, but must be without any and contrary to all reason.' 

Zorn v. Zorn (Mo.), 64 S.W. (2d) 626, 628."

Sec. 1099-Note 42. 

Higgins v. Smith et al. (App.), 150 S.W. (2d) 539.

Sec. 1099-Note 53. 

Rex v. Masonic Home of Missouri, 341 Mo. 589, 108 S.W. (2d) 72.

A delusion to make a testator incapable of making a will must be a delusion as to or affecting some matter necessarily involved in making of will.

Sec. 1099-Note 61. 

In Higgins v. Smith (App.), 150 S.W. (2d) 539, 1.c. 543, the court said: "The fact that in a discordant family the testatrix might turn against first one member of the family and then another, who differed with her, with no fixed delusion as to any one particular one, or any particular subject, and conclude they were persecuting her or mean to her because of such indifferences, might be some evidence of an unsound mind, but it would not be proof of an insane delusion."

Sec. 1099-Note 63. 

In Higgins v. Smith (App.), 150 S.W. (2d) 539, it was held that the pleading must set forth the insane delusion relied on; that the general allegation in the petition "that she was subject to insane delusions and hallucinations as to her relatives, friends, acquaintances, affairs, and the nature and extent of her property," was not sufficient.

Sec. 1113-Note 82. 

Palm v. Maguire et al., 347 Mo. 189, 146 S.W. (2d) 636.

No verbal request to witness the will is necessary if the acts and conduct indicate that the testator is signing a will in the presence of the witnesses. 

Sec. 1117.

It has been held that where at the time a witness signed the will, the witness, testatrix, and another attesting witness were all in room together, will was attested "in the presence of the testatrix" within requirement of statute even if testatrix did not actually see witness sign. Callaway et al. v. Blankenbaker, 346 Mo. 383, 141 S.W. (2d) 810.

Sec. 1117-Note 33. 

Baxter v. Bank of Belle, 340 Mo. 952, 104 S.W. (2d) 265. 55 The above case is a good illustration as to what not to do in the execution and witnessing of a will. The will is set out by photostat copy.

Only one of the purported witnesses was held to have been a proper witness. One signed who was not present at its execution and a third certified as notary public without any evidence that he was requested to witness or that he intended to sign as a witness. 

Sec. 1122.

The mere fact that two wills on their face bear similar provisions and appear to be reciprocal does not make them such unless they are made by mutual agreement upon valid consideration. mons v. Pemberton (App.), 117 S.W. (2d) 392. 

Sec. 1122. 

Plemmons v. Pemberton (App.), 117 S.W. (2d) 392.

See Plem- An agreement to execute reciprocal and mutual wills need not be established by direct evidence, and if the agreement does not expressly appear in the language of the wills, it may be supplied by competent witnesses testifying to testators' admissions, or an express promise may be shown. The nature of such indirect or circumstantial testimony may be facts showing that each party acted with the knowledge of the other, that the two wills were drawn by the same person, at the same time, and at the joint request or directions of both parties, and, even though their dates differ slightly, that they were in fact executed in pursuance of a common purpose and understanding. Such an agreement, i.e., to make reciprocal and mutual wills to remain unrevoked, must be established by clear, definite, convincing, unequivocal, and satisfactory testimony. 

Sec. 1122.

A contract to make mutual wills to remain unrevoked at the death of the parties, is valid and enforcible if fair and just, definite and certain in its terms and as to the subject matter and based upon sufficient consideration, and if such a will is afterwards revoked by one of the testators, after the death of the other, an action may be brought upon the contract by the beneficiary under the will of deceased, such action not being for the revocation of the will but upon the contract or agreement. This is especially true where the survivor avails himself of the provision of the will in his favor and accepts the benefits thereunder.

However, mere making by two persons of wills at the same time

with reciprocal testamentary dispositions will not in itself establish such a contract. It is not enough that the wills were simultaneously made, and similar in their reciprocal provisions. The existence of a clear and definite contract must be alleged and proved, either by proof of an express agreement, or by unequivocal circumstances. See 

Plemmons v. Pemberton, 346 Mo. 45, 139 S.W. (2d) 910, and cases cited therein.

Sec. 1122-Note 49. 

Plemmons v. Pemberton (App.), 117 S.W. (2d) 392. See also, same case, 346 Mo. 45, 139 S.W. (2d) 910.

Even if evidence other than mutual wills themselves shows that wills were made pursuant to some agreement, that is insufficient to show that they were made in pursuance of a contract to make wills to remain unrevoked at testator's deaths. 

Sec. 1127-Note 86. 

Idle v. Moody, 344 Mo. 594, 127 S.W. (2d) 660.

The Supreme Court in this case assents to the rule of law that: 

It is immaterial whether or not the scrivener thought that the will he drew expressed the testator's purposes and wishes. If the testator told him to draw it one way and he drew it another, and testator signed it under the belief that it was written as he had directed, it is not his will. See Cowan et al. v. Shaver et al., 197 

Mo. 203, 95 S.W. 200, and Bradford v. Blossom, 207 Mo. 177, 105 S.W. 

289. The court in the Idle case, however, upholds the verdict of a jury in favor of proponents where the young lawyer who drew a codicil admitted on cross-examination that he had never drawn a codicil before; that the testatrix had instructed him that she only wanted by making a codicil to the will to place a recently purchased note in trust for one of her relatives; but the scrivener in drafting the codicil made the same relative who received the benefit of the note in trust also the sole residuary legatee, whereas the will had provided for several relatives as the residuary legatees. The testatrix was intelligent, had had the opportunity of reading the codicil and there was no intimation that her mind was feeble or unsound nor was there any allegation of undue influence. Under such circumstances the facts are sufficient for the jury to find for the proponents and having done so their verdict was upheld. A directed verdict in favor of contestants would not be justified. 

Sec. 1128.

In a will contest involving issue of undue influence, proponents offering previous wills to prove contested will was executed volun-

tarily did not have the burden of showing that previous wills were not procured by undue influence. Pulitzer v. Chapman, 85 S.W. (2d) 

400, 337 Mo. 298.

Sec. 1128. 

1 

Clark et al. v. Powell et al. (Sup.), 175 S.W. (2d) 842.

The beneficiary was not related to testatrix. He received a substantial legacy. The evidence of contestants tended to show that beneficiary stood in a confidential relation to testatrix and was active in procuring the will. The confidential relationship consisted in the fact that beneficiary was administrator of the estate of testatrix' daughter from whom testatrix would inherit. A verdict setting aside the will on the ground of undue influence was upheld. 

See this case also for evidence of circumstances tending to show undue influence and instructions as to undue influence.

In which the Supreme Court in a will contest holds the evidence insufficient both as to testamentary incapacity and as to undue influence and that the facts were insufficient to submit to the jury. 

Sec. 1128-Note 10. 

The influence which will warrant rejecting a will must be "undue influence," and must be of sufficient potency to destroy free agency of testator at time of making will, and must rise to such overpersuasfon, coercion, force, fraud or deception as breaks the will power of testator and puts in its stead, the will of another, but the influence of natural affection is not sufficient, and there must be more than mere opportunity to influence or mere suspicion. Hahn v. 

Brueseke, 348 Mo. 708, 155 S.W. (2d) 98.

Sec. 1128-Note 10. 

"Undue influence" which will invalidate a will is such influence as develops from overpersuasion, coercion, fraud or deception; an influence that restrains, controls, directs and diverts or coerces the will; that overcomes and confuses the mind, beclouds the judgment and is of such potency as destroys or enfeebles the will power of the testator, rendering it inoperative and substituting the will of another. 

O'Reilly v. O'Reilly (App.), 157 S.W. (2d) 220.

Sec. 1128-Note 10. 

"Undue influence" to invalidate a will should be of sufficient potency to destroy the free agency of testator at the time of making

the will, and the influence of natural affection is not sufficient. 

O'Reilly v. O'Reilly (App.), 157 S.W. (2d) 220.

Sec. 1128-Note 16. 

"Undue influence" to be effective in breaking a will, need not be shown by direct evidence, but may be shown indirectly and arise as a natural inference from other facts in case, but it must not rest on mere opportunity to influence or on mere suspicion. v. Alt, 348 Mo. 53, 152 S.W. (2d) 135.

Sec. 1128-Note 21. 

Walter

The existence of a fiduciary relation between testatrix and officers of charity to which residue of her property was devised does not in itself give rise to presumption or inference that execution of will was procured through exercise of undue influence by such officers, but facts must be shown in addition to fiduciary relation from which it can be fairly and reasonably inferred that such fiduciary actively exercised undue influence in making of will. 

Such undue influence in execution of the will need not be proven by direct evidence but may be shown by or inferred from facts and circumstances in evidence, but more must be shown than mere opportunity to influence or mere suspicion.
