Sec. 1129-Unnatural Disposition of Property. 

Proffer v. Proffer, 342 Mo. 184, 114 S.W. (2d) 1035.

A harsh and unnatural disposition of property by will is a circumstance which tends to discredit the maker's testamentary capacity. 

Sec. 1129-Note 32. 

Hennings v. Hallar, 347 Mo. 827, 149 S.W. (2d) 338. Kadderly v. 

Vossbrink (Mo.), 149 S.W. (2d) 869. 

Sec. 1129. 

Gaume v. Gaume, 340 Mo. 758, 102 S.W. (2d) 636.

The court reaffirms the principle that unequal distribution of testator's property by his will, standing alone, will not constitute sufficient evidence from which jury can legitimately find testator's incapacity.

Sec. 1129-Note 28. 

Carl v. Ellis (App.), 110 S.W. (2d) 805.

Unnatural disposition of property by will may be considered on the question of testamentary capacity where there are other circumstances having the same tendency. 

Sec. 1130. 

Gaume v. Gaume, 340 Mo. 758, 102 S.W. (2d) 636. 

See the discussion of Cooley, Commissioner, as to insane delusion and unnatural disposition of property. The court discusses and reviews the previous case law in this state; among other cases discussed, are: 

Stevens v. Meadows et al., 340 Mo. 252, 100 S.W. (2d) 281, and 

Hall v. Mercantile Trust Co., 332 Mo. 802, 59 S.W. (2d) 664. 

Sec. 1137. 

Weaver et al. v. Allison et al., 340 Mo. 815, 102 S.W. (2d) 884.

The contestants claimed that the will was void because of one provision thereof, which delayed, until the death of her husband,

the vesting of property devised to one of the testator's daughters. 

Since this was a will contest and not a proceeding to construe the will, the validity, effect, or construction of the provisions of the will could not be determined in such contest. 

This holding of the court might be brought in question where in a will contest the nature of the provisions were such as might be considered to determine whether such disposition of property was unnatural. In such case no doubt such provision might be construed to determine whether the will bore a meaning which disinherited the natural objects of his bounty (in connection with undue influence where other circumstances are present) or to determine whether a person contesting has such a direct pecuniary interest as to enable him to be a party to the contest. 

Sec. 1141. 

The Supreme Court in Buder v. Stocke et al., 343 Mo. 506, 121 

S.W. (2d) 852, defines ademption and discusses quite thoroughly its application to the facts in that case. It is often used in different senses: (1) The satisfaction of a legacy by delivery of the subject matter or a payment of the specific sum to the designated legatee in his lifetime; (2) any act by which a specific legacy has become inoperative on account of the withdrawal or disappearance of its subject matter from the testator's estate during his lifetime. 

In other words, ademption is merely one of the ways in which a legacy lapses in consequence of some act of the testator equivalent of revocation or indicative of an intention to revoke as to that part. 

Sec. 1144. 

The right to contest a will is not a property right and does not descend to one's heirs and such heirs of a contestant cannot be made parties to a pending contest. Campbell v. St. Louis Union Trust Co. (Mo.), 346 Mo. 200, 139 S.W. (2d) 935, 129 A.L.R. 316. But the contest is not vacated by reason of a contestant's death; the will must still be proven. (For other cases see Sec. 1144. Note 75.)

Sec. 1144. 

In re Cordes' Estate (App.), 116 S.W. (2d) 207. 

Will contest.-Parties. 

All persons interested in subject matter of suit must be made parties.

Sec. 1144 Note 67. 

McCrary v. Michael, 233 Mo. A. 797, 109 S.W. (2d) 50.

A will contest is a proceeding sui generis, a suit in rem, and has for its purpose determination of question of whether there is or is not a will.

Sec. 1144 Note 69. 

Breeding v. Pack et al. (Mo.), 164 S.W. (2d) 929.

Sec. 1144 Note 73. 

McCrary v. Michael, 233 Mo. A. 797, 109 S.W. (2d) 50.

Where contest is brought in circuit court by those who, but for will, would, under law of descents and distribution, be entitled to interests in estate of deceased, effect is to wipe out or vacate action of probate court.

Sec. 1144 Note 74. 

The Circuit Court has no jurisdiction to set aside the probate court's order probating the will. The filing of a will contest is a substantial admission that the order of the probate court is regular. 

See Canty v. Lehmkuhl (App.), 164 S.W. (2d) 132.

Sec. 1144-Note 75. 

The right of action of person contesting will was not a property right descending to his heir at his death, but was personal, and heir was not entitled to be substituted as contestant; such right of action to contest a will is neither assignable nor descendible. Campbell v. 

St. Louis Union Trust Co., 346 Mo. 200, 139 S.W. (2d) 935.

Sec. 1144 Note 75. 

Contestant must allege and prove a direct pecuniary interest in the probate of the will. See Palm v. Maguire et al., 347 Mo. 189, 146 

S.W. (2d) 636; Campbell v. St. Louis Union Trust Co., 346 Mo. 200, 139 S.W. (2d) 935, 129 A.L.R. 316; Jensen v. Hinderks, 338 Mo. 459, 92 S.W. (2d) 108. In the first case the court said, l.c. (S.W.) 638, "Appellants contend that the petition does not state facts sufficient to show that plaintiff has such an interest in the probate of the will as entitles him to contest it. Ordinarily appellants, having gone to trial on the merits without filing a demurrer, would be precluded from now making this objection. But in a will contest it is a jurisdictional requirement that a contestant both allege and prove a direct pecuniary interest in the probate of the will." (Citing cases.) 

Sec. 1147-Costs In Will Contest. 

McCrary v. Michael, 233 Mo. A. 797, 109 S.W. (2d) 50.

Costs would be taxed against unsuccessful will contestants under statute providing that in all civil actions, or proceedings of any

kind, party prevailing shall recover costs against other party, except in those cases in which different provision is made by law, since there are no special statutory provisions relating to costs in will contests. 

Sec. 1147-Note 98. 

McCrary v. Michael, 233 Mo. A. 797, 109 S.W. (2d) 50.

In a will contest, authority of the executor, if he has an interest in the estate, is suspended by statute pending the will contest, and, in event contestants are successful, executor, if a party, at once becomes functus officio and no one is left who has duty to look after interest of estate. 

Sec. 1148-Note 3. 

It is the established law in Missouri that a will contest cannot be dismissed even by the contestant. The filing of a contest makes it obligatory to have an adjudication upon the will. A recent case on this is Campbell v. St. Louis Union Trust Co., 343 Mo. 1041, 124

S.W. (2d) 1068, in which the contestees sought to enjoin the contest proceeding. Hazlett Kyle Campbell was the only surviving heir of 

Hugh Campbell and the former was insane. It was alleged that certain persons had procured the appointment of a guardian for him for the sole purpose of a contest. There had been a substantial legacy to Hazlett Kyle Campbell left in trust for him. 

It was held that the contest itself was the remedy and not injunction. Some cases cited among them, Primeau v. Primeau, 317 Mo. 

828, 297 S.W. 382, were cited by contestant, but the court indicated they should be confined to the facts in those cases. which were in the main indicative of an election by the plaintiff to take under the will prior to his filing a contest. 

Sec. 1148-Note 3. 

McCrary v. Michael, 233 Mo. A. 797, 109 S.W. (2d) 50.

Heirs bringing suit in circuit court to contest will may abandon contest against will, but have no right to dismiss suit or prevent circuit court from acting on will. 

Sec. 1149. 

Weaver v. Allison, 340 Mo. 815, 102 S.W. (2d) 884.

The burden of establishing that testator was of sound mind at the time of his signing the will remains with the proponent throughout the trial in a will contest, and while the burden of evidence shifts after proponent makes a prima facie case, the burden of establishing such fact by a preponderance or greater weight of the

evidence remains with proponents. The presumption of sanity alone is insufficient to establish testamentary capacity and absent proof of sanity on behalf of proponents they will not be entitled to a judgment sustaining the will.

Sec. 1152. 

Primary rule for construction of will is to determine the true intent and meaning of testator as expressed in his will and such intent and meaning will control unless it contravenes some established rule of law: 

Kemp v. Hutchinson (App.), 110 S.W. (2d) 1126. 

Garrett v. Damron (Mo.), 110 S.W. (2d) 1112. 

Rowe v. Strother, 341 Mo. 1149, 111 S.W. (2d) 93. 

Coleman v. Haworth, 320 Mo. 852, 8 S.W. (2d) 931.

This being the controlling principle of construction, all technical rules of construction must yield: 

Humphreys v. Welling, 341 Mo. 1198, 111 S.W. (2d) 123. 

Kemp v. Hutchinson (App.), 110 S.W. (2d) 1126.

In ascertaining testator's intention from his will sentences may be transposed, if necessary,1 "or", will be construed to mean "and", where the will from its four corners requires such constuction,2 and, in ascertaining testator's intention, words may be supplied or omitted if necessary; likewise where such words as "want," "desire," etc., are used they may be construed to be mandatory or precatory, depending upon the context and the circumstances shown tending to indicate the sense in which such words are apparently used: 4 

1 Humphreys v. Welling, 341 Mo. 1198, 111 S.W. (2d) 123. 

2 Garrett v. Damron (Mo.), 110 S.W. (2d) 1112. 

3 Humphreys v. Welling, 341 Mo. 1198, 111 S.W. (2d) 123. 

4 Rowe v. Strother, 341 Mo. 1149, 111 S.W. (2d) 93.

Sec. 1152 (a)-Note 20. 

Kemp v. Hutchinson (App.), 110 S.W. (2d) 1126. 

Courts will not attempt to write a will for testatrix. 

Sec. 1152 (b). 

Masterson v. Masterson, 344 Mo. 1188, 130 S.W. (2d) 629.

Intent of testator primary rule for the construction of wills. 

Sec. 1152 (b)-Note 30. 

Shelton et al. v. Shelton et al., 348 Mo. 820, 155 S.W. (2d) 187. In this case Judge Douglas says: "The language of one will is rarely, if ever, like another and frequently a slight difference in the words used calls for different constructions of testamentary provisions simi-

lar in other respects. Even identical words properly receive divers interpretations when used in contexts or under circumstances which are not the same. Therefore, decisions construing similar testamentary provisions are of small value as precedents and must be considered with caution."

Sec. 1152(c)-Note 31. 

Ostmann v. Ostmann et al., 169 S.W. (2d) 81. A will speaks as of the date of testator's death and where such a will provided that none of the realty devised should be partitioned within a period of ten years after testator's death it expressed an intent to include the day of testator's death in the calculation of the ten year period, and hence partition suit filed on tenth anniversary of testator's death was not premature. It is apparent that the court distinguishes between the expression "within ten years after death" and "within ten years after date (or day) of death." If the latter expression is used the day of death is excluded.

Sec. 1152 (f)-Note 43. 

Methodist Episcopal Church v. Thomas, 235 Mo. A. 671, 145 S.W. (2d) 157, where the trial court admitted parol testimony as throwing light upon the problem whether a bequest was general or specific; the trial court's judgment of construction that the bequest was general was affirmed.

Sec. 1152 (f)-Note 43. 

As to rules for construction of will and evidence admissible where there is a patent ambiguity, see Aurien v. Security Nat. Bank Savings & Trust Co. (App.), 137 S.W. (2d) 679.

In a proceeding to construe a will which was ambiguous as to size of widow's estate, widow's will which created a life estate in her husband in all of her property, was admissible as corroborative of contention that testator intended to create a life estate in his widow. 

Aurien v. Security Nat. Bank Savings & Trust Co. of St. Louis, 137 

S.W. (2d) 679 (Transferred (Mo.), 129 S.W. (2d) 1047.) 

Sec. 1152 (g).

Buder v. Stocke et al., 343 Mo. 506, 121 S.W. (2d) 852. 

A will leaving to testator's son "all my holdings of stock" in named company and "any and all notes, obligations or claims, which I now hold of said company, whether evidenced by notes or otherwise due me on open account," passed testator's entire interest, originally represented by shares of corporate stock, in a brick business formerly operated under that name as a corporation, which after forfeiture of

charter, was operated as a partnership or as testator's individual. business under management of the son. 

Sec. 1152 (h)-Note 49. 

In Diebold v. Diebold, 235 Mo. A. 83, 141 S.W. (2d) 119, the testator provided for the payment of his debts and made certain specific bequests; his estate was then divided into aliquot parts between his children and the children of one daughter deceased; and provided that certain notes due from some of the legatees be deducted. 

The will then further provided: "It is my will that my Executors hereinafter named shall make disposition of the Personal Property within One year after my death. But no time limits shall govern the Executors to disposition of the Real-estate but they shall have the privilege to use their own Judgment as to the best opertune (Sic) time to dispose of said Real-estate for the benefit of the Benefactors, and the Signature of the Executors to the Deed shall make the sale of said Real-estate legal when acknowlaged." (Sic.) 

It was held it was the duty of executors under the will to sell the real estate. There was no express direction to do so, but the duty was implied from the fact that the executors should use their own judgment as to the time of such sale. Certain beneficiaries were not entitled to have the estate settled without a disposition of the real estate.

Sec. 1152 (k)-Note 72. 

The general rule is that the effect of republication of a will by codicil makes the will speak, with respect to the persons and things named in it, as from the date of such republication, just as though it had then been made for the first time, the codicil drawing the will down to its own date and republishing it in the form in which it was at the time of the execution of the codicil. This rule is subject to the limitation that the intention of the testator must not be defeated by such construction.

This limitation was applied in Hourigan v. McBee et al. (App.), 130 S.W. (2d) 661. The testator had made a will in 1926 devising realty to his sons and $6,000 to his daughter and thereafter the testator executed a codicil reducing the bequest to the daughter. from $6,000 to $5,000 and ratifying and confirming his will except as to the amount of bequest to daughter, but did not state that the will was republished or re-executed, and the attestation stated that the codicil was added to and should be construed as part of the will. In such case the will spoke from date of execution and not from date of codicil. 

The evidence failed to show that at the time of the execution of

the will the testator did not have sufficient personalty to pay the legacy to daughter. The inference is that if testator had not enough personalty the legacy might have been a charge on the realty of the sons, but it is not so stated. The court instead, says that the codicil should be considered a subsequent clause of the will and such title "cannot be cut down by any subsequent provisions of the will unless the later provisions of the will are as clear and definite as the language of the clause which gives the absolute title." The court cites 

Blumer v. Gillespie, 338 Mo. 1113, 93 S.W. (2d) 939; Estill v. Ballew (Mo.), 26 S.W. (2d) 778. 

Sec. 1152k.

Kemp et al. v. Hutchinson et al. (App.), 110 S.W. (2d) 1126. 

The above case is a careful discussion as to the effect of a codicil on the will, i.e., whether provisions as to certain beneficiaries are cumulative or substitutional; it also avails itself of the presumption that the testatrix did intend to dispose of her whole estate and not die intestate as to a portion thereof. 

Legg et al. v. Wagner et al. (Mo.), 155 S.W. (2d) 146. 

Sec. 1153-Note 95.

A proceeding for construction of will under Declaratory Judgment Act should go to judgment if brought in good faith and not be dismissed by the trial court and even if the court finds against the construction placed upon the will by the plaintiffs it may allow fees for plaintiff's counsel for services rendered in procuring the construction of the will. Kingston et al. v. St. Louis Union Trust Co., 348 Mo. 

448, 154 S.W. (2d) 39. 

Sec. 1154. 

Thompson v. Thompson et al. (Sup.), 175 S.W. (2d) 885.

A will devised land to testator's two sons in fee simple at life tenant's death on condition that his two sons take said farm at a valuation of $2400 to be equally divided among his four children. 

The payment of the $2400 was not a condition precedent to the vesting of the title in the two sons and they had a vested remainder impressed with a lien for the amount due the others. 

Sec. 1154 (b).

Upon the question whether clause of will is a legacy or recognizes a debt, see: 

Rowe v. Strother, 341 Mo. 1149, 111 S.W. (2d) 93.

Sec. (b)-Note 29. 

Masterson v. Masterson, 344 Mo. 1188, 130 S.W. (2d) 629. 67 Use of word "absolutely" in giving estate to widow did not enlarge estate where it was otherwise shown to be during widowhood. The use of the word "absolute" or "absolutely" in a devise of property by will does not enlarge the quantum of the estate, nor is a life estate enlarged into a fee by giving donee an added power of disposition over the fee. Such power must be exercised by the widow during her life by conveyance, and cannot be exercised by will unless expressly given in the instrument creating the power. 

Sec. 1154 (b)—Note 34. 

Union Natl. Bank in Kansas City v. Bunker et al., 232 Mo. A. 1062, 114 S.W. (2d) 193.

Language of the draftsman. 

Generally, adverbs of time or adverbial clauses designating time do not create a contingency in a devise, but merely denote the time when the enjoyment of the estate shall commence. 

Sec. 1154-Note 34. 

Thompson v. Thompson (Sup.), 175 S.W. (2d) 885. 

Adverbs of time such as "when", "there" or "after" do not necessarily create a contingency or a contingent interest but may merely denote when enjoyment of estate given by will is to commence. 

Sec. 1154 (c). 

Union Natl. Bank in Kansas City v. Bunker et al., 232 Mo. A. 

1062, 114 S.W. (2d) 193.

In this case the will of testator created a trust and directed that any balance in the trust estate remaining after payment of life tenant's funeral expenses should revert to the heirs and legatees named in the residuary clause provided that the amount devised in that clause to beneficiaries of trusts created in the will should be added to the trusts, and upon death of beneficiaries, such bequests should revert to "remaining legatees named in this paragraph." This was held to create a vested remainder in the legatees mentioned in the residuary paragraph and the word "remaining" referred to the other legatees named in the paragaph. 

Sec. 1157-Including Property In Will By Reference. 

Hourigan v. McBee (App.), 130 S.W. (2d) 661.

Where testator executed deeds to sons contemporaneously with will devising realty to sons and mentioned deeds in will and deeds were found in bank box of testator, deeds, though inoperative as deeds

68 

because of their testamentary character, would be construed as part of will and as evidencing intent of testator to pass title of realty to sons free from any other bequest in will.

Sec. 1161.-Note 19. 

Methodist Episcopal Church v. Thomas, 235 Mo. A. 671, 145 S.W. 

(2d) 157.

Sec. 1164 Note 29. 

Liggett v. Liggett, 341 Mo. 213, 108 S.W. (2d) 129. 

A devisee, who was given 80 acres of a farm by his mother's will, containing forfeiture clause disinheriting any child who should legally contest will, did not contest will so as to forfeit devise by bringing suit during life of mother and before she had executed will, for interest in farm under alleged contract, or, after death of mother, by reviving such suit and claiming 80 acre devise to him as of right under contract rather than as bounty. 

Sec. 1169.

In attempting to dispose of real property by will the essential distinction between transfer by deed and transfer by will must be kept in mind. The failure to keep this distinction in mind is well illustrated in Goins v. Melton, 343 Mo. 413, 121 S.W. (2d) 821, where a deed was held void and of no effect as a conveyance because of its testamentary character. The deed was in the usual form of a warranty deed except for the following provision: "It is the express understanding between the parties hereto that the grantor herein shall retain possession and control of all profits therefrom for and during his natural life time, also retaining to himself the right to sell and deed said land, or any part thereof during his life time, at his death the title to all, or whatever part thereof remains unsold, to pass to and vest in the grantee together with all his personal property and belongings." (Court's italics.) 

The Supreme Court calls attention to the tests laid down for a valid present conveyance, among others that in Owen v. Trail, 302 

Mo. 292, 258 S.W. 699, 1.c. 702, as follows: "If the terms of the deed show that the intention of the grantor is to pass a present irrevocable interest in the property, and that limiting condition operated only upon the present enjoyment of the premises, then it would be a valid deed."

The defect in the deed in the present case (Goins v. Melton) was that because it reserved both title and control for life no interest either present or future passed; nor could any such interest pass until death and the attempted conveyance was in fact an attempt to

pass the whole title and interest only at death, which made it testamentary in character without the statutory requirements required in making a will. See the many authorities cited in this case as well as the distinction between such conveyance and one which created a trust as in Sims v. Brown, 252 Mo. 58, 158 S.W. 624. 

Sec. 1170. 

Eisenhardt v. Siegel, 343 Mo. 22, 119 S.W. (2d) 810.

A murderer cannot inherit realty from his victim. 

Where grantor who had been adjudged sane conveyed farm to grantee on condition that farm would revert to grantor should grantee predecease him and grantee was killed under circumstances tending to show that he was killed by grantor, who was thereafter adjudged insane and who had been insane at time grantee was killed, title to the land under the deed reverted to grantor upon grantee's death. 

Sec. 1170-Note 54. 

Shelton et al. v. Shelton et al., 348 Mo. 820, 155 S.W. (2d) 187. 

Sec. 1171.

For example of devise of property to wife during the time she remained a widow with power to sell, exchange, or encumber it and reinvest the proceeds, with a provision that in the event of her death remaining estate was devised to children, and the construction thereof, see: 

Graham v. Stroh et al., 342 Mo. 686, 117 S.W. (2d) 258.

In such case it is held that such widow as a life tenant with right to convey a fee cannot convey the fee by gift. See the cases cited therein. 

Sec. 1172. 

Friesz et al. v. Friesz et al., 344 Mo. 698, 127 S.W. (2d) 714.

Under will devising realty to testator's son during his lifetime and after his death to his children upon express condition that son pay certain amount to testator's executrix within two years after testator's death, condition was only upon life estate, and fee granted to remainderman was not cut down by express terms of will other than in so far as payment might become a simple charge against land. 

Sec. 1172.

Although a base fee or a fee with possibility of reverter was descendible it was not devisable at common law. The statute of 

Missouri enables a testator to devise any estate or interest in real

property. Whether this changes the rule of common law was discussed but not decided in Davis v. Austin, 348 Mo. 1094, 156 S.W. (2d) 903; see also, University City v. Chicago, R. I. & P. Ry. Co., 347 Mo. 814, 149 S.W. (2d) 321, 1.c. (S.W.) 324. 1 

Sec. 1172-Note 94. 

McMurry v. McMurry, 340 Mo. 1094, 104 S.W. (2d) 345.

Under husband's will, leaving all his estate to his wife, “making her absolute owner thereof, her life time, she to be her own executor and no bond to be required," and providing that at her death a certain sum was to be paid to son with remainder to be divided equally among the other children, widow obtained a life estate with remainder over at her death and power to dispose of fee in her life time. 

Sec. 1174-Note 24. 

Pearson v. First Congregational Church of Joplin (App.), 106 S.W. 

(2d) 941.

Precatory words. No trust created by a clause which gave "one third of my estate to my church, and request that the ladies of the church may determine how this may be used." The court held the gift to the church was absolute and was not lessened or cut down by the subsequent request. 

Sec. 1177. 

Hanssen v. Karbe, 234 Mo. A. 663, 115 S.W. (2d) 109.

Advancements.-The word as used in statute applies to persons dying intestate, but see the construction placed thereon when used in a will by a qualified scrivener. 

Sec. 1178 (a).

Where an executor or administrator contracts with another to perform services for the estate such as selling, custody of, or suitable work, on the assets, or clerical or other services in managing the property such executor or administrator is primarily and directly liable. See Kopp v. Moffett, 167 S.W. (2d) 87 (K. C. Ct. App.). 

Sec. 1181. 

State ex rel. St. Louis Union Trust Co. v. Sartorius (Mo.), 164 

S.W. (2d) 356.

The court holds Administrator has no right to appeal from an order of final distribution in his representative capacity. Messersmith v. 

Messersmith, 264 Mo. 610, 175 S.W. 914, was overruled. The St.

Louis Union case involved right of trustee to appeal from a decree

determining the rights of the beneficiaries of the trust but the court holds the situation is analogous to that of administrators. 

Sec. 1182 (The Twelfth Category). 

An order of the probate court setting aside its previous approval of final settlement is not an order compelling legatees or distributees to refund, no matter what the reasons are for setting aside such approval, and an appeal is not authorized on behalf of the administrator on such ground. In re Rohde's Estate. Kuenzler v. Beger (App.), 157 S.W. (2d) 527.

Sec. 1184 Note 22. 

An order of the probate court revoking the letters of an administrator with the will annexed is "appealable." In re Crooks' Estate (App.), 138 S.W. (2d) 6.

Sec. 1185. 

Exceptions which merely object to the allowance of items without assigning any specific reason for objection to the items is not suf ficient to present any issue for hearing on appeal. Such statements as that the administrator's or executor's settlement is not true; that the "executor has not charged himself with all the property belonging to said estate and said executrix has taken credit for items that are not properly charged against said estate and have not been properly filed and allowed against said estate"; or that executrix is not entitled to certain items of credit; all fall within this rule and are held insufficient on appeal. See Clow's Estate v. Clow, 167 S.W. (2d) 903 (K. C. App.).

Sec. 1185. 

A probate court's order, setting aside its order for distribution of decedent's estate and discharge of administratrix thereof on motion, filed during term at which order was made is not a final order and no appeal lies therefrom. In re Rohde's Estate, 157 S.W. (2d) 527 (App.).

Sec. 1185-Note 36. 

Although appeal does not lie from annual settlement the court has distinguished between the settlement itself and specific exceptions to such settlement. In the latter if the court makes an order overruling or sustaining the exception, appeal will lie from such order. 

See Veterans' Admn. v. Boles, 227 Mo. A. 1023, 61 S.W. (2d) 757. 

See also In re Mills' Estate, Sheehan v. Rudick, 349 Mo. 611, 162 

S.W. (2d) 807.

Sec. 1188.

Proffer v. Proffer, 342 Mo. 184, 114 S.W. (2d) 1035.

Appellate jurisdiction where will devises real estate and the will is contested is in the Supreme Court. See, however (a case cited), Nettleton Bank v. McGaughey's Estate, 318 Mo. 948, 2 S.W. (2d) 771, which is distinguished. The latter case was an attempt by creditor of deceased to establish priority over the widow's right to certain land as homestead and the court concludes that title is not directly involved. 

Sec. 1190.

Upon an appeal from the probate court to the circuit court, the cause is for trial anew and the judgment of the circuit court upon a hearing of the issues determines and defines the rights of the parties. The judgment of the circuit court should be definite in its findings and in its directions so as to inform the probate court how to proceed. In re Adams' Estate. Adams et al. v. Meyers (App.), 139 

S.W. (2d) 1037, 1.c. 1038, citing In re Hamill's Estate, 315 Mo. 972, 287 S.W. 485; In re Taylor's Estate (App.), 5 S.W. (2d) 457. 

Sec. 1192. 

West St. Louis Trust Co. v. Brokaw, 232 Mo. A. 209, 102 S.W. (2d) 

792, 1.c. S.W. 796.

When the next friend of a minor plaintiff receives the proceeds of a judgment, the circuit court's authority over the particular case comes to an end. The matter of supervising the proceeds is a matter over which the probate court alone has jurisdiction. 

In the above case the circuit court undertook to make an order retaining in that court the right to control and supervise the manner in which an accounting should be made to the minor. Such order was void and ineffective as beyond the jurisdiction of the court to make. 

Sec. 1242-Note 45.

In re Ermeling's Estate (Mo. App.), 131 S.W. (2d) 912. 

A guardian and curator of insane person who made improper loans to himself from estate funds should be required to replace money, with interest at eight per cent. compounded annually from time money was borrowed to date of final or turnover settlement, which is highest legal rate, but should be credited with all interest paid or accounted for on such loans. 

Sec. 1285-Note 86. 

Orders as to the insane poor. See Van Loo v. Osage County, 346

Mo. 358, 141 S.W. (2d) 805. In this case it is held that the probate court's power to adjudge a person insane is not confined to persons having property but that it cannot make an order for the admittance of such person to a state hospital. The county court, only, can make such admittance order, but it is relieved of the inquiry as to sanity where the probate court has made the inquiry. 

Sec. 1290-Note 35. 

Ex Parte Trant (App.), 175 S.W. (2d) 161.

A father filed information that his son was insane. The son had been arrested and lodged in the county jail for his own protection from injury and when the information of insanity was lodged with the county court it was made returnable the same day. Upon hearing before the county court on that day he was committed to the State Hospital No. 2 for the insane, where he was at the time of the filing of this petition for habeas corpus. 

Upon the issue whether the notice or summons to the insane person returnable on the same day is sufficient, the court holds it is not. 

The statute (R.S. Mo. 1939, Sec. 449) requires that the notice shall be served in person on the alleged insane person a reasonable time before the date set for such hearing. After holding that such notice was insufficient, and in fact no notice, the court said as to the request that he be committed to the custody of the sheriff to await further action, as he was evidently insane: "We have concluded we cannot make such an order. A lunacy proceeding is a civil, as distinguished from a criminal proceeding; it is a proceeding in personam by the state; the public is interested in the welfare of the person alleged to be insane; and the informant who starts the proceeding cannot withdraw the complaint without the consent of the court. * * *There has been no warrant issued for the arrest of petitioner either under a criminal statute or under the proviso of Section 9336. *** We know of no authority authoriz ing us to commit the petitioner to the custody of the sheriff. The complaint is still pending in the County Court of Buchanan County and must be proceeded on in strict compliance with Article 2, Chapter 51, R.S. Mo. 1939, Mo. R.S.A., § 9321 et seq."

Sec. 1307-Note 3. 

Buder v. Stocke, 343 Mo. 506, 121 S.W. (2d) 852. 

Where the testator has made a will and thereafter becomes insane and is under guardianship until his death, the weight of authority is against holding that an ademption has resulted from the dealings of a guardian of an insane or incompetent testator with his ward's

property, where the physical facts make it possible to hold other wise. The court cites: 

30 A.L.R. 676 (note);

Lamkin v. Kaiser (App.), 256 S.W. 558; 

National Board of C. W. B. v. Fry, 293 Mo. 399, 239 S.W. 519. 

Sec. 1309.

Tock v. Tock (App.), 120 S.W. (2d) 169. 

A daughter-in-law who furnished support for her mother-in-law after the latter had been declared insane and was in need of such support, relying on her mother-in-law's agreement that the reasonable value of such support would be paid, could sue therefor on a quantum meruit, irrespective of whether such agreement was enforceable as a contract with an insane person.

Sec. 1311-Note 12. 

The investment by guardian of an insane veteran in mortgage bonds secured by deed of trust which placed all bonds upon an equality only in event of foreclosure, and some of which bonds matured earlier than those acquired by guardian, was not a "loan on prime real estate security", as such words are used in statute govening investments by guardians. In re Keisker's Estate. Hines, etc. v. American Surety Co., 168 S.W. (2d) 96 (Mo.). 

Sec. 1318.

Annual or partial settlements by guardian of insane person generally are not reviewable on appeal since they are interlocutory in character.

In re Turley (App.), 164 S.W. (2d) 169. Where the appeal is by the guardian from an order of the probate court sustaining exceptions to an annual report and surcharging certain items of guardian's account disallowed, such appeal should be allowed. The circuit court's jurisdiction on appeal is confined to the questions of law and fact which were passed on by the probate court in the entry of the particular order or judgment appealed from and where the guardian of an insane ward sought credit for a sum for back board which was not asserted in the probate court and sought to have the exceptions overruled on that ground, a finding by the circuit court in favor of the guardian on that ground was void and the probate court was justified in striking a credit for such item from the final settlement notwithstanding such judgment.
